# Script Types and Run Context

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - LocalScript does nothing: In Workspace or ReplicatedStorage -> Starter containers, or a Client-context Script in ReplicatedStorage
> - Client code runs twice: Client-context `Script` in a Starter container -> LocalScript there, or move to ReplicatedStorage
> - Input handlers multiply after respawns: Character/GUI scripts re-run; old connections leaked -> Disconnect on removal; `ResetOnSpawn = false` for persistent UI
> - One server entry Script, one client entry; everything else in modules.
> - No scripts inside Workspace models unless they are distributed assets with explicit `RunContext`.
> - Starter containers contain only LocalScripts.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~200 tok · whole note ~3.9k tok. Read more: ## 2. RunContext (Docs) · ## 3. The recommended layout (Docs) · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Whether your code runs at all, and where, depends on three things: the script's **class** (`Script`, `LocalScript`, `ModuleScript`), its **location** in the Explorer, and, for `Script`, its **`RunContext`**. Roblox's own docs call this "the fundamental challenge of adapting to Roblox scripting" (Docs: script types and locations). This note is the reference for those rules, the recommended layout, script lifecycle (enable, disable, destroy, respawn), the source and local limits that bite large scripts, and the traps: scripts that run twice, never run, or run with stale state.

---

## 1. The three script classes

| Class | Runs where | Starts when |
|---|---|---|
| `Script` | Server (Legacy/Server) or client (Client) per `RunContext` | It is enabled and in a container valid for its run context |
| `LocalScript` | Client only | It is in a client container (below), enabled |
| `ModuleScript` | Wherever it is required | When `require` is called; once per VM ([[Module Scripts and Requiring]]) |

`LocalScript` inherits from `Script` but has no run context of its own; `RunContext` is only meaningful on `Script` (Docs).

---

## 2. RunContext (Docs)

| Value | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `Legacy` (default, 0) | Classic: a `Script` runs on the server, and only in server containers such as `Workspace` and `ServerScriptService` |
| `Server` (1) | Runs on the server regardless of legacy container rules; it can also run in `ReplicatedStorage` (not recommended: its source is replicated to clients) |
| `Client` (2) | Runs on the client; valid in `ReplicatedStorage`, `ReplicatedFirst`, and Starter containers (but see the double-run trap) |
| `Plugin` (3) | Runs as plugin code when a descendant of a `Plugin` |

Changing `RunContext` while a script runs drops its threads and starts a fresh run under the new context, if possible; an actively executing thread continues until it yields or returns (Docs).

### LocalScript containers

A `LocalScript` runs when it is a descendant of: the player's `Backpack`, `PlayerGui`, `PlayerScripts`, the player's `Character` model, or `ReplicatedFirst` (Docs: data model client table; Starter containers copy into these). A `LocalScript` in `Workspace` (outside your character) or `ReplicatedStorage` does **not** run. That is the most common "my script does nothing" cause.

### Containers at a glance

| Container | Replicated to clients | Server `Script` (Legacy) | `LocalScript` | `Script` with Client context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ServerScriptService` | No | Runs | No | No |
| `ServerStorage` | No | No (storage) | No | No |
| `Workspace` | Yes | Runs | Only inside the local character | Rule of thumb: avoid |
| `ReplicatedStorage` | Yes | No | No | Runs |
| `ReplicatedFirst` | Yes, first | No | Runs | Runs |
| `StarterPlayerScripts` | Copied to `PlayerScripts` | No | Runs (copy) | Runs twice (original + copy) |
| `StarterCharacterScripts` | Copied into each character | Legacy server Scripts copied into the character also run on the server | Runs (copy, per spawn) | Runs twice |
| `StarterGui` | Copied to `PlayerGui` | No | Runs (copy) | Avoid |
| `StarterPack` | Copied to `Backpack` | Tools' server scripts run once in the character | Runs (copy) | Avoid |

The "runs twice" trap is documented: a `Script` with `RunContext = Client` placed in a Starter container runs as the original **and** as the copy (Docs). Use `LocalScript`s in Starter containers, and Client-context `Script`s only in `ReplicatedStorage`/`ReplicatedFirst`.

---

## 3. The recommended layout (Docs)

Roblox's guidance, which matches what most professional teams do:

- One `Script` with `RunContext = Server` in `ServerScriptService` as the server entry point.
- One `Script` with `RunContext = Client` in `ReplicatedStorage` as the client entry point (or a `LocalScript` in `StarterPlayerScripts`).
- Everything else in `ModuleScript`s, each exposing `start()` (and often `init()`), required by the entry scripts. Shared modules in `ReplicatedStorage`; server modules in `ServerScriptService`/`ServerStorage`.
- A minimal `ReplicatedFirst` script for the loading screen only.
- No scripts attached to Workspace instances: tag them and handle them from a module with CollectionService (CollectionService Patterns).
- Exception: models and packages distributed on the Creator Store may carry their own scripts; **set an explicit `RunContext`** on each so they behave the same wherever they are inserted.

Benefits: one place controls startup order, failing modules can be isolated, the Output window links to stable script locations (`ReplicatedStorage.Client` rather than an ephemeral copy under `Players.Name.PlayerScripts`), and nothing runs by accident because it was dragged somewhere. See Project Structure and Bootstrapping.

```lua
--!strict
-- ReplicatedStorage/ClientMain (Script, RunContext = Client)
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local controllers = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Controllers")
local order = { "InputController", "CameraController", "HudController" }

for _, name in order do
	local module = controllers:WaitForChild(name) :: ModuleScript
	local ok, controller = pcall(require, module)
	if ok and type(controller) == "table" and controller.start then
		task.spawn(controller.start, Players.LocalPlayer)
	else
		warn(`[ClientMain] failed to load {name}: {controller}`)
	end
end
```

---

## 4. Startup order on the client (Docs)

1. `ReplicatedFirst` contents arrive; its LocalScripts (and Client-context Scripts) run. They can access `ReplicatedFirst` safely but **not** other services' contents without `WaitForChild`.
2. The rest of the game loads; `game.Loaded` fires and `game:IsLoaded()` becomes true.
3. LocalScripts in `PlayerScripts` (from `StarterPlayerScripts`) and Client Scripts in `ReplicatedStorage` run; they can access `ReplicatedStorage` without `WaitForChild`.
4. The character spawns.
5. LocalScripts in the character (from `StarterCharacterScripts`) run.

With Instance Streaming, Workspace content may still be missing at any of these points ([[Instance Streaming]]).

The server has no such staging: server scripts start as the place loads. Do not assume any player exists when a server script starts; handle `Players:GetPlayers()` plus `PlayerAdded` ([[Events Signals and Connections]]).

---

## 5. Lifecycle

- **Enabled/Disabled.** Setting `Enabled = false` drops the script's references to its thread; a yielded thread is never resumed; an executing thread continues until it yields or returns. Setting it back to `true` starts a **fresh run** (Docs). Toggling is a crude restart, not a pause, and state in its locals is lost. Module state required by it persists (cached).
- **Destroying a script** (or an ancestor) stops its threads. A script whose `Parent` is set to `nil` **keeps running** if not destroyed (Docs).
- **Errors** at the top level stop the rest of that script; errors in handlers kill only that handler's thread (Error Handling and Retries).
- **Character scripts re-run on every spawn.** Anything they connect to outside the character (UserInputService, RunService, PlayerGui objects) must be disconnected when the character is removed, or each respawn adds another copy. Scripts inside the character are destroyed with it, and connections they made to signals of instances inside the character die with those instances, but connections to long-lived signals do not die by themselves if the thread is merely dropped (Rule of thumb: always clean up explicitly).
- **`ResetOnSpawn`** on ScreenGuis (default true) re-clones GUIs and their LocalScripts from StarterGui on each spawn. Persistent UI should set `ResetOnSpawn = false` so its scripts do not restart and duplicate state (ScreenGui Fundamentals).
- **Tools**: scripts inside a Tool run when the tool is in a Backpack or character; equipping moves the tool between them.

---

## 6. Size and complexity limits for one script

Large single scripts hit hard limits before they become unmaintainable:

| Limit | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `Source` length | 200,000 characters; larger sources cannot be assigned or saved ("Unable to assign property Source") | Measured in the reference project |
| Active locals per function, including the main chunk | 200 | Luau compiler (Docs, luau-lang source) |
| Upvalues per closure | 200 | Luau bytecode format (Docs) |
| Registers per function | 255 | Luau bytecode format (Docs) |

In the reference project, a combat service at about 199,600 characters was frozen by team rule (new behaviour went into a separate API module); a config module and a theme module crossed the cap and had to be split into child modules before any edit was possible; a tutorial controller reached exactly 200 top-level locals so new features had to live inside a function (Measured). See [[Module Scripts and Requiring]] for the safe-split procedure and Luau Language Essentials for the local limit.

`Script.Source` is protected: game scripts cannot read or write it (Docs). Plugins and the Command Bar can; Studio tooling that edits scripts should use `ScriptEditorService:UpdateSourceAsync` so open editors stay consistent (Plugins - Using and Writing).

---

## 7. Server, client and "both" code

- `RunService:IsServer()`, `IsClient()`, `IsStudio()`, `IsRunMode()`, `IsEdit()` let shared modules branch. In Studio's Play Solo, the server and client run in one process but are still separate VMs.
- Never branch security on `IsClient()` inside shared code that the client can modify: exploiters control everything on their client. Authority stays on the server ([[Client-Server Model]], [[Server Authority and Validation]]).
- `Players.LocalPlayer` is `nil` on the server.
- Code in `ReplicatedStorage` and `ReplicatedFirst` is downloadable by clients; keep server-only logic out of it.

---

## 8. Parallel and plugin contexts

- Scripts under an `Actor` can run in parallel phases ([[Parallel Luau and Actors]]). Each Actor has its own VM and module copies.
- `RunContext = Plugin` scripts run as plugin code under `Plugin` instances; normal plugins are installed as plugin files and run in Studio only (Plugins - Using and Writing).
- The Command Bar runs in Studio's context with its own module cache (Command Bar and Studio Scripting).

---

## 9. Diagnosing "my script does not run"

Work through these in order; most cases stop at step 2.

1. **Is it enabled?** `Enabled` unchecked (or a disabled ancestor `Actor`/`Folder` does not matter, but a disabled script does).
2. **Is it a valid class for its location?** A `LocalScript` outside the client containers, or a Legacy `Script` in `ReplicatedStorage`, never runs. Check the containers table above.
3. **Did it run and error immediately?** Look at Output with the server/client filter correct (Studio's Play mode shows both; the Developer Console in live games has separate Server and Client tabs). A top-level error stops the script after its first lines.
4. **Is it yielding forever?** A `WaitForChild` on a misspelled name or on a streamed-out instance blocks everything after it; look for "Infinite yield possible" warnings. A `require` of a module that yields at load blocks the same way.
5. **Is it running on the side you think?** Put `print(script:GetFullName(), RunService:IsServer())` at the top. A Client-context script prints from `ReplicatedStorage`; a LocalScript copy prints from `Players.Name.PlayerScripts`.
6. **Is it running twice?** Two prints at startup means a duplicated copy (Starter container trap, or a script left inside a cloned model).
7. **Was it destroyed or disabled by other code?** Some systems disable scripts at runtime (for example a tool's script when unequipped, or a cleanup pass). Search for `.Enabled = false` and `:Destroy()` targeting scripts.

For the client-server mental model behind these rules, see [[Client-Server Model]] and Replication Rules. For testing both sides in Studio, Testing Modes - Play Run and Multi-Client.

## 10. Migration from scattered scripts

Older places often have hundreds of scripts inside parts and models. A safe migration path:

1. Inventory scripts by location and purpose (a Command Bar script listing `GetDescendants()` that are `LuaSourceContainer`s, with their full names and source lengths).
2. Group identical or near-identical scripts (kill bricks, spinning coins). Replace each group with one tag plus one module binder (CollectionService Patterns); remove the copies.
3. Move unique server logic into modules required by the server entry script; unique client logic into controllers required by the client entry.
4. Set explicit `RunContext` on any script that must stay inside a model (distributed packages).
5. Ship in stages, keeping the old scripts disabled (not deleted) until each stage is verified in a live server, then delete them (Safe Changes in a Shared Place).

---

## Common mistakes

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| LocalScript does nothing | In Workspace or ReplicatedStorage | Starter containers, or a Client-context Script in ReplicatedStorage |
| Client code runs twice | Client-context `Script` in a Starter container | LocalScript there, or move to ReplicatedStorage |
| Input handlers multiply after respawns | Character/GUI scripts re-run; old connections leaked | Disconnect on removal; `ResetOnSpawn = false` for persistent UI |
| Server code visible to exploiters | Server-context Script or modules in ReplicatedStorage | ServerScriptService |
| Inserted model's scripts behave differently per location | Legacy run context | Explicit `RunContext` |
| Script cannot be saved after edits | Source over 200,000 characters | Split into modules |
| Adding one local breaks compilation | 200-local limit | Group, scope, split |
| `LocalPlayer` is nil | Shared module running on the server | Guard by `IsClient()` |

## Checklist

- [ ] One server entry Script, one client entry; everything else in modules.
- [ ] No scripts inside Workspace models unless they are distributed assets with explicit `RunContext`.
- [ ] Starter containers contain only LocalScripts.
- [ ] Persistent GUIs use `ResetOnSpawn = false`; per-character scripts clean up.
- [ ] Scripts stay far below 200,000 characters and 200 top-level locals.
- [ ] Server-only code never in replicated containers.

## See also

# Task Library Coroutines and Yielding

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Client freezes on an action: Unbounded loop without yield -> Cap attempts; yield; check targets exist
> - Errors vanish: `coroutine.resume` result ignored -> Use `task.spawn`, or check `ok, err`
> - Timer drifts or fires late: Deprecated `wait`/`delay` throttling -> `task.*`
> - No `wait`, `spawn`, `delay`, `tick` in the codebase.
> - Every loop is bounded or yields each iteration.
> - Per-frame work uses the correct RunService event and is disconnectable.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~160 tok · whole note ~3.8k tok. Read more: ## 3. Coroutines · ## 5. Loops that run forever · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Roblox runs all Luau on one main thread per VM, cooperatively. A script runs until it **yields** (waits for something) or returns; then the engine's task scheduler resumes some other thread. There is no preemption: a loop that never yields freezes the whole client or server. The `task` library is how you talk to the scheduler; the `coroutine` library is the lower-level primitive underneath. This note explains both, how they interact with the frame, the deprecated globals they replace, how to cancel work, and the freeze and leak failure modes.

Parallel execution across cores is a different model, covered in [[Parallel Luau and Actors]]. The frame order (when `PreSimulation`, `Heartbeat` and friends run) is in Frame Order and RunService Timing.

---

## 1. The task library (Docs)

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `task.spawn(fnOrThread, ...)` | Calls/resumes **immediately** through the scheduler; returns the thread |
| `task.defer(fnOrThread, ...)` | Calls/resumes at the **end of the current resumption cycle** (later this frame); returns the thread |
| `task.delay(seconds, fnOrThread, ...)` | Calls/resumes on the first `Heartbeat` after `seconds` have elapsed; returns the thread |
| `task.wait(seconds?)` | Yields until `seconds` (default 0) have elapsed, resumes on the next `Heartbeat`, returns actual elapsed time |
| `task.cancel(thread)` | Closes a thread so it is never resumed |
| `task.desynchronize()` / `task.synchronize()` | Switch between parallel and serial phases (Actors only) |

Key documented guarantees:
- `task.wait` and `task.delay` do **not throttle**: the thread resumes on the first Heartbeat at which it is due. `task.wait()` with no argument equals `RunService.Heartbeat:Wait()`.
- `task.delay(0, f)` runs `f` on the very next Heartbeat.
- `task.spawn` from a serial phase resumes in the serial phase; from a parallel phase, in the parallel phase. Same for `defer`, `delay` and `wait`.
- `task.cancel` can fail on threads in certain states: the currently running thread, and threads that have resumed another coroutine, cannot be cancelled and it errors. Docs warn not to rely on these failure conditions; they may be lifted.

### Resolution

`task.wait(0.01)` cannot wait less than one frame. At 60 FPS a Heartbeat is about 16.7 ms, so `task.wait(0.01)` returns about 0.0167 (Rule of thumb; at lower frame rates, longer). Server Heartbeat runs at about 60 Hz. Anything timing-sensitive should measure elapsed time (`os.clock()`, or the returned value) instead of assuming the requested duration:

```lua
local elapsed = task.wait(0.25)   -- actually 0.25 to 0.27 at 60 FPS
```

### Deprecated globals

`wait()`, `spawn()` and `delay()` are deprecated. The old `wait` throttles (it can resume much later than requested under load, and it historically had a ~0.03 s minimum), and `spawn` does not run immediately. Replace them all; lint `DeprecatedGlobal` finds them.

| Old | New | Behaviour change |
|---|---|---|
| `wait(n)` | `task.wait(n)` | No throttling; returns only elapsed time |
| `spawn(f)` | `task.spawn(f)` or `task.defer(f)` | `spawn` started later; `task.spawn` runs now. If code relied on the delay, use `task.defer` |
| `delay(n, f)` | `task.delay(n, f)` | No throttling |

---

## 2. spawn vs defer: which one

```lua
print("A")
task.spawn(function() print("B") end)
task.defer(function() print("C") end)
print("D")
--> A, B, D, C
```

- **`task.spawn`**: the function runs **now**, up to its first yield, before the caller continues. Use it to start background work that should begin immediately, or to call a callback that might yield without blocking the caller.
- **`task.defer`**: the function runs after the current code (and the current batch of resumptions) finishes. Use it to avoid re-entrancy ("fire this after I finish updating my state"), to coalesce many changes into one update, or to break a deep call chain.

```lua
-- Coalesce: many property changes in one frame cause one rebuild
local dirty = false
local function markDirty()
	if dirty then return end
	dirty = true
	task.defer(function()
		dirty = false
		rebuildInventoryUI()
	end)
end
```

**Deferred engine events** ([[Events Signals and Connections]]) behave like `task.defer` for signal handlers when `Workspace.SignalBehavior` is `Deferred`.

---

## 3. Coroutines

The `coroutine` library (Docs: `create`, `resume`, `yield`, `wrap`, `status`, `running`, `isyieldable`, `close`, and on Roblox `finally`) is the primitive. A coroutine is a thread with its own stack that you resume manually.

```lua
local gen = coroutine.create(function(n: number)
	for i = 1, n do
		coroutine.yield(i * i)
	end
	return "done"
end)

print(coroutine.resume(gen, 3))   --> true 1
print(coroutine.resume(gen))      --> true 4
print(coroutine.resume(gen))      --> true 9
print(coroutine.resume(gen))      --> true done
print(coroutine.status(gen))      --> dead
print(coroutine.resume(gen))      --> false cannot resume dead coroutine
```

Status values: `"suspended"`, `"running"`, `"normal"` (it resumed another coroutine), `"dead"`.

**Errors are swallowed by `coroutine.resume`.** It returns `false, err` instead of throwing. Code that ignores the return value hides errors completely. `coroutine.wrap` rethrows, but the traceback points at the wrap call. `task.spawn` reports the error to the Output with a proper trace, which is usually what you want.

**`coroutine.finally(co, callback)`** (Roblox Docs, 2026) registers a callback run when `co` reaches a terminal state: `callback("finished", ...results)`, `callback("error", err)` or `callback("cancelled")` (after `coroutine.close` or `task.cancel`). Callbacks run at most once, last-registered first; registering on a dead coroutine errors; a coroutine with finalizers that ends inside a `coroutine.wrap` resume raises "cannot run finalizers from a wrapped coroutine". Useful for cleanup that must run however a task ends. Check that your Studio version has it before relying on it.

### Mixing coroutines with the engine

Rule of thumb: once a thread has been yielded **by the engine** (it is inside `task.wait`, `WaitForChild`, a web call), do not resume it yourself with `coroutine.resume`; the engine will also resume it later and you get a double resume or a confusing error. Use `task.spawn(thread, ...)` to resume threads you yielded with `coroutine.yield`, and leave engine-yielded threads alone.

A clean "wait for one of several things" helper uses a manually yielded thread:

```lua
--!strict
-- Yields until the signal fires or the timeout passes. Returns true if fired.
local function waitWithTimeout(signal: RBXScriptSignal, timeout: number): boolean
	local thread = coroutine.running()
	local fired = false
	local timeoutThread: thread? = nil
	local conn: RBXScriptConnection? = nil

	conn = signal:Once(function()
		fired = true
		if timeoutThread then task.cancel(timeoutThread) end
		task.spawn(thread)
	end)

	timeoutThread = task.delay(timeout, function()
		if conn then conn:Disconnect() end
		task.spawn(thread)
	end)

	coroutine.yield()
	return fired
end
```

Each path cancels the other before resuming, so the waiting thread is resumed exactly once.

---

## 4. What yields

Calls that yield include: `task.wait`, `RBXScriptSignal:Wait`, `Instance:WaitForChild`, `RemoteFunction:InvokeServer`/`InvokeClient`, `BindableFunction:Invoke` (if the handler yields), all `DataStore`/`MemoryStore` calls, `HttpService:RequestAsync`/`GetAsync`/`PostAsync`, `MarketplaceService` and `Players` async lookups, `TeleportService`, `ContentProvider:PreloadAsync`, `InsertService:LoadAsset`, `Player:LoadCharacterAsync` (in practice), and `require` of a module that yields. Most methods ending in `Async` yield.

`coroutine.isyieldable()` tells you whether the current context may yield. Contexts where yielding is not allowed include metamethods, `table.sort` comparators and `string.gsub` callbacks; yielding there errors ("attempt to yield across metamethod/C-call boundary" style messages).

`pcall` and `xpcall` are yieldable in Luau (Docs), so `pcall(dataStore.GetAsync, dataStore, key)` is fine.

---

## 5. Loops that run forever

### The freeze

A loop that never yields blocks the VM. On the client, the game freezes; on the server, every player lags. Studio may eventually stop it with a script timeout error. A real case from the reference project: a UI effect helper retried `while true do` until a decorative frame parented successfully. After a click destroyed the layer it parented into, every attempt failed instantly, the loop never yielded, and the client froze on every click for some item rarities (Measured). The fix: bounded attempts (max 4), return `nil` when the parent is gone, and have callers skip `nil`.

Rules:
- Every `while` and `repeat` loop either has a provable bound or yields every iteration.
- A retry loop checks that its target still exists (`instance.Parent ~= nil`) and has an attempt cap.
- Long CPU work (generation, pathfinding over many nodes) yields periodically: `if os.clock() - start > 0.005 then task.wait() start = os.clock() end`.

### Per-frame work: Heartbeat, not `while task.wait()`

```lua
-- Acceptable for coarse timers (once per second)
task.spawn(function()
	while true do
		task.wait(1)
		regenerateStamina()
	end
end)

-- Per-frame logic: connect to the RunService event that matches your phase
local conn = RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(dt: number)
	updateProjectiles(dt)
end)
```

`while true do task.wait() ... end` works but ties you to a thread that is awkward to stop. A connection can be disconnected. Choose the event by phase: `PreSimulation` to drive physics inputs, `PreRender` (client) for camera and visuals, `Heartbeat` for general post-physics logic (Frame Order and RunService Timing).

### Stopping loops cleanly

Every background loop needs an owner and a stop condition:

```lua
--!strict
local Spawner = {}
Spawner.__index = Spawner

function Spawner.new(interval: number)
	local self = setmetatable({ running = true, thread = nil :: thread? }, Spawner)
	self.thread = task.spawn(function()
		while self.running do
			spawnWave()
			task.wait(interval)
		end
	end)
	return self
end

function Spawner.Destroy(self: any)
	self.running = false
	if self.thread and coroutine.status(self.thread) == "suspended" then
		task.cancel(self.thread)   -- stop it mid-wait instead of after the next wave
	end
end
```

**Thread leaks.** A thread waiting on a signal that never fires (for example `player.CharacterAdded:Wait()` after the player left) stays suspended forever, holding its upvalues. Prefer `Once` connections that you disconnect on cleanup, or timeouts.

**Disabled or destroyed scripts.** Setting `Enabled = false` or destroying a script drops its threads: yielded threads are never resumed (Docs: BaseScript). But a thread currently running continues until it yields. Connections made by that script are disconnected when the script is destroyed or disabled (Rule of thumb: verify for connections to signals on objects outside the script if you depend on it; explicit cleanup is safer).

---

## 6. Timing patterns

```lua
-- Elapsed time for durations: os.clock() (high resolution, monotonic within a session)
local start = os.clock()
doWork()
print(("took %.2f ms"):format((os.clock() - start) * 1000))

-- Wall clock for timestamps saved to DataStores: os.time() (UTC seconds) or DateTime.now()
local nextReward = os.time() + 24 * 3600

-- Server-synchronized time shared by server and clients: workspace:GetServerTimeNow()
```

Do not use `tick()` (deprecated, timezone-dependent on some platforms). Do not use frame counts as time; frame rates vary from 20 to 240 FPS across devices.

**Fixed-step accumulation** for logic that must be frame-rate independent:

```lua
local STEP = 1 / 30
local acc = 0
RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(dt)
	acc += math.min(dt, 0.25)      -- clamp to avoid a spiral after a hitch
	while acc >= STEP do
		simulate(STEP)
		acc -= STEP
	end
end)
```

---

## 7. Yielding in event handlers and ordering

Each connected handler runs in its own thread, so one handler yielding does not block others. But it means handler code after a yield runs in a later frame, interleaved with everything else. Classic bug: a `PlayerAdded` handler loads data (yields 0.2 to 2 s), then sets up leaderstats; meanwhile another system already read the missing leaderstats. Fix by making dependents wait for an explicit "ready" signal or attribute, not by adding `task.wait(1)`.

`task.wait(n)` to "let things load" is never a fix; it is a race with a longer fuse. Wait for the actual condition (`WaitForChild`, an attribute, a signal).

---

## Common mistakes

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Client freezes on an action | Unbounded loop without yield | Cap attempts; yield; check targets exist |
| Errors vanish | `coroutine.resume` result ignored | Use `task.spawn`, or check `ok, err` |
| Timer drifts or fires late | Deprecated `wait`/`delay` throttling | `task.*` |
| "cannot resume non-suspended coroutine" | Resuming an engine-yielded or running thread | Only resume threads you yielded yourself; resume once |
| Code after `task.spawn` runs before the spawned function's later half | Expected: spawn runs until first yield | Use signals or explicit sequencing |
| Loops keep running after round end | No owner/stop flag | Owner object with `Destroy` and `task.cancel` |
| `task.cancel` errors | Cancelling the running thread | Set a flag and return instead |

## Checklist

- [ ] No `wait`, `spawn`, `delay`, `tick` in the codebase.
- [ ] Every loop is bounded or yields each iteration.
- [ ] Per-frame work uses the correct RunService event and is disconnectable.
- [ ] Background threads are owned and cancellable.
- [ ] Code re-validates state after every yield.
- [ ] Durations use `os.clock`, timestamps `os.time`/`DateTime`, cross-machine time `GetServerTimeNow`.

# Client-Server Model

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Client changes `leaderstats` or an attribute and expects the... -> Send a request; the server changes it
> - Avoid: Server reads a value the client wrote locally -> Keep authoritative values on the server only
> - Avoid: Client computes damage and sends it -> Server computes damage from server-side stats
> - Every value that grants power or currency is computed and stored on the server.
> - No secrets in ReplicatedStorage, ReplicatedFirst, Workspace, StarterGui or StarterPlayer.
> - Every remote handler validates type, value, context and rate before acting.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~180 tok · whole note ~5.0k tok. Read more: ## Latency: the other half of the model · ## A minimal correct round trip · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Every Roblox experience is a distributed program. One **server** runs the authoritative copy of the game; every player runs a **client** with a partial, delayed copy. Almost every hard bug in a multiplayer Roblox game (duplicated items, enemies that "teleport", effects only one player sees, a shop that gives free items) comes from code that forgot which side it was on, or trusted the wrong side. This note is the map: what runs where, what each side can see and change, what the latency looks like, and how to decide where a piece of logic belongs.

The rest of this section builds on it: Replication Rules (what crosses the boundary on its own), [[RemoteEvents RemoteFunctions and Unreliable Remotes]] (what you send across it), [[Network Ownership]] (who simulates physics), [[Server Authority and Validation]] and Exploits and Anti-Cheat (what to do about the fact that clients lie).

## The two DataModels

When a game starts, Roblox takes the published place (the "edit" DataModel you built in Studio) and runs a copy of it on a Roblox server as the **runtime DataModel** (Roblox docs, "Client-server runtime"). Each player who joins receives their own copy of that runtime DataModel, minus the containers the server never sends, and with Workspace content arriving gradually if [[Instance Streaming]] is on.

From that point there are N+1 DataModels: the server's, and one per client. They start identical (apart from server-only containers) and then drift. **Replication** is the engine process that pushes server changes out to clients so they stay roughly in sync. It is mostly one-way. A client can change anything in its own copy, and in almost all cases that change stays on that client.

```text
                    +-----------------------------+
                    |           SERVER            |
                    |  ServerScriptService        |
                    |  ServerStorage              |
                    |  Workspace (everything)     |
                    |  ReplicatedStorage          |
                    +------+-------------+--------+
              replication  |             |  replication
              (automatic)  |             |  (automatic)
                    +------v----+   +----v------+
                    | CLIENT A  |   | CLIENT B  |
                    | Workspace |   | Workspace |
                    | (partial) |   | (partial) |
                    | PlayerGui |   | PlayerGui |
                    +-----------+   +-----------+
        remotes, owned physics, a few engine-defined exceptions go back up
```

## Who runs what

| Side | Runs | Can see | Can change for everyone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Server | `Script` (RunContext Legacy in server containers, or `Server`) | Everything, including ServerStorage and ServerScriptService | Yes: any instance or property it changes replicates (subject to streaming on the receiving side) |
| Client | `LocalScript`, `Script` with RunContext `Client`, ModuleScripts they require | Everything replicated to it, plus anything it creates locally | Only through the narrow exceptions in Replication Rules: remotes, physics of parts it owns, its own character's animations, and a handful of engine events |

ModuleScripts run on whichever side requires them, and a module required on both sides is two independent copies with separate state. A module in ReplicatedStorage that holds a `coins` table on the server and a different `coins` table on each client is a classic source of "the UI shows 500 but the server says 20". See [[Module Scripts and Requiring]] and [[Script Types and Run Context]].

## Containers and visibility

Where an instance lives decides who receives it. This is the most important table in the section.

| Container | Sent to clients? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Workspace` | Yes | With streaming on, BaseParts and most models arrive by distance; the server always has all of it |
| `ReplicatedFirst` | Yes, first | Loaded before anything else on join; use for loading screens and the client bootstrap |
| `ReplicatedStorage` | Yes, all at join | Not streamed. Shared modules, remotes, assets the client clones |
| `Lighting`, `SoundService`, `Teams`, `StarterGui`, `StarterPack`, `StarterPlayer` | Yes | Starter containers are templates copied into each player |
| `Players.<Player>.PlayerGui`, `.Backpack` | Only to that player | Server-created UI placed here is only visible to its owner |
| `ServerScriptService` | **Never** | Server scripts and server-only modules |
| `ServerStorage` | **Never** | Server-only assets, templates, test flags, secret config |

Two consequences that matter for security:

1. **Anything in a replicated container is public.** Exploiters can read every replicated instance and decompile every replicated `LocalScript`, client `Script` and `ModuleScript`, even ones that are disabled or never required (Roblox docs, "Access control and confidentiality"). Prices in a ReplicatedStorage config module, an admin list in a client script, a "secret" code list in a ModuleScript: all of it can be read.
2. **ServerStorage and ServerScriptService are your only private storage.** One production game kept its admin panel's client UI in ServerStorage and cloned it into an admin's `PlayerGui` on join. Non-admins never receive the code at all, and the server re-checks the caller on every admin request regardless, because the client UI is a convenience, not a gate.

## What a client can do (assume all of it)

The Roblox security docs list what a determined exploiter controls. Paraphrased:

- Decompile any replicated LocalScript or ModuleScript.
- Take network ownership of their character and any unanchored parts the engine hands them, and set their position, rotation and velocity to anything, including `inf` and `NaN`.
- Trigger client-initiated events (Touched, ProximityPrompt, ClickDetector) at any range and any frequency.
- Fire or invoke any RemoteEvent or RemoteFunction with arbitrary arguments, at any rate. The only argument they cannot forge is the first `player` parameter the server receives.
- Change anything in their local DataModel without firing the usual events.
- Alter the behaviour of any code running on their machine.

So the working model is: **the client is a rendering terminal and an input device that sometimes lies.** It is extremely good at the first job and should never be trusted for anything that matters. The server's job, per the docs, is to receive input, validate that the requested action is possible and permitted, execute it, update authoritative state, and replicate results.

## Latency: the other half of the model

Even honest clients disagree with the server, because everything takes time to travel.

| Path | Typical delay |
|---|---|
| Client input to server | One-way latency, roughly half the round trip (rule of thumb: 30 to 150 ms for most players, much worse on mobile data) |
| Server change to a client | Same one-way latency, plus replication batching |
| Client A's action seen by client B | A to server, then server to B: about a full round trip |
| `Player:GetNetworkPing()` | Round-trip network latency in seconds, measured without processing time (Roblox docs) |

This creates three different "nows":

- **The owner's now.** The player sees their own character and their own predicted effects with zero delay.
- **The server's now.** The server sees the player's character where the client was about half a round trip ago.
- **Everyone else's now.** Other players see that character where it was about a full round trip ago, smoothed by interpolation.

Gameplay decisions must be made in the server's now, while presentation should happen in the viewer's now. That split is the root of most architecture choices in combat games: the attacker's client plays the swing instantly, the server decides the hit using its own state plus a latency tolerance, and the victim's client shows the result when it arrives. See Hitboxes and Hit Detection and Combat Systems Architecture.

### A shared clock

`os.clock()` and `tick()` are local to each machine. For anything both sides must agree on (an ability's start time, a round timer, an animation that every client joins part-way through), use `workspace:GetServerTimeNow()`, which returns an estimate of the server's time on any machine.

```lua
--!strict
-- Shared helper: how far into a server-started action are we, on any machine?
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local function elapsedSince(serverStartTime: number): number
	return math.max(0, Workspace:GetServerTimeNow() - serverStartTime)
end

return elapsedSince
```

The server writes the start time once (an attribute or a remote argument), and every client computes its own offset. One production game drove all enemy animation this way: the server wrote `AnimT = GetServerTimeNow()` with the clip name, and each client started the clip at `(now - AnimT) * speed` so late joiners and laggy clients were still in sync (see Enemy Animation State Protocol).

## The simulation is split three ways

Physics is not simply "on the server". Roblox uses **distributed physics**: each unanchored assembly is simulated by exactly one machine, its network owner (Roblox docs, "Network ownership").

| Thing | Simulated by | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Anchored parts | Server (always; cannot be changed) | Clients cannot move them for others |
| A player's own character | That player's client | The client decides where it is. Speed, fly and teleport hacks start here |
| Unanchored parts near a player | Often that player's client (automatic ownership) | That client can move them, fling them, fake their Touched events |
| NPCs and props you lock with `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` | Server | Authoritative, but clients see them with latency and possible jitter |

This is why "validate everything" is not only about remotes. Character position, owned parts and Touched events are all client-authored data that arrive through the engine, not through your code. See [[Network Ownership]].

A newer option, the **server authority model** (`Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server`, with client prediction and rollback), moves character and physics simulation to the server while clients predict. The Roblox docs describe it as in beta and "will be released soon" (as of October 2026); check its status before relying on it. Everything in this section assumes the classic model unless it says otherwise.

## Where should this code live? (decision table)

| Logic | Side | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Currency, inventory, progression, cooldowns that gate power | Server | Any client copy can be edited |
| Damage numbers, hit decisions, kill credit | Server | Clients would choose their own damage |
| Prices, drop tables, odds | Server (a client copy for display only) | Display copies are readable but harmless if the server never reads them back |
| Input reading, camera, UI, sounds, VFX | Client | Only the local player needs them; zero latency |
| Your own character's animation | Client (owner) | Replicates through the Animator; see Replication and Ownership |
| Enemy AI decisions | Server | Shared world state |
| Enemy animation and effects for many NPCs | Every client, driven by small server state | Server CPU and bandwidth stay flat; see Entity Component Systems |
| Pure maths both sides need (level curve, damage formula preview) | Shared module | The server result is authoritative; the client copy is prediction or display |
| Secrets (API keys, admin lists, codes) | ServerStorage or server modules, or HttpService secrets | Replicated means public |

## Responsiveness without trust

The tension is permanent: authority wants everything on the server, feel wants everything on the client. The patterns that resolve it:

1. **Predict, then confirm.** The client shows the result immediately (button press animates, swing plays, coin counter ticks), sends the request, and reconciles when the server answers. If the server rejects, roll the presentation back quietly.
2. **Request intent, not outcome.** "I swung at time T facing direction D" instead of "I hit enemy 12 for 400". The server derives the outcome. See [[Server Authority and Validation]].
3. **Replicate state, derive presentation.** The server writes small facts (attributes like `State = "Stunned"`, `AnimT`); every client turns them into animation, VFX and UI. Presentation can be rich without the server sending rich data. See Replication Rules.
4. **Data-driven timing.** When the server must know when a hit lands, it reads the time from data (marker times exported from the clip, a table of hit frames) instead of waiting for the client to say so. One production combat game computed ability hits per segment on the server from shared timing data, so the caster's client could animate freely while the server applied damage on schedule. See Markers and Events.

## A minimal correct round trip

The smallest example that shows every rule: a "claim daily reward" button.

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/DailyReward.server.luau
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local remotes = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Remotes")
local claimRemote = remotes:WaitForChild("ClaimDaily") :: RemoteEvent
local resultRemote = remotes:WaitForChild("DailyResult") :: RemoteEvent

local COOLDOWN = 20 * 60 * 60 -- seconds between claims (server-side truth)
local REWARD = 250

-- Server-owned state. In a real game this lives in the player's profile.
local lastClaim: { [Player]: number } = {}
local busy: { [Player]: boolean } = {}

claimRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player: Player)
	-- No arguments are trusted because none are accepted.
	if busy[player] then return end -- ignore re-entry while one claim is in flight
	busy[player] = true

	local now = os.time()
	local last = lastClaim[player] or 0
	if now - last >= COOLDOWN then
		lastClaim[player] = now -- mark BEFORE paying, so a re-entrant request cannot pay twice
		local coins = (player:GetAttribute("Coins") :: number?) or 0
		player:SetAttribute("Coins", coins + REWARD) -- server write: replicates to the owner's UI
		resultRemote:FireClient(player, true, REWARD)
	else
		resultRemote:FireClient(player, false, COOLDOWN - (now - last))
	end

	busy[player] = nil
end)

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
	lastClaim[player] = nil
	busy[player] = nil
end)
```

```lua
--!strict
-- StarterPlayerScripts/DailyRewardClient.client.luau
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local remotes = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Remotes")
local claimRemote = remotes:WaitForChild("ClaimDaily") :: RemoteEvent
local resultRemote = remotes:WaitForChild("DailyResult") :: RemoteEvent

local function onClaimPressed()
	-- Optimistic UI could start a spinner here; the server decides the outcome.
	claimRemote:FireServer()
end

resultRemote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(ok: boolean, value: number)
	if ok then
		print(("Claimed %d coins"):format(value))
	else
		print(("Come back in %d seconds"):format(value))
	end
end)

-- Wire onClaimPressed to a button in your UI code.
```

What makes it correct: the client sends no data the server uses, the cooldown and reward live on the server, the claim is marked before the reward is granted, the result travels back as a separate message, and per-player state is cleaned up on leave. A real version also rate-limits the remote ([[Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention]]) and saves the claim time with the profile ([[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]]).

## Nuances where the obvious answer is wrong

- **"The server sees what the client sees."** No. The server sees every player's character late, and with streaming the client does not have most of the world. Code that runs fine in Play Solo (zero latency, everything loaded) fails live. Test with network simulation and multiple clients (Testing Modes - Play Run and Multi-Client).
- **"LocalScripts can't hurt the server."** A LocalScript can do anything to the server that the server lets a remote, an owned part, a prompt or a Touched event do. The risk is in the server's handlers, not in the LocalScript.
- **"Put it in ReplicatedStorage so both sides can use it."** Fine for code that must exist on both sides. Wrong for server logic: decompilation exposes your rules and makes exploits easier to find (Roblox docs warn against mixed server/client modules).
- **"The server is fast, so do everything there."** Server CPU is shared by every player in the instance. Animation for 200 NPCs, per-frame raycasts for every projectile, or per-frame UI state on the server will drop the server's frame rate for everyone, and every server-side visual change costs bandwidth. Do decisions on the server and presentation on clients.
- **"Studio Play Solo proves it works."** Play Solo runs client and server in one process with no latency and a tiny world. Teleports do not work in Studio at all (Teleporting and Multi-Place Games), and some behaviours (like ids registered for Studio only) look like replication bugs only in live servers (Case Study - Abilities That Only Worked in Studio).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Client changes `leaderstats` or an attribute and expects the server to see it | Works for the player, reverts on rejoin, other players see old values | Send a request; the server changes it |
| Server reads a value the client wrote locally | The server sees the old value (the change never replicated) | Keep authoritative values on the server only |
| Client computes damage and sends it | Exploiters one-shot bosses | Server computes damage from server-side stats |
| One ModuleScript with server and client branches in ReplicatedStorage | Server logic visible to exploiters | Split into a server module (ServerScriptService) and a client module |
| Timers with `os.clock()` across the boundary | Effects out of sync by seconds | `workspace:GetServerTimeNow()` |
| Assuming a Workspace object exists on the client | `attempt to index nil` on join or after walking away | `WaitForChild` with timeout, tags, streaming-aware code; see [[Instance Streaming]] |

## Checklist

- [ ] Every value that grants power or currency is computed and stored on the server.
- [ ] No secrets in ReplicatedStorage, ReplicatedFirst, Workspace, StarterGui or StarterPlayer.
- [ ] Every remote handler validates type, value, context and rate before acting.
- [ ] Shared timing uses `GetServerTimeNow()`.
- [ ] Presentation (VFX, sound, camera, UI) runs on clients, driven by small replicated state.
- [ ] Tested with two or more clients and simulated latency, not only Play Solo.

# Instance Streaming

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Turning streaming off "to fix bugs" -> Fix the client code; non-streamed big worlds crash phones
> - Avoid: Persistent on many models -> Atomic for most; Persistent only for tiny essentials
> - Avoid: Expecting Atomic in ReplicatedStorage -> Streaming settings apply to Workspace only
> - Streaming on; properties chosen deliberately (radius, StreamOutBehavior, integrity mode, Improved behaviour).
> - Interactable models set to Atomic; Persistent only where justified.
> - No LocalScript indexes Workspace parts directly without a wait or a tag.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~180 tok · whole note ~4.6k tok. Read more: ## Per-model streaming: `ModelStreamingMode` · ## Writing streaming-safe client code · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

With **instance streaming** (`Workspace.StreamingEnabled`), the server sends each client only the part of the Workspace near that player, and the client drops distant parts again when it needs memory. It is enabled by default for new places (Roblox docs, "Instance streaming"), and for any world bigger than a single arena it is the difference between a 10 second join and a 60 second join, and between a phone that runs the game and one that crashes. The cost is that **client code can no longer assume any Workspace instance exists**. This note covers the exact streaming rules, every property and per-model mode, how to write client code that survives streaming, how to move players safely with `RequestStreamAroundAsync`, and a production example of tuning a big world.

Related: Level of Detail and Model Streaming (visual LOD and SLIM), Case Study - Fast Join and Deferred Loading, Memory Budgets and Leaks.

## What streams and what does not

From the Roblox docs:

- **Scope:** only descendants of `Workspace` stream. `ReplicatedStorage` and `ReplicatedFirst` are sent in full at join and never stream. An Atomic model placed in ReplicatedStorage is not atomic; the setting has no meaning there.
- **On join**, the client receives the Workspace **except**: BaseParts; models set to Atomic, Persistent or PersistentPerPlayer; Nonatomic models when `ModelStreamingBehavior` is Improved; and the descendants of all of those. Those deferred instances stream in later based on distance, device and conditions.
- **Stream out:** a client may remove regions of BaseParts, starting furthest from its replication focus. Regions inside `StreamingMinRadius` **never** stream out.
- A **Model with no BasePart descendants** (a container for scripts or values) is exempt from streaming out unless it is under a BasePart.
- Instances **created or cloned by client scripts** are exempt from streaming out unless parented under a server-created instance.
- When an instance streams out it is **parented to `nil`, not destroyed**; removal signals fire on its parent and ancestors; if it streams back in, existing Luau references reconnect. Local-only property changes on it can be lost.
- **Assemblies** stream in as complete units with their constraints and attachments, except anchored assemblies, where only the BaseParts inside the radius come in. Assemblies stream out only when all their parts are eligible. Avoid huge moving assemblies: they stream in all at once and spike.
- **The server always has everything.** Streaming only changes what clients hold.

## Workspace properties

All streaming properties are **non-scriptable**: you set them on Workspace in Studio's Properties panel; scripts cannot read or set them (Roblox docs). `StreamingEnabled` itself cannot be set by script.

| Property | Default | Docs recommendation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `StreamingMinRadius` | 64 | Keep 64 | Radius streamed at highest priority and never streamed out. Larger costs memory and server bandwidth |
| `StreamingTargetRadius` | 1024 | Keep 1024 | Maximum distance the server streams to; also the distance players see full detail |
| `StreamOutBehavior` | `LowMemory` | `Opportunistic` | LowMemory streams out beyond the min radius only under memory pressure. Opportunistic may remove regions beyond the target radius any time |
| `StreamingIntegrityMode` | `Default` | `PauseOutsideLoadedArea` | What happens when a player moves into an area not yet streamed. Enum values: `Default`, `Disabled`, `MinimumRadiusPause`, `PauseOutsideLoadedArea` |
| `ModelStreamingBehavior` | `Legacy` | `Improved` | How Nonatomic models stream (see below) |
| `PredictiveStreamingMode` | off | Opt in with `Enabled` | Engine pre-fetches likely respawn points and recently left areas |
| `EnableSLIMAvatars` | off | Per game | SLIM level of detail for avatars |

The target radius must be larger than the min radius: the ring between them is the buffer that absorbs moments when the client stops receiving (Roblox docs). Equal values mean more streaming pauses.

When integrity pausing triggers, `Player.GameplayPaused` becomes true; you can replace the default notification with `GuiService:SetGameplayPausedNotificationEnabled(false)` and your own UI.

## Per-model streaming: `ModelStreamingMode`

Enum values: `Default`, `Atomic`, `Persistent`, `PersistentPerPlayer`, `Nonatomic` (Roblox API reference). The docs describe the behaviours as:

| Mode | Streams in | Streams out | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nonatomic (default behaviour) | Legacy: the model container and its non-BasePart children (scripts) replicate at join; parts stream individually. Improved: the model streams in when one of its parts is eligible, with that part and all non-part children; it streams out with its last part | Part by part | Scenery, terrain dressing, anything client code does not walk into |
| Atomic | Everything in the model (initial descendants) arrives together when any part is eligible | Only when all parts are eligible, all together | Interactables and machines client code reads as a whole (a door with its hinge and prompt, a shop stand) |
| Persistent | Sent as a complete unit soon after join, before `Workspace.PersistentLoaded` fires | Never | Very rare: a small set of parts client code must always reach. Not a way to bypass streaming |
| PersistentPerPlayer | Persistent for players added with `Model:AddPersistentPlayer()`, Atomic for others | Per player | A player's own base or plot that must stay loaded for its owner |

The docs warn that overusing Persistent hurts performance. Each Persistent model is memory every player always pays.

### Why Atomic simplifies code

With Atomic, a client that has the model has all of it, so you `WaitForChild` the model only, never each descendant:

```lua
--!strict
-- Client: one wait for an Atomic model, then direct indexing is safe.
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local shop = Workspace:WaitForChild("ShopStand", 30)
if shop then
	-- Safe: an Atomic model's initial descendants arrive together with it.
	local counter = shop:FindFirstChild("Counter") :: BasePart
	local prompt = counter:FindFirstChildOfClass("ProximityPrompt") :: ProximityPrompt
	prompt.Triggered:Connect(function()
		-- Local feedback only (open the shop UI). Purchases are decided on the server.
	end)
end
```

With Nonatomic, `shop.Counter` may arrive before or after `shop.Counter.Prompt`, and the model may exist while its parts do not.

## Replication focus

Streaming happens around the character's `PrimaryPart` by default. You can change it with `Player.ReplicationFocus`, or add extra foci with `Player:AddReplicationFocus(part)` and `RemoveReplicationFocus`. Each extra focus costs about as much server work as another player: the docs give the example that one player with nine moving foci costs roughly as much as ten players. Client physics, including for Persistent models, only simulates in streamed areas, so add a focus near any far object that must keep simulating (Roblox docs).

Good uses: a spectator camera that flies away from the character; a cutscene camera; a scope or remote viewer looking at a distant base; a "home base" that players return to often.

## Moving players: `RequestStreamAroundAsync`

When the **server** moves a character far away (a teleport pad, respawn in another world, an admin "bring", a cutscene ending), the destination is usually not streamed in on that client. The player lands in emptiness: they fall through missing floors, hit an integrity pause, or see the world pop in.

`Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(position, timeOut)` asks the server to stream regions (parts and terrain) around a position to that player before you move them (Roblox docs):

- It **yields** and is server-callable for the target player.
- `timeOut` defaults to 0, which means effectively infinite; under low client memory the engine abandons requests regardless.
- The effect is **temporary** and there is **no guarantee** about what will be streamed.

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: move a player to a far destination with the destination streamed first.
local MAX_WAIT = 5 -- seconds; never let a slow client block the move forever

local function moveFar(player: Player, destination: CFrame)
	local character = player.Character
	if not character then return end

	-- Pre-fetch around the destination. pcall: the call can fail for players leaving.
	local ok, err = pcall(function()
		player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(destination.Position, MAX_WAIT)
	end)
	if not ok then
		warn("RequestStreamAroundAsync failed: " .. tostring(err))
	end

	-- The player may have left or respawned while we yielded.
	if player.Parent == nil or player.Character ~= character then return end
	character:PivotTo(destination)
end

return moveFar
```

Two practical details:

- Run it in its own thread if the caller should not yield (a ProximityPrompt handler can spawn it).
- Tell your movement validator that this move was server-initiated so it does not flag a "teleport" (Exploits and Anti-Cheat).

With `PredictiveStreamingMode = Enabled`, the engine also pre-fetches likely respawn points on death and keeps the area a player just left briefly streamed; it does not add a focus where you already requested one (Roblox docs).

## Writing streaming-safe client code

The rule: **a client script must handle every Workspace instance it uses appearing late, disappearing, and reappearing.**

| Pattern | Streaming-safe? | Better |
|---|---|---|
| `workspace.Map.Shop.Door.Prompt` at the top of a LocalScript | No: errors if any link is missing | `WaitForChild` on the Atomic model, or tag-based setup |
| `WaitForChild` chain with no timeout | Hangs forever if the player never goes near | Timeout, or event-driven setup |
| Looping over `workspace.Chests:GetChildren()` once at start | Misses chests that stream in later | `CollectionService` added and removed signals |
| Caching part references forever | Holds parts parented to nil; connections may die | Re-resolve on `GetInstanceAddedSignal`, clean up on removed |
| Client-side `Touched` on distant parts | Never fires; parts are not there | Server-side logic, or client logic only near the player |
| Reading attributes of an object to show UI | Fine if the object is streamed in | Keep UI-relevant state on `Player` or in ReplicatedStorage, which never stream |

The tag pattern handles all three cases in one place:

```lua
--!strict
-- Client: attach behaviour to every tagged instance as it streams in, clean up as it streams out.
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local TAG = "Chest"
local cleanups: { [Instance]: () -> () } = {}

local function attach(inst: Instance)
	if cleanups[inst] then return end
	local conns: { RBXScriptConnection } = {}
	table.insert(conns, inst:GetAttributeChangedSignal("Opened"):Connect(function()
		-- play the open animation and VFX locally
	end))
	cleanups[inst] = function()
		for _, c in conns do c:Disconnect() end
	end
end

local function detach(inst: Instance)
	local cleanup = cleanups[inst]
	if cleanup then
		cleanup()
		cleanups[inst] = nil
	end
end

for _, inst in CollectionService:GetTagged(TAG) do attach(inst) end
CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal(TAG):Connect(attach)
CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal(TAG):Connect(detach)
```

Tags travel with the instance, so tagged objects fire "added" when they stream in and "removed" when they stream out. See CollectionService Patterns.

### Keep UI state off the map

A HUD that reads "quest progress" from an attribute on a quest board in Workspace breaks when the player walks away from the board. Put anything the UI needs on the `Player`, in `ReplicatedStorage`, or send it by remote. One production game mirrored quest and inventory state as JSON attributes on the Player for exactly this reason.

### Server code is unaffected, mostly

The server sees everything, so server logic does not change. Two exceptions: server code that **asks the client** about Workspace objects (client remotes that send an Instance only work if the client has it) and server moves of players (use `RequestStreamAroundAsync`).

## Production example: a world too big to see

One production game had a hub and several themed realms, the nearest realm more than 11,000 studs from the hub. Players in the hub could see realm models on the horizon, which meant the streaming radius was far too large: every client held geometry it would not reach for minutes. The team's changes:

| Setting | Chosen value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `StreamingMinRadius` | 256 | Combat arenas needed close geometry guaranteed (the docs default is 64; the team accepted the memory cost for its arenas) |
| `StreamingTargetRadius` | 1024 | The docs default; enough for every in-zone view |
| `StreamOutBehavior` | Opportunistic | Reclaim memory on phones without waiting for pressure |
| `ModelStreamingBehavior` | Improved | Models without parts stop arriving at join; faster join |
| `StreamingIntegrityMode` | MinimumRadiusPause | Pause only if the guaranteed radius is missing (the docs recommend PauseOutsideLoadedArea; the team picked the narrower mode to pause less often) |

Before flipping the switch, the code was audited for streaming readiness:

- **Every server-initiated move streamed the destination first**: hub travel, zone travel, world travel, death respawns, boss events, admin teleports.
- Client `WaitForChild` chains into Workspace only crossed Folders and a config ModuleScript (containers that do not stream out), never parts.
- Portal and gate lookups re-scanned instead of caching once.
- Automatic model LOD was turned off on 7,861 decorative models so distant stand-in meshes did not keep far realms visible (an attribute recorded the previous value on each model so it could be reverted).

The settings had to be applied by hand in Studio's Properties panel, because they are not scriptable: tooling that edits places by script could not set them.

A related lesson from the same game: a 5,000 by 1,900 stud sea of terrain water stalled joining. Large terrain and water areas are expensive to stream and render; the team replaced it with a flat part. See Terrain Tools and Terrain API and Water Sky and Atmosphere Art.

## Streaming is not a security boundary

The security docs suggest streaming as defence in depth ("if feasible, use streaming to limit how much of the world replicates to a new player"), but do not rely on it for secrecy. Anything a player can get near streams to them, and exploit clients can move their character anywhere to pull content. Unreleased content belongs in a separate private universe, not in a far corner of the live map (Roblox docs, "Access control and confidentiality").

## Debugging streaming

- In a live game press **Shift+F3** (in Studio playtest **Shift+Ctrl+F3**, Mac **Shift+Cmd+F3**) for Network Stats, then **Shift+1** repeatedly; the fourth panel is the Streaming view, with regions coloured: red inside the min radius, yellow between min and target, blue at the target radius, green beyond (Roblox docs).
- Temporarily raise `CameraMaxZoomDistance` (for example to 1000) to see the streamed region around you.
- Studio playtests stream like live games, but with local server speed; also test on a real phone.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `attempt to index nil` in a LocalScript on join | Direct indexing into Workspace | `WaitForChild` with timeout, Atomic models, tags |
| Player falls through the floor after a teleport | Destination not streamed | `RequestStreamAroundAsync` before moving; integrity mode |
| Interactable works only after walking near it twice | Setup ran once at start and missed late arrivals | Tag added signal |
| Effects keep playing on objects far away | References to streamed-out parts never cleaned | Tag removed signal, `AncestryChanged` |
| Memory keeps growing on phones | `LowMemory` never streams out until pressure | `Opportunistic` |
| World pops in when turning around | Target radius too small for the view | Raise target radius, or fog and LOD to hide edges |
| Everything far away is visible | Target radius huge, or LOD stand-ins | Default radius; review Model LOD |
| Physics object far away stops moving | Client physics only runs in streamed areas | Server ownership, or an extra replication focus |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Turning streaming off "to fix bugs" | Fix the client code; non-streamed big worlds crash phones |
| Persistent on many models | Atomic for most; Persistent only for tiny essentials |
| Expecting Atomic in ReplicatedStorage | Streaming settings apply to Workspace only |
| Server teleports without pre-fetch | `RequestStreamAroundAsync` with a timeout |
| UI reading Workspace attributes | Move UI state to Player or ReplicatedStorage |
| Many replication foci per player | Each costs like a player; use sparingly |

## Checklist

- [ ] Streaming on; properties chosen deliberately (radius, StreamOutBehavior, integrity mode, Improved behaviour).
- [ ] Interactable models set to Atomic; Persistent only where justified.
- [ ] No LocalScript indexes Workspace parts directly without a wait or a tag.
- [ ] Every server move of a character pre-fetches the destination.
- [ ] Tested on a low-memory phone by walking far and back.

## See also
Level of Detail and Model Streaming · [[Client-Server Model]] · Replication Rules · CollectionService Patterns · Case Study - Fast Join and Deferred Loading · Memory Budgets and Leaks · Mobile and Low-End Optimization · Teleporting and Multi-Place Games · [[Network Ownership]]
