# Network Ownership

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Leaving boss NPCs on automatic ownership -> `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` after spawn
> - Avoid: Prompts and ClickDetectors on unanchored parts -> Anchor them or server-own them; server distance check
> - Avoid: `SetNetworkOwner` on anchored parts, or no way back to automatic -> Anchored parts are always server-owned...
> - Every gameplay-critical unanchored object has a deliberate owner.
> - No valuable interaction relies on client-owned Touched or prompt position alone.
> - Vehicles assign the driver on sit and reset on exit, and ownership changes nowhere else (switches cause jitter).
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~190 tok · whole note ~4.6k tok. Read more: ## When to set ownership manually · ## Security: what owned physics lets an exploiter do · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Roblox physics is **distributed**: each unanchored assembly is simulated by one machine, its **network owner**, and that machine's results are replicated to everyone else. Owner can be the server or any one client. Ownership is why your character feels instant, why a ball you kick responds immediately, and also why exploiters can fly, teleport, fling other players and fire Touched events from across the map. This note covers the documented rules, how automatic ownership behaves in practice, when and how to set ownership yourself, the security model, and the diagnosis tools.

Related: Physics Assemblies and Constraints (what an assembly is), Replication and Ownership (animation and ownership), Exploits and Anti-Cheat (movement validation).

## The documented rules

From Roblox docs, "Network ownership":

1. By default the server retains ownership of any BasePart, and the engine **automatically** assigns ownership of unanchored parts to clients based on the client's hardware capacity and the player character's proximity. Parts near a character are more likely to become that player's.
2. The server **always owns anchored parts**, and you cannot change that.
3. Ownership applies per **assembly** (a set of parts rigidly connected). If a mechanism has no anchored parts, setting ownership on one assembly sets it for every assembly in the mechanism.
4. Anchoring a lone assembly gives it to the server; unanchoring it loses its previous ownership setting and returns to automatic handling. Anchoring one assembly inside a larger mechanism moves only that assembly to the server.
5. `BasePart:SetNetworkOwner(player)` assigns ownership from the server; `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` assigns the server. `SetNetworkOwnershipAuto()` returns to automatic. `GetNetworkOwner()` returns the owning player or `nil` for the server. `CanSetNetworkOwnership()` tells you whether a call would succeed (it fails for anchored assemblies, for example).
6. Roblox cannot verify physics calculations from a client owner. A client can teleport parts it owns, move them through walls, and fire Touched events on them even if the server sees no touch.

And from "Network ownership, movement validation, and physics": a client that owns parts (including its character) can teleport to any position, set any WalkSpeed locally without firing events, play arbitrary animations, bypass collisions, and **replicate `inf` or `NaN` CFrame components and extreme velocities** that disturb other unanchored assemblies, even ones it does not own. That is the fling exploit.

## The player character is always client-owned

A player's character root is owned by that player's client in the classic model. This is non-negotiable unless you adopt the server authority model (a beta as of October 2026). Everything about anti-cheat for movement follows from it: you cannot prevent a client from putting its character anywhere; you can only detect, correct and make it worthless. See Exploits and Anti-Cheat.

Consequences people miss:

- **Anything welded to the character is part of the character's assembly**, so the client owns it too. A carried crate, a weapon with an unanchored hitbox part, a pet welded to the root: all client-controlled.
- **Humanoid state is decided by the owner.** `Humanoid:ChangeState` only works on the owner, and `SetStateEnabled` does not replicate. See Humanoid States and Animation.
- **Setting the character's CFrame from the server works** (the server can always write), but the client may immediately write its own position back. Server teleports of characters are usually respected because honest clients accept them; exploit clients may not. That is why server-initiated teleports need to be part of your movement validator (whitelisted, not flagged).

## Automatic ownership in practice

The engine hands ownership of loose parts to nearby clients. In practice this means:

| Situation | What happens | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Physics props (balls, crates) in a hub | Ownership hops between nearby players as they approach | Jitter at hand-off; any nearby exploiter can grab and fling them |
| An unanchored NPC near players | NPC may become client-owned | The client controls the NPC's position: kiting, pinning, flinging into the void |
| A ProximityPrompt on an unanchored part | Client may own the part | An exploiter moves the part to themselves and triggers it, defeating distance checks (Roblox docs) |
| A vehicle with driver and passenger seats | The first player to sit can own the whole vehicle | The driver's input lags (docs example) |

The hand-off itself takes several network cycles, and the old and new owner briefly disagree, which shows as a stutter. "Ownership ping-pong" (two players standing near the same prop) causes repeated stutters.

## When to set ownership manually

| Object | Recommended owner | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Gameplay-critical NPCs and bosses | Server: `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` on the root after spawn | No client can move them; stable server hit detection |
| Vehicles | The driver while seated; automatic when empty | Responsive driving (docs example) |
| Loose parts riding on a vehicle | The vehicle's driver too | Avoid two owners fighting (docs warning) |
| Projectiles with gameplay effect | Server, or no physics at all (server raycasts/math, client visuals) | Client-owned projectiles can be steered |
| Thrown objects the player throws | The thrower for feel, with server validation of results | Trade-off: responsiveness vs trust |
| Interactable objects with prompts | Anchored, or server-owned | Prompts on client-owned parts can be moved |
| Cosmetic debris, ragdoll limbs of dead NPCs | Leave automatic, or create them on clients only | Not worth server bandwidth |

The docs caution that server ownership "may result in jittery physics interactions for clients": a server-owned object near a player reacts to that player's pushes only after a round trip. For an NPC that is fine; for a ball players dribble, it feels bad.

### Locking an NPC to the server

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: spawn an NPC and keep it server-owned for its whole life.
local function lockToServer(model: Model)
	local root = model.PrimaryPart
	if not root then
		warn("NPC has no PrimaryPart: " .. model:GetFullName())
		return
	end
	local ok, reason = root:CanSetNetworkOwnership()
	if ok then
		root:SetNetworkOwner(nil)
	else
		warn(("Cannot set ownership on %s: %s"):format(model:GetFullName(), tostring(reason)))
	end
end

local function spawnNpc(template: Model, cframe: CFrame): Model
	local npc = template:Clone()
	npc:PivotTo(cframe)
	npc.Parent = workspace
	-- Ownership is per assembly; set it after the model is in the world and assembled.
	lockToServer(npc)
	return npc
end

return spawnNpc
```

Notes:

- Call it **after** parenting into Workspace; the assembly must exist.
- If a part of the NPC is anchored, the call fails for that assembly (`CanSetNetworkOwnership` returns false with a reason). Anchored NPCs are already server-owned.
- Welding the NPC to something else, or a constraint that joins it to a player's assembly, can merge mechanisms and change ownership. Re-assert after big structural changes (ragdoll on death, carrying).

### Vehicle seat ownership

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/VehicleOwnership: hand each tagged vehicle to its driver, back to the server when empty.
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local function driverOf(seat: VehicleSeat): Player?
	local humanoid = seat.Occupant
	return if humanoid then Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(humanoid.Parent) else nil
end

local function refreshOwner(seat: VehicleSeat)
	local ok, reason = seat:CanSetNetworkOwnership()
	if not ok then
		warn(`{seat:GetFullName()}: {reason}`) -- usually an anchored part in the vehicle
		return
	end
	local driver = driverOf(seat)
	if driver then
		seat:SetNetworkOwner(driver) -- applies to the whole assembly
	else
		seat:SetNetworkOwner(nil) -- empty vehicles stay with the server
	end
end

local function watch(instance: Instance)
	if not instance:IsA("VehicleSeat") then return end
	instance:GetPropertyChangedSignal("Occupant"):Connect(function()
		refreshOwner(instance)
	end)
	refreshOwner(instance)
end

CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("DrivableSeat"):Connect(watch)
for _, seat in CollectionService:GetTagged("DrivableSeat") do
	watch(seat)
end
```

Pinning an empty vehicle to the server (rather than leaving it on automatic) stops a nearby player from picking up ownership of a parked car and flinging it.

Driver ownership means the driver controls the car's physics. Validate what matters: speed caps checked on the server, finish lines decided by server-side checkpoints, collisions that damage other players recomputed on the server.

## Security: what owned physics lets an exploiter do

| Exploit | Mechanism | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Speed hack | Local WalkSpeed or direct CFrame writes on own character | Server displacement checks with tolerance; rubber-band (Exploits and Anti-Cheat) |
| Fly / noclip | Owner disables gravity or collisions locally | Ground and collision heuristics; make flight worthless with server distance checks on interactions |
| Teleport | Owner writes a far CFrame | Server displacement checks; server-side zone gates (see below) |
| Fling | Owner gives its own parts huge or `NaN` velocity and touches others | Server-owned NPCs; check `AssemblyLinearVelocity` for absurd values; anchor or server-own critical props |
| Touched spoofing | Owner fires Touched on a part it owns anywhere | Never award from client-owned Touched alone; server distance check at the moment of the event |
| Prompt pulling | Owner moves an unanchored part with a prompt to itself | Anchored or server-owned prompt parents; server distance check in `Triggered` |
| NPC control | Client owns a nearby NPC | `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` on NPC roots |

### Validating Touched from a client-owned part

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: a pickup that ignores touches that could not physically have happened.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local MAX_TOUCH_DISTANCE = 12 -- studs from part centre; tune to part and character size

local function onTouched(pickup: BasePart, hit: BasePart)
	local character = hit:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
	local player = character and Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
	if not player or not character then return end
	local root = character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart") :: BasePart?
	if not root then return end
	-- The server's view of the root lags the client slightly, so allow a margin.
	if (root.Position - pickup.Position).Magnitude > MAX_TOUCH_DISTANCE then
		return -- touch reported far from where the server sees the character
	end
	if pickup:GetAttribute("Taken") then return end
	pickup:SetAttribute("Taken", true) -- claim before granting
	-- grant reward from server-side data here
end

return onTouched
```

Even better is to not rely on Touched for anything valuable: on the server, check proximity on a timer or with `GetPartBoundsInRadius` against your own pickup list. See Raycasts Shapecasts and Spatial Queries.

### Server-side zone gating (a teleport defence that just works)

One production game had progression-gated worlds. Rather than trying to stop teleport hacks, a server-side guard periodically checked whether each player's character stood inside a world they had not unlocked, and if so moved them to the lobby. A teleport hack then gains nothing: rewards in that zone require server-validated presence, and the player is removed within seconds. This is the "make it worthless" principle, and it costs a few bounding-box checks per player per second.

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: return players standing in zones they have not unlocked.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

type Zone = { name: string, cframe: CFrame, size: Vector3 }
local ZONES: { Zone } = {} -- filled from map data at startup
local LOBBY = CFrame.new(0, 10, 0)

local function inside(zone: Zone, p: Vector3): boolean
	local localPos = zone.cframe:PointToObjectSpace(p)
	local half = zone.size / 2
	return math.abs(localPos.X) <= half.X and math.abs(localPos.Y) <= half.Y and math.abs(localPos.Z) <= half.Z
end

local function hasUnlocked(player: Player, zoneName: string): boolean
	-- Read from the server-side profile, never from client-writable state.
	local unlocked = player:GetAttribute("Unlocked_" .. zoneName)
	return unlocked == true
end

task.spawn(function()
	while true do
		task.wait(2)
		for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
			local character = player.Character
			local root = character and character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart") :: BasePart?
			if root then
				for _, zone in ZONES do
					if inside(zone, root.Position) and not hasUnlocked(player, zone.name) then
						-- With streaming on, stream the destination first: see Instance Streaming.
						player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(LOBBY.Position, 5)
						character:PivotTo(LOBBY)
						break
					end
				end
			end
		end
	end
end)
```

(Player attributes are server-written here; the client cannot change what the server reads. In a real game the profile table is the source of truth and the attribute is only a mirror.)

## Ownership and hit detection

Ownership decides whose view of a moving object is "true". For combat:

- **Player attacks:** the attacker's character is client-owned, so the server sees it late. Server hit checks need a latency tolerance (one production game raised its player reach from 13 to 17 studs and used a range multiplier of 1.35 for abilities, on characters scaled to 1.6x, after measuring missed hits).
- **NPC attacks:** server-owned NPCs give the server an exact position, so the server can decide hits precisely; the victim's client sees the NPC late, so dodge windows need generosity on the victim's side (the same game used a 0.40 s dodge window against boss attacks, and a 0.26 s parry window).
- **Client-animated NPCs:** if NPC animation runs only on clients (see Replication and Ownership), the server's parts do not move with the animation, so hits must be data-driven (distance, arc, marker times) rather than part-touch based.

See Hitboxes and Hit Detection and Combat Systems Architecture.

## Diagnosing ownership

- Studio: viewport **visualization options** (top right) and toggle **Network owners** during a playtest. Green: your client owns and simulates it. Red: in a buffer zone, your client simulates it but something else owns it. White or grey: server or another client. Black: nobody owns it and physics will not apply. In multi-client tests each client gets its own colour (Roblox docs).
- Server-side audit: print owners of everything moving.

```lua
--!strict
-- Command bar (server view during a playtest): list unanchored assemblies by owner.
local counts: { [string]: number } = {}
for _, d in workspace:GetDescendants() do
	if d:IsA("BasePart") and not d.Anchored and d.AssemblyRootPart == d then
		local owner = d:GetNetworkOwner()
		local key = if owner then owner.Name else "server"
		counts[key] = (counts[key] or 0) + 1
	end
end
for k, n in counts do print(k, n) end
```

Symptoms:

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| NPC stutters when players approach | Automatic ownership hand-off; set server ownership |
| Vehicle input lags for the driver | Passenger owns the vehicle; set driver ownership |
| Prop jitters between two players | Ownership ping-pong; server-own it or anchor it |
| Object frozen in the air, no physics | Black outline: no owner; check anchoring and constraints |
| `SetNetworkOwner` errors | Part is anchored or welded to an anchored part; use `CanSetNetworkOwnership` |
| Players flung by another player | Owned fling; validate velocities, protect characters with collision groups if needed |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Leaving boss NPCs on automatic ownership | `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` after spawn |
| Prompts and ClickDetectors on unanchored parts | Anchor them or server-own them; server distance check |
| `SetNetworkOwner` on anchored parts, or no way back to automatic | Anchored parts are always server-owned; `SetNetworkOwnershipAuto()` restores automatic |
| Awarding from client-owned Touched | Server proximity check or server queries |
| Calling `SetNetworkOwner` before parenting | Call after the assembly exists in Workspace |
| Treating server ownership as free | It adds latency for nearby players; use it for critical objects only |
| Flagging server-initiated teleports as cheats | Tell the movement validator about every server move |

## Checklist

- [ ] Every gameplay-critical unanchored object has a deliberate owner.
- [ ] No valuable interaction relies on client-owned Touched or prompt position alone.
- [ ] Vehicles assign the driver on sit and reset on exit, and ownership changes nowhere else (switches cause jitter).
- [ ] Movement validation accounts for latency and whitelists server teleports.
- [ ] Ownership visualised once in a multi-client test.

# Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Rate limit after expensive parsing or DataStore calls -> Rate limit first
> - Avoid: One global cooldown table keyed by player name -> Key by `Player` (or `UserId`), clear on leave
> - Avoid: Kicking on rate-limit hits -> Log and score; drop the request
> - Every client-triggerable entry point has a per-player limit as its first statement, then type and range checks on every argument.
> - Limits are 1.5x to 2x the fastest legitimate use, with logged rejections.
> - Backend calls go through server-wide budgets.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~170 tok · whole note ~4.6k tok. Read more: ## A reusable rate limiter · ## Nuances and edge cases · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Any server logic a client can trigger (remotes, Touched, ProximityPrompts, ClickDetectors, chat, trade requests) can be triggered faster than you planned: by exploiters on purpose, by auto-clickers, by a buggy client loop, or by an honest player mashing a button on a laggy connection. Rate limiting decides how often each action may run, protects the economy from timing exploits, and protects the server (and Roblox's backend services) from overload. This note covers the algorithms, how to choose limits, the engine's own limits you must stay under, coalescing and idempotency, cleanup, and production numbers.

## Why the engine's throttle is not enough

Roblox throttles client-to-server remotes at about **500 requests per second per client**, shared across all remotes of the same type (Roblox docs, `RemoteEvent` "Throttling"). Over the limit, RemoteEvents are **delayed** (queued, order kept) and UnreliableRemoteEvents are **dropped**. That protects Roblox's servers, not your game: 500 "buy" or "cast" requests a second is several hundred more than any honest player sends. Your own per-action limits sit far below it.

There is also an honest-player reason: because the budget is shared, a client loop firing a reliable remote every frame delays every other reliable remote from that client. Rate-limit your own client code too.

## Cooldown vs rate limit

They are different tools and you usually need both:

| Tool | Question | Lives in | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cooldown** | Is this game action available yet? | Game rules, saved or session state | "Fireball recharges in 6 s"; "Daily chest every 20 h" |
| **Rate limit** | Is this client sending too many requests? | Transport layer, per player per remote | "No more than 5 cast requests per second" |

A cooldown rejection is a normal outcome (show a timer). A rate-limit rejection is abnormal (drop silently, maybe log). Honest clients should almost never hit a rate limit; set limits a comfortable margin above the fastest legitimate use.

## Algorithms

| Algorithm | Behaviour | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed minimum interval** (`now - last >= interval`) | One action per interval, no bursts | Simple actions with a natural pace: "one flourish per second" |
| **Token bucket** | Bursts up to capacity, sustained rate = refill rate | Most remotes: allows a quick double-click, blocks sustained spam (the Roblox docs' recommended example) |
| **Leaky bucket accumulator** | Accumulates "excess", leaks over time, triggers past a threshold | Measurements rather than requests: movement excess, damage-per-second plausibility |
| **Sliding window counter** | At most N in the last T seconds | Moderation-style limits: "5 trade requests per minute" |
| **Global budget** | One bucket for the whole server | Protecting shared backends: DataStore, HttpService, MessagingService |

## A reusable rate limiter

Per player, per key, token bucket, with cleanup. `os.clock()` is fine on the server (monotonic, local); the Roblox docs' example uses `time()`.

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Shared/RateLimiter.luau
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

export type Limiter = {
	allow: (self: Limiter, player: Player, key: string?) -> boolean,
	reset: (self: Limiter, player: Player) -> (),
}

type Bucket = { tokens: number, last: number }

local RateLimiter = {}
RateLimiter.__index = RateLimiter

local all: { any } = setmetatable({}, { __mode = "v" }) :: any -- weak list for cleanup

-- ratePerSec: sustained rate. burst: how many may be spent at once.
function RateLimiter.new(ratePerSec: number, burst: number): Limiter
	assert(ratePerSec > 0 and burst >= 1, "bad limiter config")
	local self = setmetatable({
		rate = ratePerSec,
		burst = burst,
		buckets = {} :: { [Player]: { [string]: Bucket } },
		rejected = {} :: { [Player]: number },
	}, RateLimiter)
	table.insert(all, self)
	return (self :: any) :: Limiter
end

function RateLimiter.allow(self: any, player: Player, key: string?): boolean
	local k = key or "_"
	local now = os.clock()
	local mine = self.buckets[player]
	if not mine then
		mine = {}
		self.buckets[player] = mine
	end
	local b = mine[k]
	if not b then
		b = { tokens = self.burst, last = now }
		mine[k] = b
	else
		b.tokens = math.min(self.burst, b.tokens + (now - b.last) * self.rate)
		b.last = now
	end
	if b.tokens >= 1 then
		b.tokens -= 1
		return true
	end
	self.rejected[player] = (self.rejected[player] or 0) + 1
	return false
end

function RateLimiter.reset(self: any, player: Player)
	self.buckets[player] = nil
	self.rejected[player] = nil
end

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
	for _, limiter in all do
		limiter:reset(player)
	end
end)

return RateLimiter
```

Use it as the first line of a handler, before any parsing:

```lua
local castLimiter = RateLimiter.new(4, 6)      -- 4/s sustained, burst 6
local buyLimiter = RateLimiter.new(2, 4)
local chatLimiter = RateLimiter.new(0.5, 5)    -- the docs' "5 per 10 seconds"

castRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, slot, aim)
	if not castLimiter:allow(player) then return end
	-- validate, then act
end)
```

Or make it middleware in your remote wrapper so no handler can forget it (see [[RemoteEvents RemoteFunctions and Unreliable Remotes]]).

## Choosing limits

1. **Find the fastest legitimate use.** A combo of 4 swings at a 0.32 s pace is about 3 requests per second; a shop where a player buys in quick succession may click 5 times in a second.
2. **Set the sustained rate at 1.5x to 2x that** and the burst at the largest honest burst (a double-click, a combo string, a reconnect flush).
3. **Log rejections** for a week before tightening. Honest players hitting a limit means the limit is wrong.
4. **Never auto-ban on rate limits alone.** Mobile lag bunches inputs; retry loops resend. A player tripping limits hundreds of times is a signal for the suspicion score (Exploits and Anti-Cheat), not a verdict.

Production values from one combat and collection game (all server-side):

| Action | Limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Admin panel actions | 1 per 0.08 s | Allowlisted users only; limit exists to stop accidental loops |
| Crafting and fusion requests | 1 per 0.4 s | Plus idempotent tokens |
| Hub activities (spin, fishing, chest) | 1 per 0.5 s | Plus range check, cooldown, and a "can mutate profile" check |
| Equip flourish relay | 1 per second | Cosmetic relay to other clients |
| Custom animation relay: speed changes | Immediately if the change is 6% or more, else at most every 0.25 s | Batching continuous state |
| Custom animation relay: weight changes | At most 4 per second | |
| Ability casts | Cooldown enforced at 0.95x authored value | Tolerance for latency jitter |

## Engine and backend limits you must budget for

Several Roblox services have their own limits; exceeding them makes requests fail or queue. Budget them **server-wide**, not per player, because one player's spam can starve everyone.

| Service | Limit (as of October 2026) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Remotes (client to server) | About 500/s per client, shared per remote type | Roblox docs |
| UnreliableRemoteEvent payload | 1,000 bytes | Roblox docs |
| HttpService | About 500 requests per minute per server | Roblox docs; one production game hit it with per-clip uploads and switched to one request per batch |
| MessagingService publish | 600 + 240 x players per minute per server | Roblox docs; see Cross-Server Messaging |
| MemoryStore requests | 1,000 + 120 x concurrent users request units per minute, experience-wide | Roblox docs; see MemoryStore Service |
| DataStores | Per-server request budgets that scale with players | See [[DataStore Fundamentals]] |

A server-wide budget is just a limiter keyed on a fixed "player" slot; or a small queue that spends a fixed number of calls per second and drops or delays the rest:

```lua
--!strict
-- A server-wide budget for an expensive backend call, with a bounded queue.
local Budget = {}

local RATE = 4          -- calls per second for this service
local MAX_QUEUE = 200   -- beyond this, drop new work (log it)

local queue: { () -> () } = {}
local tokens = RATE
local last = os.clock()

function Budget.submit(job: () -> ()): boolean
	if #queue >= MAX_QUEUE then
		warn("[Budget] queue full; dropping job")
		return false
	end
	table.insert(queue, job)
	return true
end

task.spawn(function()
	while true do
		task.wait(0.05)
		local now = os.clock()
		tokens = math.min(RATE, tokens + (now - last) * RATE)
		last = now
		while tokens >= 1 and #queue > 0 do
			tokens -= 1
			local job = table.remove(queue, 1) :: () -> ()
			task.spawn(function()
				local ok, err = pcall(job)
				if not ok then warn("[Budget] job failed: " .. tostring(err)) end
			end)
		end
	end
end)

return Budget
```

## Coalescing: do less work, not just less often

Many "spam" problems are really "the same work repeated". Coalesce:

- **Save soon, not save now.** Mark the profile dirty and schedule one save a few seconds later; ten changes produce one write. One production game used a `pushState` (update the client mirror) plus `saveSoon` (debounced save) pair after every profile mutation.
- **Batch UI updates.** Send one inventory snapshot after a burst of changes rather than one remote per item.
- **Relay at a fixed rate.** Continuous state (aim, animation speed) is sampled and sent at 10 to 20 Hz, only when it changed meaningfully.

```lua
--!strict
-- Debounce helper: run `fn(key)` once, `delay` seconds after the last request for that key.
local Debounce = {}
local pending: { [any]: thread } = {}

function Debounce.soon(key: any, delay: number, fn: (any) -> ())
	local existing = pending[key]
	if existing then
		task.cancel(existing)
	end
	pending[key] = task.delay(delay, function()
		pending[key] = nil
		fn(key)
	end)
end

return Debounce
-- Usage: Debounce.soon(player, 5, saveProfile) after every mutation.
-- On PlayerRemoving and BindToClose, save immediately instead (and cancel the pending one).
```

## Idempotency: making retries harmless

Rate limits reduce volume; they do not stop a duplicated request from doing double work. Give actions that grant or consume value a client-generated token and remember recent tokens on the server (see the `Idempotency` helper in [[Server Authority and Validation]]). Purchases use the receipt's `PurchaseId` the same way ([[Purchase Data and Receipts]]).

## Abuse that is not cheating

Rate limits also protect players from each other:

| Abuse | Limit |
|---|---|
| Trade request spam | Sliding window per sender, and per sender-recipient pair |
| Friend or party invite spam | Same |
| Report spam | Per reporter per target |
| Custom chat or sign text | Token bucket plus `TextService` filtering on the server |
| Emote and effect spam near others | Per player rate; cap effects per area on receiving clients |
| Vote kick or vote skip | One vote per player per vote; cooldown per initiator |

User text must be filtered on the server with `TextService` before other players see it; never relay raw strings (Roblox Policies Ratings and Compliance).

## Client-side limiting (for honest clients)

Client debounces do not stop exploiters, but they keep honest clients well inside every limit and make the UI feel right:

- Disable a button while its request is in flight; re-enable on the server's answer or after a timeout.
- Pace continuous sends (aim, position hints) on a timer, not per frame.
- Collapse repeated presses into one request when the action is idempotent ("open shop").

## Diagnosing

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Actions feel delayed for one player under load | Their client is saturating the shared remote budget; find the per-frame remote |
| DataStore warnings about queued requests | Unbatched saves; add `saveSoon` |
| `HttpService` errors about the request limit | Per-item requests; batch |
| Honest players report "nothing happens sometimes" | Rate limit too tight; check rejection logs |
| Memory slowly grows on long servers | Rate limiter tables not cleared on `PlayerRemoving` |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Rate limit after expensive parsing or DataStore calls | Rate limit first |
| One global cooldown table keyed by player name | Key by `Player` (or `UserId`), clear on leave |
| Kicking on rate-limit hits | Log and score; drop the request |
| Rate limiting only remotes | Prompts, Touched, ClickDetectors too |
| Using `tick()` | `os.clock()` on one machine; `GetServerTimeNow()` across machines |
| Saving on every change | Debounced saves plus immediate save on leave |

## Checklist

- [ ] Every client-triggerable entry point has a per-player limit as its first statement, then type and range checks on every argument.
- [ ] Limits are 1.5x to 2x the fastest legitimate use, with logged rejections.
- [ ] Backend calls go through server-wide budgets.
- [ ] Saves and UI pushes are coalesced.
- [ ] Value-granting actions are idempotent.
- [ ] Limiter state is cleared on `PlayerRemoving`.

## See also
[[Server Authority and Validation]] · Exploits and Anti-Cheat · [[RemoteEvents RemoteFunctions and Unreliable Remotes]] · [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]] · HttpService and External APIs · Cross-Server Messaging · MemoryStore Service · [[Network Performance]]

## Nuances and edge cases

1. **Honest players burst.** A player on a laggy connection can deliver ten queued remote calls in one packet after a stall. A strict "max 1 per 100 ms" check flags them as abusers. Token buckets with a burst allowance (for example, a capacity of 10 refilling at 5 per second) accept honest bursts while capping sustained abuse. Choose capacity from the largest honest burst you measure, not a guess.
2. **Limits depend on device and input.** Auto-clickers and fast tapping on phones look similar; a player on a high-refresh mouse can click faster than a phone player can tap. Set limits from game rules (an attack cannot happen faster than its animation) rather than from input speed.
3. **Rate limiting is per resource, not per remote.** One remote that does three things (buy, equip, sell) needs separate limits per action, because buying is expensive and equipping is cheap. Key buckets by player and action.
4. **Server cost per rejected call still exists.** Even a rejected call costs deserialisation and a table lookup. Under a flood, the cheapest possible rejection matters: check the bucket before any argument parsing, and drop silently instead of replying.
5. **Scale changes what abuse costs you.** One abuser in a 6-player server ruins five players' experience; in a 50-player server they can also degrade server performance for everyone. Track per-server totals as well as per-player, and shed load from the noisiest players first.
6. **Global resources need global limits.** Per-player limits do not protect shared budgets: 50 players each staying under their own limit can together exhaust a DataStore or HTTP budget. Put a server-wide limiter in front of anything that consumes a per-server or per-experience quota.
7. **Punishment needs evidence.** Rate-limit hits are evidence of either abuse or lag. Log and score them, combine with other signals, and act on patterns. Instant kicks for a single hit produce false positives and angry support messages (see False Positives Lag and Fair Enforcement).
8. **Client-side limits are UX, not security.** Disabling a button for half a second stops accidental double-clicks and reduces load from honest players. It does nothing against exploiters, so the server limit must exist regardless.

The senior trade-off: tight limits reduce abuse and anger honest players with bad connections; loose limits do the opposite. Measure honest traffic first (log rates for a week), then set limits a comfortable margin above the honest maximum.

## Common mistakes (advanced)

1. **Fixed-interval checks with no burst.** Symptom: laggy players report actions being ignored. Fix: token buckets with measured capacity.
2. **One limit per remote for multi-action remotes.** Symptom: cheap actions are throttled by expensive ones, or the reverse. Fix: per-action buckets.
3. **Replying to every rejected call.** Symptom: floods cost server bandwidth. Fix: drop silently; notify the client at most once per window.
4. **No server-wide limits on shared budgets.** Symptom: DataStore throttling during busy periods even though every player is within limits. Fix: a global limiter per budget.
5. **Buckets never cleaned up.** Symptom: memory growth over long server lifetimes. Fix: clear per-player buckets on leave.
6. **Limits tuned only in Studio.** Symptom: real players on phones trip limits that never triggered in testing. Fix: log live rates before enforcing.

# RemoteEvents RemoteFunctions and Unreliable Remotes

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Budgeting remote traffic per remote instead of per client -> Loss-tolerant streams on an UnreliableRemoteEvent (its own pool)...
> - Avoid: `InvokeClient` for anything -> Event plus reply event with timeout
> - Avoid: Identity, price or balance taken from the payload -> The caller is `OnServerEvent`'s first argument; the server reads...
> - Client send rates budgeted per client: about 500 calls per second shared by all remotes of one type (reliable and unreliable...
> - All remotes created by the server, in one folder, from one list.
> - No `InvokeClient` anywhere.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~180 tok · whole note ~5.8k tok. Read more: ## The three types · ## Organising remotes · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Remotes are the explicit messages you send across the client-server boundary. Roblox has three kinds, each with different delivery promises, limits and failure modes. Choosing the wrong one gives you either lag (reliable traffic for data nobody needs), lost events (unreliable traffic for things that must happen), or a server thread that hangs forever (`InvokeClient`). This note covers the guarantees exactly as documented, the argument rules, the throttling and size limits, the RemoteFunction pitfalls, how to organise remotes in a project, and the production patterns that hold up: server-validated relays, request/response with timeouts, sequenced unreliable streams and honeypots.

Validation of what arrives is covered in [[Server Authority and Validation]] and rate limits in [[Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention]]. This note focuses on the transport.

## The three types

| Type | Direction | Yields the sender? | Delivery | Order | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `RemoteEvent` | Client to server, server to one client, server to all | No | Reliable: lost packets are resent while connected | Ordered per direction, **including across different RemoteEvent instances** | Requests, state changes, anything that must arrive |
| `UnreliableRemoteEvent` | Same | No | Best effort; may be dropped | **Not** ordered | Continuous or ephemeral data: aim, cosmetic effects, positions |
| `RemoteFunction` | Client to server (`InvokeServer`), server to client (`InvokeClient`) | **Yes**, until the other side returns | Reliable | Not ordered relative to RemoteEvents | Client asking the server a question and needing an answer |

All facts in this table are from the Roblox docs pages for these classes and "Remote events and callbacks" (as of October 2026).

### Delivery details worth memorising

From the docs:

- **RemoteEvent with no handler connected:** messages queue and are delivered in order when a handler connects. The queue is limited in count and memory; when full, further messages are discarded and Output logs a "Remote event invocation" error. Undelivered messages are lost if the recipient disconnects.
- **Handler ordering is about start, not finish.** If a handler yields (`task.wait`, `WaitForChild`, a DataStore call), the next message's handler can start before the earlier one resumes. Two requests from the same player can interleave in your code. This is the root of most "duplicate item" bugs.
- **RemoteFunction callbacks that yield** can return responses out of order.
- **UnreliableRemoteEvent** messages can be dropped because of transit loss, congestion, payloads over 1,000 bytes, exceeding the throttle (excess is **dropped**, not delayed), or no connected handler (discarded immediately, not queued). Later messages can arrive before earlier ones.
- Only one invocation can be in flight per calling thread, and if several callbacks are assigned to the same RemoteFunction, only the last assignment runs.

### Limits

| Limit | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Client-to-server rate | About **500 requests per second per client**, shared among all remotes **of the same type** | Roblox docs, `RemoteEvent` and `UnreliableRemoteEvent` "Throttling" |
| RemoteEvent over the rate | Excess is processed later (delayed), order kept | Roblox docs |
| UnreliableRemoteEvent over the rate | Excess is dropped | Roblox docs |
| UnreliableRemoteEvent payload | Events with payloads **larger than 1,000 bytes are dropped**; Studio's Output reports by how many bytes | Roblox docs |
| Payload size of reliable remotes | No small documented hard cap, but large payloads cost bandwidth and delay every message behind them | Rule of thumb: keep per-message payloads small; send large data rarely |

Payloads are encoded and compressed (buffers in particular), which makes it hard to know your unreliable payload size before firing (Roblox docs). Design unreliable messages to be obviously small: a few numbers, an id, a short string.

The 500/s throttle is per client and shared per remote type. One noisy system (a per-frame `FireServer` from a LocalScript) can consume the budget and delay every other RemoteEvent that client sends, including your purchase confirmation. Never fire reliable remotes per frame. RemoteEvent and UnreliableRemoteEvent are different types, so each draws on its own pool: moving a high-rate stream (aim, look direction) to an UnreliableRemoteEvent frees the reliable budget for hits and purchases.

## Argument rules

What survives the trip (Roblox docs, "Argument limitations"):

| You send | Receiver gets |
|---|---|
| Numbers, strings, booleans, `nil` | Same values. **`NaN` and `inf` are valid numbers and pass through** |
| Roblox datatypes (`Vector3`, `CFrame`, `Color3`, `EnumItem`...) | Same values |
| An `Instance` the receiver can see | A reference to its copy |
| An `Instance` the receiver cannot see (ServerStorage item to a client; client-created part to the server) | `nil` |
| A table | A **copy**: no identity, no metatable, functions removed |
| A table with non-string keys | Keys converted to strings |
| A mixed table (array part plus string keys) | Undefined; do not send |
| A table with `nil` holes | Do not send; elements may be lost |
| A function | `nil` |
| A `buffer` | A copy; compact and efficient (see Buffers and Binary Data) |

Server-side, the **first parameter of `OnServerEvent` is always the real sending `Player`**, supplied by the engine. It is the only argument you can trust. Every other argument is attacker-controlled: a client can send a table shaped like an Instance (`{Name = "Sword", ClassName = "Folder", Price = {Value = 0}}`), a `NaN`, a 10 MB string, an Instance from a part of the game it should not touch. The docs show exactly the fake-Instance-table attack against a shop.

### Payload design

- **Send ids, not objects.** `"blade_ember"` and look it up in a server catalog, rather than the Tool Instance (whose attributes the client may have edited locally).
- **Send scalars, not tables**, where possible. Each table field is another thing to validate.
- **Send intent, not outcome.** "Cast slot 2 aimed at this direction" rather than "deal 400 damage to this enemy".
- **Send small.** Quantise positions, use enums or short ids, batch several updates into one message at a fixed rate.

## RemoteFunction pitfalls

`InvokeServer` (client asks, server answers) is fine and convenient for request/response UIs (shop "can I afford this?", "load my inventory page"). Its pitfalls are manageable:

- The client thread yields until the server returns; if the server handler yields for a DataStore call, the UI waits. Show a spinner and guard against double clicks.
- If the server callback errors, the error propagates to the client caller. Do not leak internal error strings; wrap the handler and return a clean result.
- The return value is an information channel: never return state the client should not know.

`InvokeClient` (server asks a client) is the dangerous one. The docs list the failure modes:

- If the client throws an error, **the server throws too**.
- If the client disconnects during the call, `InvokeClient` errors.
- If the client never returns a value, **the server yields forever**.

An exploiter can simply set `OnClientInvoke` to a function that never returns, and your server thread leaks. If that thread held a lock (a trade in progress, a save in progress), the lock is held forever. **Do not use `InvokeClient`** for anything. If the server needs an answer from a client, send a RemoteEvent and wait for a reply RemoteEvent with a timeout:

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: ask one client a question and wait at most `timeout` seconds for the answer.
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local askRemote = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.Ask :: RemoteEvent
local replyRemote = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.Reply :: RemoteEvent

type Pending = { player: Player, thread: thread }
local pending: { [string]: Pending } = {}

replyRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player: Player, requestId: unknown, answer: unknown)
	if typeof(requestId) ~= "string" then return end
	local entry = pending[requestId]
	if not entry or entry.player ~= player then return end -- only the asked player may answer
	pending[requestId] = nil
	task.spawn(entry.thread, true, answer) -- answer is still untrusted: validate at the call site
end)

local function ask(player: Player, question: string, timeout: number): (boolean, unknown)
	local requestId = HttpService:GenerateGUID(false)
	local thread = coroutine.running()
	pending[requestId] = { player = player, thread = thread }

	task.delay(timeout, function()
		if pending[requestId] then
			pending[requestId] = nil
			task.spawn(thread, false, "timeout")
		end
	end)

	askRemote:FireClient(player, requestId, question)
	return coroutine.yield()
end

return ask
```

The server thread always resumes: either with the answer or with a timeout. Clean up `pending` entries for a player on `PlayerRemoving` in a real implementation.

## UnreliableRemoteEvent in practice

Good fits:

- Aim direction, look direction, cursor position (sent 10 to 20 times a second; a lost update is replaced by the next one).
- Cosmetic one-shots where missing one is harmless (a footstep puff, a muzzle flash for distant players).
- Server-to-client positions of many cheap objects (projectile visuals) when the authoritative state lives elsewhere.

Bad fits: anything that changes state permanently, anything the player paid for, the start or end of an ability (a lost "stop" message leaves an effect running forever), anything larger than about 1 KB.

Because order is not guaranteed, **sequence your messages** and ignore stale ones:

```lua
--!strict
-- Client: stream aim direction at 15 Hz through an UnreliableRemoteEvent.
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local aimRemote = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.Aim :: UnreliableRemoteEvent
local SEND_INTERVAL = 1 / 15

local seq = 0
local accumulator = 0
local lastSent: Vector3? = nil

RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(dt)
	accumulator += dt
	if accumulator < SEND_INTERVAL then return end
	accumulator = 0

	local camera = Workspace.CurrentCamera
	if not camera then return end
	local look = camera.CFrame.LookVector
	-- Skip if the change is too small to matter (saves the budget).
	if lastSent and lastSent:Dot(look) > 0.9995 then return end
	lastSent = look

	seq = (seq + 1) % 65536 -- small number, wraps
	aimRemote:FireServer(seq, look)
end)
```

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: accept only newer, finite, unit-length directions.
local aimRemote = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.Aim :: UnreliableRemoteEvent
local lastSeq: { [Player]: number } = {}

local function isNewer(a: number, b: number): boolean
	-- wrap-around aware comparison for a 16-bit sequence
	local diff = (a - b) % 65536
	return diff > 0 and diff < 32768
end

aimRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player: Player, seq: unknown, look: unknown)
	if typeof(seq) ~= "number" or typeof(look) ~= "Vector3" then return end
	if seq ~= seq or seq < 0 or seq >= 65536 or seq % 1 ~= 0 then return end
	local m = look.Magnitude
	if m ~= m or m < 0.9 or m > 1.1 then return end -- rejects NaN and absurd vectors
	local prev = lastSeq[player]
	if prev and not isNewer(seq, prev) then return end -- stale or duplicate
	lastSeq[player] = seq
	player:SetAttribute("Aim", look.Unit) -- other clients read it; or relay at a fixed rate
end)

game:GetService("Players").PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(p) lastSeq[p] = nil end)
```

## Pattern: the server-validated relay

Many remotes exist only so one client can trigger an effect on others: a spell, an emote, an equip flourish. The naive relay ("receive, `FireAllClients` the same arguments") lets an exploiter spam effects, send malformed data that errors every client, or use abilities they do not own. The docs' wording: **the server must be a gatekeeper, not a relay.**

The pattern used in one production combat game for ability effects and equip flourishes:

1. The caster's client plays the animation and effects immediately (instant feedback).
2. It fires one RemoteEvent with a small id: the move or flourish name.
3. The server validates: rate limit (one flourish per second per player in that game), the id exists, it belongs to the weapon the player actually holds (read from server state, not from the client's Tool), the player is alive and not stunned, the ability is off cooldown.
4. The server relays **its own validated values** (player, id, server start time) to every other client, never the raw arguments.
5. Other clients play the effect, offset by the start time so they stay in sync.

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: validated relay for cosmetic ability effects.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local fxRequest = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.FxRequest :: RemoteEvent
local fxPlay = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.FxPlay :: RemoteEvent

local RateLimiter = require(game.ServerScriptService.Shared.RateLimiter)
local Loadout = require(game.ServerScriptService.Systems.Loadout) -- server truth for held weapon

local limiter = RateLimiter.new(1, 1) -- 1 per second, burst 1

fxRequest.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player: Player, moveId: unknown)
	if typeof(moveId) ~= "string" or #moveId > 32 then return end
	if not limiter:allow(player) then return end
	local weapon = Loadout.getWeapon(player)
	if not weapon or not weapon.moves[moveId] then return end -- move must belong to held weapon
	local character = player.Character
	local humanoid = character and character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if not humanoid or humanoid.Health <= 0 then return end

	local t0 = Workspace:GetServerTimeNow()
	for _, other in Players:GetPlayers() do
		if other ~= player then
			fxPlay:FireClient(other, player, moveId, t0) -- server-built values only
		end
	end
end)
```

A relayed custom animation system in the same game went further: speed changes were relayed immediately only when they changed by 6% or more, otherwise at most every 0.25 s, and weight changes at most 4 times a second. Late joiners asked once for the currently active tracks. Those numbers are a good starting budget for any relayed continuous state.

## Organising remotes

Rules that pay off as a project grows (see Project Structure and Bootstrapping):

- **The server creates all remotes at startup**, in one folder, from one list. Clients only `WaitForChild` the folder. Never let a client create a remote, and never scatter `Instance.new("RemoteEvent")` through systems.
- **One remote per purpose**, or a small number of multiplexed remotes with an action field. Either is fine; per-purpose remotes are easier to rate-limit and to honeypot.
- **Wrap access in a module** so every server handler passes through the same validation and rate-limit middleware.
- **Never look up remotes by a name that data can also use.**

That last rule comes from a real incident. In one production game, each weapon kit kept its remotes as children of the kit folder (`Origin`, `FX`, `LocalCast`) next to animation clips named after moves. An ultimate's clip was named `Origin`. `kit:FindFirstChild("Origin")` returned the clip instead of the RemoteEvent, and every damage request for that weapon silently failed. The fix was a list of **reserved child names** (`Attack`, `Origin`, `FX`, `LocalCast`, `Moves`, `ItemRig`) that content may never use, checked by the install tooling, plus keeping remotes in their own folder. Generalise it: wherever code finds a child by name in a folder that also holds content, either separate the folders or enforce reserved names with a check.

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Net.luau: server-side remote registry with middleware.
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local Net = {}

local folder = Instance.new("Folder")
folder.Name = "Remotes"

local events: { [string]: RemoteEvent } = {}
local functions: { [string]: RemoteFunction } = {}
local unreliable: { [string]: UnreliableRemoteEvent } = {}

type Handler = (player: Player, ...any) -> ...any
type Middleware = (player: Player, name: string, ...any) -> boolean
local middleware: { Middleware } = {}

function Net.use(m: Middleware)
	table.insert(middleware, m)
end

local function passes(player: Player, name: string, ...: any): boolean
	for _, m in middleware do
		if not m(player, name, ...) then return false end
	end
	return true
end

function Net.event(name: string): RemoteEvent
	assert(not events[name], "duplicate remote " .. name)
	local r = Instance.new("RemoteEvent")
	r.Name = name
	r.Parent = folder
	events[name] = r
	return r
end

function Net.unreliable(name: string): UnreliableRemoteEvent
	assert(not unreliable[name], "duplicate remote " .. name)
	local r = Instance.new("UnreliableRemoteEvent")
	r.Name = name
	r.Parent = folder
	unreliable[name] = r
	return r
end

function Net.func(name: string): RemoteFunction
	assert(not functions[name], "duplicate remote " .. name)
	local r = Instance.new("RemoteFunction")
	r.Name = name
	r.Parent = folder
	functions[name] = r
	return r
end

function Net.on(name: string, handler: Handler)
	local r: any = events[name] or unreliable[name]
	assert(r, "unknown remote " .. name)
	local signal: RBXScriptSignal = r.OnServerEvent
	signal:Connect(function(player: Player, ...)
		if not passes(player, name, ...) then return end
		local ok, err = pcall(handler, player, ...)
		if not ok then warn(("[Net] %s handler error: %s"):format(name, tostring(err))) end
	end)
end

function Net.handle(name: string, handler: Handler)
	local r = functions[name]
	assert(r, "unknown function " .. name)
	r.OnServerInvoke = function(player: Player, ...)
		if not passes(player, name, ...) then return nil end
		local results = table.pack(pcall(handler, player, ...))
		if not results[1] then
			warn(("[Net] %s invoke error: %s"):format(name, tostring(results[2])))
			return nil -- never leak the error text to the client
		end
		return table.unpack(results, 2, results.n)
	end
end

-- Call once after all systems registered their remotes.
function Net.publish()
	folder.Parent = ReplicatedStorage
end

return Net
```

Parenting the folder only after every system has registered means clients never see a half-built remote set, and the `assert` on duplicates catches two systems claiming one name.

## Honeypots and direction checks

The Roblox docs suggest two cheap detection tricks:

- **Honeypot remotes:** a remote with a tempting name that no legitimate client script ever fires. Any traffic on it is a near-certain exploiter. Log and kick.
- **Direction tracking:** remotes meant only for server-to-client use should never receive `OnServerEvent`. Connect a handler that flags any client that fires one.

Both are high-confidence signals with almost no false positives, unlike movement heuristics. See Exploits and Anti-Cheat.

## Studio-only and test remotes

Every remote shipped in a live game is callable by every player. Debug remotes (`GiveCoins`, `SetLevel`, `SpawnBoss`) must either not exist in live servers or be gated by a server-side UserId allowlist on every call. One production game kept QA switches as **attributes on ServerStorage** (an isolated test save key, a simulated load failure flag) instead of remotes, so there was nothing for a client to call; its admin panel used a single RemoteFunction whose server handler re-checked an allowlist and throttled to one call per 0.08 s. Keep the allowlist in **one** module: the same game had the list in three places and had to remember to keep them in sync. See [[Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention]].

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Budgeting remote traffic per remote instead of per client | About 500 client-to-server calls per second per client are shared by every remote of one type; a 30 Hz aim stream on a RemoteEvent delays that client's hit reports and purchases | Loss-tolerant streams on an UnreliableRemoteEvent (its own pool); hits, purchases and state on reliable RemoteEvents |
| `InvokeClient` for anything | Server threads hang forever on a malicious or crashed client | Event plus reply event with timeout |
| Identity, price or balance taken from the payload | Anyone pays as, or harms, another player; items for free | The caller is `OnServerEvent`'s first argument; the server reads price and balance |
| Relaying raw client arguments with `FireAllClients` | Spam, client crashes, unowned abilities | Validate, rate-limit, relay server-built values |
| Reliable remote fired per frame | Uses the 500/s budget, delays everything else, bandwidth | Unreliable at 10 to 20 Hz, or send on change |
| Unreliable remote for state changes | Lost "stop" messages, stuck effects | Reliable remote or attribute |
| Unreliable payload over 1,000 bytes | Silently dropped | Smaller payloads or reliable remote |
| Trusting an Instance argument | Fake tables, wrong objects, objects out of reach | Type check, `IsDescendantOf` the expected folder, ownership and distance checks |
| Yield in a handler between check and write | Two requests both pass the check: duplication | Mark state before yielding; per-player busy flag |
| Remote found by a name content can reuse | Wrong object returned, silent breakage | Separate folders, reserved names, install-time checks |

## Checklist

- [ ] Client send rates budgeted per client: about 500 calls per second shared by all remotes of one type (reliable and unreliable pools are separate).
- [ ] All remotes created by the server, in one folder, from one list.
- [ ] No `InvokeClient` anywhere.
- [ ] Every argument after the automatic `Player` is attacker-controlled: check type, value (NaN, inf, length), context and rate, then act.
- [ ] Unreliable remotes carry small, sequenced, loss-tolerant data only.
- [ ] Relays send server-built values to other clients, never the caller's raw arguments.
- [ ] Debug remotes absent from live servers or allowlisted on the server.
- [ ] A honeypot remote and direction checks log suspicious clients.

# Server Authority and Validation

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Validating only type, not value -> Add finiteness, range, integrality, length
> - Avoid: Trusting Tool attributes or names from the client's copy -> Look up by id in server state
> - Avoid: Yield between check and write -> Mark first; plan-then-apply; busy flags
> - Every remote handler starts with rate limit and `Guard.args`.
> - Every numeric argument is checked for NaN, infinity, range and integrality.
> - Every Instance argument is checked for type, location, ownership and distance.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~160 tok · whole note ~5.1k tok. Read more: ## A reusable validation module · ## Pattern: KitGuard-style ability validation · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

**Server authority** means the server holds the true game state and decides every outcome that matters; clients render, predict and request. **Validation** is how the server turns untrusted requests into safe decisions. Together they are the only real security a Roblox game has: client-side checks can always be removed by an exploiter (Roblox docs, "Security and cheat mitigation tactics").

This note gives the layered validation model, a reusable validation module, the race conditions that cause most duplication bugs, a production-style ability validator ("KitGuard" pattern), data-driven hit validation, idempotent purchases and claims, and where the new server authority engine model fits. Exploit-specific defences are in Exploits and Anti-Cheat; rate limiting in [[Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention]].

## What the server must own

| State | Owner | Client gets |
|---|---|---|
| Currency, inventory, unlocks, progression | Server (saved profile) | Mirrors for UI (attributes or remotes) |
| Cooldowns that gate power | Server | Copies for UI sweeps, which may be wrong |
| Health, damage, kills, rewards | Server | Replicated results |
| Prices, odds, drop tables | Server | Display copies; the server never reads them back |
| Match state, timers, round results | Server | Attributes with server timestamps |
| Character position | **Client** (owner) in the classic model | Cannot be owned by the server without the server authority model; validate it instead |

The last row is the gap. Everything else can be fully server-owned with ordinary code.

## The validation layers

Validate in this order and return early, silently, on any failure. The Roblox docs describe the same layers (type and structure, value, context and permission) plus rate limiting.

| Layer | Question | Examples of failures |
|---|---|---|
| 0. Rate | Is this player sending too often? | 300 casts per second |
| 1. Type | Is each argument the expected type? | Table instead of string; table shaped like an Instance |
| 2. Structure and size | Is it within size limits? | 100,000 character string; deep nested table |
| 3. Value | Is the number finite, integral, in range? Is the id known? | `NaN`, `inf`, `-5` quantity, unknown item id |
| 4. Permission | May this player do this at all? | Using a weapon they do not own; admin action by a non-admin |
| 5. Context | Is it possible right now? | Dead, stunned, out of range, on cooldown, shop closed |
| 6. Plausibility | Could a legitimate player have produced this? | Hit 80 studs away; three hits in 0.1 s |

### NaN and infinity

`NaN` is of type `"number"` and fails every comparison: `NaN < 0` is false and `NaN > max` is false, so a range check lets it through, and it then poisons every value it touches (Roblox docs show a trade exploit built on exactly this). `math.huge` passes type checks too. The docs recommend `math.isfinite()`; the portable check is:

```lua
local function isFinite(x: number): boolean
	return x == x and x ~= math.huge and x ~= -math.huge
end
```

Vectors and CFrames can contain NaN components too; check `v.X == v.X` (or the magnitude) before using them.

## A reusable validation module

Write validators once and use them declaratively at the top of each handler. A tiny combinator module covers most needs without a dependency (the community library `t` does the same with more features).

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Shared/Guard.luau
local Guard = {}

export type Check = (value: unknown) -> boolean

local function finite(x: number): boolean
	return x == x and x ~= math.huge and x ~= -math.huge
end

function Guard.string(maxLen: number): Check
	return function(v)
		return typeof(v) == "string" and #v <= maxLen
	end
end

function Guard.int(min: number, max: number): Check
	return function(v)
		if typeof(v) ~= "number" then return false end
		local n = v :: number
		return finite(n) and n % 1 == 0 and n >= min and n <= max
	end
end

function Guard.number(min: number, max: number): Check
	return function(v)
		if typeof(v) ~= "number" then return false end
		local n = v :: number
		return finite(n) and n >= min and n <= max
	end
end

function Guard.unitVector(): Check
	return function(v)
		if typeof(v) ~= "Vector3" then return false end
		local m = (v :: Vector3).Magnitude
		return m == m and m > 0.95 and m < 1.05
	end
end

function Guard.position(maxAbs: number): Check
	return function(v)
		if typeof(v) ~= "Vector3" then return false end
		local p = v :: Vector3
		return finite(p.X) and finite(p.Y) and finite(p.Z)
			and math.abs(p.X) <= maxAbs and math.abs(p.Y) <= maxAbs and math.abs(p.Z) <= maxAbs
	end
end

function Guard.oneOf(set: { [string]: any }): Check
	return function(v)
		return typeof(v) == "string" and set[v :: string] ~= nil
	end
end

-- An Instance that really is inside `root` and of class `className`.
function Guard.instanceIn(root: Instance, className: string): Check
	return function(v)
		return typeof(v) == "Instance" and (v :: Instance):IsA(className) and (v :: Instance):IsDescendantOf(root)
	end
end

-- Validate a full argument list: Guard.args({checkA, checkB}, ...)
function Guard.args(checks: { Check }, ...: unknown): boolean
	if select("#", ...) > #checks then return false end -- extra arguments: reject
	for i, check in checks do
		if not check((select(i, ...))) then return false end
	end
	return true
end

return Guard
```

Usage at the top of a handler:

```lua
local SLOT = Guard.int(1, 6)
local AIM = Guard.unitVector()

castRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, slot, aim)
	if not Guard.args({ SLOT, AIM }, slot, aim) then return end
	-- slot and aim are now safe to use
end)
```

Rejecting extra arguments is cheap insurance: legitimate clients never send them, and probing tools often do.

### Instances as arguments

An Instance argument is a pointer into the world the client chose. Check, in order: that it is an Instance (not a lookalike table), its class, that it lives where you expect (`IsDescendantOf` a known folder), that this player may act on it (their plot, their pet, a public chest), and the distance to it. The Roblox docs show a shop exploit where a fake table imitates a `Folder` with a `Price` child of value 0; the `typeof(item) == "Instance"` and `IsDescendantOf(itemDataFolder)` checks stop it. Prefer sending an id string and looking the object up on the server.

## Races: why validated code still duplicates items

Remote handlers run concurrently. If a handler yields between checking and writing, a second request from the same player can pass the same check:

```lua
-- VULNERABLE: two fast requests both see "not claimed" while the first is saving.
if not profile.claimed[questId] then
	saveAsync(player)                -- yields
	profile.claimed[questId] = true
	grantReward(player, questId)
end
```

Production rules that close this class of bug:

1. **Mark before you pay, and before you yield.** Set the claimed flag (or deduct the price) first, then do slow work. One production game's hub activities (a lucky spin, a daily chest, fishing) all marked the claim before paying.
2. **Plan, then apply with no yield.** Compute the full outcome into a plan table (which items to remove, which to add, the new balance), validate the plan, then apply it in one synchronous block. A crafting system in the same game used exactly this: "plan-then-apply with no yield", so no other request could observe a half-applied state.
3. **Per-player busy flags** for multi-step flows that must yield (trading, DataStore-backed purchases).
4. **Idempotency tokens** for anything the client might retry: the client generates a token per action; the server remembers recent tokens and returns the previous result for a repeat instead of doing the work twice. The crafting system above used token receipts so a retried "fuse" never fused twice.
5. **Exclusive locks across systems**: items in an active trade are untouchable by salvage, sell or fuse (the same game had a `TradeBusy` state that every consuming system respected).

```lua
--!strict
-- Idempotent action helper: same token, same result, work done once.
local Idempotency = {}

type Entry = { result: { any }, expires: number }
local seen: { [Player]: { [string]: Entry } } = {}
local TTL = 120 -- seconds a token is remembered

function Idempotency.run(player: Player, token: unknown, work: () -> ...any): ...any
	if typeof(token) ~= "string" or #token < 8 or #token > 64 then
		return nil
	end
	local now = os.clock()
	local mine = seen[player]
	if not mine then
		mine = {}
		seen[player] = mine
	end
	local prior = mine[token :: string]
	if prior and prior.expires > now then
		return table.unpack(prior.result) -- replay: do not repeat the work
	end
	-- Record a placeholder BEFORE doing work so a concurrent duplicate cannot start it again.
	local entry: Entry = { result = {}, expires = now + TTL }
	mine[token :: string] = entry
	entry.result = table.pack(work())
	return table.unpack(entry.result)
end

function Idempotency.forget(player: Player)
	seen[player] = nil
end

return Idempotency
```

(A concurrent duplicate that arrives while `work()` is still running gets an empty result; for flows that yield, combine this with a busy flag.)

## Pattern: KitGuard-style ability validation

In one production combat game every weapon "kit" (a set of abilities) had a server script, and every cast passed through a shared server validator. Its responsibilities, generalised:

| Check | Detail from production |
|---|---|
| The move exists on the weapon the player **currently holds** | Held weapon read from server state (the Tool is named consistently and carries a server-set id attribute), never from client arguments |
| The move is allowed for this item | Ultimates were refused below a rarity threshold, in the server validator as well as the client UI |
| Cooldown | Enforced at **0.95x** the authored cooldown, so normal latency jitter never rejects an honest cast while spam is still blocked |
| Character state | Alive, not stunned, not already casting |
| Cast in flight | The validator exposed "the current cast" so downstream damage code could attribute and scale hits to the move being cast |
| Damage clamps | Ability damage multipliers were clamped to a maximum before any per-move adjustments |

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Systems/AbilityGuard.luau
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local Catalog = require(script.Parent.AbilityCatalog) -- server truth: weapons -> moves -> cooldowns
local Loadout = require(script.Parent.Loadout)         -- server truth: what each player holds

local COOLDOWN_TOLERANCE = 0.95 -- accept casts slightly early to absorb latency jitter

export type Cast = { player: Player, weaponId: string, moveId: string, startedAt: number }

local AbilityGuard = {}
local lastCast: { [Player]: { [string]: number } } = {}
local current: { [Player]: Cast } = {}

function AbilityGuard.tryCast(player: Player, moveId: unknown): Cast?
	if typeof(moveId) ~= "string" or #moveId > 40 then return nil end

	local weaponId = Loadout.heldWeapon(player)
	if not weaponId then return nil end
	local move = Catalog.move(weaponId, moveId :: string)
	if not move then return nil end -- not a move of the held weapon
	if move.isUltimate and not Catalog.allowsUltimate(weaponId) then return nil end

	local character = player.Character
	local humanoid = character and character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if not humanoid or humanoid.Health <= 0 then return nil end
	if character and character:GetAttribute("Stunned") then return nil end
	if current[player] then return nil end -- one cast at a time

	local now = Workspace:GetServerTimeNow()
	local times = lastCast[player]
	if not times then
		times = {}
		lastCast[player] = times
	end
	local key = weaponId .. "/" .. (moveId :: string)
	local last = times[key]
	if last and now - last < move.cooldown * COOLDOWN_TOLERANCE then return nil end

	times[key] = now -- commit the cooldown BEFORE any yielding work
	local cast: Cast = { player = player, weaponId = weaponId, moveId = moveId :: string, startedAt = now }
	current[player] = cast
	return cast
end

function AbilityGuard.finish(cast: Cast)
	if current[cast.player] == cast then
		current[cast.player] = nil
	end
end

function AbilityGuard.current(player: Player): Cast?
	return current[player]
end

function AbilityGuard.clear(player: Player)
	lastCast[player] = nil
	current[player] = nil
end

return AbilityGuard
```

The same game had a gap worth learning from: cooldown scaling existed in several places (the client bar, the server validator, a universal abilities module, the move list UI). When a cooldown upgrade was added, every one of them had to multiply by it. Keep the **effective** cooldown in one server function and have UI ask for it.

## Data-driven hit validation

The server must decide hits without trusting the client's "I hit X". Two approaches:

**Server computes the hit.** The client sends "cast move M aimed at direction D". The server knows when M's hits land (from data: marker times exported at build time, or a table of hit frames), and at each hit time it runs its own query (a shape cast or distance and angle check) from the character's server position. One production game computed ability hits per segment on the server from shared timing data, so caster animation and server damage stayed in step without any client hit messages. See Markers and Events and Hitboxes and Hit Detection.

**Client proposes, server verifies.** The client sends "I hit enemy E at time T". The server checks: E exists and is alive; the attacker had a swing in progress whose hit window contains T (with latency tolerance); distance from the attacker's server position to E is within reach plus tolerance; the angle is within the swing arc; the rate is plausible (swing pacing). The same game's swing pacing kept a per-player "bank" on the server that never refused honest clicks but capped sustained hits at the weapon's pace.

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: verify a client-proposed melee hit.
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local REACH = 17        -- studs, includes latency margin (production value for 1.6x scaled characters)
local ARC_DOT = 0.2     -- cos of the half-angle of the accepted arc (about 78 degrees)
local LATE_GRACE = 0.25 -- seconds a hit may arrive after its window closed

type Swing = { startedAt: number, windowStart: number, windowEnd: number, hitTargets: { [Model]: boolean } }

local function verifyHit(player: Player, swing: Swing?, target: unknown): boolean
	if not swing then return false end
	if typeof(target) ~= "Instance" or not (target :: Instance):IsA("Model") then return false end
	local enemy = target :: Model
	if not enemy:IsDescendantOf(Workspace.Enemies) then return false end
	if swing.hitTargets[enemy] then return false end -- one hit per target per swing

	local now = Workspace:GetServerTimeNow()
	local t = now - swing.startedAt
	if t < swing.windowStart or t > swing.windowEnd + LATE_GRACE then return false end

	local character = player.Character
	local root = character and character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart") :: BasePart?
	local enemyRoot = enemy.PrimaryPart
	if not root or not enemyRoot then return false end

	local offset = enemyRoot.Position - root.Position
	local dist = offset.Magnitude
	if dist > REACH then return false end
	if dist > 2 then
		local facing = root.CFrame.LookVector
		if facing:Dot(offset.Unit) < ARC_DOT then return false end
	end

	swing.hitTargets[enemy] = true
	return true
end

return verifyHit
```

Tolerance numbers are game-specific; measure them. In that game the player reach was raised from 13 to 17 studs and the ability range multiplier set to 1.35 after measuring how often honest hits were rejected under real latency.

## Purchases and grants

- **Developer products are granted only in `MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt`.** The docs are explicit that `PromptProductPurchaseFinished` does not mean a purchase happened and must not be used to grant. A client remote "I bought product X" is a free-items exploit.
- **Game pass ownership** is checked on the server with `MarketplaceService:UserOwnsGamePassAsync`, cached per session, and refreshed after a purchase prompt closes.
- Receipts are idempotent: store processed `PurchaseId`s with the profile so a re-delivered receipt does not grant twice. See Developer Products and ProcessReceipt and [[Purchase Data and Receipts]].

## Admin and privileged actions

- An allowlist of UserIds (or group ranks) lives in **one** server module. Every privileged handler checks it on every call; the client UI's own check is decoration.
- Privileged UI code lives in ServerStorage and is cloned to the admin's PlayerGui, so other clients never receive it.
- Admin actions that touch other players (kick, give, teleport) log who did what to whom.

## The server authority model (engine feature)

Roblox now offers an engine-level server authority model (`Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server`): the server is the source of truth for the whole simulation, including characters; clients send inputs through the Input Action System and **predict** ahead, rolling back and resimulating on misprediction. Setup requires `NextGenerationReplication`, the input action system for player scripts, deferred signals, fixed simulation and streaming; core logic runs in `RunService:BindToSimulation()` callbacks on both sides; attributes on predicted instances are compared and mismatches trigger rollback (Roblox docs, "Server authority model"). The security docs call it "currently in beta" and the most reliable fix for movement and physics exploits (as of October 2026).

It changes the trade-offs in this note: movement validation largely disappears, but you must write simulation code that is deterministic enough to resimulate, put inputs through input actions instead of `UserInputService` in simulation code, and keep presentation in `RenderStepped`. Remote validation, economy rules and purchase handling stay exactly the same.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Validating only type, not value | Add finiteness, range, integrality, length |
| Trusting Tool attributes or names from the client's copy | Look up by id in server state |
| Yield between check and write | Mark first; plan-then-apply; busy flags |
| Cooldown multipliers scattered in many files | One server function for effective cooldown |
| Client tells server "I killed it, pay me" | Server witnesses the kill |
| Granting from `PromptProductPurchaseFinished` | `ProcessReceipt` only |
| Loud errors on bad input | Silent drop plus a log line; errors teach the exploiter |

## Checklist

- [ ] Every remote handler starts with rate limit and `Guard.args`.
- [ ] Every numeric argument is checked for NaN, infinity, range and integrality.
- [ ] Every Instance argument is checked for type, location, ownership and distance.
- [ ] No yield between a check and the state change it guards.
- [ ] Retried actions are idempotent.
- [ ] Damage and rewards are computed from server data only.
- [ ] Privileged actions check one allowlist on the server.
