# Data Schema Design and Migrations

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Sharing one `DEFAULT` table between players (Every new player edits the same table; data bleeds between players)
> - Avoid: Array holes or mixed keys (Fields silently dropped or turned into strings)
> - Avoid: Saving `Vector3`/`CFrame` directly (Write fails with 104 every time)
> - `Schema` integer on every profile, `CURRENT_SCHEMA` in code.
> - Ordered, deterministic, non-yielding steps; never edited after release.
> - Newer schema refused on load.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~160 tok · whole note ~4.4k tok. Read more: ## What a data store can hold · ## Versioning: the `Schema` field · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Saved data outlives the code that wrote it. A profile written in week one is still loaded by the release you ship in month six, and during every rollout old and new servers run side by side. This note covers how to shape a profile so it survives that, how JSON serialization actually treats Luau values (the edge cases that silently corrupt data), how to build a migration framework that is safe under rolling updates, and what one production game learned doing roughly a dozen migrations and three account resets.

Prerequisites: [[DataStore Fundamentals]], [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]].

## What a data store can hold

Values are serialized to JSON. Roblox docs (`HttpService:JSONEncode`, which follows the same rules) and the data store limits page give the boundaries:

| Luau value | Saved as | Gotcha |
|---|---|---|
| number | JSON number | `inf` and `nan` are accepted but are not valid JSON; Open Cloud returns them as tagged objects like `{"t":"numeric","v":"inf"}` |
| string | JSON string | Must be valid UTF-8 or the write fails |
| boolean | boolean | |
| array table (1..n, no holes) | JSON array | A hole (`nil` in the middle) breaks it: the table may be saved as an object with string keys, or truncated |
| dictionary with string keys | JSON object | |
| table with **both** array part and string keys | Array wins, string keys are dropped | Silent data loss |
| dictionary with **number** keys that are not 1..n | Saved with the keys turned into strings | `t[5]` comes back as `t["5"]` |
| empty table `{}` | `[]` | Indistinguishable from an empty array; harmless if your code treats both as empty |
| Instance, function, thread, userdata | Not allowed | Error 103/104 |
| Vector3, CFrame, Color3, EnumItem, UDim2 | Not allowed | Convert at the boundary |
| `buffer` | Encoded to base64 by `JSONEncode` (up to 50 MiB) | Prefer explicit encoding so you control the format |

The production lesson from one game, recorded in its own rules: "Sparse Lua tables save with string keys: keep saved lists dense." A `Quests.Track.Claimed` list that had `nil` holes came back with string keys and broke `ipairs` loops on the next load. If you need sparse data, store it deliberately as a map with string keys (`Claimed["17"] = true`).

### Serializing engine types

Convert at the edge, store the smallest faithful form, and version the encoding:

```lua
--!strict
local Codec = {}

function Codec.v3(v: Vector3): { number }
	return { v.X, v.Y, v.Z }
end
function Codec.toV3(t: any): Vector3?
	if type(t) ~= "table" then return nil end
	local x, y, z = tonumber(t[1]), tonumber(t[2]), tonumber(t[3])
	return if x and y and z then Vector3.new(x, y, z) else nil
end

-- 12 numbers is exact; position + YXZ angles (6 numbers) is smaller but lossy near gimbal poles
function Codec.cf(c: CFrame): { number }
	return { c:GetComponents() }
end
function Codec.toCf(t: any): CFrame?
	if type(t) ~= "table" or #t ~= 12 then return nil end
	for i = 1, 12 do
		if type(t[i]) ~= "number" then return nil end
	end
	return CFrame.new(table.unpack(t))
end

function Codec.color(c: Color3): string
	return c:ToHex() -- "ff8800"
end
function Codec.toColor(s: any): Color3?
	if type(s) ~= "string" then return nil end
	local ok, c = pcall(Color3.fromHex, s)
	return if ok then c else nil
end

-- Enums: save the NAME, not .Value (names are stable and readable; values can be reused)
function Codec.enum(e: EnumItem): string
	return e.Name
end

return Codec
```

Never store asset references as full URLs if an id will do; never store display names (they change); never store anything you can recompute from other saved fields (derived totals drift out of sync).

## Shape of a good profile

```lua
--!strict
export type Item = { Uid: string, Id: string, Level: number, Stars: number?, Locked: boolean? }
export type ProfileData = {
	Schema: number,          -- the migration version of THIS table
	Coins: number,
	Gems: number,
	Items: { Item },         -- dense array; every entry has a stable Uid
	Equipped: { [string]: string }, -- slot -> Uid
	Unlocks: { [string]: boolean }, -- string keys only
	Settings: { [string]: any },
	Receipts: { string },    -- recent PurchaseIds, capped (see the receipts note)
	Stats: { FirstJoin: number, PlaySeconds: number },
}
```

Principles:

- **One root table per player**, one key ([[DataStore Fundamentals]]). Coupled values (currency and what it bought) live in the same key so one write saves both.
- **Every owned item has a stable unique id** (`HttpService:GenerateGUID(false)` at creation). Equips, trades, locks and receipts reference the `Uid`, never an array index. Indices shift when something is removed.
- **Store facts, not presentation.** Save `Id = "flamesword"`, not its display name, damage or icon. Item definitions live in code or config; when you rebalance, every saved item picks up the new values for free.
- **Bound everything that grows.** Inventories get a hard cap, histories keep the newest N, receipts keep the newest 100 (the reference project's number). Measure: `#HttpService:JSONEncode(data)` on your heaviest real profile, and alert above a budget (rule of thumb: keep player profiles under 100 KB; most are 2 to 30 KB). Remember the 4 MB/min per-key write throughput: a 1 MB profile can only be saved 4 times a minute.
- **Settings are small and separate in meaning, not necessarily in key.** The reference project kept settings in their own store so a progress reset did not wipe keybinds and graphics choices. That is a good reason to split.

## Versioning: the `Schema` field

Every profile carries an integer `Schema`. Code knows `CURRENT_SCHEMA`. On load, a chain of migration functions upgrades old data one step at a time.

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Data/Schema (ModuleScript)
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local CURRENT_SCHEMA = 4

local Schema = {}
Schema.Current = CURRENT_SCHEMA

local function default(): { [string]: any }
	return {
		Schema = CURRENT_SCHEMA,
		Coins = 0,
		Gems = 0,
		Items = {},
		Equipped = {},
		Unlocks = {},
		Settings = { Music = true, Sfx = true },
		Receipts = {},
		Stats = { FirstJoin = os.time(), PlaySeconds = 0 },
	}
end

function Schema.newProfile(): { [string]: any }
	return default() -- a fresh table every call: never share one template table between players
end

-- Each step takes data at version N and returns data at version N + 1.
-- Steps must be deterministic, must not yield, and must tolerate missing fields.
local STEPS: { [number]: (any) -> any } = {
	[1] = function(d)
		-- v1 stored "Gold"; v2 renames it to Coins
		d.Coins = (tonumber(d.Coins) or 0) + (tonumber(d.Gold) or 0)
		d.Gold = nil
		return d
	end,
	[2] = function(d)
		-- v2 items were bare ids { "sword", "axe" }; v3 items are records with Uids
		local out = {}
		for _, entry in ipairs(if type(d.Items) == "table" then d.Items else {}) do
			if type(entry) == "string" then
				table.insert(out, { Uid = HttpService:GenerateGUID(false), Id = entry, Level = 1 })
			elseif type(entry) == "table" and type(entry.Id) == "string" then
				entry.Uid = entry.Uid or HttpService:GenerateGUID(false)
				table.insert(out, entry)
			end
		end
		d.Items = out
		d.Equipped = {} -- old index-based equips cannot be mapped safely; re-equip on join
		return d
	end,
	[3] = function(d)
		d.Receipts = if type(d.Receipts) == "table" then d.Receipts else {}
		d.Stats = if type(d.Stats) == "table" then d.Stats else { FirstJoin = os.time(), PlaySeconds = 0 }
		return d
	end,
}

-- Fill fields added WITHOUT a schema bump (purely additive defaults). Never overwrites.
local function reconcile(data: { [string]: any }, template: { [string]: any })
	for k, v in template do
		if data[k] == nil then
			data[k] = if type(v) == "table" then table.clone(v) else v
		elseif type(v) == "table" and type(data[k]) == "table" and next(v) ~= nil and #v == 0 then
			reconcile(data[k], v) -- recurse into non-empty dictionaries only
		end
	end
end

function Schema.migrate(data: any): { [string]: any }
	if type(data) ~= "table" then
		error("profile is not a table")
	end
	local version = tonumber(data.Schema) or 1
	if version > CURRENT_SCHEMA then
		-- Written by a NEWER release (rolling update, or a rollback). Refuse: loading would
		-- drop fields this code does not know, and the next save would destroy them.
		error(`profile schema {version} is newer than this server ({CURRENT_SCHEMA})`)
	end
	while version < CURRENT_SCHEMA do
		local step = STEPS[version]
		if not step then
			error(`missing migration step from schema {version}`)
		end
		data = step(data)
		version += 1
		data.Schema = version
	end
	reconcile(data, default())
	return data
end

return Schema
```

Why each piece matters:

- **Steps, not a big "fix everything" function.** A player who last played at v1 runs steps 1, 2, 3 in order. Each step only has to understand one transition. Never edit a shipped step; add a new one.
- **Refusing newer data** is the guard for rolling updates. When you publish, Roblox does not swap every server instantly: old servers keep running until they empty or you migrate them. A player can hop from a new server (writes v4) to an old one (knows v3). Without the guard the old server loads v4 data, ignores fields it does not know, and its next save deletes them. With the guard, the old server fails the load and the player rejoins onto a new server. (Pair it with "Migrate To Latest Update" so old servers drain quickly; see Release Process and Rollbacks.)
- **`reconcile` for additive fields.** Adding `Settings.Haptics = true` does not need a step; reconcile fills it on load. Anything that renames, moves, splits, converts or deletes needs a step.
- **Run migration inside the load path, before gameplay sees the data**, and let the first save write the upgraded record. Do not write a migration back immediately on join "to be safe"; the normal save does it, and an extra write is one more chance to fail.

## Idempotent migrations (production lessons)

The reference project migrated live data many times without a reset. The patterns that worked:

- **Idempotent conversions.** When the forge material system replaced two older shard systems, the migration folded both old id sets into the new materials, summing counts. It was written so "running it again changes nothing": an old id only exists until it is converted, and the conversion deletes it. That made it safe to call on every load without a version gate, which is useful when a migration is shipped as a hotfix.
- **Version flags for one-time changes.** Re-numbering the zone ladder (old zone 7 became 10, old 8 became 11, old 14 became 20) used a dedicated `LadderV = 1` flag on the profile so the mapping could never run twice. Mapping split zones to the later half meant "nothing is lost".
- **Paying out instead of deleting.** When quests v1 were replaced, finished-but-unclaimed v1 quests were paid out during migration rather than dropped. Removed items were sold for their value on load, and when developer-only weapons were stripped from normal players the profile got an audit record `DevWeaponStrip = { t = time, ids = {...}, paid = n }`. Leave a trail in the save when a migration takes something away; support will need it.
- **Persisting paid state that lived only in memory.** A paid "Lucky Charm" boost lived only in player attributes, so rolls left were lost on leave. The fix added it to the profile on every save. Audit: anything the player paid for must be in the profile.
- **Rebuilding derived state on load** instead of saving it (UI mirrors such as `QuestsJson` attributes are republished from the profile each join).

## Resets and "new store" versioning

Sometimes you really do want everyone to start over (a wipe for a relaunch, or a beta reset). The safe way, used three times by the reference project: **change the store names** (`Game_v5` to `Game_v6`, `LB_Totals_v5` to `LB_Totals_v6`). The old data stays untouched, and "revert = rename back". They deliberately did **not** rename the receipts store, the gift-intent store or the settings store, so purchase idempotency and preferences survived the reset. Three rules:

1. Never reset by writing defaults over existing keys. You lose the 30-day version history safety net and cannot undo.
2. Keep purchase records across resets, or a retried receipt can be granted twice (see [[Purchase Data and Receipts]]). Decide what paid items mean after a wipe and communicate it; wiping paid progress without compensation is a trust and policy problem (Ethical Design and Player Trust).
3. Old stores still count toward storage until deleted, and still hold personal data (they need right-to-erasure coverage; Player Privacy and Data Deletion).

Also note the anti-pattern the same project had to guard against: an admin-only "reset my progress every join" convenience. It was written to reset **only after a successful read**, so "a DataStore outage can never turn into a blank overwrite". Any code that writes defaults must be behind that check.

## Bulk migrations with Open Cloud

Lazy migration (on load) never touches players who do not come back, which is usually fine. Do a bulk migration when you must change data for everyone at once (a currency revaluation, or a leaderboard that reads profiles directly). Use the Open Cloud data store APIs from an external script (Open Cloud APIs):

- List keys with the prefix, read each entry, transform, write back. Open Cloud has no `UpdateAsync`-style transform, so a game server can write between your read and your write: check the endpoint reference for a conditional-update option (unverified here) and otherwise only touch keys with no live lease.
- Rate-limit it: Open Cloud shares the experience-wide budget with live servers.
- Respect session leases: skip keys whose lease is live, or the live server's next save will overwrite your change (or, with fencing, your change will make that server's session `lost`).
- Take a snapshot first.

Roblox's open-source Data Stores Batch Processor is meant for exactly these large jobs.

## Testing migrations

Migrations are pure functions; test them without Studio data:

```lua
--!strict
-- Run in the command bar or a TestEZ spec (see the testing notes)
local Schema = require(game.ServerScriptService.Data.Schema)

local v1 = { Gold = 50, Items = { "sword", "axe" } }
local out = Schema.migrate(table.clone(v1))
assert(out.Schema == Schema.Current, "schema not current")
assert(out.Coins == 50 and out.Gold == nil, "gold not renamed")
assert(#out.Items == 2 and type(out.Items[1].Uid) == "string", "items not converted")

-- idempotence on current data
local again = Schema.migrate(out)
assert(#again.Items == 2, "second migrate changed items")

-- newer data must be refused
assert(not pcall(Schema.migrate, { Schema = Schema.Current + 1 }), "newer schema was accepted")
print("migrations ok")
```

Keep a folder of anonymised real profiles from each schema era (exported through Open Cloud or the Data Stores Manager) and run every one through `migrate` in CI (Testing Strategies and Frameworks). The interesting bugs live in data shapes nobody remembers writing.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Sharing one `DEFAULT` table between players | Every new player edits the same table; data bleeds between players |
| Array holes or mixed keys | Fields silently dropped or turned into strings |
| Saving `Vector3`/`CFrame` directly | Write fails with 104 every time |
| Editing a shipped migration step | Players who already ran it and players who did not end up with different data |
| Deleting a field "because nothing uses it" without a step | During the rollout an old server re-saves it, or a new server deletes it while old code still needs it |
| No refusal of newer schemas | Rolling updates and rollbacks destroy new fields |
| Resetting by overwriting keys | No undo; purchase history lost |
| Equips by array index | Removing one item re-points equips to the wrong item |

## Checklist

- [ ] `Schema` integer on every profile, `CURRENT_SCHEMA` in code.
- [ ] Ordered, deterministic, non-yielding steps; never edited after release.
- [ ] Newer schema refused on load.
- [ ] Additive defaults through reconcile; structural changes through steps.
- [ ] Engine types converted at the boundary; arrays dense; enums by name.
- [ ] Every item has a stable `Uid`.
- [ ] Profile size measured and bounded.
- [ ] Migrations unit-tested on real historical shapes.
- [ ] Snapshot before shipping a migration.

# DataStore Fundamentals

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Key name over 50 characters, or a value over 4 MB serialized -> Short keys like `Player_{UserId}`; measure...
> - Avoid: `GetAsync` then `SetAsync` for player data -> `UpdateAsync` plus session locking
> - Avoid: Treating a `nil` load result after an error as "new player" -> Distinguish "no data" from "call failed" (Data Loss Prevention and...
> - Transform handles `nil` (new key), never yields, may run more than once, returns `nil` to cancel; keys at most 50 characters.
> - Every data store call is in `pcall`, with transient-error retry and backoff.
> - Player data is written only through one module, with `UpdateAsync` and a session lock.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~200 tok · whole note ~5.6k tok. Read more: ## UpdateAsync, precisely · ## Limits (Roblox docs, as of October 2026) · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

`DataStoreService` is the only durable, cross-server storage built into the engine. Everything a player expects to still exist tomorrow (currency, inventory, settings, purchase history) ends up in a data store. This note explains what a data store actually is, the exact limits and budgets it enforces (as of October 2026), how the 4 second read cache works and bites, how versioning gives you free backups, and which API to call for which job. The rest of this folder builds on it: [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]], [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]], [[Data Schema Design and Migrations]].

## The mental model

A data store is a remote key-value table:

- **Data store name** (up to 50 characters) picks the table, for example `PlayerData`.
- **Scope** (up to 50 characters, default `global`) is a legacy prefix glued onto every key. Roblox docs now say: new games should use key **prefixes** instead of scopes.
- **Key** (up to 50 characters) picks the row, for example `User_123456`.
- **Value**: anything that serializes to JSON (numbers, strings, booleans, tables with either array or string keys). Up to **4,194,304 characters per key** after serialization (Roblox docs).

Every call is a web request from the game server to Roblox's storage backend. That has three consequences that shape every design decision in this folder:

1. **Calls yield** (tens to hundreds of milliseconds, sometimes seconds under throttling).
2. **Calls fail.** Network errors, throttling, backend incidents and shutdown all throw. Every call goes in `pcall`.
3. **A failed write may still have happened.** The docs are explicit: an error means the server did not receive a success response, not that the backend did nothing. Design writes to be safe to repeat (see [[Purchase Data and Receipts]]).

Data stores are **per experience (universe)**, not per place. Every place in the universe reads and writes the same stores. Only server `Script`s can call the API; a `LocalScript` call errors.

### Studio access

By default, Studio play sessions cannot touch data stores (error `403 StudioAccessToApisNotAllowed`). Enabling **File > Experience Settings > Security > Enable Studio Access to API Services** makes Studio read and write the **same live data** your players use. Roblox recommends enabling it only on a separate test experience. The reference project did enable it on the live place and paid for that with a set of safety rules (a Studio-only test-profile key, a load-failure simulator, a "never reset the real save" rule); see Data Loss Prevention and Recovery.

Contrast: MemoryStoreService data is isolated between Studio and production automatically (MemoryStore Service). Data stores are not.

## Choosing the API

| Need | Call | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Read a value | `GetAsync(key, options?)` | Cached 4 s (see below). Returns `value, DataStoreKeyInfo` |
| Read-modify-write, or anything another server might also write | `UpdateAsync(key, transform)` | Reads latest, retries your transform on conflict. Costs one read **and** one write |
| Overwrite with a value that does not depend on the old one | `SetAsync(key, value, userIds?, options?)` | Write budget only. Races with other servers |
| Add to an integer | `IncrementAsync(key, delta, userIds?, options?)` | Atomic add; value must be an integer |
| Delete | `RemoveAsync(key)` | Writes a tombstone version; old versions stay reachable until they expire |
| See history | `ListVersionsAsync`, `GetVersionAsync`, `GetVersionAtTimeAsync` | Standard (non-ordered) stores only |
| Enumerate | `DataStoreService:ListDataStoresAsync(prefix?, pageSize?, cursor?)`, `DataStore:ListKeysAsync(prefix?, pageSize?, cursor?, excludeDeleted?)` | Lists only stores that contain at least one object |
| Ranked numbers | `GetOrderedDataStore` + `GetSortedAsync` | Integers only. See OrderedDataStores and Leaderboards |

`GetDataStore(name, scope?, options?)` returns the same object for the same name and scope, so caching the object in a module is fine but not required. `GetGlobalDataStore()` returns the default store (scope `u`); do not use it for new work, a named store is clearer.

`OnUpdate` is deprecated (it polled once a minute). Use MessagingService for change notification (Cross-Server Messaging).

## UpdateAsync, precisely

`UpdateAsync` is the workhorse. Its exact contract (Roblox docs):

- The transform receives `(currentValue, keyInfo)`. `keyInfo` is `nil` for a key that does not exist yet.
- It returns up to three values: `newValue, userIds, metadata`.
- **If you return only a value, existing user ids and metadata are cleared.** If you use either, pass them through: `return newValue, keyInfo:GetUserIds(), keyInfo:GetMetadata()`.
- If another server wrote the key between the read and the write, the engine **calls your transform again** with the newer value and discards the previous result. It repeats until the write lands or you return `nil`.
- Returning `nil` cancels the write. The call still succeeds and returns.
- **The transform cannot yield.** No `task.wait`, no other `*Async` calls, no `RemoteFunction` invokes.

Two consequences people miss:

1. **Side effects inside the transform can run several times.** Do not grant items, fire remotes, increment counters in outer scope, or log "saved" inside it. Set plain flags (`claimed = true`) and reset them at the top of the transform, because the last invocation is the one that counts. The reference project's lease code does exactly that: every flag is reset on entry.
2. **Your transform must be a pure function of its input** plus captured constants. If it captures a live in-memory profile table and mutates it, a retried call sees the mutation from the first attempt.

```lua
--!strict
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")

-- Atomically add coins without clobbering anything another server wrote.
local function addCoins(userId: number, amount: number): (boolean, number?)
	local newTotal: number? = nil
	local ok, err = pcall(function()
		store:UpdateAsync(`User_{userId}`, function(old: any, keyInfo: DataStoreKeyInfo?)
			newTotal = nil -- reset: this function may run more than once
			local data = if type(old) == "table" then old else { Coins = 0 }
			data.Coins = (tonumber(data.Coins) or 0) + amount
			newTotal = data.Coins
			if keyInfo then
				-- preserve user ids and metadata, or they are wiped
				return data, keyInfo:GetUserIds(), keyInfo:GetMetadata()
			end
			return data, { userId }
		end)
	end)
	if not ok then
		warn(`addCoins failed for {userId}: {err}`)
		return false, nil
	end
	return true, newTotal
end
```

This is a teaching example. Live player data should not be written like this from arbitrary code while the player is in a session; it goes through the session-locked profile ([[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]]).

## Limits (Roblox docs, as of October 2026)

### Size limits

| Item | Maximum |
|---|---|
| Data store name | 50 characters |
| Scope | 50 characters |
| Key name | 50 characters |
| Value | 4,194,304 characters per key (serialized) |
| Metadata key name | 50 characters |
| Metadata value | 250 characters |
| Metadata total | 300 characters |

Strings must be valid UTF-8. A single byte above 127 that is not part of a valid multi-byte sequence makes the write fail. This bites people who store raw `buffer` or `string.pack` output as a string: base64 it first, or use `buffer` through `HttpService:JSONEncode`-safe encoding (see Buffers and Binary Data).

### Per-key throughput

Each key, across all servers and Open Cloud, is measured over a rolling 60 seconds:

| Kind | Calls | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Read | `GetAsync`, `GetVersionAsync`, `GetVersionAtTimeAsync`, `ListVersionsAsync`, `UpdateAsync` | 25 MB per minute |
| Write | `SetAsync`, `IncrementAsync`, `UpdateAsync`, `RemoveAsync` | 4 MB per minute |

Each request is rounded **up** to the next KB. Writing an 800-byte value and a 1.2 KB value counts as 3 KB. So a 400 KB profile can be written at most about 10 times per minute before that key throttles. Heavy profiles and frequent saves collide here first.

> Older guides (and some skills) state a "one write per key every 6 seconds" rule. The current limits page does not contain it; the per-key limit is now expressed as throughput. Spacing writes to one key by several seconds is still a good rule of thumb: the reference project never saves a profile more often than every 2 s and normally waits about 8 s since the last save before a "save soon".

### Experience-wide budgets (shared by all servers **and** Open Cloud)

Requests per minute, CCU = concurrent users:

| Type | Standard stores | Ordered stores |
|---|---|---|
| Read | 300 + CCU x 40 | 300 + CCU x 40 |
| Write | 300 + CCU x 20 | 300 + CCU x 20 |
| List | 300 + CCU x 2 | 300 + CCU x 2 |
| Remove | 300 + CCU x 40 | 300 + CCU x 40 |

`UpdateAsync` spends one read and one write. Open Cloud scripts (support tools, migrations, RTBF bots) draw from the same pool, so a careless bulk script can throttle live servers. See Open Cloud APIs.

> Historical (before 2026-07-29): the base was 250 (250 + CCU x 40 get, 250 + CCU x 20 set), and some pages, such as the Extended Services pricing table, may still show it. Since the 2026-07-29 unification the limits page says **300**; use the table above. See Data and Cloud Changes 2025-2026.

### Per-server defaults (configurable)

| Type | Standard | Ordered |
|---|---|---|
| Read | 60 + players x 40 | 60 + players x 40 |
| Write | 60 + players x 40 | 30 + players x 5 |
| List | 5 + players x 2 | 5 + players x 2 |
| Remove | 60 + players x 40 | 30 + players x 5 |

New servers get a one-time startup burst on top (size not documented). `DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType(Enum.DataStoreRequestType.X)` returns the current budget; `SetRateLimitForRequestType(requestType, baseLimit, perPlayerLimit)` can lower these per-server defaults (**Unverified** whether it can raise them above the defaults; call once at startup; `UpdateAsync` and `OnUpdate` cannot be configured). The newer enum members are `StandardRead`, `StandardWrite`, `StandardList`, `StandardRemove`, `OrderedRead`, `OrderedWrite`, `OrderedList`, `OrderedRemove`; the legacy ones (`GetAsync`, `SetIncrementAsync`, `UpdateAsync`, `GetSortedAsync`, `SetIncrementSortedAsync`, `ListAsync`, ...) still exist.

Studio Run mode uses its own static limits, which can be lower. Test rate-limit behaviour in a Team Create session or a live test server, not solo Play.

### Queues and the 30-request cliff

When over budget, requests wait in one of four queues (Set, Ordered set, Get, Ordered get). Each queue holds **30** requests. The calling thread just yields longer while queued. Once a queue is full, new requests fail immediately with errors 301 to 306 (`GetAsyncThrottle`, `SetAsyncThrottle`, `IncreAsyncThrottle`, `UpdateAsyncThrottle`, `GetSortedThrottle`, `RemoveAsyncThrottle`).

What it looks like: saves that normally take 0.2 s take 10 to 30 s, then a burst of `30x` errors in the console, usually right after a server-wide event (everyone saving on the same tick, a leaderboard refresh loop in every server, a migration loop).

### Storage

Per experience: **500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime users** of the latest version of every key, measured **compressed**. Old versions and deleted keys do not count. Roblox compresses for you; do not pre-compress (it wastes CPU and hurts their compression). Going over shows estimated monthly costs in the Data Stores Manager and is billable through Extended Services ($0.12 per GB per month as listed in October 2026). Historical (before 2026-07-29): the free allowance was 100 MB + 1 MB per lifetime player; a page still quoting 100 MB is out of date. See Data and Cloud Changes 2025-2026.

## The 4 second cache

`GetAsync` caches each key **locally on the server for 4 seconds** after a backend read (Roblox docs):

- A `GetAsync` within those 4 seconds returns the cached value without a request. Cache hits do not count against any budget.
- `SetAsync` and `UpdateAsync` on that key **apply to the cache immediately** and restart the timer.
- The cache belongs to the data store object instance. Two objects for the same store but different scope settings (for example one with `AllScopes`) have separate caches and can disagree.
- `GetVersionAsync`, `ListVersionsAsync`, `ListKeysAsync`, `ListDataStoresAsync` never use the cache.
- To bypass it, pass a `DataStoreGetOptions` with `UseCache = false`. Such reads always count against budgets.

```lua
--!strict
local function readFresh(store: DataStore, key: string): (boolean, any)
	local options = Instance.new("DataStoreGetOptions")
	options.UseCache = false
	return pcall(function()
		return store:GetAsync(key, options)
	end)
end
```

The trap, measured in one production game: you save from one script (or one server), then immediately "verify" with a plain `GetAsync` from a tool or another server that read the key a moment earlier, and you see the **old** value for up to about 4 seconds. Developers then conclude "the save failed" and start debugging the wrong thing. The reference project's rule: every verification read uses `UseCache = false`. The cache also explains a second symptom: a server that polls a shared key with `GetAsync` every second really only reaches the backend every 4 seconds.

The cache does not make `GetAsync` safe for read-modify-write. Another server can write the key the instant after your read. Use `UpdateAsync`.

## Versioning: the backups you already have

Standard data stores keep history automatically (Roblox docs):

- `SetAsync`, `UpdateAsync` and `IncrementAsync` create a **versioned backup on the first write to each key in each UTC hour**. Later writes in the same hour overwrite the current version in place. So you get roughly one restore point per key per hour of activity.
- A backup **expires 30 days after a newer write supersedes it**. The latest version never expires.
- `RemoveAsync` writes a tombstone: `GetAsync` returns `nil` afterwards, but earlier versions stay readable through the version APIs until they expire. Removed objects are deleted permanently after 30 days.
- `RemoveVersionAsync` is deprecated.
- `GetVersionAtTimeAsync(key, timestampMs)` returns the version current at that time. Timestamps are milliseconds since the epoch and may not be more than ten minutes in the future.
- Ordered data stores have **no** versioning.

This is the basis of every rollback tool in Data Loss Prevention and Recovery. It also has a sharp edge: if a bug corrupts a profile and the player keeps playing for an hour, the "hourly" backup can itself be corrupt. For that reason Roblox recommends taking an Open Cloud **snapshot** (available once a day per experience) right before publishing any update that changes data logic (Open Cloud APIs).

## Metadata and user ids

Each key in a standard store carries:

- **Service metadata** (read-only through `DataStoreKeyInfo`): `Version`, `CreatedTime`, `UpdatedTime` (ms since epoch).
- **User-defined metadata**: set with `DataStoreSetOptions:SetMetadata({...})` or returned as the third value from an `UpdateAsync` transform. Max 300 characters total.
- **User ids**: an array passed to `SetAsync`/`IncrementAsync` or returned from the transform. Roblox calls them "highly recommended to assist with GDPR tracking/removal". The upper count is reported only as an error (`512 UserIdLimitExceeded`) with no published number.

Rule from the docs: when you write with `SetAsync`, `IncrementAsync` or `UpdateAsync`, always supply the metadata again, even if it did not change, or it is lost. Metadata is a good home for small, query-free facts like a schema version or a lock id (Roblox's own sample stores its session lock there).

## Keys and stores: how to lay them out

Roblox's best-practices page (October 2026) recommends:

- **Few data stores, organised by key.** One `PlayerData` store with `User_{UserId}` keys, not a store per player or per feature per player.
- **One key per player** when it fits under 4 MB: atomic updates across all fields, one read on join, easy rollback. Split into a few deterministic keys only when parts have different access patterns or approach the size/throughput limits, and keep anything that must change together in the same key.
- **Static key patterns** built from stable ids (`User_{UserId}`), never display names. Static patterns are what make automated right-to-be-forgotten deletion possible (Player Privacy and Data Deletion).
- **Prefixes** for grouping, for example `User_123/Profile/Warrior`, then `ListKeysAsync("User_123/Profile")`.

The reference project's layout, as a real example: one profile store (key `P_<userId>`), a skills store keyed `..._S_<userId>`, a receipts store keyed by `PurchaseId`, a gift-intent store keyed by buyer id, a settings store, a support-report store and several ordered stores for boards. Its one regret worth copying: skills lived in a separate key from the currency that bought them, so a crash could persist one without the other. They later moved the skill list into the main profile write ("charge and record in one step"). Keep coupled data in one key.

## Errors you will actually see

| Code | Name | Usual cause |
|---|---|---|
| 101 / 102 | KeyNameEmpty / KeyNameLimit | Empty or over-50-character key (usually a bug building the key) |
| 103 / 104 | ValueNotAllowed / CantStoreValue | Transform returned an Instance, function, mixed table or invalid UTF-8 |
| 105 | ValueTooLarge | Over 4 MB serialized |
| 106 / 107 | Ordered paging errors | Page size outside 1 to 100, non-integer min/max, max < min |
| 301 to 306 | `*Throttle` | Queue full, request dropped |
| 401 / 402 | DataModelNoAccess / LuaWebSrvsNoAccess | Called too late during shutdown |
| 403 | StudioAccessToApisNotAllowed | Studio API access off |
| 502 | RequestRejected | Backend rejected (often transient) |
| 509 | OperationNotAllowed | Writes blocked on a personal RCC |
| 511 / 512 / 513 | Metadata too large / too many user ids / bad metadata type | |

Distinguish **permanent** errors (1xx, 403, 511 to 513: retrying cannot help) from **transient** ones (3xx, 5xx: retry with backoff). The retry helper in [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]] does this.

## What does not belong in a data store

| Data | Better home |
|---|---|
| Matchmaking queues, live auction prices, "who is online" | MemoryStore Service |
| Feature flags, tuning values, event start times | Experience configs (Global State and Live Config) |
| API keys, webhook URLs | Secrets store (HttpService and External APIs) |
| Per-round state, cooldowns, buffs that end with the session | Plain Luau tables on the server |
| Anything the client sent you, unvalidated | Nowhere until validated ([[Server Authority and Validation]]) |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Key name over 50 characters, or a value over 4 MB serialized | The write errors every time for that key | Short keys like `Player_{UserId}`; measure `#HttpService:JSONEncode(data)` |
| `GetAsync` then `SetAsync` for player data | Occasional rollbacks, duplicated items after server hops | `UpdateAsync` plus session locking |
| Treating a `nil` load result after an error as "new player" | A player's whole save replaced by defaults | Distinguish "no data" from "call failed" (Data Loss Prevention and Recovery) |
| Yielding inside the transform | Error "Callbacks cannot yield" or a silently failed save | Compute everything before calling `UpdateAsync` |
| Returning only the value from a transform | User ids and metadata vanish | Pass `keyInfo:GetUserIds()`, `keyInfo:GetMetadata()` through |
| Verifying a save with plain `GetAsync` | "Save failed" false alarms | `UseCache = false` |
| Studio API access enabled on the live game with no guard | Test sessions overwrite real saves | Separate test experience, or a Studio-only test key (Data Loss Prevention and Recovery) |
| Saving every coin pickup | 30x throttle errors at peak | Buffer in memory, autosave ([[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]]) |
| Unbounded arrays (logs, history) in the profile | Profile grows until writes throttle or hit 4 MB | Cap and rotate |
| Sparse arrays | Data saved with string keys or truncated at the first hole | Keep arrays dense, or store maps with string keys deliberately |
| Storing `inf`/`nan` | Open Cloud tools receive tagged objects instead of numbers | Clamp numbers before saving |

## Checklist

- [ ] Transform handles `nil` (new key), never yields, may run more than once, returns `nil` to cancel; keys at most 50 characters.
- [ ] Every data store call is in `pcall`, with transient-error retry and backoff.
- [ ] Player data is written only through one module, with `UpdateAsync` and a session lock.
- [ ] Load failure and "new player" are different code paths.
- [ ] Keys follow `Prefix_{UserId}`; user ids passed on write.
- [ ] Profile size is measured (`#HttpService:JSONEncode(profile)`) and bounded.
- [ ] Verification reads use `UseCache = false`.
- [ ] Studio access is either off on the live game or guarded by a test-key scheme.

# Purchase Data and Receipts

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Returning `PurchaseGranted` before saving (Paid items lost on crash or failed save)
> - Avoid: Granting without checking `PurchaseId` (Double grants on retries and concurrent servers)
> - Avoid: Grant and id saved in different writes or keys (A crash keeps one without the other)
> - Exactly one `ProcessReceipt`, covering every product id.
> - Waits for the profile; refuses when it cannot save.
> - Grant and `PurchaseId` recorded together, synchronously, in the same key.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~160 tok · whole note ~4.2k tok. Read more: ## The handler · ## Two-layer design for gifts (production lesson) · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

A developer product purchase is the one write in your game where a bug costs a player real money or costs you a refund dispute. The rules come from two places: the exact guarantees `MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt` gives (and does not give), and the data store's failure modes. This note covers both, then gives a complete idempotent receipt handler built on a session-locked profile, the extra ledger needed for gifting, and the production lessons from one game that sold boosts, bundles, gifts and one-time packs. The monetization side (pricing, product design) lives in Developer Products and ProcessReceipt and Monetization Overview; this note is about getting the data right.

Prerequisites: [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]], [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]].

## What ProcessReceipt guarantees (Roblox reference, October 2026)

- You set `MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt` **once**, in one server `Script`, and it handles every product.
- It is called for **unresolved** purchases when a purchase completes, when a successful purchase prompt appears, and **when the user joins a server**.
- A purchase is **resolved** only when your callback returns `Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted` **and** Roblox records that on its backend.
- **No time-based retry.** If you return `NotProcessedYet` (or error), the callback runs again only when the user starts another product purchase or rejoins any server of the experience.
- **No timeout.** The callback may yield as long as the server runs; a late result is still accepted.
- The user must be **in the server** for the callback to be invoked. They do not have to still be there when it returns.
- The callback for one purchase **can run on two servers at the same time**, if the user joins a second server before the first returns.
- Even after you return `PurchaseGranted`, recording can fail, and the purchase stays unresolved: **you will see the same `PurchaseId` again** later.
- Multiple pending purchases arrive in a non-deterministic order.
- Unresolved purchases are **not** removed or refunded when escrow expires.
- If you never set a callback, receipts are auto-acknowledged and cannot be recovered.

The `receiptInfo` table: `PurchaseId` (unique per purchase), `PlayerId`, `ProductId`, `PlaceIdWherePurchased`, `CurrencySpent`, `CurrencyType` (always Robux), and `ProductPurchaseChannel` (`InExperience`, `ExperienceDetailsPage`, `AdReward`, `CommerceProduct`).

Two consequences drive everything below:

1. **Grants must be idempotent by `PurchaseId`.** The same purchase can arrive twice (concurrently, or after a lost acknowledgment).
2. **Return `PurchaseGranted` only after the grant is durable.** If you grant in memory, return granted, and then the save fails, the player paid for something that vanishes at the next crash.

## Roblox's definition of "handled"

Roblox's player-data guide defines a handled purchase as: not previously handled, reflected in the current session, and **saved to a data store**. Its required order:

1. Verify the `PurchaseId` is not already recorded as handled.
2. Award the purchase in the in-memory player data.
3. Record the `PurchaseId` in the same in-memory data.
4. Save that data to the data store.
5. Return `PurchaseGranted` if the save succeeded, `NotProcessedYet` if not.

And the subtle case: if the id is recorded **in memory but not yet saved**, do not grant again; just try the save again and answer accordingly. Session locking is what makes this sound: with one owner per profile, the in-memory receipt list is the newest one that exists, so checking it is enough.

## The handler

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Monetization/ReceiptHandler (Script): the ONLY ProcessReceipt in the game
local MarketplaceService = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ServerScriptService = game:GetService("ServerScriptService")

local Profiles = require(ServerScriptService.Data.Profiles)
local ProfileManager = require(ServerScriptService.Data.ProfileManager)

local MAX_RECEIPTS = 100 -- newest PurchaseIds kept in the profile

type Grant = (data: { [string]: any }) -> boolean -- must not yield; returns false if it cannot apply

-- Product id -> grant. Prices and ids live in config; these numbers are placeholders.
local GRANTS: { [number]: Grant } = {
	[0000000001] = function(data)
		data.Gems = (tonumber(data.Gems) or 0) + 500
		return true
	end,
	[0000000002] = function(data)
		-- once-per-player starter pack: refuse a second grant (the shop should never prompt it)
		data.Once = data.Once or {}
		if data.Once.StarterPack then
			return false
		end
		data.Once.StarterPack = true
		data.Coins = (tonumber(data.Coins) or 0) + 10000
		return true
	end,
}

local function hasReceipt(data: { [string]: any }, purchaseId: string): boolean
	local list = data.Receipts
	if type(list) ~= "table" then
		return false
	end
	for _, id in list do
		if id == purchaseId then
			return true
		end
	end
	return false
end

local function recordReceipt(data: { [string]: any }, purchaseId: string)
	local list = if type(data.Receipts) == "table" then data.Receipts else {}
	table.insert(list, purchaseId)
	while #list > MAX_RECEIPTS do
		table.remove(list, 1)
	end
	data.Receipts = list
end

local function saveNow(player: Player): boolean
	local profile = Profiles._get(player)
	if not profile or profile.State ~= "active" then
		return false
	end
	for _ = 1, 3 do
		local result = ProfileManager.save(profile, false)
		if result == "saved" then
			return true
		elseif result == "lost" then
			return false
		end
		task.wait(1 + math.random())
	end
	return false
end

MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt = function(receipt): Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision
	local WAIT = Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet
	local purchaseId = receipt.PurchaseId
	local grant = GRANTS[receipt.ProductId]
	if type(purchaseId) ~= "string" or not grant then
		warn(`[Receipts] unknown product {receipt.ProductId}`)
		return WAIT -- never acknowledge what we cannot deliver
	end
	local player = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(receipt.PlayerId)
	if not player then
		return WAIT
	end
	-- The player may have just joined: wait for their profile (it can also fail or lock).
	local status = Profiles.waitReady(player, 60)
	if status ~= "ready" or not Profiles.canMutate(player) then
		return WAIT
	end

	local applied = false
	local refused = false
	Profiles.mutate(player, function(data)
		if hasReceipt(data, purchaseId) then
			return -- already granted in this profile (saved or not): do not grant again
		end
		-- no yields between the grant and the record: a save snapshot sees both or neither
		if not grant(data) then
			refused = true
			return
		end
		recordReceipt(data, purchaseId)
		applied = true
	end)
	if refused then
		warn(`[Receipts] grant refused for {purchaseId}`)
		return WAIT -- leave it unresolved; support can resolve it (see "refused grants" below)
	end

	-- Granted now or earlier: acknowledge only once the profile with this id is saved.
	if saveNow(player) then
		if applied then
			-- side effects that must happen once: analytics, announcements, spend boards
		end
		return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
	end
	return WAIT
end
```

Why each step is the way it is:

- **`waitReady` first.** A purchase from the Store tab (`ExperienceDetailsPage`) or a pending one arrives the moment the player joins, before their profile loads. Granting into nothing is impossible; answering `NotProcessedYet` immediately means it only comes back on the next purchase or rejoin. Waiting is allowed (no timeout) and is what Roblox's sample does, while also giving up if the player leaves.
- **Refuse if the profile cannot save** (`lost`, failed load, locked). Granting into a session that will never be written takes the money and gives nothing.
- **Grant and record inside one non-yielding mutation.** The save takes a deep-copy snapshot of the profile; because the grant and the receipt id are added in the same synchronous step, every snapshot contains either both or neither.
- **Already recorded but unsaved**: we skip the grant and just save. That matches Roblox's "recorded but not reflected in the data store: return NotProcessedYet until it is".
- **Concurrent servers**: session locking means only one server holds an active profile. The other's `waitReady` fails (`locked`) and it answers `NotProcessedYet`; the purchase is resolved by the owner.
- **Bounded receipt list.** Roblox only re-delivers unresolved purchases; once one is resolved it does not come back, so a recent window suffices. The reference project kept the newest 100 ids per profile.
- **One-off side effects after the durable save**, gated by `applied`: a retried receipt must not re-announce or re-count spend.

## Two-layer design for gifts (production lesson)

Gifting breaks the simple model: the **buyer** triggers the receipt, but the **recipient's** profile gets the grant, and the recipient may leave before it lands. One production game handled this with a second store, a **receipt ledger** keyed by `PurchaseId`, failing closed everywhere ("anything uncertain answers NotProcessedYet, and Roblox retries the receipt later instead of us guessing"):

1. **Claim the purchase id** in the ledger with `UpdateAsync` before any grant. The record stores who it pays (`R = recipientUserId`), the product key and a timestamp. If a record already exists, read it instead: a retry must pay the **same** person.
2. If the record says `Done`, return `PurchaseGranted` immediately.
3. If the recipient is in the server, call the grant hook, which writes grant + purchase id into the **recipient's** profile and answers true only after that save.
4. If the recipient has left: check whether their **saved** profile already contains the purchase id (a fresh read). If yes, mark done and acknowledge. If not, give them a grace period (the buyer sees "your gift is waiting for its player to join your server"), and after it **re-point** the ledger record to the buyer (only if it still points at the recipient and is not done) before granting to the buyer, so a later retry cannot pay both.
5. After the grant is saved, mark the ledger record `Done` (best effort: if that write fails, the retry finds the id in the profile).
6. The gift target chosen in the purchase prompt was also saved in a small **intent store** (buyer id to product to recipient), because the receipt can arrive on a different server than the one where the player chose the recipient.

The general lesson: when a purchase can touch more than one profile, the profile receipt list is not enough, because no single session lock covers both. A ledger keyed by `PurchaseId` and claimed atomically is the coordination point.

Other lessons from the same project:

- **Every paid thing must be in the profile.** A paid boost that lived only in player attributes was lost on leave; it was moved into the profile.
- **Once-per-player products** were recorded in a profile `Once` table, and the shop refused to prompt a second time (asking the profile owner `ownsOnce`, which answered `nil`, "can't tell", while the profile was loading, so the shop refused then too).
- **Products whose grant could not be paid** (a placeholder id of 0, or a grant type the profile code did not support) were never prompted: "it must never take Robux for nothing".
- **Spend tracking** for a Robux leaderboard fired exactly once, when the ledger record flipped to `Done` for the first time.
- Account resets renamed progress stores but **kept the receipts and intent stores**, so idempotency survived the reset ([[Data Schema Design and Migrations]]).

## Refused and stuck grants

What if `grant` cannot apply (inventory full, one-time pack already owned because of a client-side race)? Options:

| Policy | Effect |
|---|---|
| Return `NotProcessedYet` (above) | Robux stays in escrow; the purchase comes back on rejoin. Unresolved purchases are not refunded automatically when escrow ends, so you must resolve it eventually |
| Grant an equivalent (currency of the same value) | Resolves cleanly; communicate it |
| Make the grant always succeed (overflow storage, mailbox) | Best: design products so a valid purchase can always be delivered |

Prevent the race at prompt time: validate on the server before calling `PromptProductPurchase`, and re-validate in the grant.

## Game passes and subscriptions are different

Game passes are owned permanently by the user, not delivered by receipts. Check `MarketplaceService:UserOwnsGamePassAsync(userId, passId)` on join (cache the result; it can fail, so retry and treat failure as "unknown", not "not owned"), and react to `PromptGamePassPurchaseFinished` for in-session purchases. Do **not** store pass ownership as the source of truth in your data store; store only derived state (for example, a one-time bonus already given). The reference project stored bundle passes it granted itself (passes sold as developer products) in a profile `OwnedPasses` table, which is a different thing: those are products. Note its test-key rule as well: Studio test profiles ignore owned passes so a fresh-profile test is really fresh. Subscriptions have their own APIs (Subscriptions and Premium Payouts).

## Refunds

Roblox can send a **Transaction Refunded** webhook (developer products, passes, private servers, paid access; not subscriptions) to an endpoint you configure on the Creator Dashboard (Open Cloud APIs). What you do with it is policy: many games log it and, for abuse patterns, claw back the currency through a support tool, never by silently deleting items mid-session. Any clawback is a profile write and must go through the session-locked path (or Open Cloud when the player is offline and no lease is live).

## Testing

- In Studio, product prompts complete as test purchases; `ProcessReceipt` runs. Use a test profile key ([[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]]).
- Force the failure paths: make `saveNow` return false and confirm the handler answers `NotProcessedYet` and the next trigger (another purchase, rejoin) resolves it without a double grant.
- Simulate a duplicate: call the handler twice with the same fake receipt and assert one grant.
- Simulate "recorded but unsaved": grant, block the save, unblock, call again.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Result |
|---|---|
| Returning `PurchaseGranted` before saving | Paid items lost on crash or failed save |
| Granting without checking `PurchaseId` | Double grants on retries and concurrent servers |
| Grant and id saved in different writes or keys | A crash keeps one without the other |
| Answering `NotProcessedYet` instantly when the profile is still loading | Store-tab purchases stay stuck until the next rejoin |
| Granting into a profile that failed to load | Robux taken, nothing persists |
| Multiple scripts setting `ProcessReceipt` | Only the last assignment is used; products handled elsewhere never grant |
| Side effects (announce, analytics) before the durable save | Repeated on every retry |
| Trusting the client about what was bought | Exploitable; the receipt is the only truth |

## Checklist

- [ ] Exactly one `ProcessReceipt`, covering every product id.
- [ ] Waits for the profile; refuses when it cannot save.
- [ ] Grant and `PurchaseId` recorded together, synchronously, in the same key.
- [ ] `PurchaseGranted` only after a confirmed save.
- [ ] Receipt list bounded; kept across resets.
- [ ] Gifts and cross-profile grants use a ledger claimed with `UpdateAsync`.
- [ ] One-off side effects run once.
- [ ] Unknown or undeliverable products are never prompted.

# Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: No `BindToClose` (Every update or shutdown loses up to one autosave interval for...)
> - Avoid: Saving players one by one in `BindToClose` (Large servers time out; the last players lose data)
> - Avoid: Not waiting for `PlayerRemoving` saves in `BindToClose` (Last player in an emptying server loses progress)
> - Save on: autosave (staggered), leave (with release), shutdown (parallel, with a deadline), purchases.
> - Autosave interval below the lease.
> - No save path exists for a profile that failed to load.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~170 tok · whole note ~4.4k tok. Read more: ## When to write · ## The loader: wiring it all together · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Loading is one call at the start of a session. Saving is where data actually gets lost: on a server crash, during a shutdown with 30 players, in a throttled minute, or because a save ran before the load finished. This note gives the timing rules (with official numbers and the values one production game settled on), a retry helper that knows which errors are worth retrying, and a complete loader script that wires load, autosave, "save soon", leave-saves and `BindToClose` together on top of the module from [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]].

## When to write

Roblox's player-data guide names exactly four moments to touch the store:

1. **Initial read** at the start of the session.
2. **Final write** when the player leaves (and releases the session lock).
3. **Periodic writes** so a crash loses minutes, not the whole session. These also renew the lease.
4. **Writes at critical checkpoints**, above all while processing a purchase ([[Purchase Data and Receipts]]).

Everything else (coin pickups, kills, equips) only changes the in-memory profile.

### Timing values

| Value | Roblox sample | One production game | Rule of thumb |
|---|---|---|---|
| Autosave interval | 180 s (with a random first offset per player, added in the October 2026 guide) | 120 s, one loop for all players | 60 to 180 s, below the lease, staggered |
| Lease | (configurable) | 90 s, renewed by every save and every 30 s | 2 to 3 autosave periods |
| "Save soon" after something valuable | n/a | 2 s minimum, normally waits until 8 s since the last save | 2 to 10 s debounce |
| Retry after a failed autosave | queue-based backoff | re-queue after 15 s | exponential with jitter, capped |
| `BindToClose` window | 30 s (engine) | waits up to 25 s for in-flight saves | finish by ~25 s |

Why stagger: if every server starts its autosave loop on boot, and many servers boot together after an update, they all save on the same tick, forever. Roblox's best-practices page says assign a random initial offset per server or player and add bounded jitter. A single loop that saves all players back to back also bursts the server's write budget; spreading each player on their own offset keeps it smooth.

Why not save more often: each save costs one read and one write from both the server budget (60 + 40 per player per minute) and the experience budget (300 + 20 x CCU writes per minute), and counts against the per-key 4 MB/min throughput. At 120 s per player you use under 1 write per player per minute, leaving lots of headroom for purchases and other stores.

## The retry helper

Retry only what can succeed on retry, back off exponentially with jitter, cap attempts, and keep retries for one key in order (the module serializes saves per profile).

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Data/Retry (ModuleScript)
local Retry = {}

-- Data store errors usually begin with their numeric code, e.g. "104: Cannot store ..."
-- (observed format; the codes themselves are listed on the Roblox limits page).
local PERMANENT: { [number]: boolean } = {
	[101] = true, [102] = true, [103] = true, [104] = true, [105] = true,
	[106] = true, [107] = true, [403] = true, [509] = true,
	[511] = true, [512] = true, [513] = true,
}

function Retry.isPermanent(err: any): boolean
	local code = tonumber(string.match(tostring(err), "^(%d%d%d)"))
	return code ~= nil and PERMANENT[code] == true
end

-- Calls fn until it returns without erroring, or attempts run out.
-- Returns ok, ...results  (ok = false, lastError on failure)
function Retry.call<T...>(attempts: number, fn: () -> T...): (boolean, ...any)
	local delay = 1
	local lastErr: any = nil
	for attempt = 1, attempts do
		local results = table.pack(pcall(fn))
		if results[1] then
			return true, table.unpack(results, 2, results.n)
		end
		lastErr = results[2]
		if Retry.isPermanent(lastErr) then
			break
		end
		if attempt < attempts then
			task.wait(delay * (0.5 + math.random())) -- jitter: 0.5x to 1.5x
			delay = math.min(delay * 2, 16)
		end
	end
	return false, lastErr
end

return Retry
```

Note the module from [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]] already wraps `UpdateAsync` in `pcall` and returns `"error"`; the loader below decides how many times to call it again, because the right number depends on context (autosave can wait for the next cycle, a final save cannot).

## Never save before the load succeeded

The single most destructive bug in Roblox persistence is: load fails, the code falls back to a default profile, and the leave-save writes that default over the player's real data. The reference project's rule, stated at the top of its persistence code: a profile is written back only once it has been read successfully (or the player is confirmed brand new). A failed read leaves the session **unsaved** rather than letting a blank profile overwrite real progress. The module enforces this structurally: there is no profile object to save unless the claim succeeded.

A second, quieter version of the same bug: values that live outside the profile (leaderstats values, attributes) and are copied into it on save. If the save runs before those were restored from the profile, it writes zeros. The reference project only marks a profile ready once its Cash/Gems/Rolls are back in leaderstats. Better still: make the profile the single source of truth and drive leaderstats from it, never the other way round.

## The loader: wiring it all together

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Data/PlayerDataLoader (Script)
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local ProfileManager = require(script.Parent.ProfileManager)
local Profiles = require(script.Parent.Profiles)

local AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL = 120     -- desired interval; clamped below so each save renews the lease in time
local FINAL_SAVE_ATTEMPTS = 4
local SHUTDOWN_BUDGET = 25         -- seconds of the 30 s BindToClose window we allow ourselves

-- A 90 s lease needs saves (renewals) more often than every 90 s.
AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL = math.min(AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL, math.floor(ProfileManager.LeaseSeconds / 3))

local inFlight = 0
local saveQueued: { [Player]: boolean } = {}
local lastSaveAt: { [Player]: number } = {}

local function notify(player: Player, text: string)
	-- hook into your UI; an attribute keeps the example self-contained
	player:SetAttribute("DataNotice", text)
end

local function saveWithRetries(player: Player, release: boolean, attempts: number): boolean
	local profile = Profiles._get(player)
	if not profile or profile.State ~= "active" then
		return false
	end
	inFlight += 1
	local result = "error"
	local delay = 1
	for attempt = 1, attempts do
		result = ProfileManager.save(profile, release)
		if result ~= "error" then
			break
		end
		if attempt < attempts then
			task.wait(delay * (0.5 + math.random()))
			delay = math.min(delay * 2, 8)
		end
	end
	inFlight -= 1
	lastSaveAt[player] = os.clock()
	if result == "lost" and player.Parent then
		notify(player, "Your data was opened on another server. Rejoin to keep playing safely.")
	end
	return result == "saved"
end

-- Debounced save after something valuable (a big purchase, a rare drop, a trade).
local function saveSoon(player: Player)
	if saveQueued[player] then
		return
	end
	saveQueued[player] = true
	local since = os.clock() - (lastSaveAt[player] or -math.huge)
	local delay = math.max(2, 8 - since) -- at least 2 s, and about 8 s between writes to one key
	task.delay(delay, function()
		saveQueued[player] = nil
		if player.Parent then
			saveWithRetries(player, false, 2)
		end
	end)
end

-- gameplay code calls Profiles.saveSoon(player) after valuable changes
(Profiles :: any).saveSoon = saveSoon

local function startAutosave(player: Player)
	task.spawn(function()
		task.wait(math.random() * AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL) -- per-player offset: no synchronized bursts
		while player.Parent do
			local profile = Profiles._get(player)
			if not profile or profile.State ~= "active" then
				break
			end
			-- a failed autosave just waits for the next cycle (or the leave-save)
			saveWithRetries(player, false, 1)
			task.wait(AUTOSAVE_INTERVAL + math.random() * 5) -- small jitter each cycle
		end
	end)
end

local function onPlayerAdded(player: Player)
	Profiles._set(player, "loading", nil)
	local status, profile = ProfileManager.load(player)
	if status == "left" then
		return
	end
	if not player.Parent then
		-- left after we claimed: release immediately so their next server can load
		if profile then
			ProfileManager.save(profile, true)
		end
		return
	end
	if status ~= "ready" or not profile then
		Profiles._set(player, status, nil)
		if status == "locked" then
			player:Kick("Your data is still saving from your last server. Please rejoin in a minute.")
		else
			player:Kick("Your data couldn't load. Nothing was changed; please rejoin.")
		end
		return
	end
	Profiles._set(player, "ready", profile)
	startAutosave(player)
end

local function onPlayerRemoving(player: Player)
	saveQueued[player] = nil
	saveWithRetries(player, true, FINAL_SAVE_ATTEMPTS) -- final write + release the lease
	Profiles._clear(player)
	lastSaveAt[player] = nil
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(onPlayerRemoving)
for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
	task.spawn(onPlayerAdded, p) -- players who joined before this script ran
end

game:BindToClose(function(reason: Enum.CloseReason)
	if RunService:IsStudio() then
		-- Studio: save but do not hold the window open (stopping Play stays fast). Leases left
		-- behind are handled by the Studio takeover rule / test key in the locking note.
		for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
			task.spawn(saveWithRetries, p, true, 1)
		end
		task.wait(1)
		return
	end
	-- Live: save everyone in PARALLEL (sequential saves of 30 players will not fit in 30 s).
	for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
		task.spawn(saveWithRetries, p, true, 3)
	end
	local started = os.clock()
	task.wait(0.5) -- let the spawned saves (and PlayerRemoving saves) register as in flight
	while inFlight > 0 and os.clock() - started < SHUTDOWN_BUDGET do
		task.wait(0.1)
	end
	if inFlight > 0 then
		warn(`[Data] shutdown ({reason.Name}) ended with {inFlight} saves still running`)
	end
end)
```

Notes on the loader:

- **The autosave interval and the lease must agree.** The production game paired a 90 s lease with a 120 s autosave, which only worked because it had a separate 30 s renewal loop. The loader above folds renewal into the autosave by clamping the interval to a third of the lease. If you want 120 to 180 s autosaves, use a 300 s or longer lease.
- **Kick on `locked` and `failed`.** This is the conservative choice. The alternative (play in a no-save mode with a banner) is described in [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]]; if you choose it, also block purchases.
- **`saveSoon` is for value, not for frequency.** Call it after a purchase grant (the receipt flow saves synchronously anyway), a trade, a rare drop, a rebirth. Do not call it on every currency tick.
- **PlayerRemoving during shutdown.** When a server closes, players are removed and `PlayerRemoving` fires while `BindToClose` runs. Both paths call `saveWithRetries`; the module's per-profile serialization makes the second call wait, then it sees `State = "released"` and returns. No double write races.
- **`inFlight` covers both paths**, so `BindToClose` waits for leave-saves started by `PlayerRemoving`, which the production game called out explicitly ("these and the leave-saves PlayerRemoving is running").

## BindToClose, precisely

From the `DataModel:BindToClose` reference (October 2026):

- You can bind several functions; **they run in parallel**.
- The server waits **30 seconds** for all of them, then shuts down regardless.
- If the bound function takes a parameter it receives an `Enum.CloseReason`: `Unknown`, `RobloxMaintenance`, `DeveloperShutdown`, `DeveloperUpdate`, `ServerEmpty`, `OutOfMemory`, `Moderation`. Useful for logging and for skipping non-essential work; save on every reason.
- Use `RunService:IsStudio()` to avoid making Studio wait.
- Data store calls made too late fail with 401/402 (DataModel or web services unavailable during shutdown).

What eats the 30 seconds:

| Cost | Typical | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| One `UpdateAsync` | 0.1 to 1 s, much longer when throttled | Parallel saves |
| 30 players saved one after another | Can exceed 30 s under load | `task.spawn` each |
| Other stores (leaderboards, analytics) | Adds requests to the same queues | Write critical player data first; skip non-critical stores or give them a short budget |
| Retries | Exponential waits | Fewer attempts in shutdown (3, short delays) |
| Write queue already full (30 requests) | New requests fail with 30x | Stop non-critical writers when shutdown begins |

`ServerEmpty` shutdowns are the common case: the last player left, `PlayerRemoving` already started their save, and `BindToClose` just needs to wait for it. Forgetting to wait is the classic "last player's progress is lost" bug.

Roblox's sample adds one more trick: on shutdown, drop queued stale requests and send only the latest state per key. With per-profile serialization plus snapshots there is never more than one queued save per profile, so this is automatic.

## Saving other stores

Not every store needs the profile's guarantees:

| Store | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Player profile | Session-locked, fenced `UpdateAsync` (this note) |
| Receipts ledger | `UpdateAsync` claim per `PurchaseId` ([[Purchase Data and Receipts]]) |
| Leaderboard (ordered) | `SetAsync` of the current value on leave and on a slow loop, only if the profile loaded; skipped in Studio test sessions (OrderedDataStores and Leaderboards) |
| Settings | Separate key, `UpdateAsync` on change with a debounce |
| Analytics, reports | Best effort; never block shutdown on them |

The reference project's leaderboard service applied the most important rule here: "never write a profile we failed to read, or we would wipe their history". Its totals were only written for players whose leaderboard state had loaded, and never while a Studio test key was active.

## Verifying that saves work

- In Studio with API access on a **test experience** (or with the test key), play, change data, stop, and read the key back with `UseCache = false` ([[DataStore Fundamentals]]): a plain `GetAsync` may serve a value up to 4 s old.
- Simulate failure: a flag that forces the load to fail (the reference project's `SimulateLoadFailure` attribute) proves the no-save path works. Also simulate save errors (a flag that makes `ProfileManager.save` return `"error"`) to see the retry and the "will retry" UI.
- Watch the Data Stores observability dashboard after a release: Request Count by Status for throttling and errors, Write Request Type Quota Usage for headroom (Data Loss Prevention and Recovery).
- Test a shutdown with players in the server (a live test server, "Shut Down All Servers"), then confirm every player's `SavedAt` is after the shutdown time.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What happens |
|---|---|
| No `BindToClose` | Every update or shutdown loses up to one autosave interval for every player |
| Saving players one by one in `BindToClose` | Large servers time out; the last players lose data |
| Not waiting for `PlayerRemoving` saves in `BindToClose` | Last player in an emptying server loses progress |
| Yielding in `PlayerRemoving` before the save | Delays the save; widens the session-overlap window |
| Saving defaults after a failed load | Real data overwritten |
| Autosave interval longer than the lease | Healthy servers lose their own lease and sessions turn `lost` |
| Same-tick autosave in every server | Throttling at the same moment every few minutes |
| Saving on every change | 30x throttle errors; per-key throughput exceeded |
| Holding `BindToClose` open in Studio | Every Stop takes 25 s |

## Checklist

- [ ] Save on: autosave (staggered), leave (with release), shutdown (parallel, with a deadline), purchases.
- [ ] Autosave interval below the lease.
- [ ] No save path exists for a profile that failed to load.
- [ ] `BindToClose` waits for in-flight leave-saves.
- [ ] Studio does not wait in `BindToClose`.
- [ ] Retries back off with jitter and stop on permanent errors.
- [ ] Non-critical stores never block shutdown.
