# Session Locking and Profile Libraries

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Items duplicated after teleports: No lease, or saves not fenced -> Search for `SetAsync` / unfenced `UpdateAsync` on player keys
> - "Progress saved on another server" messages in normal play: Two servers both loaded the key (version-only guard) -> Add a lease
> - Players cannot rejoin for ~1 to 5 minutes after a server crash: Lease length -> Expected; shorten the lease or show a countdown
> - Lease written and checked inside the same `UpdateAsync` as the data.
> - Every save is fenced by a per-session token; "lost" stops all writes.
> - Autosave interval is shorter than the lease and renews it.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~190 tok · whole note ~6.4k tok. Read more: ## A complete session-locked profile module · ## Exposing the profile to the rest of the game (the bridge) · ## Failure modes and diagnosis · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Every serious Roblox game keeps a player's data **in server memory** for the session and writes it back periodically. That design is only safe if **one server at a time** owns a given player's data. Session locking is the mechanism that guarantees it. This note explains why it is needed (with the exact failure sequences), how to build a lease-based lock on `UpdateAsync` correctly, the production lessons from one shipped game (including a 90 second lease that blocked Studio test loads), and how the common libraries (ProfileStore, ProfileService, Roblox's sample) compare.

Prerequisites: [[DataStore Fundamentals]]. Follow-ups: [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]], [[Data Schema Design and Migrations]], [[Purchase Data and Receipts]].

## Why "load, play, save" is not enough

Roblox only lets a client connect to one server at a time, so it is tempting to assume one player's data is only ever live in one place. It is not. Roblox's own player-data guide lists the ways a player's next session can start before the last one finished saving:

1. Server A's final save fails and is retrying while the player joins server B.
2. Server A is throttled and the final `UpdateAsync` sits in the queue (see the 30-request queues in [[DataStore Fundamentals]]).
3. Code on `PlayerRemoving` in server A yields (a remote call, an analytics post) before the save starts.
4. Server A is so loaded that the save runs late.

Teleports make all four common, because the player is on the new server within seconds. Now trace it:

```text
t=0   Server A has Coins=100 in memory. Player trades 50 coins worth of items away.
t=1   Player teleports. A starts its final save (slow).
t=2   Server B loads the key: still the OLD value (Coins=100, items present).
t=3   A's save lands: Coins=50, items gone.
t=60  B autosaves its copy: Coins=100, items present again.  -> items duplicated
```

The reverse ordering loses progress instead of duplicating it. Players discover the duplicating version deliberately: it is the classic Roblox trade dupe. `UpdateAsync` alone does not fix it, because B's autosave is a perfectly valid read-modify-write of B's stale copy.

The fix has two halves:
- **Exclusion on load**: B must not start a session while A still owns the key.
- **Fencing on save**: if A somehow lost ownership (its lease expired, someone forced a takeover), A's late writes must be refused.

## Leases, not locks

A lock that is only released by its owner is a disaster when the owner crashes: the player can never load again. So every practical scheme is a **lease**: the owner writes `{ Token, ExpiresAt }` into the key and must keep renewing it. If the owner dies, the lease expires and another server may claim it.

Lease length is a trade-off:

| Lease | Upside | Downside |
|---|---|---|
| Short (30 to 60 s) | A crashed server's players can rejoin quickly | Must renew often; a slow backend can make a healthy server lose its own lease |
| Long (90 to 300 s) | Robust through backend hiccups | After a crash, or a release that failed, the player waits that long |

Rules of thumb: renew at a third of the lease or more often; make the autosave interval shorter than the lease (Roblox's best-practices page says the same: "shorter than any session-lock expiration"); fold renewal into the autosave so it costs nothing extra.

One production game used **a 90 second lease, renewed every 30 seconds**, claim attempts 6 times with waits of 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 s (7.5 s total) before giving up.

### Where to store the lease

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| A field in the value (`record.Session`) | Simple, visible in Data Stores Manager, one write updates data and lease together. Used by the reference project |
| Key metadata (`LockId` via `SetMetadata` / transform's third return) | What Roblox's sample does. Keeps the value clean. Metadata is capped at 300 characters, and you must pass it through on every write or it is erased |
| A MemoryStore hash map entry | Fast and expiring, but a second system that can disagree with the data store. Only worth it for very advanced setups |

Either of the first two is fine. The important part is that **the lease check and the data write happen in the same `UpdateAsync`**.

### Clocks

`ExpiresAt` uses `os.time()`. Different servers' clocks are close but not identical. With leases measured in tens of seconds, a few seconds of skew is harmless; just never use leases shorter than about 30 s, and never compare `os.clock()` values across servers (it is per-process).

## The fencing token, and why a version counter alone is not enough

The owner generates a random token (`HttpService:GenerateGUID(false)`) when it claims the key. Every save checks "is the token in the stored record still mine?" inside the transform. If not, the save aborts and the session stops writing.

The reference project's first version used a different guard: a `SaveVersion` counter. Each save required the stored counter to equal what this server last wrote, then incremented it. That does stop stale overwrites, but it has two weaknesses the team ran into:

1. **It does not stop two servers from loading the same version.** Both load v7, both play; the first save makes it v8, the second server's save is refused and its **whole session** is thrown away. No dupe, but lost progress, and the player saw "Your progress was saved on another server". The team added the lease ("makes quick teleports wait for the old server to release the key") on top.
2. **Unknown-outcome writes look like a stranger's write.** A save can error after the backend actually committed it ([[DataStore Fundamentals]]). The stored counter is now one ahead of what the server believes, and a strict "must equal" check marks the server's own data as foreign. With a token, the rule is simpler and correct: if the stored token is mine, every write since my claim was mine, whatever the counter says.

So: use the token as the authority, keep a version counter for diagnostics and for refusing writes from old code that predates tokens.

## A complete session-locked profile module

This is a self-contained server module. It claims with retries, builds or migrates the profile, saves with fencing, releases on leave, and exposes state for the rest of the game. Autosave, `BindToClose` and the retry helper live in [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]]; migrations in [[Data Schema Design and Migrations]].

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Data/ProfileManager (ModuleScript)
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")

local Schema = require(script.Parent.Schema) -- newProfile(), migrate(data) (see the migrations note)

local STORE_NAME = "PlayerData_v1"
local LEASE_SECONDS = 90
local CLAIM_ATTEMPTS = 6

local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore(STORE_NAME)
local IS_STUDIO = RunService:IsStudio()

export type LoadStatus = "ready" | "locked" | "failed" | "left"
export type Profile = {
	UserId: number,
	Key: string,
	Token: string,
	Data: { [string]: any },
	SaveVersion: number,
	IsNew: boolean,
	State: "active" | "lost" | "released",
	Saving: boolean,
}

type SessionRecord = { Token: string, JobId: string, PlaceId: number, ExpiresAt: number, Studio: boolean? }

local ProfileManager = {}
ProfileManager.LeaseSeconds = LEASE_SECONDS

-- Studio-only isolated key: ServerStorage attribute TestProfileKey = "fresh1" plays on a
-- separate save so tests never touch the real one. Ignored on live servers.
local function keyFor(userId: number): string
	if IS_STUDIO then
		local test = ServerStorage:GetAttribute("TestProfileKey")
		if type(test) == "string" and test ~= "" and #test <= 20 then
			return `TEST_{test}_{userId}`
		end
	end
	return `User_{userId}`
end
ProfileManager.keyFor = keyFor

local function deepCopy<T>(value: T): T
	if type(value) ~= "table" then
		return value
	end
	local out = {}
	for k, v in value :: any do
		out[deepCopy(k)] = deepCopy(v)
	end
	return out :: any
end
ProfileManager.deepCopy = deepCopy

local function newSession(token: string): SessionRecord
	return {
		Token = token,
		JobId = game.JobId,
		PlaceId = game.PlaceId,
		ExpiresAt = os.time() + LEASE_SECONDS,
		Studio = if IS_STUDIO then true else nil,
	}
end

-- One claim attempt. Returns outcome plus the stored record when claimed.
local function tryClaim(key: string, userId: number, token: string): (string, any, number?)
	local outcome, lockedUntil = "error", nil :: number?
	local ok, result = pcall(function()
		return store:UpdateAsync(key, function(old: any, keyInfo: DataStoreKeyInfo?)
			outcome, lockedUntil = "error", nil -- reset: the transform can run several times
			if old ~= nil and type(old) ~= "table" then
				outcome = "malformed"
				return nil
			end
			local record = old or { SaveVersion = 0 }
			local held = record.Session
			if type(held) == "table" and held.Token ~= token then
				local expires = tonumber(held.ExpiresAt) or 0
				-- A lease left by a Studio test session may be taken by another Studio session
				-- (see "the 90 second Studio trap" below). Live leases are always honoured.
				local studioTakeover = IS_STUDIO and held.Studio == true
				if expires > os.time() and not studioTakeover then
					outcome, lockedUntil = "locked", expires
					return nil
				end
			end
			record.Session = newSession(token)
			outcome = "claimed"
			local userIds = if keyInfo then keyInfo:GetUserIds() else { userId }
			local metadata = if keyInfo then keyInfo:GetMetadata() else nil
			return record, userIds, metadata
		end)
	end)
	if not ok then
		warn(`[ProfileManager] claim error for {key}: {result}`)
		return "error", nil, nil
	end
	return outcome, result, lockedUntil
end

function ProfileManager.load(player: Player): (LoadStatus, Profile?)
	local userId = player.UserId
	local key = keyFor(userId)
	local token = HttpService:GenerateGUID(false)
	local lastOutcome = "error"
	for attempt = 1, CLAIM_ATTEMPTS do
		if not player.Parent then
			return "left", nil
		end
		local outcome, record, lockedUntil = tryClaim(key, userId, token)
		lastOutcome = outcome
		if outcome == "claimed" and type(record) == "table" then
			local isNew = record.Data == nil
			local okMigrate, data = pcall(function()
				return if isNew then Schema.newProfile() else Schema.migrate(record.Data)
			end)
			if not okMigrate then
				-- Data we cannot read (corrupt, or written by a NEWER release). Never overwrite it.
				warn(`[ProfileManager] migrate failed for {key}: {data}`)
				ProfileManager.releaseUnsaved(key, token)
				return "failed", nil
			end
			local profile: Profile = {
				UserId = userId,
				Key = key,
				Token = token,
				Data = data,
				SaveVersion = tonumber(record.SaveVersion) or 0,
				IsNew = isNew,
				State = "active",
				Saving = false,
			}
			return "ready", profile
		elseif outcome == "malformed" then
			return "failed", nil
		elseif outcome == "locked" and attempt == 1 and lockedUntil then
			warn(`[ProfileManager] {key} held by another server, lease ends in {lockedUntil - os.time()} s`)
		end
		if attempt < CLAIM_ATTEMPTS then
			task.wait(math.min(8, attempt * 1.5) + math.random()) -- backoff with jitter
		end
	end
	return if lastOutcome == "locked" then "locked" else "failed", nil
end

-- Writes Data (and optionally clears the lease). Fenced by the token.
-- Returns "saved" | "lost" | "error". Callers retry "error" (see the saving note).
function ProfileManager.save(profile: Profile, release: boolean): string
	if profile.State ~= "active" then
		return "lost"
	end
	while profile.Saving do -- one write per profile at a time, in order
		task.wait(0.1)
	end
	if profile.State ~= "active" then
		return "lost"
	end
	profile.Saving = true
	local snapshot = deepCopy(profile.Data) -- the transform must not see later gameplay mutations
	local result = "error"
	local writtenVersion = profile.SaveVersion
	local ok, err = pcall(function()
		store:UpdateAsync(profile.Key, function(old: any, keyInfo: DataStoreKeyInfo?)
			result = "error"
			if type(old) ~= "table" or type(old.Session) ~= "table" or old.Session.Token ~= profile.Token then
				result = "lost" -- someone else owns this key now: never write
				return nil
			end
			-- The token is ours, so any version bump since our claim was our own unacknowledged write.
			writtenVersion = math.max(tonumber(old.SaveVersion) or 0, profile.SaveVersion) + 1
			old.Data = snapshot
			old.SaveVersion = writtenVersion
			old.SavedAt = os.time()
			old.Session = if release then nil else newSession(profile.Token)
			result = "saved"
			local userIds = if keyInfo then keyInfo:GetUserIds() else { profile.UserId }
			local metadata = if keyInfo then keyInfo:GetMetadata() else nil
			return old, userIds, metadata
		end)
	end)
	profile.Saving = false
	if not ok then
		warn(`[ProfileManager] save error for {profile.Key}: {err}`)
		return "error"
	end
	if result == "lost" then
		profile.State = "lost"
		return "lost"
	end
	if result == "saved" then
		profile.SaveVersion = writtenVersion
		if release then
			profile.State = "released"
		end
	end
	return result
end

-- Drops our lease without writing data (load refused after the claim).
function ProfileManager.releaseUnsaved(key: string, token: string)
	pcall(function()
		store:UpdateAsync(key, function(old: any, keyInfo: DataStoreKeyInfo?)
			if type(old) ~= "table" or type(old.Session) ~= "table" or old.Session.Token ~= token then
				return nil
			end
			old.Session = nil -- Data (if any) is left exactly as it was
			return old, if keyInfo then keyInfo:GetUserIds() else nil, if keyInfo then keyInfo:GetMetadata() else nil
		end)
	end)
end

return ProfileManager
```

Design notes on the module:

- **New players**: the claim writes `{ SaveVersion = 0, Session = ... }` with no `Data`. That record is the lock; the first save fills `Data`. A crash in between leaves a record with no data, which loads as a new player next time: correct.
- **Deep copy before save**: gameplay keeps mutating `profile.Data` while the save yields. Without the copy, a retried transform could serialize a half-applied change (for example, an item removed but the coins not yet added). Copying at the start makes each save a consistent snapshot as of that instant. Make every gameplay mutation synchronous (no yields between related changes), so any snapshot is consistent.
- **One save at a time**: `Saving` serializes writes per profile. Roblox's sample goes further and queues every request per key in order ("an older request that retries after a newer one succeeds can overwrite newer data"). With token fencing plus serialization this module cannot reorder its own writes.
- **"lost" is terminal**: once the token is gone, the session must stop saving and tell the player. Do not try to re-claim silently; the other owner's data is newer.
- **Expired but still ours**: the save accepts the write when the token matches even if `ExpiresAt` has passed. If the lease lapsed during a backend outage and nobody claimed it, the token is still ours and writing is safe. If someone did claim it, the token differs and we refuse. (The reference project also refused its own expired lease. That is safe but throws away a session for no reason after a long outage.)

## The 90 second Studio trap (production lesson)

Measured in one production game: after adding the 90 s lease, developers testing in Studio started getting "Your saved progress couldn't load" on the **second** Play in a row.

What happened:

1. Play session 1 claims `User_123` with token T1, expires at now + 90.
2. The developer presses Stop. Studio shuts the test server down. The project, like most, skips or shortens the `BindToClose` wait in Studio so stopping is not painful, so the releasing save never lands.
3. Within 90 s the developer presses Play again. Session 2 sees T1, unexpired, not its own token, and retries for 7.5 s, then gives up: load failed.

Fixes, from least to most effort:

| Fix | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| Wait 90 s between Play sessions | Annoying, people forget |
| A **Studio-only test-profile key** (`ServerStorage` attribute `TestProfileKey` gives key `TEST_<name>_<uid>`; new name = fresh profile) | Also isolates tests from the real save. The project used this throughout. Remember to clear it: one developer left a test key set and later "lost" their real progress, which was simply on the other key |
| Mark leases written from Studio (`Studio = true`) and let another Studio session take them over (the module above does this) | Live servers never honour or create Studio takeovers. Two developers testing the same account at once in Team Create can clobber each other; acceptable for tests |
| Let the `BindToClose` release run in Studio | Stopping waits for a save each time |

The project's related rules, worth copying: the test key is read **only** when `RunService:IsStudio()`, so it cannot leak into a live server; never set the test key before Play has actually started; the key also skips developer grants and disables the leaderboard writes, so test sessions do not pollute boards; and a second attribute, `SimulateLoadFailure`, forces the "load failed, nothing will be saved" path so it can be tested on purpose.

## Handling a load that did not succeed

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `ready` | Claimed and loaded | Play |
| `locked` | Another server still owns the lease after all retries | Tell the player their data is still saving elsewhere; kick with a "rejoin in a minute" message, or keep them in a no-save lobby and retry |
| `failed` | Backend errors, malformed or future-schema data | Never give them a default profile that saves. Either kick, or let them play in a clearly marked no-save mode |
| `left` | Player left during load | Release if you claimed (the module only claims on success) |

Roblox's sample recommends letting the player play with default data, marked as errored so it is never written, and showing a clear message, rather than kicking. The roblox-datastores playbook and many studios prefer a kick. Both are defensible; what is never acceptable is a default profile that can save over real data. Also block purchases while a profile is not `ready` (Roblox's sample checks `hasErrored` before prompting), or a purchase lands in a session that can never be saved ([[Purchase Data and Receipts]]).

## Exposing the profile to the rest of the game (the bridge)

Only one module should own `DataStoreService` calls for player data. Every other system goes through it. The reference project called this the **ProfileBridge**: a single entry point that other server scripts use to "touch this profile safely", with actions such as `ready` (can this profile be changed and saved right now?), `waitReady` (yield until loaded or failed, 90 s cap), `receiptSaved` (is this purchase id in the saved profile?), and combined "charge and record" operations so currency and the thing it bought are always written by the same save.

In a ModuleScript-based codebase the bridge is just the module's public API:

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Data/Profiles (ModuleScript): the only API gameplay code uses
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ProfileManager = require(script.Parent.ProfileManager)

type Profile = ProfileManager.Profile

local profiles: { [Player]: Profile } = {}
local loadState: { [Player]: string } = {}
local readyEvent = Instance.new("BindableEvent")

local Profiles = {}

function Profiles.canMutate(player: Player): boolean
	local p = profiles[player]
	return p ~= nil and p.State == "active"
end

-- Synchronous mutation. The callback must not yield, so related changes are atomic
-- with respect to any snapshot taken by a save.
function Profiles.mutate(player: Player, fn: (data: { [string]: any }) -> ()): boolean
	local p = profiles[player]
	if not p or p.State ~= "active" then
		return false
	end
	fn(p.Data)
	return true
end

function Profiles.waitReady(player: Player, timeout: number?): string?
	local deadline = os.clock() + (timeout or 90)
	while player.Parent and os.clock() < deadline do
		local s = loadState[player]
		if s == "ready" or s == "failed" or s == "locked" then
			return s
		end
		readyEvent.Event:Wait()
	end
	return nil
end

-- used by the loader script
function Profiles._set(player: Player, status: string, profile: Profile?)
	loadState[player] = status
	profiles[player] = profile
	readyEvent:Fire(player)
end

function Profiles._get(player: Player): Profile?
	return profiles[player]
end

function Profiles._clear(player: Player)
	profiles[player] = nil
	loadState[player] = nil
	readyEvent:Fire(player)
end

return Profiles
```

`readyEvent:Wait()` wakes on any player's state change, which is fine at Roblox server sizes. If the owner is a classic `Script` (as in the reference project), a `BindableFunction` in `ServerScriptService` plays the same role; just keep the rule that callbacks never yield between a check and the change it guards. Gameplay rules for the bridge:

- Check `canMutate` before granting anything valuable. A profile in `lost` state still exists in memory; granting into it gives the player something that will never save.
- Never hand out the `Data` table for long-lived storage elsewhere; other systems keep ids, not references.
- Replicate to the client from the owner (attributes or a single remote), never let clients write ([[Server Authority and Validation]]).

## Libraries

| Library | Status (October 2026) | Locking model | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ProfileStore** (by loleris) | Maintained successor to ProfileService | Session lock in the record, auto-save, session end signals | API: `ProfileStore.New(name, template)`, `store:StartSessionAsync(key, { Cancel = fn, Steal = bool })`, `profile.Data`, `profile:Reconcile()`, `profile:AddUserId()`, `profile:EndSession()`, `profile:IsActive()`, `profile.OnSessionEnd`, `store:GetAsync` / `VersionQuery` / `MessageAsync`, and `.Mock` for tests. Timing constants (`AUTO_SAVE_PERIOD`, `ASSUME_DEAD`, `SESSION_STEAL`, ...) are settable with `SetConstant`; check the source for defaults |
| **ProfileService** (same author) | Older; superseded by ProfileStore | Session lock | Many existing games still run it; migration path documented by the author |
| **Roblox sample** (`SessionLockedDataStoreWrapper`) | Reference code, Roblox says do not ship as-is without extensive testing | Lock id in metadata, per-key ordered queue, 180 s autosave | Good to read for the ordering argument |
| **DataStore2** | Legacy | One store per player (ordered backups) | Roblox says do not use for new games; offers a migration tool |
| Hand-rolled (the module above) | Yours | Lease + token | Choose this when you need control over purchases, gifting, cross-key operations, or you want to understand every failure |

Roblox's advice before adopting any module: check ownership and maintenance, and make sure you can read and migrate your data **without** the module. A library that stores data in a private format is a lock-in risk.

## Failure modes and diagnosis

| Symptom | Likely cause | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Items duplicated after teleports | No lease, or saves not fenced | Search for `SetAsync` / unfenced `UpdateAsync` on player keys |
| "Progress saved on another server" messages in normal play | Two servers both loaded the key (version-only guard) | Add a lease |
| Players cannot rejoin for ~1 to 5 minutes after a server crash | Lease length | Expected; shorten the lease or show a countdown |
| Second Studio Play fails to load | Lease from the previous test still live | Studio takeover rule, test key, or wait |
| Real progress "gone" after testing | `TestProfileKey` still set | Clear it; data is on `User_<id>` untouched |
| Session flips to `lost` during an outage | Another server claimed after expiry | Expected and safe; longer lease if frequent |

## Checklist

- [ ] Lease written and checked inside the same `UpdateAsync` as the data.
- [ ] Every save is fenced by a per-session token; "lost" stops all writes.
- [ ] Autosave interval is shorter than the lease and renews it.
- [ ] The final save releases the lease; failure to release only delays the next join.
- [ ] Load returns distinct `ready` / `locked` / `failed`; none of them saves defaults over real data.
- [ ] Purchases and grants check `canMutate` first.
- [ ] Studio has a test-key path and a plan for leftover leases.

# Responsive UI for Phone Tablet Console and PC

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: `TouchEnabled` used as "is a phone".
> - Avoid: One global `UIScale` with no floor; phone text at 6 px.
> - Avoid: Zoom-and-pan instead of real phone layouts.
> - Device profile separates layout family from input.
> - Five viewports plus a notched phone in every test pass.
> - Numbers enforced: 12 px text, 44 px taps, 8 px gaps, 0 overlaps.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~130 tok · whole note ~4.1k tok. Read more: ## 1. Classify by capability, not by guessing the device · ## 4. Four strategies for small screens, ranked by what survived · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Roblox players arrive on 4.7 inch phones, tablets, laptops, ultrawide monitors and living-room TVs, and the same player may switch device between sessions. Mobile is a large share of the audience, so a UI signed off only at Studio's default desktop window is broken for many of your players. This note is about strategy: how to classify devices without guessing, which viewports to test, the measurable rules (text size, tap size, gaps, overlaps) that define "fits", and why the reference project ended up building real phone layouts instead of shrinking or zooming desktop ones.

Sources: **Docs** ("Cross-platform development", `GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize`, `UserInputService.PreferredInput`, styling queries; October 2026), the **reference project** (one production game whose phone UI was rebuilt screen by screen; numbers measured there), and **rule of thumb**.

Mechanics of sizing are in Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints; notches and the top bar are in Safe Areas and Insets; gamepad specifics in Gamepad and Console UX.

---

## 1. Classify by capability, not by guessing the device

Roblox does not tell you "this is an iPhone". It tells you capabilities, and you combine them:

| Signal | What it means | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `Camera.ViewportSize` | Render size in pixels | Layout maths |
| `GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize` | `Small` (most phones, tablets, handhelds), `Medium` (laptops, monitors), `Large` (TVs) (Docs) | Picking a layout family |
| `UserInputService.PreferredInput` | `KeyboardAndMouse`, `Gamepad`, `Touch`, `MicroGamepad`; updates as the player switches (Docs) | Which prompts and controls to show |
| `UserInputService.TouchEnabled` | The device has a touch screen | Not "is a phone": many laptops have touch |

Docs: "attempting to predict screen size by pixels often leads to misinterpretation", and `GuiService:IsTenFootInterface()` is deprecated in favour of `ViewportDisplaySize`.

### The reference project's phone rule

`phone = TouchEnabled and shortSide < 520` (short side of the viewport in pixels). It was chosen because the phones they cared about report 375 to 430 px short sides in landscape (667 x 375, 844 x 390, 932 x 430) while the smallest tablets report 600 or more. An earlier rule (`TouchEnabled and uiScale < 0.75`) mis-classified a touch laptop and missed a large phone, which is why a size threshold on the **short** side replaced it.

A practical device profile combines all of it:

```lua
--!strict
local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

export type Profile = {
	kind: "phone" | "tablet" | "desktop" | "tv",
	input: Enum.PreferredInput,
	viewport: Vector2,
	shortSide: number,
}

local PHONE_SHORT_SIDE = 520 -- reference project threshold (px, landscape short side)

local function profile(): Profile
	local camera = Workspace.CurrentCamera
	local vp = if camera then camera.ViewportSize else Vector2.new(1920, 1080)
	local short = math.min(vp.X, vp.Y)
	local display = GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize
	local kind: "phone" | "tablet" | "desktop" | "tv"
	if display == Enum.DisplaySize.Large then
		kind = "tv"
	elseif UserInputService.TouchEnabled and short < PHONE_SHORT_SIDE then
		kind = "phone"
	elseif display == Enum.DisplaySize.Small then
		kind = "tablet"
	else
		kind = "desktop"
	end
	return {
		kind = kind,
		input = UserInputService.PreferredInput,
		viewport = vp,
		shortSide = short,
	}
end

local Device = {}
Device.changed = Instance.new("BindableEvent")
Device.current = profile()

local function recompute()
	local p = profile()
	local old = Device.current
	Device.current = p
	if p.kind ~= old.kind or p.input ~= old.input or p.viewport ~= old.viewport then
		Device.changed:Fire(p)
	end
end

UserInputService:GetPropertyChangedSignal("PreferredInput"):Connect(recompute)
GuiService:GetPropertyChangedSignal("ViewportDisplaySize"):Connect(recompute)
local camera = Workspace.CurrentCamera
if camera then
	camera:GetPropertyChangedSignal("ViewportSize"):Connect(recompute)
end

return Device
```

Keep layout family (`kind`) and input (`input`) separate. A tablet with a Bluetooth keyboard is a small-screen layout with keyboard prompts. A phone with a gamepad needs selection rings on the phone layout.

---

## 2. The viewports to test

Studio's Device Emulator and Controller Emulator are the baseline tools (Docs). The reference project standardised on a fixed list and ran its automated checks at every one of them:

| Viewport | Represents | Why it is on the list |
|---|---|---|
| 1920 x 1080 | Desktop baseline | Design resolution |
| 1366 x 768, 1024 x 600 | Laptops, small tablets | Where "compact desktop" layouts start |
| 932 x 430 | Large phone | Widest phone; side-by-side layouts fit here |
| 844 x 390 | Common phone | Primary phone target |
| 667 x 375 | Small phone | Worst case; every overlap shows here first |

Plus a notched variant of 844 x 390 (the notch eats width, see Safe Areas and Insets) and, for TV, 1920 x 1080 with the `Large` display size and gamepad input.

**Landscape only?** Games that lock orientation (the reference project uses landscape sensor) do not need portrait layouts. If you allow portrait (`PlayerGui.ScreenOrientation`), every layout needs a portrait test too, and the phone short side becomes the width.

---

## 3. Define "fits" as numbers, then measure them

"Looks fine" is not testable. These are the reference project's pass criteria (measured on the drawn result, after all scaling):

| Rule | Threshold | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Smallest drawn text | 12 px | `TextScaled` text measured at the size the engine actually draws |
| Smallest drawn tap target | 44 px (48 for HUD buttons, 54 design units in phone panels) | Invisible tap pads count |
| Gap between tap targets | 8 px | Fat-finger mis-taps below this |
| Overlaps between interactive objects | 0 | At every viewport and scenario |
| Objects outside the screen | 0 | Except deliberate overhangs, listed by name |
| Desktop round trip | 0 differences | Switching phone layout on and off restores desktop exactly |

Docs say only "Do not use MinTextSize values lower than 9". The 12 px floor is stricter on purpose: 9 px is legible on a monitor at arm's length, not on a 375 px tall phone in a moving car.

### Automate it

The reference project wrote three Edit-mode tools, and they paid for themselves within a week:

- **A phone check** lays out each screen's phone arrangement on a copy, off-screen (at x = -20000), at 844 x 390 and 667 x 375, and reports minimum text, minimum tap, minimum gap, overlaps, out-of-bounds objects and the desktop round trip. Copies are always destroyed afterwards.
- **A HUD overlap check** places every HUD element with the same placement code the game uses, across five viewports and several scenarios (lobby, combat, boss bar showing, quest dock open, tutorial running), and counts rectangle intersections. Target: 0.
- **A tap check** measures the drawn size of every touch target, including invisible pads.

The key design decision: **the checks call the real placement code**, not a copy of its numbers. Every time a check had its own copy of the maths, the game and the check drifted apart and the check went green while players saw overlaps.

```lua
--!strict
-- Core of an overlap check: given placed GuiObjects, report intersecting pairs.
local function rectsOverlap(a: GuiObject, b: GuiObject, tolerance: number): boolean
	local ap, as = a.AbsolutePosition, a.AbsoluteSize
	local bp, bs = b.AbsolutePosition, b.AbsoluteSize
	return ap.X + as.X - tolerance > bp.X
		and bp.X + bs.X - tolerance > ap.X
		and ap.Y + as.Y - tolerance > bp.Y
		and bp.Y + bs.Y - tolerance > ap.Y
end

local function findOverlaps(objects: { GuiObject }): { string }
	local hits = {}
	for i = 1, #objects do
		for j = i + 1, #objects do
			local a, b = objects[i], objects[j]
			if a.Visible and b.Visible and rectsOverlap(a, b, 1) then
				table.insert(hits, a:GetFullName() .. " x " .. b:GetFullName())
			end
		end
	end
	return hits
end
```

---

## 4. Four strategies for small screens, ranked by what survived

### 4.1 Shrink (one global UIScale)

Fast, and what most games ship. It fails the 12 px rule as soon as the panel was designed for a monitor: 15 px text at the 667 x 375 scale of 0.347 draws at 5 px. It is fine for elements designed big (a giant roll button, a currency pill).

### 4.2 Zoom and pan

The reference project's first phone pass: on a phone, an open panel zoomed until its smallest authored text drew at 12 px (capped at 1.0 overall), and the player panned the oversized panel with a one-finger drag. It was quick to build for 40 screens and it met the text rule. Players disliked it: half of every panel was off-screen, and dragging a panel competes with scrolling lists inside it. It was **retired** once real layouts existed and is kept only as a reference.

### 4.3 Real phone layouts (what shipped)

Each screen got a second arrangement for phones, applied and removed by code:

- **Fixed panel height, computed scale.** Panels are laid out at `W x 430` design units and scaled by `s = 0.97 * screenHeight / 430`. At 844 x 390 that is `s = 0.880` with `W = 930`; at 667 x 375, `s = 0.846` with `W = 764`. Width comes from the screen's aspect ratio; height is always the full usable height.
- **Minimum tap 54 units, gap 10 units**, so at `s = 0.846` taps draw at about 46 px and gaps at 8.5 px.
- **Pages instead of panes.** Desktop shows list and detail side by side; on phones the detail opens as a full-panel page with a BACK button. On wide phones (an available area of 890 units or more, so 844 x 390 and 932 x 430) the detail card still fits beside the list; on 667 x 375 it becomes a page.
- **Horizontal strips for navigation.** Tabs, filter chips and categories move into horizontal scrolling strips so the main content owns vertical scrolling.
- **Bigger cards, fewer columns.** Cards scale by a per-screen factor (1.37 for shop cards, 1.48 for pet cards) and the grid drops columns.
- **Store, set, restore.** Before applying the phone arrangement, every property it will touch is stored; switching back restores desktop exactly. The automated "round trip" check proves it.

Results across 24 screens: every screen at or above 12 px text, 44 px taps, 8 px gaps, 0 overlaps, 0 round-trip differences.

### 4.4 Separate screens per device family

Building a dedicated phone UI from scratch is the cleanest result and the most expensive to maintain (every feature ships twice). The reference project's approach (one tree, two arrangements) was the compromise: same instances, same names (so tutorials and controllers keep working), different placement.

### Tablets and compact desktops

Tablets landed between: the reference project's backpack used a scale of 0.92 to 1.1 with 50-unit taps on tablets, a static desktop design wherever its 15-unit text still drew at 12 px or more, and a compact desktop variant (scale 0.8) for 1024 x 600 laptops.

---

## 5. Scale by device kind with style queries (engine option)

Roblox's UI styling system supports **style queries**: conditions such as viewport display size and preferred input that switch style tokens without code. Docs mention intrinsic selectors like `@ViewportDisplaySizeSmall` and `@PreferredInputTouch` that let UI "automatically swap tokens for text sizes, container dimensions" and more. If your UI is built on `StyleSheet`s (UI Design Systems), this is the least-code way to make text and tap sizes larger on small screens. It does not rearrange layouts (pages instead of panes); that still needs code or separate arrangements.

---

## 6. Phone HUD rules

The HUD is where phones hurt most, because the thumb zones (bottom-left movement stick, bottom-right jump and action buttons) and the Roblox top bar take space you cannot use. The reference project's phone HUD rules after its fixes:

- **Hide, do not shrink.** On phones the HUD keeps only what is needed in moment-to-moment play. Secondary squares move into a menu; the right rail of tabs folds into one row at the top right.
- **Panels hide the HUD on phones** (desktop keeps it). A full-height phone panel over a HUD just creates overlaps.
- **Every top-down slot starts below the top bar.** An elite enemy health bar placed at a fixed y sat half under the Roblox top bar on phones. HUD slots gained a "below inset" flag that adds `GuiService.TopbarInset` height.
- **Boss bars shrink to fit** instead of meeting the stamina bar on short phones (scale 0.64 to 0.72 in the boss scenario on phones).
- **Combat buttons are separated by a final real-rectangle pass.** Six touch buttons (attack, dash, throw, slide, run, block) were placed by percentages; on some phones slide sat on attack. A last pass reads every button's actual rectangle and pushes overlapping ones apart.
- **Tap pads.** Small visual buttons get an invisible 48 px `ImageButton` under them that forwards the press.

See HUD Design for the layout system behind this.

---

## 7. TV and console

- Treat `ViewportDisplaySize.Large` plus gamepad as "ten-foot UI": players sit 2 to 3 m away. Text that is fine at 1080p on a monitor is small on a TV; a rule of thumb is to raise body text by about 1.25 to 1.5x relative to desktop.
- Cap growth: with pure Scale, a 4K TV makes panels enormous (Docs warn about this). Use a `UISizeConstraint` or a scale clamp (rule of thumb: stop growing at about 1.2 times the design size).
- Everything must be reachable with a gamepad and show a visible selection. See Gamepad and Console UX.
- Older TVs overscan; keep critical UI out of the outer few percent of the screen (rule of thumb, roughly 5%).

---

## 8. Testing workflow that worked

1. Build at 1920 x 1080.
2. Run the automated checks at all five viewports.
3. Look at screenshots at 667 x 375 first: it fails first.
4. Test a notched phone emulation for safe areas.
5. Test with the Controller Emulator for selection.
6. Play on a real phone before release. Emulators do not show thumb occlusion, heat, or how small 12 px really is in your hand.

The reference project's changelog shows the cost of skipping step 6: many phone passes were marked "Edit only, not play-tested", and the "fix phone GUI" pass that followed (folded rail colliding with the touch combat cluster, elite bar under the top bar, overlapping combat buttons) came straight from a player's phone screenshot.

---

## Common mistakes

- `TouchEnabled` used as "is a phone".
- One global `UIScale` with no floor; phone text at 6 px.
- Zoom-and-pan instead of real phone layouts.
- Tap targets that pass on desktop and draw at 30 px on a phone.
- Checks with their own copy of placement numbers (they drift).
- Never testing 667 x 375 or a notched device.
- Signing off phone UI without playing on a phone.

## Checklist

- [ ] Device profile separates layout family from input.
- [ ] Five viewports plus a notched phone in every test pass.
- [ ] Numbers enforced: 12 px text, 44 px taps, 8 px gaps, 0 overlaps.
- [ ] Phone arrangements store and restore desktop exactly.
- [ ] Automated checks call the game's own placement code.
- [ ] HUD hides secondary items on phones; top-down slots start below the top bar.
- [ ] TV text enlarged and growth capped.
- [ ] Played on a real phone.

See also: Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints, Safe Areas and Insets, HUD Design, Gamepad and Console UX, Accessibility, Mobile and Low-End Optimization, QA Checklists Before Release, Case Study - Phone UI Overhaul.

# UI Layout Objects - Lists Grids and Pages

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Tweening `Position` of a child under a layout (nothing happens).
> - Avoid: `SortOrder = Name`, then a rename reorders the menu.
> - Avoid: Duplicate `LayoutOrder`s (order varies between sessions).
> - Every layout uses `SortOrder = LayoutOrder` with gapped, unique orders.
> - Laid-out slots are static; animation happens on inner faces.
> - Tab bars use flex `Fill`; card rows with uneven content use `Stretch`.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~4.5k tok. Read more: ## 3. Flex layouts · ## 7. ScrollingFrame with layouts · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Layout objects arrange the siblings they sit next to. Insert a `UIListLayout` into a frame and every other `GuiObject` child of that frame is positioned (and possibly sized) by the layout instead of by its own `Position`. This note covers `UIListLayout` (including wrapping and flex), `UIFlexItem`, `UIGridLayout`, `UIPageLayout`, `UITableLayout` and `ScrollingFrame` with automatic canvas size, plus the performance and ordering traps that show up in shops and inventories with hundreds of entries.

Sources: **Docs** (engine reference, "List and flex layouts", "Grid and table layouts", "Scrolling frames", October 2026), the **reference project** (one production game), and **rule of thumb**. Single-object sizing is in Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints.

---

## 1. What a layout takes over

Docs warn that once a layout is inserted it "either overrides or influences" `Position`, `Rotation` and/or `Size` of its siblings, so editing those in Properties or scripts "will not have the normal effect". In practice:

| Property of a child | Under `UIListLayout` (no flex) | Under flex | Under `UIGridLayout` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Position` | Ignored | Ignored | Ignored |
| `Size` | Used | Overridden on the flex axis | Overridden by `CellSize` |
| `AnchorPoint` | Ignored for placement | Ignored | Ignored |
| `Visible = false` | Skipped, no gap left | Skipped | Skipped |
| `LayoutOrder` | Sort key (if `SortOrder = LayoutOrder`) | Same | Same |

Two consequences:

- **You cannot animate a child's `Position` inside a layout.** To slide or bob an item, animate an inner frame inside the item, or a `UIScale`, never the laid-out child itself. This is why production cards are usually two levels deep: a laid-out "slot" and a free "face" inside it.
- **Hiding a child collapses the gap.** Great for HUD rails that hide locked buttons; bad when you want a stable grid (use transparency instead of `Visible` for placeholders).

`UIGridStyleLayout` (the base of list, grid and page layouts) exposes `AbsoluteContentSize`, the pixel size of everything laid out. It is the number you need for sizing a container to its content when `AutomaticSize` is not enough, and `ApplyLayout()` forces an immediate re-layout (Docs).

---

## 2. UIListLayout

Core properties (Docs):

- `FillDirection`: `Horizontal` or `Vertical`.
- `SortOrder`: `LayoutOrder` (ascending integers) or `Name` (alphanumeric). `Custom` with `SetCustomSortFunction` also exists on the base class.
- `HorizontalAlignment` / `VerticalAlignment`: where the whole list sits in the container, and how items align to each other.
- `Padding`: a `UDim` gap **between** items only. Use `UIPadding` on the container for space around the list.
- `Wraps`: when items exceed the container on the fill axis, continue on a new line.

### Sort order rules that save time

- Always use `SortOrder = LayoutOrder` in production. Sorting by `Name` means renaming an item reorders the menu.
- Leave gaps: order items 10, 20, 30, not 1, 2, 3, so a new item can slot in at 15 without renumbering.
- To reverse a horizontal list (right to left), negate the orders (Docs suggest `0, -1, -2, -3`).
- Ties fall back to the order the objects were added in (**Roblox docs**, GuiObject.LayoutOrder). That order changes when items are re-parented or rebuilt, so give every item a unique `LayoutOrder` when the order matters.

### Wrapping: grids without UIGridLayout

`Wraps = true` turns a list into a flowing grid where items keep their own sizes. The reference project's HUD rail is a vertical `UIListLayout` with `Wraps` on, so the button column flows into a second column when it runs out of height, giving a two-wide grid of square buttons whose count can change (shop, upgrades, index, worlds, forge, and so on) without hand placement. On phones a script hides two of the squares and sets the rail's height so it wraps three high by two wide; their measured rule was that a three-wide rail collided with the hotbar and boss bar at 667 x 375.

---

## 3. Flex layouts

Flex adds distribution of spare space to `UIListLayout` (Docs):

- `HorizontalFlex` (horizontal lists) and `VerticalFlex` (vertical lists) take a `UIFlexAlignment`: `None`, `Fill`, `SpaceAround`, `SpaceBetween`, `SpaceEvenly`.
  - `Fill`: items resize to fill the line, overriding their own size on that axis. The number of items per line does not change.
  - The three `Space*` modes keep item sizes and distribute gaps.
- `ItemLineAlignment` (`Automatic`, `Start`, `Center`, `End`, `Stretch`) aligns items across the line. `Stretch` makes every item fill the line's cross size, which evens out cards whose content heights differ.

`UIFlexItem`, parented to one child, overrides flex for that child alone (Docs):

| `FlexMode` | Effective grow:shrink | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `None` | 0:0 | Keeps its size |
| `Grow` | 1:0 | Takes spare space, never shrinks below its size (can overflow) |
| `Shrink` | 0:1 | Gives up space when cramped, never grows |
| `Fill` | 1:1 | Always fills the line |
| `Custom` | `GrowRatio` : `ShrinkRatio` | Your ratios |

`UIFlexItem.ItemLineAlignment` overrides the cross alignment for that item.

### When flex is the right answer

- **Tab bars.** `HorizontalFlex = Fill` gives equal tabs whatever their count; Docs use this exact example. Adding a sixth tab needs no maths.
- **Slider rows.** Fixed-width labels at both ends, one bar with `UIFlexItem` `Fill` between them.
- **Footer pill bars.** Pills keep their text widths with `SpaceBetween`.
- **Cards with uneven text.** `ItemLineAlignment = Stretch` so every card in a row is the same height.

### When it is not

Docs: flex "adds a slight performance cost above non-flex, especially when resizing the layout or dynamically adding/removing flex items", and a grid layout is preferable when items must align in both X and Y. Do not put flex on a list that gets items added every frame (a kill feed, a damage log); use a plain list.

```lua
--!strict
-- Equal-width tab bar that adapts to any number of tabs.
local function buildTabBar(parent: GuiObject, names: { string }): Frame
	local bar = Instance.new("Frame")
	bar.Name = "TabBar"
	bar.Size = UDim2.new(1, 0, 0, 48)
	bar.BackgroundTransparency = 1

	local list = Instance.new("UIListLayout")
	list.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Horizontal
	list.SortOrder = Enum.SortOrder.LayoutOrder
	list.HorizontalFlex = Enum.UIFlexAlignment.Fill
	list.Padding = UDim.new(0, 6)
	list.Parent = bar

	for i, name in names do
		local tab = Instance.new("TextButton")
		tab.Name = "Tab_" .. name
		tab.LayoutOrder = i * 10
		tab.Size = UDim2.new(0, 80, 1, 0) -- 80 is the basis; Fill overrides width
		tab.Text = name
		tab.TextSize = 18
		tab.Parent = bar
	end

	bar.Parent = parent
	return bar
end
```

---

## 4. UIGridLayout

For strict two-dimensional grids where every cell is the same size (Docs):

- `CellSize` (`UDim2`) and `CellPadding` (`UDim2`).
- `FillDirection`: which axis fills first.
- `FillDirectionMaxCells`: cap on cells per row (or column) before wrapping. 0 means as many as fit.
- `StartCorner`: which corner the grid starts from.
- `AbsoluteCellSize` and `AbsoluteCellCount` (read-only): what the engine actually used.

### Responsive cell counts

A Scale `CellSize` like `UDim2.fromScale(0.2, 0.2)` gives five columns but non-square cells. The robust pattern computes Offset cell sizes from the container's width and a target column count:

```lua
--!strict
-- Keeps square-ish cards, picks how many fit, recomputes on resize.
local function fitGrid(container: GuiObject, grid: UIGridLayout, minCell: number, gap: number, aspect: number)
	local function apply()
		local width = container.AbsoluteSize.X
		if width <= 0 then
			return
		end
		local columns = math.max(1, math.floor((width + gap) / (minCell + gap)))
		local cell = math.floor((width - gap * (columns - 1)) / columns)
		grid.CellPadding = UDim2.fromOffset(gap, gap)
		grid.CellSize = UDim2.fromOffset(cell, math.floor(cell / aspect))
		grid.FillDirectionMaxCells = columns
	end
	container:GetPropertyChangedSignal("AbsoluteSize"):Connect(apply)
	apply()
end
```

Note the trap: `AbsoluteSize` here is post-`UIScale`. If the grid lives inside a scaled panel, compute in design units (divide by the scale) or the column count changes when the panel pops open from 0.92 to 1 and the grid jumps mid-animation. The reference project hit exactly this class of bug: its card pops had to be made relative to the card's own base scale after phones drew cards larger.

### Grid versus wrapped list

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Identical cells, both axes aligned (inventory, index) | `UIGridLayout` |
| Items of different widths flowing like text (tags, chips) | `UIListLayout` with `Wraps` |
| Rows of uneven cards that should share a height | `UIListLayout` with `Wraps` and `ItemLineAlignment = Stretch` |

---

## 5. UIPageLayout

Turns children into pages shown one at a time with an animated scroll (Docs). Useful properties and members:

- `Animated`, `TweenTime`, `EasingStyle`, `EasingDirection`, `Circular`, `Padding`.
- Input switches, all default true: `GamepadInputEnabled` (overrides `NextSelection*` to page), `ScrollWheelInputEnabled`, `TouchInputEnabled` (swipe).
- `CurrentPage`, `JumpTo(page)`, `JumpToIndex(index)` (wraps modulo the page count), `Next()`, `Previous()`.
- Events `PageEnter`, `PageLeave`, `Stopped`.

Good for onboarding carousels, a codex, and "pick your world" pickers. Two cautions:

- **Built-in input can fight your input.** Touch swiping a page also scrolls a `ScrollingFrame` inside it; the mouse wheel pages when the player meant to scroll a list. Turn off the inputs you do not want.
- **All pages exist at once.** A page layout with ten heavy pages holds all ten in memory. For big tabbed menus, prefer one container with `Visible` tabs (or build pages on demand). Use `PageEnter` and `PageLeave` to start and stop page animation.

---

## 6. UITableLayout

Treats children as rows (or columns, via `MajorAxis`) and their children as cells, aligning columns across rows (Docs: `FillEmptySpaceColumns`, `FillEmptySpaceRows`, `MajorAxis`, `Padding`). It suits stat tables and leaderboards where the columns must line up. For most game UI a vertical list of row frames, each with a horizontal flex list and fixed-width columns, is easier to style and animate.

---

## 7. ScrollingFrame with layouts

The modern recipe:

1. A `ScrollingFrame` with `AutomaticCanvasSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.Y` (or X for horizontal strips) and `CanvasSize = UDim2.new()`.
2. A `UIListLayout` or `UIGridLayout` inside.
3. `UIPadding` inside for edge spacing.
4. `ScrollingDirection` set to the one axis you mean.

Docs: `AutomaticCanvasSize` "behaves the same" as `AutomaticSize` but resizes the canvas. Other properties worth knowing: `ElasticBehavior` (touch overscroll), `ScrollBarThickness`, `VerticalScrollBarInset` (whether the canvas is narrowed by the bar), and `CanvasPosition` for programmatic scrolling. `GetScrollVelocity` and `ResetScrollVelocity` control inertia (Docs).

Two production traps:

- **Scrollbar overlap.** With `VerticalScrollBarInset = None`, a 12 px bar covers the right edge of every card. Use `ScrollBar` inset, or pad the right side by the bar thickness.
- **Phones and nested scrolling.** A horizontal strip inside a vertical scroller is fine; two scrollers on the same axis fight for the finger. The reference project's phone layouts turned tabs, chips and categories into **horizontal** strips precisely so the main content could own vertical scrolling.

### Scrolling to the selected item

```lua
--!strict
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

-- Bring a child into view (vertical scroller), e.g. after gamepad selection.
local function scrollIntoView(scroller: ScrollingFrame, child: GuiObject, margin: number)
	local top = child.AbsolutePosition.Y - scroller.AbsolutePosition.Y + scroller.CanvasPosition.Y
	local bottom = top + child.AbsoluteSize.Y
	local viewTop = scroller.CanvasPosition.Y
	local viewBottom = viewTop + scroller.AbsoluteWindowSize.Y
	local target = viewTop
	if top - margin < viewTop then
		target = top - margin
	elseif bottom + margin > viewBottom then
		target = bottom + margin - scroller.AbsoluteWindowSize.Y
	end
	if target ~= viewTop then
		TweenService:Create(scroller, TweenInfo.new(0.15), {
			CanvasPosition = Vector2.new(scroller.CanvasPosition.X, math.max(0, target)),
		}):Play()
	end
end
```

The engine already scrolls to a gamepad-selected child, but not with your margin and not for selection you set from code; this helper makes both consistent. Note that this computes in absolute pixels, so it works inside a `UIScale`d panel too.

---

## 8. Big lists: when the layout itself is the problem

A layout recomputes when a child is added, removed, resized or reordered. For a backpack with 600 items, building 600 cards means 600 instances times every card's children (often 10 to 20 each), so 6,000 to 12,000 instances, and a re-layout every time one changes.

Measured guidance (rule of thumb, consistent with the reference project's inventory work):

| Item count | Approach |
|---|---|
| Under about 100 | Build all cards; fine everywhere |
| 100 to 500 | Build all, but reuse cards (pool) when filtering instead of destroying and rebuilding; batch inserts in one frame |
| Over 500 | Virtualise: build only the cards in view plus a buffer, place them by `Position` yourself (no layout), and set `CanvasSize` from the item count |

```lua
--!strict
-- Minimal vertical virtualiser: fixed row height, pooled rows, no UIListLayout.
type RowBinder = (row: Frame, index: number) -> ()

local function virtualList(scroller: ScrollingFrame, template: Frame, rowHeight: number, count: number, bind: RowBinder)
	scroller.AutomaticCanvasSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.None
	scroller.CanvasSize = UDim2.fromOffset(0, rowHeight * count)

	local pool: { Frame } = {}
	local function rowAt(i: number): Frame
		local row = pool[i]
		if not row then
			row = template:Clone()
			row.Parent = scroller
			pool[i] = row
		end
		return row
	end

	local function refresh()
		local viewH = scroller.AbsoluteWindowSize.Y
		local first = math.max(1, math.floor(scroller.CanvasPosition.Y / rowHeight))
		local visible = math.ceil(viewH / rowHeight) + 2
		for slot = 1, visible do
			local index = first + slot - 1
			local row = rowAt(slot)
			if index <= count then
				row.Visible = true
				row.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(0, (index - 1) * rowHeight)
				bind(row, index)
			else
				row.Visible = false
			end
		end
		for slot = visible + 1, #pool do
			pool[slot].Visible = false
		end
	end

	scroller:GetPropertyChangedSignal("CanvasPosition"):Connect(refresh)
	scroller:GetPropertyChangedSignal("AbsoluteWindowSize"):Connect(refresh)
	refresh()
end
```

Rebinding only writes properties that changed in a well-written `bind` (compare before assigning), which keeps the ScreenGui cache valid most frames (ScreenGui Fundamentals).

---

## 9. Layout objects and animation

- Animate faces inside slots, not slots (section 1).
- To animate an item entering a list, add it with a `UIScale` at 0 and tween to 1; the layout reserves its full size immediately, so neighbours jump. If that jump is ugly, animate the slot's `Size` on the fill axis from 0 instead (layouts do use child `Size` when flex is off).
- A pressed button inside a list that scales up overlaps its neighbours; that is fine for a 1.06 hover, ugly at 1.2. The reference project's hover scale is 1.06 with a 3 px lift for this reason.
- Grids keep scaled cells centred only if the scaling happens on an inner child with `AnchorPoint (0.5, 0.5)`. The same project re-anchored every zoom target to its centre in place, and for list items moved the scaled visuals into a centred inner "HoverContent" frame.

---

## Common mistakes

- Tweening `Position` of a child under a layout (nothing happens).
- `SortOrder = Name`, then a rename reorders the menu.
- Duplicate `LayoutOrder`s (order varies between sessions).
- Flex on a list that changes every frame.
- Scale `CellSize` that stretches cards on wide screens.
- Grid maths reading post-`UIScale` sizes during an open animation.
- A `UIPageLayout` swallowing the mouse wheel meant for a list.
- Building 600 cards with 15 children each on menu open.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every layout uses `SortOrder = LayoutOrder` with gapped, unique orders.
- [ ] Laid-out slots are static; animation happens on inner faces.
- [ ] Tab bars use flex `Fill`; card rows with uneven content use `Stretch`.
- [ ] Grids compute Offset cell size from available width.
- [ ] Scrollers use `AutomaticCanvasSize` on one axis and pad for the scrollbar.
- [ ] Lists over a few hundred items are pooled or virtualised.

See also: Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints, [[Responsive UI for Phone Tablet Console and PC]], Menu Archetypes - Shop Settings Codes Rewards, Gamepad and Console UX, UI and GUI Animation, [[Script Performance]].
