# UI Motion Language and Timing

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Hiding on `Completed` without checking state -> Check `Enum.PlaybackState.Completed` and current intent
> - Avoid: Back In on exits -> Quad or Quint In
> - Avoid: Input disabled until entrance ends -> Accept input from first visible frame
> - All UI tweens go through one module with named tokens.
> - Exits are faster than entrances and use In easing without overshoot.
> - Moves scale duration with screen-space distance, clamped.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~6.4k tok. Read more: ## 5. Interruption: where most UI motion breaks · ## 8. A motion module that enforces the language · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

A motion language is the small set of rules that decides how every piece of UI moves: which direction things come from, how long they take, which easing they use, what happens when the player interrupts them, and what all of it collapses to when the player asks for reduced motion. Without one, every panel gets tuned by whoever built it, and the game ends up with 40 different "open" animations that feel like 40 different products.

This note goes past the button numbers already listed in UI Design Systems and Game Feel and Juice, and the pattern catalogue in UI and GUI Animation. It is about the decisions behind the numbers: timing that scales with distance, interruption, choreography, what property to animate, and the failure modes that only show up when real players mash buttons on a phone at 30 fps.

---

## 1. What motion is for

UI motion has exactly four jobs. If an animation does none of them, cut it.

| Job | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Orientation** | Where did this come from, where did it go? | The shop slides in from the shop button; closing it shrinks back toward the button |
| **Causality** | What did my input do? | Press squash on a button; a coin flying from the enemy into the counter |
| **Hierarchy** | What should I look at first? | The reward card arrives before the "Claim" button; the button arrives last |
| **State** | Is this busy, ready, locked, new? | A breathing glow on a claimable reward; a shake on a locked one |

"It looks nice" is not on the list. Decorative motion is allowed, but it is idle life (see UI and GUI Animation, looping tweens) and it has a budget, not a job.

The corollary: **motion must be consistent to carry meaning.** If the shop enters from the right and the inventory enters from the bottom for no reason, players learn nothing from direction. If every panel that is "on top of the world" scales in from centre and every panel that is "part of the HUD" slides from its edge, direction starts to mean something.

---

## 2. The vocabulary: five verbs

Define motion as verbs, not as per-element tweens. Every animation in the game should be one of these:

| Verb | Use | Easing family | Duration (rule of thumb) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Enter** | Something appears | Out (decelerate into rest); Back Out for playful styles | 0.18 to 0.30 s |
| **Exit** | Something leaves | In (accelerate away); never Back In for anything that blocks input | 0.10 to 0.18 s |
| **Move** | Something already visible changes place or size | InOut (Quad or Sine) | 0.20 to 0.40 s, scaled by distance |
| **Feedback** | Confirm an input | Out, very short; springs if interruptible | 0.06 to 0.12 s down, 0.20 to 0.30 s back |
| **Emphasis** | Draw the eye to a change | Back Out pop, or a spring kick | 0.25 to 0.45 s |

Why exits are faster than entrances: the player chose to leave, so the old content is no longer interesting, and anything blocking the screen delays the next action. A good rule of thumb is exit time = 0.6 to 0.75 of enter time. The reference project landed on 0.26 s in and 0.14 s out for its popups, a ratio of about 0.54, and players read it as "snappy", not "abrupt".

Why Back In is dangerous on exits: Back In first moves the element *the wrong way* (it grows slightly before shrinking). On a close button that reads as hesitation, and on a fast double tap it reads as the panel refusing to close. Use Quad In or Quint In for exits; save overshoot for arrivals.

Roblox's `Enum.EasingStyle.Back` has a fixed overshoot (you cannot pass a tension parameter to `TweenInfo`). If Back is too bouncy for a large element, either shorten it, animate a smaller range (scale from 0.92, not from 0), or use a spring where you control damping (Springs Damping and Smoothing).

---

## 3. Timing numbers and why they scale

### Perception bands (rule of thumb)

| Duration | How it reads |
|---|---|
| Under 0.1 s | Instant; the motion itself is barely seen, only its result |
| 0.1 to 0.2 s | Snappy; ideal for feedback and exits |
| 0.2 to 0.35 s | Visible motion; ideal for entrances and small moves |
| 0.35 to 0.6 s | Deliberate; only for big reveals or large travel |
| Over 0.6 s | Slow; the player is waiting on you. Acceptable only in a reward sequence the player is enjoying, never in navigation |

These are not Roblox facts, they are general interaction design guidance, but they hold on Roblox with one twist: **frame rate**. A 0.12 s tween at 30 fps is 3 or 4 frames. At that length the easing curve is not visible at all, only the endpoints. On low-end phones, very short tweens degrade into a pop, so durations below about 0.08 s are pointless except as a way of saying "instant but not jarring".

### Duration should scale with distance

A fixed 0.3 s for every move makes short moves look sluggish and long moves look frantic. Scale duration with distance, with a floor and a ceiling:

```
duration = clamp(base + k * sqrt(distance_in_px), minT, maxT)
```

The square root is the important part: doubling distance should not double time. With base 0.12, k 0.012, min 0.15, max 0.45 (rule of thumb starting values, tune by eye):

| Distance | Duration |
|---|---|
| 40 px | 0.19 s |
| 200 px | 0.29 s |
| 600 px | 0.41 s |
| 1200 px | 0.45 s (capped) |

Size matters too: a full-screen panel entering should be slower than a 60 px toast, even over the same distance, because more of the screen is changing. A practical shortcut is to give large surfaces their own token (`enterLarge`) about 1.3 times the small one, rather than computing area.

### Distance should be in screen space, not UDim

If you compute distance from `UDim2.Scale`, a move of 0.5 scale is 400 px on a phone and 1,280 px on a 2560 px monitor. Compute it from `AbsolutePosition` differences, or accept that durations will be "wrong" on one end. Reading `AbsolutePosition` is cheap; just do not read it every frame.

---

## 4. Easing choices that hold up

| Situation | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Panel enters | Back Out (playful) or Quint Out (clean) | Decelerating into rest feels like arrival |
| Panel exits | Quad In or Quint In | Accelerating away feels like departure |
| Tab indicator slides between tabs | Quad InOut or a critically damped spring | Starts and ends at rest; spring handles rapid tab switching |
| Progress bar fills | Quad Out | Fast start reads as responsive, slow end as precise |
| Number count-up | Quad Out, or Exponential Out for huge numbers | Most of the change happens early; the last digits settle |
| Looping idle (bob, breathe) | Sine InOut with `Reverses = true` | No visible seam at the turnaround |
| Shake | Not a tween; a decaying noise or spring kick | Tweens cannot express oscillation that decays |

**Linear is almost never right** for spatial motion. It is right for things that represent time (a cooldown sweep, a timer bar) because the player reads the bar as a clock.

**Elastic and Bounce styles** look fun in isolation and terrible at scale. Elastic overshoots several times; on a panel that means the content wobbles while the player tries to read it. Use them for single icons in a reward moment only.

---

## 5. Interruption: where most UI motion breaks

Players do not wait for animations. They double tap, they open the shop while the inventory is closing, they press B on a gamepad mid-entrance. Every animation must answer "what happens if this is interrupted at any frame?"

### What the engine does

- Creating and playing a new tween on a **property that another tween is already animating** on the same instance overrides the older tween; the older one stops and its `Completed` fires with `Enum.PlaybackState.Cancelled` (Roblox docs, "Tween Conflict" sample on `TweenBase`; the older reference wording described it as cancelled and overwritten). The new tween starts from **the current value**, not the old start value.
- Tweens animating **different properties** of the same instance run side by side.
- `Tween:Cancel()` stops the tween and leaves the property wherever it was; it does not snap back. The tween can be replayed from the start.
- `Tween:Pause()` keeps progress; `Play()` resumes.

### The three rules that follow

**Rule 1: never hide or destroy on `Completed` without checking the state.** The classic bug: close starts, `Completed` will set `Visible = false`; the player reopens before it finishes; the open tween overrides the close tween; the close tween's `Completed` fires with `Cancelled`; the handler hides the panel anyway. The player sees the shop open and then vanish.

```lua
closeTween.Completed:Connect(function(state: Enum.PlaybackState)
	if state == Enum.PlaybackState.Completed then
		panel.Visible = false
	end
end)
```

**Rule 2: drive animations from state, not from events.** Store "this panel should be open" as a boolean. Every input flips the boolean and calls one function that animates toward the state. Rapid toggling then always converges to the last requested state, and you never need "is it animating?" flags.

**Rule 3: retarget with proportional time.** If a close is interrupted at 80% by a reopen, the panel is only 20% away from fully open, so the reopen should take about 20% of the entrance time, not all of it. The remaining distance decides the time. For scale and transparency animations, compute the fraction left:

```lua
-- fraction of the way from `from` to `to` still remaining, given the current value
local function remainingFraction(current: number, from: number, to: number): number
	if from == to then
		return 0
	end
	return math.clamp((to - current) / (to - from), 0, 1)
end

local t = token.time * remainingFraction(scale.Scale, 0.9, 1)
```

Without this, a panel that was 95% closed when the player reopened it takes the full entrance time to travel 5% of the way, which feels like input lag.

### When to use springs instead

Springs handle interruption natively: a spring keeps velocity, so retargeting mid-motion curves smoothly instead of restarting an easing curve from zero velocity. That is why tab indicators, sliders, drag-and-release, and HUD tiles that get poked often are better as springs. The cost is a per-frame update while moving. The reference project ran one shared render-step connection that existed only while any spring was unsettled and disconnected when everything came to rest, so idle UI cost zero Lua per frame (HUD Design, section 7). The math and frame-rate-independent integrators are in Springs Damping and Smoothing.

Newer engine builds also list a `TweenService:SmoothDamp(current, target, velocity, smoothTime, maxSpeed?, dt?)` method that returns the new value and new velocity (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). It is a critically damped follower in the style of other engines. It is a reasonable built-in for "follow the target smoothly" motion; it does not overshoot, so it cannot replace a bouncy spring. The docs page lists the signature but little behavioural detail, so test it before building a system on it.

---

## 6. Choreography: several things moving at once

### Stagger

When a grid of reward cards or a list of quests appears, staggering their entrances tells the eye the reading order. Two numbers matter: the per-item step and the total cap.

| Item count | Step | Total |
|---|---|---|
| 2 to 5 | 0.05 to 0.07 s | under 0.3 s |
| 6 to 12 | 0.03 to 0.04 s | 0.3 to 0.4 s |
| More than 12 | Stagger only the first row or the first 8, then show the rest together | 0.4 s cap |

The cap is the important part. A 40-item inventory staggered at 0.05 s takes 2 s to finish appearing, and the player cannot click item 30 until it arrives. Compute the step as `min(step, cap / (count - 1))`.

### Lead and follow

In a composite panel, one element leads and the rest follow:

1. The **container** enters (scale or slide), 0.2 to 0.26 s.
2. The **content** fades or rises 0.04 to 0.08 s later, over a shorter duration, so it finishes about the same time as the container.
3. The **primary action button** arrives last, with emphasis (a small pop), because it is what the player does next.

Exits reverse the hierarchy but compress it: everything leaves together. Nobody wants to watch a choreographed goodbye.

### Overlap, not sequence

Chained animations (`Completed:Wait()` then the next) add up. Three 0.25 s steps in sequence is 0.75 s of the player waiting. Overlap them: start step 2 when step 1 is about 60% done. A `task.delay` with the right offset is simpler and more robust than waiting on `Completed`, which also never fires if the tween is overridden in some code paths you did not expect.

---

## 7. What property to animate

The property you tween decides the cost and the side effects.

| Property | Cost and side effects | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `UIScale.Scale` | Cheap; scales the whole subtree including text and strokes; does not change layout slots | Pops, panel entrances, press squash |
| `Size` | Triggers layout of siblings and re-wraps text every frame; `TextScaled` text recomputes | List items growing into place on purpose (see [[UI Layout Objects - Lists Grids and Pages]], section 9) |
| `Position` | Cheap unless a layout owns the element (layouts overwrite it) | Slides, flying gains |
| `Rotation` | Cheap; children rotate with it; clipping (`ClipsDescendants`) does not rotate with content | Wiggles, spinners |
| `BackgroundTransparency` / `ImageTransparency` per element | One tween per element; children are unaffected | Single-element fades |
| `CanvasGroup.GroupTransparency` | One property fades the whole subtree correctly, but the group renders to an off-screen texture (memory, and text inside can look soft) | Whole-panel fades |
| `UIGradient.Offset` / `Rotation` | Cheap; great for shine sweeps | Shine, shimmer |
| Text content (count-up) | Every write re-shapes text and invalidates the ScreenGui cache | Counters, at a capped update rate |

Two non-obvious points:

- **Scaling a panel with `UIScale` makes `TextScaled` text and `UIStroke` thickness scale too**, which is usually what you want for a pop. Tweening `Size` instead makes `TextScaled` text jump between font sizes as the box grows, which shows as visible stepping in the text. If a pop "shimmers", check whether it is a `Size` tween.
- **Fading without a CanvasGroup** means tweening each element's transparency, so remember each element's designed base transparency (an attribute set the first time) and fade toward it. Otherwise a frame designed at 0.3 fades in to 0 and the design changes after the first open.

---

## 8. A motion module that enforces the language

The point of a module is not convenience. It is that nobody can write `TweenInfo.new(0.37, Enum.EasingStyle.Elastic)` in a panel script without it being obvious in review.

```lua
--!strict
-- Motion: the only place TweenInfo is created for UI.
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")

export type TokenName = "feedback" | "release" | "enter" | "enterLarge" | "exit" | "move" | "emphasis"

local TOKENS: { [TokenName]: TweenInfo } = {
	feedback = TweenInfo.new(0.08, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out),
	release = TweenInfo.new(0.30, Enum.EasingStyle.Back, Enum.EasingDirection.Out),
	enter = TweenInfo.new(0.24, Enum.EasingStyle.Back, Enum.EasingDirection.Out),
	enterLarge = TweenInfo.new(0.30, Enum.EasingStyle.Quint, Enum.EasingDirection.Out),
	exit = TweenInfo.new(0.14, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.In),
	move = TweenInfo.new(0.28, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.InOut),
	emphasis = TweenInfo.new(0.36, Enum.EasingStyle.Back, Enum.EasingDirection.Out),
}

-- Properties that are "motion" (removed under reduced motion). Fades stay.
local MOTION_PROPS = { Position = true, Size = true, Rotation = true, Scale = true }

local Motion = {}

-- A game-level override so players can reduce motion even if the OS setting is off.
Motion.forceReduced = false

function Motion.reduced(): boolean
	return Motion.forceReduced or GuiService.ReducedMotionEnabled
end

local function scaledInfo(info: TweenInfo, fraction: number): TweenInfo
	return TweenInfo.new(info.Time * math.clamp(fraction, 0, 1), info.EasingStyle, info.EasingDirection)
end

-- Animate `inst` toward `goals` with a named token.
-- fraction (optional) shortens the tween when retargeting mid-motion.
function Motion.to(inst: Instance, token: TokenName, goals: { [string]: any }, fraction: number?): Tween?
	local info = TOKENS[token]
	if fraction then
		info = scaledInfo(info, fraction)
	end

	if Motion.reduced() then
		local fades: { [string]: any } = {}
		local hasFade = false
		for prop, value in goals do
			if MOTION_PROPS[prop] then
				(inst :: any)[prop] = value -- jump straight to the end state
			else
				fades[prop] = value
				hasFade = true
			end
		end
		if not hasFade then
			return nil
		end
		goals = fades
		info = TweenInfo.new(math.min(info.Time, 0.15), Enum.EasingStyle.Linear)
	end

	local tween = TweenService:Create(inst, info, goals)
	tween:Play()
	return tween
end

-- Stagger a callback over items with a capped total duration.
function Motion.stagger(items: { GuiObject }, step: number, cap: number, fn: (GuiObject, number) -> ())
	local n = #items
	local s = if n > 1 then math.min(step, cap / (n - 1)) else 0
	if Motion.reduced() then
		s = 0
	end
	for i, item in items do
		if s == 0 then
			fn(item, i)
		else
			task.delay((i - 1) * s, function()
				if item.Parent then -- the list may have been rebuilt meanwhile
					fn(item, i)
				end
			end)
		end
	end
end

return Motion
```

Notes on the module:

- `Motion.to` returns `nil` when there is nothing to animate (reduced motion with only motion properties). Callers that wait on `Completed` must handle that; a helper that returns a finished state immediately is a good addition.
- `GuiService.ReducedMotionEnabled` is a read-only, client-side property that mirrors the player's Roblox reduced-motion setting (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). Read it on the client. Also offer your own in-game toggle (`forceReduced`), because many players never find the platform setting.
- The `fraction` argument is how panels implement Rule 3 from section 5.

### A panel controller using it

```lua
--!strict
local Motion = require(script.Parent.Motion)

local function makePanel(panel: CanvasGroup)
	local scale = panel:FindFirstChildOfClass("UIScale") or Instance.new("UIScale")
	scale.Parent = panel
	local wantOpen = false

	local function apply()
		if wantOpen then
			panel.Visible = true
			local fraction = 1 - math.clamp((scale.Scale - 0.9) / 0.1, 0, 1)
			Motion.to(scale, "enter", { Scale = 1 }, math.max(fraction, 0.3))
			Motion.to(panel, "enter", { GroupTransparency = 0 }, math.max(fraction, 0.3))
		else
			local t = Motion.to(panel, "exit", { GroupTransparency = 1 })
			Motion.to(scale, "exit", { Scale = 0.9 })
			if t then
				t.Completed:Connect(function(state: Enum.PlaybackState)
					if state == Enum.PlaybackState.Completed and not wantOpen then
						panel.Visible = false
					end
				end)
			else
				panel.Visible = false
			end
		end
	end

	return function(open: boolean)
		if open == wantOpen then
			return
		end
		wantOpen = open
		apply()
	end
end

return makePanel
```

The `max(fraction, 0.3)` floor keeps a reopen from being so short it pops; tune it. The `not wantOpen` check in `Completed` is belt and braces on top of the state check.

---

## 9. Panel stacking and navigation motion

- **One panel on top at a time** for most Roblox games. When panel B opens from panel A (shop to a product detail), either replace A (A exits, B enters, overlapped) or stack B on A with a backdrop dim on A. Do not slide both around.
- **Backdrop dim**: a full-screen black frame at 0.5 to 0.6 transparency fading in with the panel (same token). It doubles as the click-outside-to-close target. Fade it, never scale it.
- **Back navigation reverses direction**. If going deeper slides content left, going back slides it right. Players read direction as depth.
- **Gamepad selection** should not wait for the entrance. Set `GuiService.SelectedObject` at the start of the entrance, not on `Completed`, or a fast player presses A on nothing (Gamepad and Console UX).
- **Input during entrance**: buttons should accept input from the first frame they are visible. Disabling input until the animation finishes is the most common reason a UI "feels slow" even with short tweens.

---

## 10. Performance

- **Tweens run in the engine**, not in Lua, so a few dozen concurrent tweens are cheap. The cost of UI motion is mostly in what the tween invalidates: layout passes (`Size` under a layout), text shaping (text changes, `TextScaled`), and CanvasGroup re-renders.
- **Every property change invalidates the ScreenGui's cached render** (ScreenGui Fundamentals). Constantly animated pieces belong in their own small ScreenGui so the static HUD keeps its cache.
- **Infinite tweens** (`RepeatCount = -1`) keep running while invisible. Pause or cancel idle loops when their panel closes. A closed shop with six breathing glows still pays for them.
- **Per-frame Lua springs** should share one connection that disconnects when idle. A spring per button with its own `RenderStepped` connection is the most common motion-related performance leak.
- Low-end phone check: open the busiest panel at the lowest graphics setting on a real device and watch the MicroProfiler for layout or text spikes during entrance ([[MicroProfiler Guide]], Mobile and Low-End Optimization).

---

## 11. Reduced motion, done properly

"Reduced motion" does not mean "no feedback". It means no spatial movement that the player did not cause directly, and no large or looping motion.

| Normal | Reduced |
|---|---|
| Panel scales in from 0.9 | Panel fades in, 0.1 to 0.15 s |
| Button squash and lift on hover/press | Colour or brightness change only |
| Cards stagger in | All cards appear together |
| Coin flies to counter | Counter pulses its colour once |
| Screen shake on a big reward | No shake; a brief flash or sound |
| Idle bobbing icons | Static |

The reference project's rule was "fades only, no scale or lift" under reduced motion, and its camera effects kept only a halved FOV punch. Also see Accessibility.

---

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | How to spot it | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Hiding on `Completed` without checking state | Panel opens then vanishes when reopened quickly | Check `Enum.PlaybackState.Completed` and current intent |
| Back In on exits | Close looks hesitant; panel briefly grows | Quad or Quint In |
| Input disabled until entrance ends | "UI feels laggy" reports with short durations | Accept input from first visible frame |
| Same duration for every distance | Small moves sluggish, big moves frantic | Scale with sqrt of pixel distance, clamp |
| Unbounded stagger | Long lists take seconds to appear | Cap total at about 0.4 s |
| Tweening `Size` for a pop | Text steps between sizes; siblings jitter | Tween a `UIScale` |
| Full-time idle loops on closed panels | Frame time cost with nothing on screen | Pause loops when hidden |
| Each panel creates its own `TweenInfo` | Inconsistent feel; review cannot catch it | One motion module with tokens |
| Reduced motion means "do nothing" | No feedback at all for those players | Swap motion for fades and colour |
| Gamepad selection set on `Completed` | First A press does nothing | Select at start of entrance |

---

## Checklist

- [ ] All UI tweens go through one module with named tokens.
- [ ] Exits are faster than entrances and use In easing without overshoot.
- [ ] Moves scale duration with screen-space distance, clamped.
- [ ] Every hide or destroy on `Completed` checks the playback state and the current intent.
- [ ] Rapid toggling (10 taps per second) always ends in the last requested state.
- [ ] Retargeted tweens use proportional duration.
- [ ] Staggers are capped at about 0.4 s total.
- [ ] Pops use `UIScale`, not `Size`.
- [ ] Idle loops pause when their panel is hidden; springs share one connection that stops when idle.
- [ ] `GuiService.ReducedMotionEnabled` plus an in-game toggle swap motion for fades.
- [ ] Input and gamepad selection work from the first visible frame.
- [ ] Tested on a low-end phone at its lowest graphics level.

# VFX Performance Budgets and Culling

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Fine alone, lags with a full server: No onlooker share or global cap -> Governor with a global cap; onlookers at half or less
> - Hitch every few seconds in long fights: Cloning and destroying per hit -> Pools with a cap
> - Phones lag only when an effect is near the camera: Overdraw from big transparent pieces -> Shrink, raise transparency on the camera line, fewer stacked layers
> - Budgets written per cast, per caster window and per client, with onlooker share and distances.
> - Cost estimation script run on every template; worst offenders listed.
> - Gameplay effects flagged; never skipped, only simplified.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~200 tok · whole note ~6.3k tok. Read more: ## 2. Budget units that actually work · ## 4. Culling and degrading: the governor · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

VFX Design Playbook tells you how to make an effect look good, and Particle Emitters In Depth covers the emitter properties and their traps. This note is about the other half of the job: keeping the frame rate when eight players fire their best effects at once on a mid-range phone. It covers where VFX cost actually goes, how to turn "it lags in big fights" into budgets you can count, how to cull and degrade effects by distance, view and importance, and how to measure all of it. The working code is a small client-side **governor** that decides, per effect, whether to play it in full, reduced or not at all.

Source labels: **Roblox docs (as of October 2026)**, **measured in the reference project** (one live action game with hundreds of ability effects), **rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. Where VFX cost goes

People say "particles are expensive" as if there were one cost. There are at least seven, and they fail differently.

| Cost | Driven by | What it looks like | Main lever |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fill rate / overdraw** | Screen area covered by transparent pixels, times the number of layers | FPS drops when the effect is close to the camera or fills the screen; fine from far away | Smaller sprites, fewer stacked layers, keep big pieces off the camera line |
| **Particle simulation** | Particles alive (rate times lifetime, plus bursts) | Steady CPU cost that grows with the number of casters, even off-screen if nothing stops it | Particle budgets, shorter lifetimes, fewer streams |
| **Draw calls** | Distinct emitters, beams, trails and textures | Cost scales with the *number* of pieces, not their size. Docs: "Decals, textures, and particles don't batch well and add draw calls" | Fewer, richer emitters; shared textures |
| **Instance churn** | Cloning and destroying effect instances per hit | Garbage collector spikes, hitching every few seconds in long fights | Pools |
| **Property churn** | Scripts writing emitter properties every frame | Docs: "property changes to ParticleEmitters can have a dramatic impact on performance" | Set once, `Emit`, leave alone |
| **Lights and shadows** | Light instances, especially shadow-casting ones | Lighting update cost; worse under realistic lighting | Few lights, `Shadows = false`, short range |
| **Script per frame** | Tweens, `RenderStepped` loops animating meshes and beams | CPU time in your scripts; worst with many concurrent effects each owning a loop | One shared stepper, idle gates |

Two facts drive most of the decisions below:

1. **Overdraw scales with screen area, not particle count.** One 40-stud smoke puff in front of the camera can cost more than 300 tiny sparks across the room. The docs list overlapping transparency as the cause: overlapping partially transparent objects force the engine to render the same pixels several times.
2. **Simulation scales with particles alive.** Alive particles are roughly `Rate * Lifetime` for a stream and the burst count for an `Emit`, summed over every emitter in the effect. This is the number you can budget.

The server does no rendering (Roblox docs). Every cost in this note is a client cost, which is one more reason effects are built on clients ([[Client-Server Model]]).

---

## 2. Budget units that actually work

A budget only helps if you can count it before you ship. These units are countable from the template alone:

| Unit | How to count | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Peak particles alive** | Sum of burst counts plus `Rate * Lifetime.Max` of enabled streams | Simulation cost |
| **Pieces** | Emitters plus beams plus trails plus meshes | Draw calls and per-piece overhead |
| **Large pieces** | Pieces bigger than some screen fraction at typical camera distance | Overdraw |
| **Lights** | Light instances, and how many cast shadows | Lighting cost |
| **Highlights** | Highlight instances live | Each one is a separate outline pass; the old engine limit was 31, the docs now say 255 (see Highlights and Selection Effects) |
| **Lifetime** | Longest life of any piece | How long all the above stays on the bill |
| **Screen share** | Fraction of the screen covered at peak | Readability and overdraw together |

The reference project's budgets, as measured and enforced in code (see also the summary in VFX Design Playbook):

| Budget | Value (measured in the reference project) |
|---|---|
| Premium effect library | 3,200 particles per 2 s per caster; ultimate caster 5,600; onlookers half |
| One sword swing | At most about 140 beams and 30 emitters (measured max 128 and 28); finisher 210 and 44 |
| Low-detail swing | 44 beams and 10 emitters |
| Emitters per ability kit folder | 16 (cut from 24 in a readability pass) |
| Lights per ability kit | 2 (range 18, brightness 1.6); stylised effect lights at most 4 at once (range 14, brightness 1.5) |
| Highlights in the shared tier layer | 3 |
| Large non-floor pieces per cast | 3, plus one ground "floor" at a time |
| Screen share per cast | 35 percent, 55 percent during an ultimate (scale pieces down to no less than 0.6, else drop them) |
| Life caps | 1.4 s (floors 2.2 s; ultimate 2.0 and 2.8 s) |
| Others' effects | Decoration layers dropped beyond about 160 studs, small juice beyond 220 |

Notice the shape: a per-cast budget (what one effect may contain), a per-caster budget over a window (what one player may produce over time), and a distance rule for other people's effects. You need all three. A per-cast budget alone lets a player who casts four times a second exceed everything; a window budget alone lets one ultimate spike a single frame.

### Worked arithmetic: will a full server hold?

Rule-of-thumb starting point: a mid-range phone stays smooth with a few thousand simple particles alive and a few dozen effect pieces on screen. Do the sum before you build:

- 8 players in one fight, each swinging about twice a second.
- One swing effect: a 30-particle spark burst (life 0.4 s), two 6-particle slash cards (life 0.3 s), one 20-particle-per-second haze stream (life 1 s). Peak alive per swing is about 30 + 12 + 20 = 62. With two swings overlapping per player, about 124 per player.
- Your own swings: 124. Seven onlookers at half detail: 7 * 62 = 434. Total about 560 alive. Fine.
- Now everyone presses their ultimate in the same second, each 5,600 for the caster and 2,800 for onlookers: 5,600 + 7 * 2,800 = 25,200. Not fine on any phone.

That last line is the real design question. Either the ultimate budget is per server view (a global cap, section 4), or the onlooker share for ultimates is far below half, or both. The reference project used half for onlookers plus distance drops, and fights rarely had all ultimates at once; a governor with a global cap is the safer answer.

---

## 3. Count it: cost estimation from templates

Put the counting in code so the budget is checked by a script, not by eye. Effects authored for the VFX Forge style runtime carry their burst size in an `EmitCount` attribute; plain templates can carry your own attribute. This function estimates peak particles alive and piece counts for any effect root:

```lua
--!strict
-- Estimate the cost of an effect template. Run in the command bar or at load.
export type Cost = {
	particles: number, -- peak alive, approximate
	emitters: number,
	beams: number,
	trails: number,
	meshes: number,
	lights: number,
	shadowLights: number,
	highlights: number,
	longestLife: number,
}

local function estimateCost(root: Instance): Cost
	local c: Cost = {
		particles = 0, emitters = 0, beams = 0, trails = 0, meshes = 0,
		lights = 0, shadowLights = 0, highlights = 0, longestLife = 0,
	}
	for _, d in root:GetDescendants() do
		if d:IsA("ParticleEmitter") then
			c.emitters += 1
			local burst = d:GetAttribute("EmitCount")
			if type(burst) == "number" then
				c.particles += burst
			end
			if d.Enabled then
				-- A stream holds about Rate * Lifetime particles once it is warm.
				c.particles += d.Rate * d.Lifetime.Max
			end
			local delay = d:GetAttribute("EmitDelay")
			local extra = if type(delay) == "number" then delay else 0
			c.longestLife = math.max(c.longestLife, d.Lifetime.Max + extra)
		elseif d:IsA("Beam") then
			c.beams += 1
		elseif d:IsA("Trail") then
			c.trails += 1
			c.longestLife = math.max(c.longestLife, d.Lifetime)
		elseif d:IsA("MeshPart") then
			c.meshes += 1
		elseif d:IsA("Light") then
			c.lights += 1
			if d.Shadows then
				c.shadowLights += 1
			end
		elseif d:IsA("Highlight") then
			c.highlights += 1
		end
	end
	return c
end

return estimateCost
```

Run it across every template folder and print the worst offenders. In the reference project an audit of this kind found ability kit folders far over their instance budget (2,973 to 5,249 instances against 2,500), and a readability audit found 170 of 373 moves below the *minimum* layer count for their tier. Budgets cut both ways: the same script tells you which effects are too thin.

Things the estimate misses, so treat it as a lower bound: scripted spawns at runtime (bolt segments, debris), effects that call `Emit` in a loop, and the screen area of big sprites (overdraw cannot be counted from properties alone; you have to look).

---

## 4. Culling and degrading: the governor

Culling means not playing an effect; degrading means playing less of it. Both need a decision made **once, when the effect starts**, from facts the client has:

| Fact | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Owner | Is this mine, my party's, or a stranger's? |
| Gameplay flag | Is this information (telegraph, hazard, objective) or decoration? |
| Distance to camera | Will anyone see the detail? |
| In view | Is it on screen now, or about to be? |
| Current load | How many particles are already alive on this client? |
| Detail setting | What did the player (or your device heuristic) choose? |

The rule that must never bend: **gameplay information is never culled for performance.** A telegraph that disappears on low settings is a fairness bug. Gameplay effects can be simplified (fewer layers, no sparks), never skipped. Mark them with an attribute on the template and let the governor exempt them.

```lua
--!strict
-- FxGovernor: one place that decides how much of each effect to play on this client.
-- Returns a detail scale: 0 = skip, 1 = full, values between = play reduced.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

export type Request = {
	cost: number,          -- estimated peak particles (estimateCost(...).particles)
	position: Vector3,
	radius: number,        -- rough size of the effect in studs
	life: number,          -- seconds the cost stays on the bill
	owner: Player?,
	gameplay: boolean?,    -- telegraphs and hazards: never skipped
}

local FxGovernor = {}

local BUDGET = 3000        -- particles alive on this client (rule of thumb starting point)
local FAR_DECOR = 160      -- studs: others' effects lose decoration beyond this
local FAR_ALL = 220        -- studs: others' small effects are skipped beyond this
local ONLOOKER = 0.5       -- others' effects play at half detail

local live = 0
local detail = 1           -- player setting, 0..1

function FxGovernor.setDetail(d: number)
	detail = math.clamp(d, 0, 1)
end

function FxGovernor.liveParticles(): number
	return live
end

-- Conservative view test: is any part of a sphere inside the camera's horizontal or vertical cone?
local function inView(pos: Vector3, radius: number): boolean
	local cam = workspace.CurrentCamera
	if not cam then
		return true
	end
	local cf = cam.CFrame
	local to = pos - cf.Position
	local dist = to.Magnitude
	if dist <= radius then
		return true -- the camera is inside the effect
	end
	local vp = cam.ViewportSize
	local halfV = math.rad(cam.FieldOfView) * 0.5
	local halfH = math.atan(math.tan(halfV) * vp.X / math.max(vp.Y, 1))
	local half = math.max(halfV, halfH)
	local angle = math.acos(math.clamp(cf.LookVector:Dot(to / dist), -1, 1))
	return angle <= half + math.asin(math.min(radius / dist, 1))
end

function FxGovernor.request(r: Request): number
	local cam = workspace.CurrentCamera
	local dist = if cam then (r.position - cam.CFrame.Position).Magnitude else 0
	local mine = r.owner == Players.LocalPlayer

	local scale = detail
	if not mine then
		scale *= ONLOOKER
	end

	if r.gameplay then
		-- Never skipped. Still counted, so decoration makes room for it.
		scale = math.max(scale, 0.5)
	else
		if not mine then
			if dist > FAR_ALL then
				return 0
			end
			if not inView(r.position, r.radius) then
				return 0
			end
			if dist > FAR_DECOR then
				scale *= 0.5
			end
		end
		local cost = r.cost * scale
		if live + cost > BUDGET then
			-- Try once at half before refusing; your own effects get the benefit of the doubt.
			if mine and live + cost * 0.5 <= BUDGET * 1.2 then
				scale *= 0.5
			else
				return 0
			end
		end
	end

	local spent = r.cost * scale
	live += spent
	task.delay(r.life, function()
		live -= spent
	end)
	return scale
end

return FxGovernor
```

How the effect player uses the scale: layers carry a `MinDetail` attribute (0 to 1). At scale 0.5, layers with `MinDetail > 0.5` are not played and burst counts are multiplied by the scale. That keeps degradation **authored**: the artist decides which layers are decoration, not the code. The same pattern is in the burst helper in Particle Emitters In Depth.

### Design choices hidden in that code

- **Decide at start, not per frame.** Re-evaluating every frame (turning emitters on and off as the camera moves) causes popping and costs script time. An effect's life is under 2 seconds; decide once.
- **Off-screen culling is for strangers only.** Your own effects play even when the camera faces away, because you will turn around mid-effect after a dash and an empty ultimate looks broken. For strangers, a missed 1-second decoration is invisible.
- **The view test is conservative.** It uses the wider of the two half-angles and adds the effect's angular radius, so an effect at the edge of the screen still plays. Prefer playing a few invisible effects over cutting visible ones.
- **No occlusion culling by raycast.** Raycasting from camera to every effect costs more than it saves for short effects, and partial occlusion (behind a thin pillar) is common. The engine already skips drawing objects outside the field of view and occluded objects (Roblox docs); your job is to skip *simulation and spawning*, which the engine cannot know is optional.
- **Global cap, then distance, then view.** The order matters only for clarity. What matters is that a global cap exists: distance and view rules do not protect you when eight players stand in one spot.
- **Hysteresis on distance.** If something long-lived (an aura, a portal) is culled by distance, use two thresholds (turn off beyond 230, back on inside 200) so standing at the boundary does not make it flicker.

### Long-lived effects: sleep, do not cull

Auras, portals, waterfalls and station effects run for minutes. They need a different rule: a periodic check (every 0.5 to 1 s, staggered) that **sleeps** them beyond a distance and wakes them inside it, by toggling `Enabled` on streams and pausing the script that animates them. The reference project slept waterfalls and station effects beyond about 650 studs, trimmed portal layers on graphics quality 1 to 3 and slept them beyond 300 studs. Sleep means `Enabled = false` and stopping loops; the instances stay, so waking is instant.

```lua
--!strict
-- Sleep long-lived ambient effects by distance, with hysteresis and a staggered check.
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

type Sleeper = { root: Instance, pos: Vector3, sleepAt: number, wakeAt: number, awake: boolean }
local sleepers: { Sleeper } = {}

local function setAwake(s: Sleeper, awake: boolean)
	s.awake = awake
	for _, d in s.root:GetDescendants() do
		if d:IsA("ParticleEmitter") or d:IsA("Beam") or d:IsA("Trail") then
			d.Enabled = awake
		end
	end
	s.root:SetAttribute("Asleep", not awake) -- animating scripts read this and idle
end

local function register(root: Instance, pos: Vector3, sleepAt: number)
	table.insert(sleepers, { root = root, pos = pos, sleepAt = sleepAt, wakeAt = sleepAt * 0.85, awake = true })
end

local index = 0
RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function()
	-- Check a few sleepers per frame instead of all of them every frame.
	local cam = workspace.CurrentCamera
	if not cam or #sleepers == 0 then
		return
	end
	for _ = 1, math.min(4, #sleepers) do
		index = index % #sleepers + 1
		local s = sleepers[index]
		local d = (s.pos - cam.CFrame.Position).Magnitude
		if s.awake and d > s.sleepAt then
			setAwake(s, false)
		elseif not s.awake and d < s.wakeAt then
			setAwake(s, true)
		end
	end
end)

return register
```

One caveat on beams: setting `Beam.Enabled = false` hides it immediately. If you sleep something in view (because of a quality change, say), fade it first.

---

## 5. Churn: pools and lifetimes

Most "random hitch every few seconds in fights" reports are instance churn: every hit clones a 40-instance template and destroys it 2 seconds later. The fixes, from Particle Emitters In Depth and the reference project:

- **Clone templates once per client** into a pool, reposition, `Emit`, release after the longest lifetime.
- **Do not destroy an emitter while its particles live.** Destroying the emitter destroys its particles; release after `Lifetime.Max` plus any emit delay.
- **`Clear()` before reusing** a pooled emitter for an unrelated hit, or the old burst shows with the new one.
- **Pool size is a budget too.** A pool that grows without bound in a long fight is a leak. Cap it (rule of thumb: enough for your peak concurrency plus 25 percent) and refuse or recycle the oldest when it is full. See Memory Budgets and Leaks.

Memory note: pooled instances hold memory until destroyed. That is the trade: steady memory instead of churn. Measure `Instances` and the graphics memory categories in the Developer Console and Stats before and after a 5-minute fight; the curve should flatten, not climb.

---

## 6. The traps that break budgets silently

| Trap | Why it bites | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Emit` ignores engine quality scaling | Measured in the reference project: bursts were not thinned on low settings, so a burst-heavy style ran at full cost on phones | Your own detail scalar applied to `EmitCount` |
| You cannot read the effective quality level | `UserGameSettings.SavedQualityLevel` reports the saved setting, which is `Automatic` for most players | An in-game preset; see Mobile and Low-End Optimization |
| Streams do not run in Edit | Rate emission does not run in Edit and Studio only steps particles while it renders (measured) | Count in Edit, judge cost in Play |
| Server-built effects | Instances replicate to everyone and arrive late | Server sends an event; clients build |
| Big sprites near the camera | Overdraw explodes when a ground ring or dome surrounds the camera | Force pieces on the camera line to at least 0.75 transparency (reference project), or shrink them |
| Beams with high `Segments` and many copies | Each beam is a draw; staggered beam slashes multiply them | Budget beams like emitters (the swing budget above) |
| Effect lights left with shadows on | Shadow-casting lights are the expensive kind (Roblox docs) | `Shadows = false` on all VFX lights; cap per kit |
| Highlights per hit | Every live Highlight is an outline pass | Pool a few, cap them (3 in the tier layer, 8 for enemy hit flashes in the reference project) |
| One `RenderStepped` loop per effect | 30 effects, 30 loops, each allocating | One shared stepper that iterates live effects |
| EditableImage or EditableMesh for runtime VFX | Fails in published games unless the experience setting allows it, with strict memory budgets (Roblox docs) | Bake offline, upload |

---

## 7. Measuring

Budgets are hypotheses until measured on a device.

1. **Draw calls:** Studio's Render Stats (Timing) or Shift+F2 in a client (Roblox docs). Compare a quiet frame with a full-party ultimate.
2. **MicroProfiler:** the docs name "Prepare and Perform" for overall rendering and `computeLightingPerform`, `ShadowMapSystem` for lighting and shadows. If lights in effects are the problem, the lighting scopes grow during casts. See [[MicroProfiler Guide]].
3. **Script cost:** label your effect stepper with `debug.profilebegin("FxStep")` / `debug.profileend()` so it shows as its own bar.
4. **Particles alive:** expose `FxGovernor.liveParticles()` in a debug overlay. If it sits at the cap during normal fights, your cap or your effects are wrong.
5. **The stress protocol** (rule of thumb): one phone, one tablet, one PC in the same server, plus 4 to 8 test clients or friends. Everyone casts their strongest ability at the same spot, then at the phone's camera, then 200 studs away. Record FPS on each device for all three. Then repeat at the lowest and highest graphics quality. See Multi-Client and Live Testing.

A useful target from practice: the phone's frame time during the worst repeatable fight should stay under about 33 ms (30 FPS) at its default setting. If it does not, cut in this order: onlooker share, decoration layers on others' effects, big transparent pieces, stream lifetimes, then your own effects.

One thing this note cannot confirm: whether the engine stops simulating particles of an emitter that is entirely off-screen. The docs say the engine skips *drawing* objects outside the view; they do not say simulation stops. Assume it does not and cull spawning yourself.

---

## 8. When not to do this

- **Small games with few simultaneous casters.** A solo-player puzzle game with one effect at a time does not need a governor; a template audit and pools are enough.
- **Do not cull your own feedback.** The player's own hit confirmation is the most important effect on their screen. Degrade others' effects to zero before you touch it.
- **Do not distance-cull bosses, telegraphs or objectives.** Simplify them instead.
- **Do not tune budgets on a PC.** A budget tuned on a desktop GPU will be wrong by a factor of several on phones.
- **Do not make the budget invisible to artists.** If the governor silently drops layers, artists will add more layers to compensate. Put the cost estimate next to the template (an attribute or a build report) so everyone sees it.

---

## Common mistakes

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Fine alone, lags with a full server | No onlooker share or global cap | Governor with a global cap; onlookers at half or less |
| Hitch every few seconds in long fights | Cloning and destroying per hit | Pools with a cap |
| Phones lag only when an effect is near the camera | Overdraw from big transparent pieces | Shrink, raise transparency on the camera line, fewer stacked layers |
| Low settings do not help | Bursts via `Emit` bypass engine thinning | Own detail scalar on burst counts |
| Particles cut off mid-effect | Emitter destroyed or recycled too early | Release after the longest lifetime |
| Ambient effects cost frame time across the map | Never sleep | Distance sleep with hysteresis |
| Telegraph missing on a phone | Gameplay effect culled as decoration | Gameplay flag; simplify, never skip |
| Effect flickers at a distance boundary | Single threshold re-checked often | Two thresholds |

## Checklist

- [ ] Budgets written per cast, per caster window and per client, with onlooker share and distances.
- [ ] Cost estimation script run on every template; worst offenders listed.
- [ ] Gameplay effects flagged; never skipped, only simplified.
- [ ] Governor decides once per effect: owner, distance, view, global load, detail setting.
- [ ] Layers carry `MinDetail`; degradation is authored, not guessed.
- [ ] Long-lived effects sleep by distance with hysteresis.
- [ ] Pools capped; release after the longest lifetime; `Clear()` on reuse.
- [ ] VFX lights without shadows, capped per kit; Highlights pooled and capped.
- [ ] Measured on a real phone with a full party, at low and high quality.

See also: VFX Design Playbook, Particle Emitters In Depth, Beams and Trails, Highlights and Selection Effects, Light Sources and Shadows, Rendering Performance, Mobile and Low-End Optimization, Art Budgets - Triangles Draw Calls Memory, Animation LOD, Ability Kits Architecture, Cinematic Ultimates, Game Feel and Juice.

# MicroProfiler Guide

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Studio skews the picture. Server and client share the process in a solo test, and Studio has its own UI cost.
> - The profiler has overhead. Capturing, especially at many frames or with X-Ray, costs time.
> - One frame is an anecdote. Look at 30 to 90 frames; use Timers for totals.
> - Profiled on the device class with the problem, not only in Studio.
> - Captured enough frames to see the pattern (30 to 90), and looked at Timers mode.
> - Identified the family: script, physics, render, network, UI.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~170 tok · whole note ~4.3k tok. Read more: ## 3. The labels that matter · ## 4. Your own labels · ## 7. Gotchas · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

The MicroProfiler is the one tool that shows **where inside a frame** the time goes: which engine job, which script event, which of your own labelled functions. Everything else (fps counters, Script Profiler totals, memory charts) tells you *that* something is slow; the MicroProfiler tells you *what* and *when*. This note covers opening it everywhere (Studio, desktop, phone, live server), reading it, the labels that matter, adding your own labels with `debug.profilebegin`/`debug.profileend`, and the diagnosis recipes that come up again and again.

Source labels: **Docs** (Creator Hub, as of October 2026), **Measured** (the reference project), **Rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. Opening it

| Where | How (Docs) |
|---|---|
| Studio | Ctrl+F6 (Cmd+F6 on Mac) per the MicroProfiler reference page |
| Desktop client | Ctrl+F6 (Cmd+F6) |
| Phone or tablet | in the in-game Settings menu, set MicroProfiler to On; then on a computer on the same network, open the IP address and port the device shows in a browser (the Docs example uses port 1338) |
| Live server | join on the desktop client with edit permission, open the Developer Console (Ctrl+F9 / F9), choose MicroProfiler, Server tab, set frames (max 60) and start delay (max 4 s), click Begin server recording; the console prints the file path a few seconds later |

**Docs disagree on the shortcut.** The MicroProfiler reference says Ctrl+F6; the "use the MicroProfiler" walkthrough and the "identify performance issues" page say **Ctrl+Alt+F6**. If one does nothing, try the other. The Performance Summary overlay is Ctrl+Shift+F5 in the walkthrough. Tracked for Open Questions - Whole Vault.

### Pausing and dumps
- **Pause** with Ctrl+P (Cmd+P) or the Pause menu item. Pausing switches to the detailed view so you can inspect a frame.
- **Dump** from the Dump menu (Studio and desktop). Files are saved to the Roblox logs folder (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Roblox\logs` on Windows, `~/Library/Logs/Roblox` on macOS) as an HTML file you can open in any browser.
- A dump contains only the selected number of frames, except Counters mode data, which runs from start-up to the dump.

### The web UI (phones and dumps)
- Shows the 30 most recent frames by default; append `/90` (or another number) to the URL to fetch more (Docs).
- **Re-capture** fetches fresh frames; **Save to file** writes `microprofile-<date>-<time>.html`.
- **X-Ray** colours memory allocation; press **C** to switch between allocation count and total size. Very useful for hunting per-frame garbage.
- **Export** produces CPU or memory flame graphs; drag a second dump in to diff two captures ("Combine & Compare").

---

## 2. Reading the frame graph

The top of the screen is a bar per frame; height is frame time.

| What you see | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Uniformly tall bars | a steady cost every frame: a per-frame loop, physics load, scene density |
| Mostly short bars with occasional tall ones | spikes: bursts of creation, GC, synchronised timers, first-use loads |
| Bars alternating tall and short | something runs every 2nd frame (a cadence scheduler, physics catch-up) |
| Orange bars | jobs (scripts, physics, animation) took longer than render (Docs) |
| Blue bars | the render thread dominated (Docs) |
| Red bars | render dominated **and** GPU wait exceeded 2.5 ms (Docs): GPU-bound, usually scene complexity, textures, effects |

Docs caveat: small tasks at the end of a frame can skew the wall-time comparison, so trust frame time more than colour.

Reference lines: 16.67 ms is 60 fps, 33.33 ms is 30 fps. On a 60 fps target anything over the first line is a dropped frame.

### Navigation (desktop, Docs)
- Left-drag to pan, scroll to zoom.
- Labels directly below a label are its children.
- **Right-click a label to zoom to exactly its duration.**
- Left-click a frame bar to jump to it.
- Left-click a label to add its per-frame time to the line graph at the bottom right; right-click the graph to hide it.
- Ctrl+F searches task names (case-insensitive); F3 or Enter for next, Shift+F3 for previous. In a dump, Ctrl+F jumps to the most expensive task.
- The **Groups** and **Threads** menus filter what is drawn.

### Modes (Docs)
| Mode | Use it for |
|---|---|
| Frame / Detailed | the normal timeline; detailed is what you get when paused |
| **Timers** | a table of labels with time and call counts; sort to find the biggest total, not just the biggest single call |
| **Counters** | instance counts and memory by category over time (the Developer Console is recommended for memory work) |
| Groups (web only) | average, max and total per group, by thread |
| Threads (web only) | per thread, by group: is work spread or piled on one thread |
| Hidden (desktop only) | hides the bars but keeps the menu and the line graph; good for watching one label over time |

Timers mode is underused. A label that costs 0.05 ms but is called 2,000 times per frame will not stand out in the timeline; in Timers it is at the top.

---

## 3. The labels that matter

From the Docs tag reference. You do not need all of them; you need to recognise which family a wide bar belongs to.

### Scripts
| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Heartbeat` / `RunService.Heartbeat` | your Heartbeat handlers (`PostSimulation` lands here too) |
| `Simulation/gameStepped/RunService.Stepped` | Stepped / `PreSimulation` handlers |
| `Render/PreRender/RunService.RenderStepped` | RenderStepped / `PreRender` handlers |
| `fireBindToRenderSteppedCallbacks` | functions bound with `BindToRenderStep` |
| `WaitingHybridScriptJob` | resuming threads waiting on `WaitForChild` or waits; has a time budget and is throttled if scripts run too long |
| `GC` | Luau garbage collection; reduce temporary allocations, reuse tables |

Under these you see the individual script and, if you added them, your own labels.

### Physics and simulation
| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `physicsStepped` | the physics step overall |
| `worldStep`, `stepContacts`, `stepWorld` | discrete physics steps, contact updates, constraint solving |
| **`stepWorldThrottled`** | the engine is overloaded and is only simulating real-time assemblies such as Humanoids (Docs). Seeing this is an alarm. |
| `stepHumanoid` | Humanoid state and movement |
| `stepAnimation` | Animators advancing tracks |
| `interpolateNetworkedAssemblies` | smoothing parts owned by someone else |
| `Distributed Physics Ownership` | deciding network owners; frequent ownership changes add cost |
| `handleFallenParts` | removing parts below the fallen-parts height |

### Rendering
| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Prepare` / `updateInvalidParts` | parts whose properties changed or were added |
| `updateInvalidatedFastClusters` | rebuilding Humanoid and skinned mesh geometry; Docs: over 4 ms suggests excessive avatar invalidations |
| `updateDynamicParts` | Beams, ParticleEmitters, Humanoids |
| `Perform` / `queryFrustumOrdered` | culling |
| `computeLightingPerform`, `LightGridCPU` | lighting near the camera, voxel light grid |
| `ShadowMapSystem`, `Scene/Shadows` | shadow maps, only at quality level 4 and above |
| `Id_Opaque`, `Id_Transparent`, `Id_Decals` | the draw passes |
| `fillGuiVertices` | UI vertex buffers |
| `Present/waitUntilCompleted` | **GPU wait**: the CPU is waiting for the GPU to finish the previous frame; frequent long waits mean you are drawing too much |

### UI
| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `UpdateUILayouts` | recomputing UI positions and sizes |
| `Rebuild Z-order list` | draw-order rebuild after adding, removing or reordering UI |
| `Render/PreRender/TweenService` | client tweens (on the server, TweenService runs inside Heartbeat) |

### Networking
| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Net PacketReceive`, `deserializePacket` | receiving packets |
| `Replicator/ProcessPackets` | applying incoming motion, events, property changes |
| `Allocate Bandwidth and Run Senders` | outgoing: physics, data (properties, remotes, new instances), streaming |
| `ModelCompleteness Mega Job` | server tracking when models are fully sent |

### Navigation
`rasterizeTile`, `computePath`, `getPrimitivesOverlapping`: pathfinding (see Pathfinding).

---

## 4. Your own labels

Engine labels stop at "LocalScript X spent 3 ms in Heartbeat". To see *which part* of your code, add labels.

```lua
--!strict
-- debug.profilebegin(label) opens a label; debug.profileend() closes the most recent one (Docs).
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local enemies: { any } = {}

RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(dt: number)
	debug.profilebegin("EnemyAI")

	debug.profilebegin("EnemyAI.sense")
	for _, enemy in enemies do
		-- cheap distance checks, target selection
	end
	debug.profileend()

	debug.profilebegin("EnemyAI.move")
	for _, enemy in enemies do
		-- steering, ground snapping
	end
	debug.profileend()

	debug.profileend() -- closes "EnemyAI"
end)
```

Nested labels show as children, exactly like engine labels.

### Rules for labels

1. **Begin and end must pair, on the same thread, without yielding in between** (rule of thumb). A `task.wait()` or a yielding call inside a label leaves it open across frames, and the timeline becomes nonsense.
2. **An error between them leaves the label open.** If the code inside can throw, protect it:

```lua
--!strict
-- Profile a block that might error, keeping begin/end balanced.
local function profiled(label: string, fn: () -> ())
	debug.profilebegin(label)
	local ok, err = pcall(fn)
	debug.profileend()
	if not ok then
		error(err, 0) -- rethrow without adding a new position prefix
	end
end
```

`pcall` has a small cost; use the wrapper at system level (once per system per frame), not per object.

3. **Use constant label strings.** `debug.profilebegin("Enemy_" .. enemy.Id)` allocates a new string every call (more GC) and produces hundreds of distinct labels that are impossible to read. Label the system, and if you need per-object detail, add an attribute counter instead.
4. **Label at the granularity you will act on.** One label per system and one per expensive phase is plenty. Labels on every function make the view unreadable.
5. **Leave the important ones in.** Labels are cheap enough to ship at system granularity (rule of thumb), and they are exactly what you need when a live server misbehaves at 2 a.m. and you capture a server dump.

### Parallel Luau
Work done after `task.desynchronize()` (or in `ConnectParallel` handlers inside an Actor) runs on worker threads, so its labels appear on worker thread rows, not under the main thread's Heartbeat. When checking whether parallelism helped, use the **Threads** view to see whether work is really spread or serialised on one worker (rule of thumb). See [[Parallel Luau and Actors]].

---

## 5. Diagnosis recipes

### Recipe: "fps drops in one area of the map"
1. Stand in the slow area; Ctrl+F6; Ctrl+P on a slow frame.
2. Bar colour blue or red? Rendering. Check `Prepare` vs `Perform` vs `waitUntilCompleted`.
   - Big `Perform` with many draw passes: too many distinct meshes or materials. See Rendering Performance.
   - Big `ShadowMapSystem`: many shadow-casting lights; check at quality level 4+.
   - Long `waitUntilCompleted`: GPU-bound (overdraw from transparency and particles, texture size).
3. Orange? Look under Heartbeat/Stepped for a script that is only active near that area (ambient FX, an NPC group).

### Recipe: "periodic hitch every few seconds"
1. Pause right after a hitch frame (watch the frame graph for the tall bar).
2. Look for `GC` (allocation churn), a burst of `updateInvalidParts` (many parts changed at once), `Rebuild Z-order list` (a big UI was built), or a script spike.
3. If a script spikes on a fixed period, find the timer: something like "every 3 s, recompute all enemy targets" is a classic. Spread it with a random phase per entity.

### Recipe: "server feels laggy for everyone"
1. Record a server dump (Developer Console, MicroProfiler, Server, 60 frames).
2. Frames over 16.67 ms on the server are a problem (Docs).
3. Look for script Heartbeat cost, `stepWorldThrottled`, pathfinding (`computePath`), or `Allocate Bandwidth and Run Senders` dominating.
4. If it is outbound replication, see [[Network Performance]]: something is replicating too much (big attribute writes, per-frame property changes, server tweens).

### Recipe: "UI is slow when a menu is open"
1. Open the menu, profile.
2. `UpdateUILayouts` large every frame means layouts are being invalidated every frame: something writes `Size`, `Position` or `Text` every frame even when unchanged, or a `UIListLayout` with hundreds of children is re-flowing.
3. Under PreRender, look for your UI scripts. The fix is almost always "update only on change" plus "stop the loop while hidden".

### Recipe: "first use of an ability stutters"
Check for asset loading and instance cloning on that frame. Preload the clip and the VFX template when the kit is equipped, not when the button is pressed. See Engine Gotchas (first use of a clip is late).

---

## 6. Worked examples

### Docs walkthrough (Docs)
The official walkthrough plants a `RunService.Stepped` handler that casts 1,500 rays per second in random directions. In the MicroProfiler the stacked bars show the LocalScript and a Raycast child; wrapping the function in `debug.profilebegin("Raycast Spam")` confirms it. Removing it takes the frame rate from 45 to 60 fps.

### Idle UI loops (Measured)
In the reference project, a tutorial tips controller kept a `RenderStepped` handler running every frame to animate a pointing hand and highlight ring, **even when no tip was showing**. It was cheap per frame, but it was one of many such idle loops. The fix was an idle gate: when nothing is visible, the loop does nothing (and better, disconnects). In the same pass, a quest tracker's countdown timer that rewrote its text every frame was moved to 4 Hz and to write only when the displayed value changed. Neither showed up as a single big bar; both showed up in **Timers mode** as steady per-frame costs under PreRender.

### One driver for many animated cards (Measured)
An inventory screen gave each rare item card its own animation loop (glow pulse, sparkles). With a full grid that was dozens of loops. It was rebuilt as **one** `RenderStepped` driver that iterates only on-screen entries, with a pool of at most 60 sparkle frames shared by all cards. The MicroProfiler went from a forest of small script entries to one label.

---

## 7. Gotchas

- **Studio skews the picture.** Server and client share the process in a solo test, and Studio has its own UI cost. Confirm on the desktop client or a phone (Performance Fundamentals).
- **The profiler has overhead.** Capturing, especially at many frames or with X-Ray, costs time. Compare captures taken the same way.
- **One frame is an anecdote.** Look at 30 to 90 frames; use Timers for totals.
- **A frozen client cannot be profiled.** If a script never yields (an infinite `while` loop), the frame never ends and the profiler UI freezes with it. That is a debugging job (Debugger Breakpoints and Logging). In the reference project, a UI helper looped `while true` until a child parented successfully; when the parent had been destroyed by a card rebuild, it looped forever and froze the client on click. The fix capped retries at 4 and returned nil.
- **Labels in modules required by the command bar** run in a separate module instance; they will not show the live game's work.

## Checklist

- [ ] Profiled on the device class with the problem, not only in Studio.
- [ ] Captured enough frames to see the pattern (30 to 90), and looked at Timers mode.
- [ ] Identified the family: script, physics, render, network, UI.
- [ ] Added constant-string labels around suspect systems; begin/end balanced and never across a yield.
- [ ] For server issues, recorded a server dump from the Developer Console.
- [ ] Re-profiled after the fix in the same scenario and kept the useful labels.

## See also

Performance Fundamentals · Developer Console and Stats · [[Script Performance]] · Rendering Performance · Physics Performance · [[Network Performance]] · Frame Order and RunService Timing · [[Parallel Luau and Actors]] · Debugging Animation Problems
