# Testing Your Own Remotes - Fuzzing and Abuse Tests

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Harness reachable in live servers -> Three-layer gate: location, `IsStudio`, no remote entry
> - Avoid: Fuzzing against real DataStore data -> Studio API access off or test scope
> - Avoid: Only testing "valid but wrong" values -> Include NaN, inf, huge, deep, wrong types
> - Handlers registered through a router as plain functions.
> - Harness gated by location, `RunService:IsStudio()`, and no remote trigger.
> - Fuzzing never touches live data.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~5.2k tok. Read more: ## The payload corpus · ## A direct fuzzer with invariants · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

You cannot know whether your remote handlers are safe by reading them. The bugs that lead to exploits are almost always things the author did not think of: a `NaN` that slips past a range check, a table where a string was expected, an error thrown halfway through a handler that leaves state half-written, a request that arrives twice in one frame. **Fuzzing** means throwing large numbers of wrong, extreme and malformed inputs at your own code and watching for errors, broken invariants and resource growth. **Abuse tests** are targeted versions: spam, races, out-of-order calls.

This note builds a Studio-only harness that does both against your own game, explains how to gate it so it can never run in a live server, lists the payload corpus and what each payload is designed to catch, and shows how to turn findings into regression tests. It complements the general testing notes (Testing Strategies and Frameworks, Automated Testing with TestEZ and Jest-Lua) and the gated cheat tooling in Multi-Client and Live Testing.

Everything here is defensive testing of code you own, in your own Studio session. Nothing is aimed at other people's games.

## Two ways to fuzz

| Approach | How | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direct (server-side)** | Call each handler function on the server with a test player and generated arguments | Fast (thousands of cases per second), deterministic, no client needed, easy to assert on state | Skips the real network serialisation; requires handlers to be callable as functions |
| **Through the wire (client-side)** | A Studio-only LocalScript fires the real remotes with generated arguments | Exercises real serialisation and the engine throttle; finds bugs in remote routing | Slower; what arrives is what survives serialisation, so some payloads change in transit |

Do both. Direct fuzzing finds most logic bugs; wire fuzzing confirms the router and validators see what you think they see.

## Make handlers fuzzable

The direct approach needs handlers that are plain functions, registered through one router, rather than anonymous closures connected inline. That design also makes rate limiting and logging uniform, so it is worth doing anyway.

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Net/Router.luau
-- Every client-to-server remote is registered here. The router applies rate limits and
-- error isolation, and exposes handlers to the Studio-only fuzzer.
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

export type Handler = (player: Player, ...unknown) -> ...any

local Router = {}
local handlers: { [string]: Handler } = {}

function Router.on(name: string, handler: Handler)
	assert(handlers[name] == nil, "duplicate handler " .. name)
	handlers[name] = handler
	local remote = ReplicatedStorage.Remotes:FindFirstChild(name)
	if remote and remote:IsA("RemoteEvent") then
		remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, ...)
			-- Rate limiting goes here (from the remote manifest).
			local ok, err = pcall(handler, player, ...)
			if not ok then
				warn(("[Router] %s errored for %d: %s"):format(name, player.UserId, tostring(err)))
			end
		end)
	elseif remote and remote:IsA("RemoteFunction") then
		remote.OnServerInvoke = function(player, ...)
			local results = table.pack(pcall(handler, player, ...))
			if not results[1] then
				warn(("[Router] %s errored for %d: %s"):format(name, player.UserId, tostring(results[2])))
				return nil
			end
			return table.unpack(results, 2, results.n)
		end
	end
end

-- Test-only access. The fuzzer requires this; production code never calls it.
function Router._handlersForTests(): { [string]: Handler }
	return handlers
end

return Router
```

The `pcall` in the router is error isolation, not error handling: it stops one bad request from breaking the connection's behaviour, and logs. The handler itself should still validate and return early instead of erroring. The fuzzer treats **any error** as a finding, because an error thrown midway through a handler may have left state half-written.

## Gating: the harness must never reach production

A fuzzer is a tool that fires every remote with garbage. In a live server it is at best noise and at worst a griefing tool if it is ever reachable. Gate it in three layers:

1. **Location:** keep the harness in a folder (for example `ServerStorage/TestOnly`) that your publish step deletes, or keep it out of the place entirely and insert it only in local test sessions. If you use Rojo, keep it in a separate project file used only for test builds (External Tooling - Rojo Wally Selene StyLua).
2. **Runtime guard:** the first line of every harness script returns unless `RunService:IsStudio()` is true.
3. **No remote entry point:** the harness is started from the command bar or a Studio plugin button, never by a remote. A "run tests" remote is a remote an attacker can fire.

```lua
--!strict
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
if not RunService:IsStudio() then
	return {} -- never run outside Studio
end
```

Also guard against your harness writing to real player data. In Studio, DataStore access depends on the "Enable Studio Access to API Services" setting; run the fuzzer with it off, or with your profile module pointed at a test scope, so a fuzz run cannot corrupt a real profile. A production lesson in [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]] shows how Studio sessions can collide with live data.

## The payload corpus

A good corpus is mostly boring values chosen to sit on boundaries. Each row says what bug it is designed to reveal.

| Payload | Reveals |
|---|---|
| `nil` | Missing nil checks (indexing nil, arithmetic on nil) |
| `true`, `false` | Type confusion where a number or string was assumed |
| `0`, `-1`, `1`, `-0` | Off-by-one, sign handling, negative quantities |
| `0.5`, `1e-9` | Missing integrality checks (half an item) |
| `2^31`, `2^53`, `2^53 + 1`, `-2^53` | Integer overflow assumptions, precision loss |
| `math.huge`, `-math.huge` | Missing finiteness checks |
| `0/0` (NaN) | Range checks that NaN passes (all comparisons false) |
| `""`, `" "`, a 10,000 character string | Empty-string handling, length limits, memory |
| Strings with control characters or invalid UTF-8 (built with `string.char`) | Text processing, filtering calls that error |
| `"__index"`, `"constructor"`, `"../"` style keys | Code that uses strings as table keys or paths without checking |
| `{}` | Empty tables where a list was expected |
| `{1, 2, 3}` vs `{a = 1}` vs `{[1] = 1, a = 2}` | Array vs dictionary assumptions; mixed tables are not sent intact over remotes, so test what arrives |
| A table nested 50 deep | Recursive validators that overflow the stack |
| An array of 10,000 entries | Loops over client-sized tables (CPU), unbounded storage |
| A table shaped like an Instance (`{Name = "Price", Value = 0}`) | Missing `typeof(x) == "Instance"` checks (the shop exploit from the Roblox docs) |
| Real instances from wrong places (`workspace.Terrain`, another player's character, a part in ServerStorage the client cannot see) | Missing `IsDescendantOf` and ownership checks; client-invisible instances arrive as nil |
| `Vector3.new(0/0, 0, 0)`, `Vector3.new(1e9, 0, 0)`, `Vector3.zero` | NaN propagation into physics and CFrames; normalising a zero vector |
| `CFrame` with NaN, `Color3`, `EnumItem`, `UDim2` | Wrong-type userdata where a Vector3 was assumed |
| Extra arguments beyond the expected count | Handlers that ignore extras are fine; validators that reject them are better |

Add **domain payloads** for your own game: every valid item id, an item id from the wrong category, a valid id for an item the test player does not own, a slot number one past the last slot, a trade id that belongs to another player.

## A direct fuzzer with invariants

The fuzzer below calls every registered handler with every combination of corpus values up to the handler's arity (configured), plus random combinations, and after each call checks invariants on the test player's state. It records errors, invariant violations and slow calls.

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerStorage/TestOnly/RemoteFuzzer.luau
-- Studio-only. Run from the command bar:
--   require(game.ServerStorage.TestOnly.RemoteFuzzer).run(game.Players:GetPlayers()[1])
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
if not RunService:IsStudio() then
	return {}
end

local ServerScriptService = game:GetService("ServerScriptService")
local Router = require(ServerScriptService.Net.Router)
local Profiles = require(ServerScriptService.Data.Profiles) -- your profile access

local Fuzzer = {}

local function deep(n: number): { any }
	local t = {}
	local cur = t
	for _ = 1, n do
		local nxt = {}
		cur[1] = nxt
		cur = nxt
	end
	return t
end

local function bigArray(n: number): { number }
	local t = table.create(n, 1)
	return t
end

local CORPUS: { any } = {
	"<nil>", true, false, 0, -1, 1, -0, 0.5, 1e-9, 2 ^ 31, 2 ^ 53, -2 ^ 53,
	math.huge, -math.huge, 0 / 0,
	"", " ", string.rep("A", 10000), string.char(0, 255, 254), "__index",
	{}, { 1, 2, 3 }, { a = 1 }, { Name = "Price", Value = 0 }, deep(50), bigArray(10000),
	Vector3.new(0 / 0, 0, 0), Vector3.new(1e9, 0, 0), Vector3.zero,
	CFrame.new(0 / 0, 0, 0), Color3.new(1, 0, 0), Enum.Material.Plastic,
	workspace.Terrain,
}

local function decode(v: any): any
	if v == "<nil>" then return nil end -- tables cannot hold nil, so it is encoded
	return v
end

export type Finding = { remote: string, kind: string, args: string, detail: string }

local function describe(args: { any }, n: number): string
	local parts = {}
	for i = 1, n do
		local v = args[i]
		local s = typeof(v) == "string" and #v > 20 and ("string(" .. #v .. ")") or tostring(v)
		table.insert(parts, typeof(v) .. ":" .. s)
	end
	return table.concat(parts, ", ")
end

-- Invariants on the test player's profile. Extend for your game.
local function checkInvariants(profile: any): string?
	for key, value in profile.currency do
		if typeof(value) ~= "number" or value ~= value or value < 0 or value % 1 ~= 0 or value > 1e15 then
			return "currency " .. tostring(key) .. " = " .. tostring(value)
		end
	end
	for uid, item in profile.items do
		if typeof(uid) ~= "string" or typeof(item) ~= "table" or typeof(item.itemId) ~= "string" then
			return "bad item entry " .. tostring(uid)
		end
	end
	if profile.busy then
		return "profile left busy" -- a handler errored or returned without clearing its flag
	end
	return nil
end

local function snapshotValue(profile: any): number
	local total = 0
	for _, v in profile.currency do total += v end
	local count = 0
	for _ in profile.items do count += 1 end
	return total + count * 1e6 -- crude: detects value creation from garbage input
end

function Fuzzer.run(player: Player, opts: { maxArity: number?, randomCases: number?, slowMs: number? }?)
	local o = opts or {}
	local maxArity = o.maxArity or 2
	local randomCases = o.randomCases or 300
	local slowMs = o.slowMs or 5
	local findings: { Finding } = {}
	local handlers = Router._handlersForTests()
	local profile = Profiles.get(player)
	assert(profile, "test player has no profile loaded")

	local function try(name: string, handler: any, args: { any }, n: number)
		local before = snapshotValue(profile)
		local t0 = os.clock()
		local ok, err = pcall(handler, player, table.unpack(args, 1, n))
		local ms = (os.clock() - t0) * 1000
		if not ok then
			table.insert(findings, { remote = name, kind = "error", args = describe(args, n), detail = tostring(err) })
		end
		local broken = checkInvariants(profile)
		if broken then
			table.insert(findings, { remote = name, kind = "invariant", args = describe(args, n), detail = broken })
			profile.busy = false
		end
		if snapshotValue(profile) > before then
			table.insert(findings, { remote = name, kind = "valueCreated", args = describe(args, n), detail = "garbage input increased value" })
		end
		if ms > slowMs then
			table.insert(findings, { remote = name, kind = "slow", args = describe(args, n), detail = ("%.1f ms"):format(ms) })
		end
	end

	for name, handler in handlers do
		-- Exhaustive single-argument and pairwise cases.
		for _, a in CORPUS do
			try(name, handler, { decode(a) }, 1)
			if maxArity >= 2 then
				for _, b in CORPUS do
					try(name, handler, { decode(a), decode(b) }, 2)
				end
			end
		end
		-- Random combinations up to 4 arguments.
		local rng = Random.new(12345)
		for _ = 1, randomCases do
			local n = rng:NextInteger(0, 4)
			local args = {}
			for i = 1, n do
				args[i] = decode(CORPUS[rng:NextInteger(1, #CORPUS)])
			end
			try(name, handler, args, n)
		end
		task.wait() -- let the server breathe between remotes
	end

	print(("[Fuzzer] %d findings"):format(#findings))
	for _, f in findings do
		print(("[Fuzzer] %s %s (%s): %s"):format(f.remote, f.kind, f.args, f.detail))
	end
	return findings
end

return Fuzzer
```

Notes:

- A fixed seed (`Random.new(12345)`) makes runs reproducible, so a finding can be replayed after a fix.
- "valueCreated" is the most important finding type: a garbage input that increased the player's value is an exploit. Give the test player a known starting state (some currency, a few items) so spending paths are exercised.
- "slow" catches handlers that loop over client-sized tables. A handler that takes 5 ms on one call can be driven to stall the server by a client sending many of them.
- Handlers that legitimately grant value (a daily reward) will report "valueCreated" on the first call. Reset the profile between remotes, or mark those handlers in your manifest and check that the grant happened at most once.

## Abuse tests: spam, races and order

Fuzzing finds bad values. Abuse tests find bad timing. Write them as small targeted scripts, using the same direct-call approach:

**Same-frame duplicates.** Call a spending handler several times concurrently and check the result.

```lua
--!strict
-- Studio-only race test: does RollWeapon ever spend the same coins twice?
local function raceTest(player: Player, handler: (Player, ...any) -> ...any, profile: any)
	profile.currency.Coins = 100     -- exactly one roll's worth (set cost to 100 in test config)
	local before = 0
	for _ in profile.items do before += 1 end
	for _ = 1, 10 do
		task.spawn(handler, player)   -- all start in the same frame
	end
	task.wait(1)
	local after = 0
	for _ in profile.items do after += 1 end
	assert(after - before <= 1, ("race: %d items for one roll's coins"):format(after - before))
	assert(profile.currency.Coins >= 0, "negative balance")
end
```

`task.spawn` starts each call immediately until its first yield, so a handler with a yield between check and write will fail this test, and a synchronous one will pass. Run every spending, claiming and trading handler through it.

**Out-of-order calls.** Call `TradeAccept` before `TradeOffer`; `ClaimReward` for a quest that was never started; `EquipWeapon` for a slot after selling its item. Every one should be a silent no-op.

**Spam at the engine limit.** From a Studio client, fire a remote in a tight loop for a few seconds and watch server CPU in the MicroProfiler ([[MicroProfiler Guide]]) and memory in the Developer Console. The engine throttles client remotes (about 500 requests per second per client, shared across remotes of the same type, Roblox docs as cited in [[Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention]]); your per-remote limits should drop the vast majority of those cheaply. If server frame time climbs, the handler does too much work before rate limiting.

**Leave mid-action.** Start a trade, a multi-step craft or a purchase prompt, then disconnect the client. Check that busy flags clear, escrow resolves and nothing is left half-applied after `PlayerRemoving`.

**Server shutdown mid-action.** In a local server test, trigger a long action and stop the server; confirm `BindToClose` saves a consistent state ([[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]]).

## Through-the-wire fuzzing

The wire fuzzer is a LocalScript placed only in a test build (for example under `StarterPlayerScripts` in the test-only project), guarded by `RunService:IsStudio()`. It iterates the remotes folder and fires each `RemoteEvent` with each corpus value, and invokes each `RemoteFunction` inside `task.spawn` with a timeout so a handler that never returns does not hang the test. The server side needs nothing special: the router logs errors. Compare the server error log after a wire run with the direct run. Differences reveal serialisation effects, such as mixed tables that arrive altered, non-replicated instances that arrive as `nil`, or values your router transforms.

Keep the wire fuzzer's fire rate below your own rate limits for the value tests (or temporarily raise limits in the test build), otherwise the rate limiter drops most cases and you test nothing.

## From findings to regression tests

Every real finding becomes a permanent test case:

1. Reproduce it with the fixed seed or the exact arguments.
2. Fix the handler (usually a missing `Guard` check or a yield in the wrong place).
3. Add the arguments to a per-remote "known bad inputs" list that a unit test runs on every build (Automated Testing with TestEZ and Jest-Lua).
4. Ask whether neighbouring handlers share the pattern; fuzz them again.

Over time the corpus grows into a record of every mistake your codebase has made, which is exactly the list the next new remote should be tested against.

## When to run it

| Moment | Run |
|---|---|
| New remote added | Direct fuzz of that remote, race test if it spends or grants |
| Before every release | Full direct fuzz, race tests on all economic handlers |
| After refactoring the router or validators | Full direct and wire fuzz |
| After an exploit report | Add the exploit's input to the corpus; full run |

A full direct run over 30 remotes with pairwise cases is around 30 x 33 x 33, roughly 33,000 calls; at well under a millisecond each, that is seconds to tens of seconds (rule of thumb; depends on your handlers).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Harness reachable in live servers | Three-layer gate: location, `IsStudio`, no remote entry |
| Fuzzing against real DataStore data | Studio API access off or test scope |
| Only testing "valid but wrong" values | Include NaN, inf, huge, deep, wrong types |
| Treating handler errors as harmless because the router catches them | Every error is a finding; it may leave half-written state |
| No invariant checks | Check balances, items and busy flags after every call |
| Random only, no seed | Fixed seeds for reproducibility |
| No race tests | Concurrent `task.spawn` calls on every spending handler |

## Checklist

- [ ] Handlers registered through a router as plain functions.
- [ ] Harness gated by location, `RunService:IsStudio()`, and no remote trigger.
- [ ] Fuzzing never touches live data.
- [ ] Corpus covers nil, booleans, boundaries, NaN, inf, long strings, deep and huge tables, fake instances, wrong-place instances, bad vectors.
- [ ] Domain payloads for your own ids and slots.
- [ ] Invariants checked after each call; value creation flagged.
- [ ] Race, out-of-order, spam, leave-mid-action and shutdown tests.
- [ ] Wire fuzz compared with direct fuzz.
- [ ] Findings become regression tests.

# Debugging Client-Server Desync

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Debugging one side only. Always look at both.
> - Avoid: Sending state as events (late joiners and re-streams break).
> - Avoid: Client code writing replicated server state "just for display".
> - Desync classified: missing, stale, divergent or out of order.
> - Both sides inspected (Client/Server toggle or inspector tool).
> - Server-owned state is read-only on the client, with a check that flags violations.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~4.6k tok. Read more: ## 2. Replication facts that cause desync · ## 4. A desync inspector · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

A desync is any bug where the client and the server disagree about the state of the game: the client shows 1,500 coins and the server has 1,200; a door is open for one player and closed for another; an enemy is dead on the server and still walking on a client. Desyncs are hard because each side, looked at alone, seems fine. This note gives a classification of desyncs, the replication facts that cause each kind, a debug tool that compares both sides directly, and fixes that remove whole families of the bug.

The rules of what replicates and when are in Replication Rules and [[Client-Server Model]]. Prediction for combat (where some desync is intended) is in Client Prediction and Reconciliation for Combat. Physics-specific desync (positions, ownership) is in Debugging Physics and Network Ownership.

Source labels: **Docs** (Creator Hub, as of October 2026), **Measured** (the reference project), **Rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. Four kinds of desync

Naming the kind narrows the cause immediately.

| Kind | Symptom | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| **Missing** | client has no copy at all (nil, or "not a valid member") | not replicated (server-only container), not streamed in, created on the client only |
| **Stale** | client has an old value that never updates | client wrote locally, so it no longer matches; or the server changed and reverted within one batch; or the UI cached a value and stopped listening |
| **Divergent** | both sides change the value independently | duplicated logic (client simulates and server simulates, with different inputs or timing) |
| **Out of order** | correct final state, wrong intermediate one; or an event handled before the data it refers to | remote arrives before an instance; unreliable remote reordered; deferred handlers |

Most desync bugs are **stale** (rule of thumb from reviewing many of them), and most stale bugs are one of two things: a client-side write to a replicated value, or a UI that read a value once.

---

## 2. Replication facts that cause desync

### 2.1 Client writes are local and sticky

When a LocalScript changes a property or attribute on a replicated instance, the change stays on that client only (Docs: changes on the client do not replicate, except for specific cases such as owned physics and some character properties). The server value has not changed, so **the server will not send it again** until it changes on the server. The client now shows its own value indefinitely.

Example: a client sets `player:SetAttribute("Coins", 0)` as a "reset display" while a menu is open. The server still has 1,500. No new value arrives until the next server change, so the UI shows 0 until the player earns a coin.

Rule: replicated state that the server owns is **read-only on the client**. Enforce it by convention and by a Studio check (section 5).

### 2.2 Batching hides quick changes

The server sends changes in batches (Docs describe replication as not instant; Replication Rules covers the details). A value set to 5 and back to 0 within one frame may never reach clients at all. If the client is supposed to react to "it happened", a property flip is the wrong channel: send an event, or use a counter (see 4.2).

### 2.3 Ordering between remotes and instances

A common out-of-order bug: the server creates an instance and fires a remote referring to it in the same frame. On the client, the handler runs, but the instance is not there yet, or the Instance argument arrives as nil (an Instance the client cannot see serialises as nil). Replication Rules covers what is and is not guaranteed. The robust approach is not to rely on the guarantee at all: send ids and let the client resolve the instance when it appears, or put the data on the instance as attributes so it arrives with it.

### 2.4 Unreliable remotes drop and reorder

`UnreliableRemoteEvent` (Docs) can drop or reorder messages. That is fine for cosmetic, frequently refreshed data (a laser pointer position). It is a desync generator for anything stateful: "door opened" sent unreliably may never arrive. If you see occasional permanent desync on a system using unreliable remotes, that is the first suspect ([[RemoteEvents RemoteFunctions and Unreliable Remotes]]).

### 2.5 Streaming removes things

With `StreamingEnabled`, parts of the world stream out on the client. A client script that held a reference to a streamed-out part now holds a part with `Parent == nil`. When it streams back in, it is **a different instance** (rule of thumb: treat any streamed instance as replaceable). Desync appears as "my highlight disappeared after walking away and back". Fix: rebind on `CollectionService` tag added/removed, not on references held at startup ([[Instance Streaming]], CollectionService Patterns).

### 2.6 Time

`os.time()` and `os.clock()` differ between machines. Using them to compare client and server events (cooldowns, timers, countdowns) produces "the timer ends early on my client". Use `workspace:GetServerTimeNow()` (Docs: a server-synchronised clock on clients) for anything shown to the player that must match the server. Still never trust the client's notion of time for authority ([[Server Authority and Validation]]).

---

## 3. Attributes vs remotes: choosing to avoid desync

The channel decision is a desync decision.

| Need | Channel | Why it resists desync |
|---|---|---|
| Persistent state of an object ("door open", "enemy health") | attribute or property set by the server | late joiners and re-streamed clients get the current value automatically |
| A moment ("explosion here", "level up") | RemoteEvent | an event is not state; a late joiner does not need it |
| High-rate cosmetic data | UnreliableRemoteEvent | loss is acceptable because the next update fixes it |
| Private per-player data (inventory) | RemoteEvent with full snapshots or versioned deltas | attributes on the Player are visible to every client |
| Large structured state | a replicated value container or remotes with snapshots | attributes are flat; big tables do not fit well |

The most common design error behind desyncs: **state sent as events.** "Door opened" fired as a remote works until someone joins late, streams the door back in, or misses a message. Then that client's door is closed forever. If it is state, make it state.

The reverse error also exists: **events sent as state** (a "LastHit" attribute that flips) loses events through batching and fires again on re-stream.

### 3.1 Snapshots and versions for remote-driven state

When state must go through remotes (private inventories, for example), send it in a way a client can recover from:

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: each change bumps a version; deltas carry the version they produce.
type Delta = { version: number, op: "add" | "remove", itemId: string, count: number }

-- Client: apply deltas in order; on a gap, ask for a full snapshot.
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Remotes = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Remotes")
local InventoryDelta = Remotes:WaitForChild("InventoryDelta") :: RemoteEvent
local RequestSnapshot = Remotes:WaitForChild("RequestInventorySnapshot") :: RemoteFunction

local inventory: { [string]: number } = {}
local version = 0
local resyncing = false

local function resync()
	if resyncing then
		return
	end
	resyncing = true
	local ok, snap = pcall(function()
		return RequestSnapshot:InvokeServer()
	end)
	if ok and type(snap) == "table" then
		inventory = snap.items
		version = snap.version
	end
	resyncing = false
end

InventoryDelta.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(d: Delta)
	if d.version <= version then
		return -- old or duplicate
	end
	if d.version ~= version + 1 or resyncing then
		task.spawn(resync) -- gap: something was missed or reordered
		return
	end
	version = d.version
	local cur = inventory[d.itemId] or 0
	inventory[d.itemId] = if d.op == "add" then cur + d.count else math.max(0, cur - d.count)
end)
```

Design notes: deltas that arrive during a resync are dropped and the snapshot covers them; the snapshot handler on the server must validate and rate-limit like any remote (Remote Abuse Patterns and Rate Limiting in Practice). The version number turns silent desync into a detected, self-healing one, and a counter of resyncs is an excellent health metric.

---

## 4. A desync inspector

The fastest way to debug desync is to stop inferring and **compare both sides directly**. A Studio-gated tool that asks the server for its view of an instance and diffs it against the client's.

### 4.1 Server side

```lua
--!strict
-- ServerScriptService/Debug/DesyncInspector.server.luau (Studio or allow-listed only)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local ALLOWED: { [number]: boolean } = {} -- developer UserIds for live use; empty = Studio only

local remote = Instance.new("RemoteFunction")
remote.Name = "DebugInspect"
remote.Parent = ReplicatedStorage

local function snapshot(inst: Instance): { [string]: any }
	local out: { [string]: any } = {}
	for k, v in inst:GetAttributes() do
		out["@" .. k] = v
	end
	if inst:IsA("BasePart") then
		out.Position = inst.Position
		out.Anchored = inst.Anchored
		out.Transparency = inst.Transparency
	end
	out.ChildCount = #inst:GetChildren()
	return out
end

remote.OnServerInvoke = function(player: Player, target: unknown)
	if not (RunService:IsStudio() or ALLOWED[player.UserId]) then
		return nil
	end
	if typeof(target) ~= "Instance" then
		return nil -- instance the server cannot see, or bad input
	end
	return snapshot(target)
end
```

### 4.2 Client side

```lua
--!strict
-- Client debug helper: compare one instance. Call from a debug UI or the client console.
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Inspect = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("DebugInspect") :: RemoteFunction

local function localSnapshot(inst: Instance): { [string]: any }
	local out: { [string]: any } = {}
	for k, v in inst:GetAttributes() do
		out["@" .. k] = v
	end
	if inst:IsA("BasePart") then
		out.Position = inst.Position
		out.Anchored = inst.Anchored
		out.Transparency = inst.Transparency
	end
	out.ChildCount = #inst:GetChildren()
	return out
end

local function diff(inst: Instance)
	local server = Inspect:InvokeServer(inst)
	if server == nil then
		warn("server cannot see", inst:GetFullName(), "(client-only instance?)")
		return
	end
	local client = localSnapshot(inst)
	for k, v in server do
		local c = client[k]
		local same = c == v
		if typeof(v) == "Vector3" and typeof(c) == "Vector3" then
			same = (v - c).Magnitude < 0.5 -- positions drift; tolerance
		end
		if not same then
			print(("DIFF %s  server=%s  client=%s"):format(k, tostring(v), tostring(c)))
		end
	end
	for k, c in client do
		if server[k] == nil then
			print(("ONLY CLIENT %s = %s"):format(k, tostring(c)))
		end
	end
end
```

Reading the output:
- "server cannot see": the client is looking at a client-created instance (missing kind, in reverse).
- An attribute that differs and **stays** different across several checks: stale. Search for client code that writes it.
- Positions that differ by a lot on unanchored parts: ownership, see Debugging Physics and Network Ownership.
- `ChildCount` differs: streaming, or children created client-side.

Security: this remote exists only in Studio or for an allow-list, validates its input, and returns only data the client could see anyway. Even so, do not ship it to live servers without the gate ([[Server Authority and Validation]]).

### 4.3 Catching client-side writes in Studio

To find the stale-kind cause (a client writing server state), log every attribute change on the client and compare with the server's log: a change that appears on the client without a matching server change is a local write.

```lua
--!strict
-- Studio-only client watcher: report attribute changes on tagged instances.
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

if RunService:IsStudio() then
	local function watch(inst: Instance)
		inst.AttributeChanged:Connect(function(name)
			print(("[C attr] %s.%s = %s @%.2f"):format(
				inst:GetFullName(), name, tostring(inst:GetAttribute(name)), workspace:GetServerTimeNow()))
		end)
	end
	for _, inst in CollectionService:GetTagged("DebugWatch") do
		watch(inst)
	end
	CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("DebugWatch"):Connect(watch)
end
```

Run the same on the server (prefix `[S attr]`). Using `GetServerTimeNow` on both sides gives comparable timestamps. The attribute signal does not tell you who wrote the value; if a client change has no server counterpart, search client code for `SetAttribute("<name>"`.

---

## 5. Divergent desync: duplicated logic

Divergent desync happens when both sides compute the same thing. Typical: a client counts down a cooldown locally and the server counts its own. A dropped frame, a hitch, or a different start time makes them disagree, and the player sees "ready" while the server rejects the attack.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. **One source of truth, others display it.** The server sets `CooldownEndsAt` (server time) as an attribute. The client shows `CooldownEndsAt - workspace:GetServerTimeNow()`. No independent counting.
2. **Prediction with reconciliation.** If responsiveness demands that the client acts first, the client predicts and the server corrects, explicitly (Client Prediction and Reconciliation for Combat).
3. **Deterministic simulation** (same inputs, same code, same order) is rarely achievable in Roblox for anything involving physics or floats across machines. Avoid relying on it (rule of thumb).

---

## 6. UI desync

A specific and very common case: the data is right on the client, the UI is wrong.

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| UI shows the value at join, never updates | read once in a setup function, never subscribed |
| UI updates, then shows an older value | two listeners (old UI instance not destroyed) write the same label |
| UI correct after reopening the menu | the menu rebuilds on open, but does not listen while open |
| UI correct for the first character, wrong after respawn | listeners bound to the old character's Humanoid ([[Debugging Race Conditions and Yield Order]]) |

Debug move: print from the place that **writes the label**, not from the data. If the label writer is not running, the subscription is missing; if it runs with the wrong value, the data is wrong; if two writers run, you have duplicate UI.

---

## 7. A worked example

**Report:** "Sometimes the shop says I cannot afford something, but I have enough gems."

1. **Kind?** The client UI shows 900 gems; the item costs 800; the server rejects the purchase. Server value: 700. So the client is stale or divergent, not the server.
2. **Inspector.** `@Gems` on the Player: server 700, client 900. Stays that way.
3. **Watcher.** The client log shows `Gems = 900` with no matching server change. A local write.
4. **Search.** A LocalScript for an "instant spend" visual effect had done `SetAttribute("Gems", current - spent)`, then later a refund path did `+ spent`, but only on the client, after a failed purchase. The server never changed, so it never sent a correction.
5. **Fix.** The client never writes `Gems`. The animated counter shows a local display value that always converges to the replicated attribute.
6. **Guard.** The Studio watcher stays as a debug tool; a lint rule (Selene custom check or a simple grep in CI) flags `SetAttribute("Gems"` in client code (External Tooling - Rojo Wally Selene StyLua).

---

## 8. Measured notes from the reference project

- A recurring class of "works in Studio, broken live" bugs was assets (animations, sounds) that only the developer's account could load, which looks like desync ("others do not see it") but is permissions. Check permissions before debugging replication (Replication Rules lists it).
- A cosmetic weapon flourish that every client must see uses both channels on purpose: the owning client fires a remote, the server checks it against the tool's attribute (rate-limited to 1 per second) and then writes character attributes (which flourish, and a start time). Every client samples the motion from those attributes on its own clock. The attributes are the state; nobody depends on catching a single event, so a client that looks over late still plays the right frame.

---

## Common mistakes

- Debugging one side only. Always look at both.
- Sending state as events (late joiners and re-streams break).
- Client code writing replicated server state "just for display".
- Comparing client and server times with `os.clock()` or `os.time()`.
- Holding references to streamed instances across stream-out.
- Unreliable remotes for stateful messages.
- Independent client and server timers for the same cooldown.

## Checklist

- [ ] Desync classified: missing, stale, divergent or out of order.
- [ ] Both sides inspected (Client/Server toggle or inspector tool).
- [ ] Server-owned state is read-only on the client, with a check that flags violations.
- [ ] State goes through attributes or snapshots; moments go through remotes.
- [ ] Remote-driven state carries versions and can resync.
- [ ] Timers shown to players use `GetServerTimeNow` and a server-set end time.
- [ ] Debug remotes are Studio or allow-list gated and validate input.

# Debugging DataStore Problems

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Verifying a save with a cached `GetAsync`.
> - Avoid: Debugging on the real key, or testing migrations in Studio against live stores.
> - Avoid: Retrying throttled requests immediately in a loop (makes throttling worse).
> - Symptom classified; uncached read done before anything else.
> - Budget logged periodically and before bursts.
> - Autosaves staggered; leaderboards and counters batched.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~140 tok · whole note ~4.8k tok. Read more: ## 2. Throttling and budgets · ## 3. Stuck session locks · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

DataStore bugs are the most expensive bugs in a Roblox game: they lose progress, duplicate items, and generate support tickets you cannot answer. They are also hard to debug because the evidence (what is actually stored) lives in a cloud service, the failure often happened on a server that no longer exists, and Studio behaves differently from live. This note is a diagnostic guide: how to read throttling and budget problems, how to tell a stuck session lock from a real outage, how to look at the actual saved data safely, and how Studio access changes what you see.

The limits, error codes and caching rules are in [[DataStore Fundamentals]]; leases and fencing in [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]]; correct save flow in [[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]]; recovery in Data Loss Prevention and Recovery. This note links to them rather than repeating the tables.

Source labels: **Docs** (Creator Hub, as of October 2026), **Measured** (the reference project), **Rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. Classify the symptom first

| Symptom | Most likely family | First check |
|---|---|---|
| Saves take 10 to 30 s, then errors 301 to 306 | throttling, queue full | budget logging (section 2) |
| "Data failed to load" for some players at peak times | experience-wide budget, or backend incident | budget logging, Roblox status page |
| Player cannot load after a server crash; works after a few minutes | stuck lease | read the lease (section 3) |
| Progress rolled back by minutes or hours | save not reaching the store, or stale overwrite | version history of that key (section 4) |
| Items duplicated | missing lease or fencing, or a trade race | version history, audit log (Trading Systems Without Duplication) |
| Works in live, fails in Studio (or the reverse) | Studio API access, Studio limits, test keys | section 5 |
| Value "did not save" when you verify right after | the 4 second `GetAsync` cache | re-read with `UseCache = false` ([[DataStore Fundamentals]]) |
| `105 ValueTooLarge` or `104 CantStoreValue` | data shape | section 6 |

The single biggest time-waster (measured in the reference project, also described in [[DataStore Fundamentals]]): concluding "the save failed" because a verification `GetAsync` returned the cached old value. Always verify with an uncached read before debugging anything else.

---

## 2. Throttling and budgets

### 2.1 What throttling looks like

When a server exceeds its request budget, requests go into a queue and the calling thread yields longer. When the queue (30 requests per type, per [[DataStore Fundamentals]]) is full, new requests fail with a `30x` throttle error. Output usually shows a warning that a request was added to the queue before the errors start (exact wording unverified; it mentions the queue and the key).

The sequence in logs:
1. Normal saves at 0.1 to 0.5 s.
2. A burst event (everyone saves at once, a leaderboard refresh, a migration loop).
3. Queue warnings, saves taking seconds.
4. Throttle errors; saves dropped.

### 2.2 Measure the budget, do not guess

`DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType(requestType)` returns the current budget (Docs). Log it around your heavy operations and every minute:

```lua
--!strict
-- Server: periodic DataStore budget log (keep at warn only when low).
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")

local TYPES = {
	Enum.DataStoreRequestType.GetAsync,
	Enum.DataStoreRequestType.SetIncrementAsync,
	Enum.DataStoreRequestType.UpdateAsync,
	Enum.DataStoreRequestType.GetSortedAsync,
}
local LOW = 10

task.spawn(function()
	while true do
		task.wait(60)
		for _, t in TYPES do
			local budget = DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType(t)
			if budget < LOW then
				warn(("[ds budget] %s low: %d"):format(t.Name, budget))
			end
		end
	end
end)
```

The newer request type members (`StandardRead`, `StandardWrite` and so on) are listed in [[DataStore Fundamentals]]; use whichever set matches your engine version (both exist as of October 2026 per that note).

Before a burst operation (a migration, a bulk leaderboard write), check the budget and pace yourself:

```lua
--!strict
local function waitForBudget(t: Enum.DataStoreRequestType, need: number, maxWait: number): boolean
	local start = os.clock()
	while DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType(t) < need do
		if os.clock() - start > maxWait then
			return false
		end
		task.wait(1)
	end
	return true
end
```

### 2.3 Find the burst

Throttling is almost always a burst, not a steady overload. Common culprits (rule of thumb, all seen in production games):

| Culprit | Fix |
|---|---|
| Autosave timer started at the same moment for all players (server start) | stagger: each player's autosave starts at a random offset |
| Leaderboard refresh with `GetSortedAsync` every few seconds in every server | refresh every 60 s or more, cache, or use MemoryStore (OrderedDataStores and Leaderboards) |
| `IncrementAsync` per kill for global stats | batch per server per minute |
| Saving on every inventory change | mark dirty, save on a timer and on leave |
| A migration or cleanup loop in game code | run it through Open Cloud at a controlled rate, or pace it with budget checks |
| Retries without backoff | exponential backoff with jitter (Error Handling and Retries) |

Remember the experience-wide budget is shared by **all servers and Open Cloud** ([[DataStore Fundamentals]]). A support tool or migration script running from outside can throttle every live server. When throttling starts at a time nobody shipped anything, ask who ran a script.

### 2.4 Per-key limits

A single hot key (a global counter, a shared guild record) hits per-key throughput long before the experience budget. Symptoms: only operations on that key throttle, and server-wide budgets look fine. Fix: shard the key (N keys, sum when reading), batch writes, or move the hot value to MemoryStore and persist periodically (MemoryStore Service).

---

## 3. Stuck session locks

A session lock (lease) prevents two servers from owning one profile. When a server dies without releasing, the lease stays until it expires. [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]] has the full design; here is how to debug one.

### 3.1 Is it stuck, or is another server really using it?

Read the lease. In a lease-based design the profile key (or a separate lock key) contains the owning server's `JobId` and an expiry time. From Studio with API access (on a copy of the data, section 4.3) or through a support tool:

```lua
-- Command bar (Studio, API access on): read the lease without changing anything.
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local options = Instance.new("DataStoreGetOptions")
options.UseCache = false
local value, keyInfo = store:GetAsync("User_0000000000", options)
if value and value.lease then
	print("owner job", value.lease.jobId, "expires in", value.lease.expiresAt - os.time(), "s")
end
print("version", keyInfo and keyInfo.Version, "updated", keyInfo and keyInfo.UpdatedTime)
```

(Field names depend on your schema; `lease.jobId` and `lease.expiresAt` are examples.)

Interpretation:
- **Expiry in the future, owner job id is a live server**: the player really is in another server (or their old server is still shutting down). Not a bug; show "your data is in use, retrying".
- **Expiry in the future, owner is gone**: a crashed server. Expected to clear at expiry. If this happens often, your servers are crashing (check the Performance dashboard, Crash and Error Telemetry) or your leases are too long.
- **Expiry in the past and loads still fail**: a bug in your claim logic (clock assumptions, comparison direction, or the claim `UpdateAsync` returning nil without retry).
- **Owner job id equals the current server**: the same server is trying to claim twice, often a rejoin before `PlayerRemoving` finished. Allow reclaim by the same job id.

### 3.2 The Studio lease trap

In Studio every play test is a new "server". If a play test ends abruptly, the lease from that session stays until expiry, so the next test cannot load. The reference project measured this at about 90 seconds of "cannot load" after each stop until it added a Studio takeover rule ([[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]] covers the fix). If loading fails only in Studio, only on the second test, think lease first.

### 3.3 Never "fix" a lock by hand in production

Clearing a lease on a live key while its owner server is still alive creates exactly the two-owner situation the lock exists to prevent. If you must force-release, do it only after confirming the owner server is gone (its job id not in your server registry, or the lease well past expiry), and log it.

---

## 4. Reading the actual saved data

When a player reports loss, the stored data is the only ground truth. Look at it before touching code.

### 4.1 Tools

| Tool | Good for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Creator Dashboard **Data Stores Manager** | browsing keys and values, quick checks | Docs; read-only browsing is safe; check what edit actions your version offers before clicking anything |
| Studio command bar with API access | `GetAsync`, `ListVersionsAsync`, `GetVersionAsync` in Luau | runs against the **live** stores of the published experience (see 5.1) |
| Open Cloud DataStore API | scripted support tools, bulk reads | shares the experience budget (Open Cloud APIs) |
| Open Cloud Luau Execution | running Luau (including DataStore calls) in a headless server for a place version | section 4.4 |

### 4.2 Version history is your time machine

Each write creates a version (Docs; versions are kept for a limited time, see [[DataStore Fundamentals]]). To investigate a rollback:

```lua
-- Command bar: list recent versions of one key, newest first.
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local pages = store:ListVersionsAsync("User_0000000000", Enum.SortDirection.Descending)
local page = pages:GetCurrentPage()
for i, info in page do
	if i > 20 then break end
	print(info.Version, DateTime.fromUnixTimestampMillis(info.CreatedTime):ToIsoDate(), info.IsDeleted)
end
```

Then fetch specific versions with `GetVersionAsync(key, version)` and compare a few fields (level, currency, item count). Patterns:
- **A sudden drop between two versions written by different servers**: a stale overwrite (no lease, or unfenced save). If your saves record the writing `JobId` and a session counter in the value, this is immediately visible. Record them; it costs a few bytes.
- **No versions at all during the period the player played**: saves never reached the store (errors swallowed, budget exhaustion, server crash before autosave).
- **Many versions seconds apart**: you are saving too often (and burning per-key throughput).

### 4.3 Never debug on the real key

Copy the value to a test key, then experiment on the copy. Reading is safe; any write while investigating risks making the loss permanent. A small support module that does "copy key X version V to key `Debug_X`" is worth writing once (Data Loss Prevention and Recovery).

### 4.4 Open Cloud Luau Execution (as of October 2026)

The Open Cloud Luau Execution API (Docs, endpoints marked stable) runs a Luau script in a headless server: a server launches, loads the place (or a specific place version), and runs your script. Documented properties:
- Server and local scripts in the place **do not** run automatically; physics does not run.
- Scripts up to 4 MB, running up to 5 minutes; returned values up to 4 MB after JSON encoding; logs keep at most about 450 KB.
- At most ten incomplete tasks per place; task results are retained for 24 hours.
- Data model changes are local to the task unless saved explicitly, but **DataStore calls are real** (the docs warn to take care).
- Rate limits (Roblox docs, as of October 2026): 5 task creations per minute, 200 task reads per minute and 45 log reads per minute, all per API key owner. Recheck the reference page, as these change.

What this means for debugging: it is **not** a way to attach to a live game server. It is a way to run your own modules (for example, your profile loader and migration code) against real stored data without opening Studio, from a CI job or a support tool. Use it to answer "does this player's stored profile load with the current migration code?" against a copy of their data. Treat it as production access: the API key that can run it can read and write every data store.

---

## 5. Studio versus live

### 5.1 Studio API access

DataStores in Studio require **Enable Studio Access to API Services** in Game Settings, Security (Docs). Without it, calls fail with error 403. With it, **Studio reads and writes the real live data stores** of that experience. There is no separate Studio database.

Consequences:
- A play test can overwrite your own real profile with test data. Use test keys or a separate store name in Studio (for example a `"PlayerData_Studio"` store chosen when `RunService:IsStudio()`), or a separate test experience.
- A bug in a migration tested in Studio can damage live data. Test migrations against a copy.
- Turning access off in Studio is a safe default for people who do not need it.

### 5.2 Studio limits differ

Studio uses its own request limits (Docs mention static limits for Studio; [[DataStore Fundamentals]]). Throttling in Studio does not prove throttling live, and the reverse. Test budget behaviour with several clients in a live test server (Multi-Client and Live Testing).

### 5.3 BindToClose in Studio

When you stop a play test, Studio closes the server and runs `BindToClose` callbacks, but the time available and the order relative to `PlayerRemoving` differ from a live shutdown (rule of thumb; the precise Studio timing is not documented). Saves that work live can fail in Studio and the reverse. Do not treat "it saved when I stopped the test" as proof of correct shutdown saving. Test shutdown in a live test server with a soft shutdown (Server Lifecycle and Shutdown).

---

## 6. Data shape errors

| Error | Usual cause | How to find it |
|---|---|---|
| `104 CantStoreValue` | an Instance, function, mixed table, NaN or invalid UTF-8 in the value | walk the table before saving (below) |
| `105 ValueTooLarge` | profile over the size limit, usually an unbounded log or history | measure `#HttpService:JSONEncode(value)` per top-level field |
| Silent loss of fields | sparse arrays or mixed keys get mangled by serialisation | same walker; keep arrays dense and dictionaries string-keyed |
| Numbers changed slightly | floats round-trip, huge integers beyond 2^53 lose precision | store large ids as strings |

A Studio-only validator that walks the profile before each save:

```lua
--!strict
local function validate(value: any, path: string, problems: { string })
	local t = typeof(value)
	if t == "number" then
		if value ~= value or value == math.huge or value == -math.huge then
			table.insert(problems, path .. ": NaN or inf")
		end
	elseif t == "string" then
		if utf8.len(value) == nil then
			table.insert(problems, path .. ": invalid UTF-8")
		end
	elseif t == "table" then
		local hasNumber, hasString = false, false
		for k, v in value do
			if type(k) == "number" then hasNumber = true
			elseif type(k) == "string" then hasString = true
			else table.insert(problems, path .. ": key of type " .. type(k)) end
			validate(v, path .. "." .. tostring(k), problems)
		end
		if hasNumber and hasString then
			table.insert(problems, path .. ": mixed keys")
		end
	elseif t ~= "boolean" and t ~= "nil" then
		table.insert(problems, path .. ": unsupported " .. t)
	end
end
```

Run it in Studio on every save and log problems; in live, run it on a sample, or only after a `104` error.

---

## 7. A worked example

**Report:** several players say they lost about an hour of progress after an update.

1. **Classify.** Rollback by about an hour. Version history family.
2. **Versions.** For three affected players: normal versions every few minutes, then a version at the update time with values from an hour earlier. The rollback version was written by a server whose session counter was lower than the one before it.
3. **Explain.** During the update, servers were shutting down. Old servers saved on shutdown; one old server had a stale copy of the profile because the player had moved to a new server an hour earlier, and the old server's copy was never released (a leak of profile references after `PlayerRemoving` failed). On shutdown it saved everything it held.
4. **Fix.** Fence saves with the lease (a server that no longer owns the lease cannot save), and remove profiles from the server's table when release completes or fails.
5. **Recover.** For affected keys, restore the last good version with a reviewed support script, after copying current values to a backup key.
6. **Guard.** Count "save rejected: not owner" events. A non-zero count now proves the fence works and shows how often the old bug would have struck.

---

## Common mistakes

- Verifying a save with a cached `GetAsync`.
- Debugging on the real key, or testing migrations in Studio against live stores.
- Retrying throttled requests immediately in a loop (makes throttling worse).
- Clearing leases by hand while the owner might be alive.
- Saving the whole profile on every change.
- No writer identity in saved data, so stale overwrites cannot be proven.
- Treating Studio stop as a test of shutdown saving.

## Checklist

- [ ] Symptom classified; uncached read done before anything else.
- [ ] Budget logged periodically and before bursts.
- [ ] Autosaves staggered; leaderboards and counters batched.
- [ ] Lease contents readable by a support tool; same-server reclaim allowed.
- [ ] Saved values include writer job id and session counter.
- [ ] Version history checked for every loss report.
- [ ] Studio uses test keys or a separate store; API access only for those who need it.
- [ ] Profile validator runs in Studio before saves.
- [ ] Open Cloud keys that can run Luau or touch data stores are treated as production credentials.

# Debugging Race Conditions and Yield Order

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: `task.wait(n)` as a fix for load order.
> - Avoid: Connecting `PlayerAdded` or `CharacterAdded` after a yield, without handling players or characters already present.
> - Avoid: Holding a character reference across a yield without re-checking it is still current.
> - Every "on added" subscription uses connect, then iterate existing, with a double-init guard.
> - Character bindings clean up on respawn and re-check `player.Character == character` after waits.
> - Server handlers change state before yielding, or hold a per-player busy flag.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~180 tok · whole note ~4.6k tok. Read more: ## 5. Character load order · ## 8. Tools for catching races · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Luau in Roblox runs one thread at a time per Luau VM (outside Parallel Luau), so people often assume races cannot happen. They happen constantly. A race in Roblox is not two threads writing the same memory at the same instant; it is **two pieces of code whose relative order is not fixed**, where one order works and the other does not. The order changes with network latency, device speed, streaming, deferred signals and which script the engine happens to start first. That is why race bugs show up on phones and in live servers and hide in Studio.

This note is about finding and fixing them. The `task` library itself and the basic ordering of `spawn` and `defer` are covered in [[Task Library Coroutines and Yielding]]; signal behaviour in [[Events Signals and Connections]].

Source labels: **Docs** (Creator Hub, as of October 2026), **Measured** (the reference project), **Rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. Where races come from

A Luau thread runs until it **yields**. Every yield is a point where other code can run and change the world. So the race surface of a function is exactly its yields:

| Yields (common) | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `task.wait`, `task.delay` callbacks | obvious |
| `WaitForChild` (when the child is not there yet) | resumes at an unknown later time |
| `require` of a module whose top level yields | the requirer waits on someone else's load |
| DataStore, MemoryStore, HttpService, MarketplaceService calls | 50 ms to many seconds |
| `RemoteFunction:InvokeServer` / `InvokeClient` | a full network round trip, or forever |
| `Players:GetUserIdFromNameAsync` and other `Async` calls | network |
| `Event:Wait()` | until someone fires |
| `Humanoid:MoveToFinished:Wait()`, tween `Completed:Wait()` | gameplay time |

And there are races without any yield in your code:
- **Scripts start in an order you do not control.** Two server Scripts in ServerScriptService run in an order that is not guaranteed (rule of thumb: never rely on it).
- **Deferred signals.** Under `SignalBehavior = Deferred`, handlers run at the next resumption point, after the code that fired them has moved on.
- **Replication.** On the client, instances arrive over time, in batches.

The debugging consequence: when you suspect a race, **list the yields between the cause and the symptom**. Each one is a candidate.

---

## 2. `task.spawn`, `task.defer`, `task.delay`: ordering traps

The basic order (spawn runs now up to its first yield, defer runs after the current work) is in [[Task Library Coroutines and Yielding]]. The traps:

### 2.1 spawn runs before your next line

```lua
local state = { ready = false }
task.spawn(function()
	print(state.ready) -- false: runs before the line below
end)
state.ready = true
```

If the spawned function needs the caller to finish setting things up, `task.spawn` is wrong; use `task.defer`, or finish setup first.

### 2.2 defer is not "later, safely"

`task.defer` runs at the next resumption point in the current frame cycle, not "after everything has loaded". Deferring a lookup of a replicated child does not wait for replication. Only an explicit wait for the condition does.

### 2.3 `task.wait(n)` as a fix is a longer fuse

`task.wait(1)` before reading something "makes it work" because on your machine it arrives in 0.2 s. On a phone on a bad network it arrives in 1.5 s. You have moved the failure from 30% of players to 3%, which is harder to debug. Wait for the **condition**: a child, an attribute, a signal.

### 2.4 Re-entrancy through events

A handler that fires an event that is handled by code that calls back into the first system is a race in disguise: the second call sees half-updated state. Under Deferred signals the order flips compared with Immediate, so code that "worked" for years can break when the place switches. Fix by updating all state first, then firing, and by making handlers tolerate being called at any moment ([[Events Signals and Connections]]).

---

## 3. `WaitForChild` pitfalls

`WaitForChild` is the most used race fix in Roblox and a common race cause.

| Pitfall | What happens | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting on the **old** character or GUI | the child is added to the new one; you wait forever | re-acquire the parent on respawn (section 5) |
| Waiting on the client for a server-only instance | never arrives; "Infinite yield possible" after 5 s (Docs) | keep shared things in ReplicatedStorage; server-only in ServerStorage |
| Waiting on the server for an instance another script creates | works only if that script runs; deadlock if it waits on you | create shared instances in one bootstrap, or create them where they are defined |
| Two children with the same name | returns whichever it finds first | unique names; never rely on name order |
| Streaming | a workspace child outside the streaming radius never streams in | use tags and `GetInstanceAddedSignal`, or `Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync` ([[Instance Streaming]]) |
| Chained waits `a:WaitForChild("b"):WaitForChild("c"):WaitForChild("d")` on every call | slow join and yields in hot paths | resolve once at startup and cache, revalidating on respawn |
| No timeout where nil is legal | silent hang after the warning | pass a timeout and handle nil |

A rule of thumb that removes most of them: **replicated containers are waited for once, at startup, by a single loader; gameplay code receives references, it does not wait.**

---

## 4. "PlayerAdded fired before I connected"

The classic: a server script does

```lua
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded)
```

and in Studio Play Solo, `onPlayerAdded` never runs for you. The player joined before the script reached that line, because something above it yielded (a `require` of a module that loads config, a `WaitForChild`), or simply because in Play Solo the local player can exist very early.

Live servers have the same bug in a rarer form: a server that starts with a player already teleporting in.

The fix is a pattern, not a delay:

```lua
--!strict
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local initialised: { [Player]: boolean } = {}

local function onPlayerAdded(player: Player)
	if initialised[player] then
		return -- already handled (connect and loop can both see the same player)
	end
	initialised[player] = true
	-- ... setup ...
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded) -- connect FIRST
for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do -- then catch anyone already here
	task.spawn(onPlayerAdded, player)
end

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player: Player)
	initialised[player] = nil
end)
```

Why connect first: if you loop first and then connect, a player who joins between the loop and the connect is missed. Why the guard: with connect first, a player who joins in that window is seen by both. Why `task.spawn`: each setup may yield (data load), and players should not wait for each other.

The same pattern applies to `CharacterAdded` (section 5), `CollectionService` tags (`GetTagged` plus `GetInstanceAddedSignal`), `ChildAdded` with existing children, and attribute signals (read the current value, then subscribe).

---

## 5. Character load order

Characters are the richest source of race bugs because they are created repeatedly and replicate in pieces.

### 5.1 The sequence (rule of thumb, verify per feature)

On the server, when a character spawns:
1. The character model is built and `player.Character` is set.
2. `Player.CharacterAdded` fires.
3. The model is parented into the workspace.
4. Appearance (accessories, clothing) loads; `Player.CharacterAppearanceLoaded` fires when done (Docs).

On the client, the model arrives through replication, and **children can arrive after `CharacterAdded` fires** on the client. Code that does `character.Humanoid` in a client `CharacterAdded` handler works on fast connections and fails on slow ones.

### 5.2 Patterns

```lua
--!strict
-- Client: robust character binding with cleanup on respawn.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

local connections: { RBXScriptConnection } = {}

local function cleanup()
	for _, c in connections do
		c:Disconnect()
	end
	table.clear(connections)
end

local function onCharacter(character: Model)
	cleanup()
	local humanoid = character:WaitForChild("Humanoid", 10) :: Humanoid?
	local root = character:WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart", 10) :: BasePart?
	if not humanoid or not root then
		return -- slow or broken spawn; the next CharacterAdded will try again
	end
	if player.Character ~= character then
		return -- respawned while we were waiting: this character is already stale
	end
	table.insert(connections, humanoid.Died:Connect(function()
		-- ...
	end))
	-- ... bind UI, camera, input to this humanoid ...
end

player.CharacterAdded:Connect(onCharacter)
if player.Character then
	task.spawn(onCharacter, player.Character)
end
```

The key line is `if player.Character ~= character then return end` **after** the waits. Without it, a quick double respawn (reset twice) leaves two bindings, one to a dead character. That is the source of many "UI shows health 0 after respawn" and "ability fires twice after reset" bugs.

Where to put character code:
- `StarterCharacterScripts`: a fresh copy runs in every new character; its references are naturally scoped to that life. Simplest for per-life logic.
- `StarterPlayerScripts`: runs once per session; must rebind on each `CharacterAdded` (as above). Better for systems that persist across lives (inventory UI, settings).

Mixing both for one system is a common source of duplicated handlers.

### 5.3 Server races around death and leaving

- A damage handler yields (plays a sound, waits for a tween), then applies a reward. If the target left or respawned in between, the reward goes to a stale reference. Re-check `target.Parent` and the player's current character after every yield.
- `PlayerRemoving` while a data load is still in flight: the save on leave runs before the load finished and saves an empty profile. This is the most expensive race in Roblox. Track the load state and refuse to save a profile that never finished loading ([[Saving Correctly - Autosave and BindToClose]], [[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]]).

---

## 6. Request races on the server

Two requests from the same player can be in flight at once whenever a handler yields. That is the root of most duplication bugs.

```lua
-- BROKEN: two quick clicks both pass the check before either spends.
Remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, itemId)
	local profile = getProfile(player)
	if profile.Gems >= PRICE then
		local ok = grantFromExternal(player, itemId) -- yields
		if ok then
			profile.Gems -= PRICE
		end
	end
end)
```

Both handler threads read `Gems >= PRICE` before either subtracts, because the first one yielded in between. Fixes, in order of strength:
1. **Do the state change before any yield** (spend first, refund on failure).
2. **A per-player busy flag** for that action (reject or queue while one is in flight).
3. **Idempotency keys** for anything crossing servers or DataStores (Trading Systems Without Duplication).

```lua
--!strict
local busy: { [Player]: boolean } = {}

Remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player: Player, itemId: unknown)
	if typeof(itemId) ~= "string" or busy[player] then
		return
	end
	busy[player] = true
	local ok, err = pcall(function()
		local profile = getProfile(player)
		if profile and profile.Gems >= PRICE then
			profile.Gems -= PRICE -- spend before yielding
			if not grantFromExternal(player, itemId) then
				profile.Gems += PRICE -- refund
			end
		end
	end)
	busy[player] = nil -- always released, even on error
	if not ok then
		warn("purchase handler failed: " .. tostring(err))
	end
end)
```

Rate limiting is a separate defence (Remote Abuse Patterns and Rate Limiting in Practice); it does not prevent this race, because two requests within the limit are enough.

---

## 7. Module initialisation races

Two common shapes:
- **A module that yields at require time** (waits for data, `WaitForChild` on something created elsewhere). Every requirer stalls until it finishes, and if two modules wait on each other's top-level work you get a deadlock that only shows as missing behaviour plus "Infinite yield possible" warnings.
- **Init order assumptions**: system B's `init` reads something system A's `init` creates. Works while the bootstrap happens to start A first.

Fixes: keep module top levels free of yields (define functions and tables only), and use an explicit bootstrap that calls `init` then `start` on every system in a defined order (Project Structure and Bootstrapping). For cross-system readiness, publish a ready flag (an attribute such as `DataLoaded` on the Player, or a signal) and have dependents wait for that, not for a timer.

---

## 8. Tools for catching races

### 8.1 A sequence log

When order matters, timestamps alone are not enough within one frame. Add a frame number and a global sequence counter:

```lua
--!strict
-- Shared/Seq.luau: ordered debug events, Studio only.
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local Seq = {}
local n = 0
local frame = 0
local enabled = RunService:IsStudio()

if enabled then
	RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function()
		frame += 1
	end)
end

function Seq.mark(tag: string, detail: string?)
	if not enabled then
		return
	end
	n += 1
	print(("[seq %d f%d %.3f] %s %s"):format(n, frame, os.clock(), tag, detail or ""))
end

return Seq
```

Mark both sides of the suspected race (`Seq.mark("load:start")`, `Seq.mark("ui:readCoins")`). When the bug happens, the log shows the bad order. Compare it with a good run.

### 8.2 Injected jitter

Make races frequent: in Studio, add a random small wait at suspected yield points.

```lua
--!strict
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local JITTER = RunService:IsStudio() and workspace:GetAttribute("DebugJitter") == true

local function jitter()
	if JITTER then
		task.wait(math.random() * 0.3)
	end
end
```

Call `jitter()` before data loads complete, before remotes fire, in character setup. If a bug's rate jumps with jitter on, you have confirmed a race and narrowed where.

### 8.3 Network latency and slow devices

Studio's network simulation adds replication lag; combined with multi-client tests it reproduces most client load-order races (Testing Modes - Play Run and Multi-Client, Multi-Client and Device Playtesting Protocols). A low-end phone is the final test: it changes timing more than any setting.

### 8.4 Assertions for invariants

Some races leave a detectable fingerprint. Assert the invariant where it must hold:
- "A profile is never saved before it loaded."
- "A player never has two active character bindings."
- "An item id is never granted twice for one receipt."

Log violations with a traceback (Studio) or a counter (live). They turn silent races into visible ones (Crash and Error Telemetry).

---

## 9. A worked example

**Report:** "On mobile, sometimes the whole HUD is empty after joining. Rejoining fixes it."

1. **Reproduce.** PC Studio: 0 of 10. With 300 ms incoming lag: 3 of 10. A race.
2. **List yields** between join and HUD build: the HUD script does `player:WaitForChild("leaderstats")`, then reads `Coins`, then `WaitForChild("Data")` on a folder the data system creates after the profile loads.
3. **Sequence log.** In the failing runs, `hud:start` happens after `data:ready`... and the HUD still fails. Odd.
4. **Look closer.** The HUD reads `Data` with `FindFirstChild` in one function and `WaitForChild` in another. The `FindFirstChild` path runs first, finds nothing, and builds an empty HUD. It never rebuilds.
5. **Explain.** On fast connections `Data` happens to be there; on slow ones it is not. The UI is built once and never updates.
6. **Fix.** The data system sets a `DataLoaded` attribute on the Player when ready. The HUD waits for it (or subscribes to the attribute change) and then builds. All reads go through one accessor.
7. **Verify.** 0 of 20 with 300 ms lag; 0 of 5 on a real low-end phone.
8. **Guard.** HUD logs a warning if it builds with missing data.

---

## Common mistakes

- `task.wait(n)` as a fix for load order.
- Connecting `PlayerAdded` or `CharacterAdded` after a yield, without handling players or characters already present.
- Holding a character reference across a yield without re-checking it is still current.
- Handlers that yield between checking and spending.
- Yielding module top levels.
- Relying on the start order of scripts.
- Saving a profile that never finished loading.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every "on added" subscription uses connect, then iterate existing, with a double-init guard.
- [ ] Character bindings clean up on respawn and re-check `player.Character == character` after waits.
- [ ] Server handlers change state before yielding, or hold a per-player busy flag.
- [ ] Module top levels never yield; a bootstrap defines init order.
- [ ] Readiness is an explicit flag or signal, never a delay.
- [ ] Races are reproduced with latency, jitter and a real phone before and after the fix.
- [ ] Invariants that races break are asserted and counted.
