# Debugging UI Layout and Input

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Debugging layout in Edit mode instead of the device emulator in a play test.
> - Avoid: Raising `ZIndex` on a child when its ancestor is the problem.
> - Avoid: Trusting `ClipsDescendants` with rotated children.
> - Studio debug tools: object-at-pointer, outline toggle, absolute size chain, selection logger.
> - DisplayOrder bands written down and assigned to every ScreenGui.
> - Rotated or rounded clipping uses CanvasGroup, sparingly.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~4.9k tok. Read more: ## 1. See what the engine sees · ## 4. AutomaticSize problems · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

UI bugs are reported vaguely ("the button does not work on my phone", "the shop looks broken") and caused precisely: a transparent frame on top eating clicks, a `ZIndex` that only applies among siblings, a `ClipsDescendants` that does not clip rotated children, an `AutomaticSize` that feeds back into itself, two `UIScale` objects multiplying, a gamepad selection that lands on an invisible button. This note gives the tools to see what the engine sees and a cause list for each family of symptom.

Layout fundamentals are in Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints and [[UI Layout Objects - Lists Grids and Pages]]; input APIs in Input - UserInputService and ContextActionService; gamepad design in Gamepad and Console UX; device testing in [[Responsive UI for Phone Tablet Console and PC]] and Multi-Client and Device Playtesting Protocols.

Source labels: **Docs** (Creator Hub, as of October 2026), **Measured** (the reference project), **Rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. See what the engine sees

UI is the one place where looking is cheaper than reasoning. Three tools.

### 1.1 What is under the pointer?

`PlayerGui:GetGuiObjectsAtPosition(x, y)` (Docs, on `BasePlayerGui`) returns the GUI objects at a screen point, topmost first. It answers "what is eating my click?" in one call.

```lua
--!strict
-- Client, Studio only: print what is under the mouse on middle click.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

if RunService:IsStudio() then
	local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui") :: PlayerGui
	UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input)
		if input.UserInputType ~= Enum.UserInputType.MouseButton3 then
			return
		end
		local p = UserInputService:GetMouseLocation()
		local inset = GuiService:GetGuiInset()
		-- GetMouseLocation is in full-screen space; GUI positions usually exclude the top inset.
		local objects = playerGui:GetGuiObjectsAtPosition(p.X - inset.X, p.Y - inset.Y)
		print(("--- %d objects at %d,%d"):format(#objects, p.X, p.Y))
		for i, o in objects do
			print(i, o:GetFullName(), o.ClassName, "Active=" .. tostring(o.Active),
				"Visible=" .. tostring(o.Visible), "Z=" .. o.ZIndex)
		end
	end)
end
```

The inset subtraction is a common source of off-by-36-pixel confusion; whether `GetGuiObjectsAtPosition` expects coordinates with or without the inset is not stated clearly in the reference (unverified). If the list looks shifted, try without the subtraction. The first object in the list with `Active = true` (or a button) is usually the one taking input.

### 1.2 Outline everything

A Studio-only toggle that adds a thin `UIStroke` to every `GuiObject` in a ScreenGui reveals invisible frames, overlaps and zero-size containers instantly:

```lua
--!strict
local function outline(root: Instance, on: boolean)
	for _, d in root:GetDescendants() do
		if d:IsA("GuiObject") then
			local s = d:FindFirstChild("_DebugStroke")
			if on and not s then
				local stroke = Instance.new("UIStroke")
				stroke.Name = "_DebugStroke"
				stroke.Thickness = 1
				stroke.Color = Color3.fromHSV((#d:GetFullName() % 12) / 12, 1, 1)
				stroke.ApplyStrokeMode = Enum.ApplyStrokeMode.Border
				stroke.Parent = d
			elseif not on and s then
				s:Destroy()
			end
		end
	end
end
```

Caveats: on `TextLabel`s and `TextButton`s, a `UIStroke` with the default `ApplyStrokeMode` outlines the text, which is why the code sets `Border`. A UIStroke also affects layout slightly in some setups (Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints mentions UIStroke as layout-affecting), so turn it off before measuring sizes.

### 1.3 Print absolute values

When a layout is wrong, the authored `Size` tells you little; `AbsoluteSize`, `AbsolutePosition` and `AbsoluteRotation` tell you what the engine computed. Print them for the element and its ancestors up to the ScreenGui. The first ancestor with an unexpected absolute size is where the problem starts (the "first wrong value" rule from [[The Debugging Method - Reproduce Isolate Bisect]]).

```lua
-- Command bar or client debug: ancestor chain of absolute sizes.
local function chain(g: GuiObject)
	local cur: Instance? = g
	while cur and cur:IsA("GuiObject") do
		print(cur.Name, cur.AbsoluteSize, cur.AbsolutePosition, cur.Size)
		cur = cur.Parent
	end
end
```

In Edit mode, StarterGui content is laid out in the Studio viewport size; on a device it is different. Always check absolute values in a play test with the device emulator, not in Edit mode.

---

## 2. Draw order: ZIndex, DisplayOrder and friends

### 2.1 How order is decided

| Level | Controlled by |
|---|---|
| Between ScreenGuis | `ScreenGui.DisplayOrder` (higher on top) (Docs) |
| Within a ScreenGui, `ZIndexBehavior = Sibling` | children always draw above their parent; among siblings, `ZIndex` decides (Docs) |
| Within a ScreenGui, `ZIndexBehavior = Global` | `ZIndex` compared across the whole ScreenGui, regardless of hierarchy (Docs) |
| Equal ZIndex among siblings | order is effectively creation or child order; do not rely on it (rule of thumb) |
| World-space UI | `BillboardGui.AlwaysOnTop`, `SurfaceGui.AlwaysOnTop`; otherwise 3D depth (World-Space UI - BillboardGui and SurfaceGui) |

Sibling is the behaviour new ScreenGuis use (Docs), and it is the sane one: a popup's children stay on top of the popup.

### 2.2 Symptoms

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Setting `ZIndex = 100` on a button does nothing | Sibling mode: the button's **ancestor** is under another branch; raise the ancestor, or move the button |
| A tooltip appears under the next card in a grid | tooltip is a child of one card; later siblings draw above it. Put tooltips in a separate top-level ScreenGui with a higher DisplayOrder |
| A modal sometimes appears under the HUD | two ScreenGuis with equal DisplayOrder; set explicit values for every ScreenGui |
| Core UI (top bar, chat) covers your button | your UI is inside the inset area; see section 6 |
| Order flips when content is rebuilt | equal ZIndex siblings relying on creation order |

A rule of thumb that prevents most of these: a written list of DisplayOrder bands (HUD 0 to 9, menus 10 to 19, modals 20 to 29, toasts 30, debug 100) and every ScreenGui assigned from it (UI Design Systems, Notification and Toast Systems).

---

## 3. Clipping

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Rotated child is not clipped by its `ClipsDescendants` parent | Docs: `ClipsDescendants` does not clip rotated descendants | use a `CanvasGroup` as the clipping container, or avoid rotation inside clipped areas |
| Rounded corners do not clip children | `UICorner` rounds the frame itself, not children | `CanvasGroup` with a `UICorner` clips children to the rounded shape |
| Content of a ScrollingFrame shows outside it | a descendant is in a different ScreenGui or uses a `CanvasGroup` that renders separately (rule of thumb); or `ClipsDescendants` turned off | check the ancestor chain; ScrollingFrames clip by default |
| `CanvasGroup` content looks blurry or pixelated | CanvasGroups render to a texture; resolution limits and memory apply (Docs mention texture memory considerations) | use CanvasGroups only where needed (fades, rounded clipping), not as general containers (Rendering Performance) |
| Children vanish when the parent has `Visible = false` | expected: visibility is inherited | check every ancestor's `Visible`, and `Enabled` on the ScreenGui |

`CanvasGroup` has a cost: texture memory per group. On phones, dozens of CanvasGroups in a list can cost real memory (Mobile and Low-End Optimization).

---

## 4. AutomaticSize problems

`AutomaticSize` (Docs) grows a GuiObject to fit its content. It is powerful and the source of a specific family of bugs.

### 4.1 Circular sizing

**Symptom:** a container sized with `AutomaticSize` collapses to zero, or its children appear at zero size, or the layout jumps between two states.

**Cause:** the children use **Scale** sizes relative to the auto-sized parent on the same axis. The parent's size depends on the children; the children's size depends on the parent. The engine resolves it in some order, and the result is rarely what you wanted (rule of thumb: treat it as undefined).

**Fix:** on the axis that is automatic, children use **Offset** sizes (or their own AutomaticSize, such as text labels sized by their text). Scale on the other axis is fine: a vertical list with `AutomaticSize = Y` can hold children with `Size = UDim2.new(1, 0, 0, 40)`.

### 4.2 TextScaled with AutomaticSize

**Symptom:** text in an auto-sized label is tiny or does not grow.

**Cause:** `TextScaled` fits text to the box; `AutomaticSize` fits the box to the text. Combining them on the same axis is circular (rule of thumb; the engine picks one).

**Fix:** with `AutomaticSize`, use a fixed `TextSize` (scaled globally with `UIScale`) instead of `TextScaled`. Use `TextScaled` only for fixed boxes, with a `UITextSizeConstraint` to cap the range (Text Fonts and Rich Text).

### 4.3 Lists that do not grow

**Symptom:** a ScrollingFrame does not scroll to the end, or its canvas is too small.

**Cause:** `CanvasSize` fixed while items were added, or `AutomaticCanvasSize` set on the wrong axis, or padding in a `UIListLayout` not included in a manual calculation.

**Fix:** `AutomaticCanvasSize` on the scroll axis (Docs), or set `CanvasSize` from `UIListLayout.AbsoluteContentSize` plus padding, updated on its change signal. For very large lists, virtualise (Virtualized Lists and Large Inventories).

### 4.4 Layout thrash

Changing a size inside a handler for `AbsoluteSize` changes of the same subtree can loop for several frames, visible as flicker or a layout that "settles" slowly. Under deferred signals it may stop after a re-entrancy limit (Reading Luau Errors and Stack Traces). Fix: never write sizes in response to your own subtree's size changes; compute from the parent's size instead, and coalesce with `task.defer`.

---

## 5. UIScale versus TextScaled

These solve different problems, and mixing them is a common source of "text is too small on phones".

| Approach | What scales | Good for | Trap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design at a fixed resolution with Offset sizes, then one `UIScale` per ScreenGui | everything, uniformly, including text, strokes and corner radii | consistent look across devices | two UIScales on one branch multiply (Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints) |
| Scale sizes plus `TextScaled` | boxes by screen proportion, text to fit each box | simple screens | text sizes differ between neighbouring labels; long translations shrink text unreadably |
| Mixed | whichever wins locally | rarely right | unpredictable on new devices |

**Debugging double scaling:** search the ancestors of a wrong-sized element for `UIScale` objects. A UIScale in a reusable component plus one on the ScreenGui gives `0.8 x 0.8 = 0.64`. Print the product along the ancestor chain:

```lua
local function effectiveScale(g: Instance): number
	local s = 1
	local cur: Instance? = g
	while cur do
		local ui = cur:FindFirstChildOfClass("UIScale")
		if ui then
			s *= ui.Scale
		end
		cur = cur.Parent
	end
	return s
end
```

**Measured note.** The reference project's first phone pass put one `UIScale` on every ScreenGui so a 1920 x 1080 layout fitted the screen. It "worked" on the single mock viewport it was checked on, but a 14 px label drew at about 5 px on a 390-pixel-tall phone and a 40 px button became about 15 px. When "text is too small on phones" is the bug, compute the effective scale (above) and the resulting pixel size before touching fonts: the answer is often a layout that needs a real phone variant, not a bigger number (Case Study - Phone UI Overhaul, fwjelaa UI Design System).

---

## 6. Insets and safe areas

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Top 36 to 58 pixels of the screen covered by core UI | content in the top bar area; `ScreenGui.ScreenInsets` set to `None` or legacy `IgnoreGuiInset` on |
| Buttons under a phone's notch or rounded corners | content outside device safe insets |
| Click positions off by the inset | mixing `GetMouseLocation` (full screen) with GUI positions (inset-relative) |

`ScreenGui.ScreenInsets` (Docs) chooses which inset the ScreenGui respects (`None`, `DeviceSafeInsets`, `CoreUISafeInsets`, `TopbarSafeInsets`). Full-screen backgrounds use `None`; interactive content uses `CoreUISafeInsets` or `DeviceSafeInsets`. Details in Safe Areas and Insets.

---

## 7. Input that does not arrive

### 7.1 Sinking: who took the input?

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Clicks on a button do nothing in one area | an invisible or transparent `GuiObject` with `Active = true` on top (use the tool in 1.1) |
| A button works with mouse, not with touch | a touch-specific overlay (thumbstick, jump button area) covers it; core touch controls take input in their zones |
| World clicks fire while the shop is open | your world-click handler ignores `gameProcessedEvent` (second argument of `InputBegan`, Docs) |
| World clicks never fire | a full-screen frame with `Active = true` sinks them; set `Active = false` on decorative full-screen frames |
| Keybinds stop when a TextBox has focus | expected: input goes to the TextBox; `gameProcessedEvent` is true |
| A ContextActionService action never fires | another binding with higher priority returned `Sink` (Input - UserInputService and ContextActionService) |
| A button ignores all input | `Interactable = false` (GuiObject property, Docs as of October 2026), `Visible = false` on an ancestor, ScreenGui `Enabled = false`, or the button is outside the screen |

Always respect `gameProcessedEvent` in world input handlers:

```lua
--!strict
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input: InputObject, gameProcessed: boolean)
	if gameProcessed then
		return -- UI, chat or a TextBox already used this input
	end
	if input.UserInputType == Enum.UserInputType.MouseButton1
		or input.UserInputType == Enum.UserInputType.Touch then
		-- world click / tap
	end
end)
```

### 7.2 Input logging

When the cause is unclear, log every input event with its type, state and `gameProcessedEvent` for a few seconds:

```lua
UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(i, gp)
	print("began", i.UserInputType.Name, i.KeyCode.Name, "processed=" .. tostring(gp))
end)
```

If the event never appears, the platform or a core script took it. If it appears with `processed = true`, your UI or a TextBox took it. If it appears with `false` and nothing happens, the bug is in your handler.

---

## 8. Gamepad selection

Gamepad bugs are invisible to anyone testing with a mouse. Test with a controller (or Studio's controller emulation, Testing Modes - Play Run and Multi-Client) from the first build of every menu.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Opening a menu selects nothing; the player is stuck | nothing set `GuiService.SelectedObject` (Docs) | select the primary button when a menu opens |
| Selection jumps to the HUD behind the menu | selection is free to move anywhere selectable | `SelectionGroup = true` on the menu container (`GuiService:AddSelectionParent` is deprecated) to keep selection inside (Docs) |
| Selection lands on an invisible element | a hidden but `Selectable` object | set `Selectable = false` on hidden elements, or hide with `Visible = false` (not transparency) |
| D-pad navigation goes in surprising directions | automatic neighbour detection in irregular layouts | set `NextSelectionUp/Down/Left/Right` explicitly on tricky elements (Docs) |
| Selection lost after rebuilding a list | the selected object was destroyed | after rebuild, reselect the equivalent item by id |
| Selection highlight invisible against the art | default selection image does not fit the style | custom `SelectionImageObject` (Docs) |

A debug label that prints `GuiService.SelectedObject` on change helps enormously:

```lua
--!strict
local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")
GuiService:GetPropertyChangedSignal("SelectedObject"):Connect(function()
	local o = GuiService.SelectedObject
	print("selected:", if o then o:GetFullName() else "nil")
end)
```

---

## 9. A worked example

**Report:** "On phones, the Claim button in daily rewards does nothing. Works on PC."

1. **Reproduce.** Device emulator, phone preset: tap does nothing 10 of 10. PC: works.
2. **What is under the tap?** Tool 1.1 at the button's position: the first object is `RewardsGui.Root.Background`, `Active = true`, then the button.
3. **Why only phones?** On phones, a responsive rule enlarges the background panel to fill the screen; the panel is a sibling **after** the button's container, so in Sibling mode it draws over it and, being `Active`, takes the tap. On PC the panel is smaller and does not overlap the button.
4. **Fix.** Background `Active = false` (it is decorative) and `ZIndex` of the background lower than the content container. Explicit DisplayOrder for the rewards ScreenGui.
5. **Verify.** Phone, tablet and PC presets, plus a real phone. Controller: opening the menu selects Claim.
6. **Guard.** UI checklist item: decorative frames are never Active (QA Checklists Before Release).

---

## Common mistakes

- Debugging layout in Edit mode instead of the device emulator in a play test.
- Raising `ZIndex` on a child when its ancestor is the problem.
- Trusting `ClipsDescendants` with rotated children.
- Scale-sized children inside an auto-sized parent on the same axis.
- `TextScaled` combined with `AutomaticSize`.
- Two `UIScale`s on one branch.
- World input handlers that ignore `gameProcessedEvent`.
- Full-screen decorative frames with `Active = true`.
- No `SelectedObject` when a menu opens; no controller testing.

## Checklist

- [ ] Studio debug tools: object-at-pointer, outline toggle, absolute size chain, selection logger.
- [ ] DisplayOrder bands written down and assigned to every ScreenGui.
- [ ] Rotated or rounded clipping uses CanvasGroup, sparingly.
- [ ] Auto-sized containers use Offset (or auto) children on the automatic axis.
- [ ] One UIScale per branch; text sizing strategy chosen per screen.

# The Debugging Method - Reproduce Isolate Bisect

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Starting to change code before having a repro.
> - Avoid: Fixing the visible wrong value instead of the first wrong value.
> - Avoid: Bisecting in a shared place and breaking other people's tests.
> - Repro written down with start state, steps, expected, actual and a rate.
> - Cheat service, test profiles and seeded RNG exist, Studio-gated.
> - Server or client answered first.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~140 tok · whole note ~4.6k tok. Read more: ## 2. Reproduce · ## 4. Bisect · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Debugger Breakpoints and Logging gives a five-step outline (reproduce, locate, explain, fix, verify). This note goes deeper into the part where most time is lost: getting from "it sometimes breaks" to "this line, with this value, in this order". The core moves are the same in every engine. The Roblox-specific parts are how you get a repeatable state, how you cut a place down to the smallest thing that still breaks, and how you bisect when the bug lives in a 400-script place that several people edit.

Source labels: **Docs** (Creator Hub, as of October 2026), **Measured** (the reference project), **Rule of thumb**.

---

## 1. Why a method at all

Debugging by intuition works when the bug is near the code you just wrote. It fails badly in three situations that are common in Roblox:

- **The symptom is far from the cause.** A UI shows the wrong coin count. The cause is a DataStore migration that ran twice, three systems away.
- **The bug depends on timing.** Client and server run on different machines, replication is batched, and `SignalBehavior` defers handlers. Things that "never happen" in Play Solo happen on a phone on 4G.
- **The place is shared.** Other people edit and test the same place. Your mental model of the code is already out of date.

A method stops you guessing. Each step produces something concrete (a written repro, a smaller place, a narrowed commit range), so even a failed hour leaves you closer.

---

## 2. Reproduce

A bug you cannot reproduce on demand cannot be fixed with confidence. You can only change code and hope. So the first job is a **repro script**: written steps, from a known starting state, that show the bug at least most of the time.

### 2.1 Write the repro down

Format that works (rule of thumb):

```
Start: fresh data, Studio, 2 clients, network latency 200 ms
1. Client A equips the bow.
2. Client A opens inventory, unequips, re-equips within 1 s.
3. Client B looks at A.
Expected: B sees the bow on A's back.
Actual: B sees nothing; A sees the bow. 7 of 10 attempts.
```

The last line matters. "7 of 10" tells you the bug is timing-sensitive, and gives you a baseline: after a fix, 0 of 20 is evidence; 0 of 3 is not.

### 2.2 Get to the state fast

Most repros fail because reaching the state takes ten minutes of grinding. Build the tools once:

- A **gated cheat service** (Studio and allow-listed developers only) that sets level, grants items, teleports to zones and fires world events. The pattern is in Multi-Client and Live Testing.
- **Test profiles**: a way to load a named fake profile instead of the real one ("fresh", "endgame", "legacy schema v3"). Keep test keys away from real player keys ([[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]] covers the trap of leaving a test key set).
- **Seeded randomness**: any RNG the bug depends on should accept a seed in Studio. `Random.new(seed)` makes drops, spawns and AI choices repeatable.

```lua
--!strict
-- Shared/Rng.luau: one place to make randomness repeatable in Studio.
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local Rng = {}

local seedAttr = workspace:GetAttribute("DebugSeed") -- set by hand in Studio
local seed: number = if RunService:IsStudio() and typeof(seedAttr) == "number"
	then seedAttr
	else (os.time() + math.floor(os.clock() * 1000))

local generator = Random.new(seed)

function Rng.seed(): number
	return seed
end

function Rng.integer(min: number, max: number): number
	return generator:NextInteger(min, max)
end

function Rng.number(): number
	return generator:NextNumber()
end

return Rng
```

Log the seed at server start. When a tester reports "the boss dropped two legendaries", the seed lets you replay the exact rolls, as long as the order of calls is the same. (One shared generator is only repeatable if the sequence of calls is; per-system generators are more robust.)

### 2.3 Turn intermittent into reliable

If the bug shows 1 time in 30, change conditions until it shows more often. Each change that raises the rate is also a clue.

| Lever | How in Roblox | What a higher rate tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Studio network simulation (incoming replication lag) | ordering or replication timing |
| Low frame rate | a throwaway script that burns CPU each frame on the client | per-frame logic assumes a frame length |
| More clients | multi-client test with 3 to 8 players | contention, shared state, ownership |
| Spam the action | an auto-clicker loop in a debug script | missing debounce, race between requests |
| Slow storage | wrap your DataStore layer with an artificial `task.wait(2)` in Studio | load-order assumptions |
| Streaming | enable `StreamingEnabled`, shrink the target radius | client assumes an instance exists |

A good trick is the **injected delay**: put `task.wait(math.random() * 0.5)` before a suspicious step in Studio only. If the failure rate jumps, you have found the race. [[Debugging Race Conditions and Yield Order]] goes further.

### 2.4 When you cannot reproduce

Then reproduce in the logs instead. Add tagged debug logging at the boundaries of the systems involved, ship it (at `warn` level or gated per tag), and wait for the next report. Each report should come with: place version, server job id, platform, time, and the player's recent actions. Debugging Live Servers covers collecting this without flooding anything.

---

## 3. Isolate

Once you can reproduce, shrink the search space. Two ways: shrink the **code** (which system?) and shrink the **data** (which input?).

### 3.1 Find the first wrong value

Every bug is a chain: correct input, some step produces a wrong value, later steps faithfully propagate it. You are looking for the **first** wrong value, not the most visible one.

Work backward from the symptom:
1. The UI shows 0 coins. Is the attribute on the player 0? (Client/Server toggle, or print on the client.)
2. Is the server value 0? If the server says 1,500 and the client says 0, it is a replication or UI bug ([[Debugging Client-Server Desync]]). If the server says 0, keep going.
3. Was the profile loaded with 0, or did something set it to 0 later? A conditional breakpoint or a logged setter tells you.

A **tripwire** catches the moment a value goes wrong without stepping through everything:

```lua
--!strict
-- Studio-only tripwire: report the first time an attribute takes a bad value.
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local function tripwire(inst: Instance, attr: string, isBad: (any) -> boolean)
	if not RunService:IsStudio() then
		return
	end
	local fired = false
	inst:GetAttributeChangedSignal(attr):Connect(function()
		local v = inst:GetAttribute(attr)
		if not fired and isBad(v) then
			fired = true
			warn(("[tripwire] %s.%s became %s\n%s"):format(
				inst:GetFullName(), attr, tostring(v), debug.traceback("", 2)))
		end
	end)
end

-- Example: coins should never drop below zero or become NaN.
tripwire(somePlayer, "Coins", function(v)
	return typeof(v) ~= "number" or v < 0 or v ~= v
end)
```

Caveat: the traceback here is the traceback of the **signal handler**, not of the code that set the attribute. Attribute signals do not tell you who wrote the value; with deferred signals the writer has already moved on. To catch the writer, funnel writes through one setter function and put the check (and a `debug.traceback()`) there. That is one more argument for a single owner of each piece of state.

### 3.2 Shrink the data

If the bug happens with one player's profile and not with a fresh one, the data is the input to isolate. Load a copy of that profile under a test key (never edit the real key while investigating, see [[Debugging DataStore Problems]]), then delete half of the fields or items and retry. Repeat. Within six or seven rounds a 100-item inventory is down to the one item whose old schema breaks the loader.

### 3.3 Ask "which side?"

In Roblox the first isolation question is almost always "server or client?". Answer it before anything else:
- Error text in Output is green for server and blue for client during play tests (Docs).
- `RunService:IsServer()` printed in the code path.
- The Client/Server toggle shows each DataModel.

Many hours are lost debugging the server copy of a ModuleScript when the failing call was on the client (or the other way round).

---

## 4. Bisect

Bisection is binary search over anything ordered: scripts, commits, place versions, data, frames. It needs only one thing: a yes/no test (the repro). With N candidates it needs about log2(N) tests. 400 scripts: 9 tests. 1,000 commits: 10 tests.

### 4.1 Bisecting by disabling scripts

When you do not know which system causes a bug (a freeze, a memory climb, a stray error at join), disable half the scripts and test.

Rules that make it work:
- **Work on a copy.** File, Save to File As, or a separate test place. Never bisect in the live shared place: disabling scripts there breaks other people's tests (Safe Changes in a Shared Place).
- **Disable, do not delete.** `Script.Enabled = false` (Docs: disabling stops the script; re-enabling runs it again). ModuleScripts cannot be disabled, so bisect the scripts that require them.
- **Respect dependencies.** If script B waits for something A creates, disabling A makes B hang. That is not the bug; it is a new failure. Bisect by system (groups of scripts that belong together), not file by file.
- **Record each step.** "Half A off: bug gone. A1 off: bug present. A2 off: bug gone..."

A command bar helper for a test copy:

```lua
-- Command bar (Edit mode, on a COPY of the place): list and toggle server scripts by folder.
local function setFolder(folder: Instance, enabled: boolean)
	local n = 0
	for _, d in folder:GetDescendants() do
		if d:IsA("Script") then -- includes LocalScript (subclass of Script)
			d.Enabled = enabled
			n += 1
		end
	end
	print(folder:GetFullName(), enabled and "enabled" or "disabled", n)
end

setFolder(game.ServerScriptService.Systems.Combat, false)
```

Note: in current Studio, `LocalScript` inherits from `Script`, so `IsA("Script")` matches both (rule of thumb from the class hierarchy; check `ClassName` if you need to separate them). Scripts with `RunContext` set behave like their context, not their location ([[Script Types and Run Context]]).

### 4.2 Bisecting by version

"It worked last week" is a gift: the bug lives between two versions.

- **With Rojo and Git**: `git bisect start`, mark a known bad and known good commit, build and test each step, mark good or bad. Git picks the midpoint. This is the cleanest option and the main reason to keep code in Git (Git and Source Control for Roblox).
- **Without Git**: Version History (Docs: published versions of a place are listed with dates and can be restored) gives you older builds. Restore a version midway in time into a separate test place (never into the live place), test, repeat. See Version History and Backups for how to do this safely. It is slower, and data in DataStores is shared between versions, so a bug caused by stored data shows in old versions too. That itself is a useful result: if every old version shows the bug, suspect data, not code.
- **Packages and dependencies**: a package auto-update can change behaviour without a commit in your repo. Check package versions when the commit range contains nothing suspicious (Packages and Asset Reuse).

### 4.3 Bisecting in time

For bugs that appear "after a while" (memory growth, a frame-time climb, a desync that builds up), bisect in time: log a value every 30 seconds and find the first interval where it changed. The full memory version of this is in Hunting Memory Leaks Step by Step.

---

## 5. Minimal repro places

A minimal repro is a small place that shows the bug with as little else as possible. It is the strongest debugging tool there is, for three reasons:

1. Building it often reveals the cause (you find which part is required).
2. It separates "my bug" from "engine bug". If a 20-line place with one part and one script shows it, it is probably not your game's architecture.
3. It is what an engine bug report on the DevForum needs. Reports with a repro file get attention; reports with a video of a full game rarely do.

How to build one:
1. New baseplate.
2. Copy only the instances the bug touches (a model, a ScreenGui), not the whole game.
3. Replace your frameworks with direct code. If the bug disappears when you remove your framework, the framework is involved.
4. Remove things one at a time until removing anything makes the bug vanish. What remains is the repro.
5. Write the expected and actual behaviour in a comment at the top of the script.

When not to: if the bug obviously depends on the interaction of many systems with real data (an economy exploit, a matchmaking stall), a minimal place costs more than it saves. Use logs and bisection in a test copy instead.

---

## 6. Explain before you fix

The rule from Debugger Breakpoints and Logging bears repeating with an example of what goes wrong without it.

**Measured case, with a counterfactual.** In the reference project, an inventory click occasionally froze the client, only for rare items, so it looked random. The cause was an unbounded retry loop that tried to parent a decoration to a frame the click had just destroyed. The fix was a cap on the loop plus a check for a gone parent. Now imagine the tempting guess: a `task.wait()` in the click handler. It would have changed the timing, the freeze would have become rarer, and the bug would have looked fixed while the unbounded loop stayed in the code.

Signs a fix is a guess:
- It adds a `task.wait` or a longer timeout.
- It wraps something in `pcall` and ignores the error.
- It works "most of the time".
- You cannot say, in one sentence, what sequence of events produced the bad value.

---

## 7. Verify, then guard

After a fix:
1. Run the original repro, under the conditions that made it frequent (latency, many clients). Use the same count: if it failed 7 of 10, run 20.
2. Remove any injected delays and debug toggles.
3. Leave a **guard** that would catch the bug or its family next time: an assertion at the boundary, a validation on the remote, a unit test for pure logic (Automated Testing with TestEZ and Jest-Lua), or a tripwire that stays on in Studio.
4. Write one line in your changelog or bug log: symptom, cause, fix. Over time this log is the most valuable debugging document you own (Documentation and Knowledge Bases).

---

## 8. Heisenbugs: when debugging changes the bug

Some bugs vanish when observed:

| You add | It changes | So |
|---|---|---|
| A breakpoint | timing; other machines keep running | use timestamped logs for races |
| A `print` with `GetFullName()` on many instances | frame time | log only on change, rate-limit |
| `WaitForChild` in a debug script | the moment the script resumes | read with `FindFirstChild` and log nil |
| A second client | network ownership and load | test with and without |

If a bug vanishes under the debugger, that itself says "timing". Move to logs with `os.clock()` timestamps and sequence numbers.

---

## 9. A worked session

Symptom report: "Sometimes after rejoining, my pet is gone."

1. **Reproduce.** Fresh test profile, equip a pet, leave, rejoin. 0 of 10. Add latency: 0 of 10. Leave and rejoin within 3 s: 4 of 10. The quick rejoin matters.
2. **Isolate.** Which side? Server profile on rejoin has no pet. So it is data. Was it saved? The save log shows the leave-save started but the new server loaded first.
3. **Explain.** On a fast rejoin, the new server read the key before the old server's leave-save landed. The new server then saved its stale copy over the good one. This is the classic missing session lock ([[Session Locking and Profile Libraries]]).
4. **Fix.** Use the lease-based profile module; the second server waits for the lease.
5. **Verify.** Fast rejoin 0 of 20, with latency.
6. **Guard.** A server counter for "load waited for lease" so you can see how often it happens live (Crash and Error Telemetry).

Total: six tests and one read of a log. Without the method, the common outcome is a `task.wait(5)` before loading and a bug that returns at peak hours.

---

## Common mistakes

- Starting to change code before having a repro.
- Fixing the visible wrong value instead of the first wrong value.
- Bisecting in a shared place and breaking other people's tests.
- Bisecting file by file through dependent scripts and chasing hangs you created.
- Declaring a timing bug fixed after three clean runs.
- Using Version History bisection for a bug that lives in stored data.
- Leaving injected delays or debug seeds enabled in a published build.

## Checklist

- [ ] Repro written down with start state, steps, expected, actual and a rate.
- [ ] Cheat service, test profiles and seeded RNG exist, Studio-gated.
- [ ] Server or client answered first.
- [ ] First wrong value found (tripwire or single setter).
- [ ] Bisection done on a copy, by system, with each step recorded.
- [ ] Cause explained in one sentence before the fix.
- [ ] Verified with at least twice the original run count under stress conditions.
- [ ] A guard left behind, and one line written in the bug log.

## See also

# Readable Text and UI Scale

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: `TextScaled` for content, so the player's text size does nothing.
> - Avoid: Fixed-height text boxes that clip at `Largest`.
> - Avoid: Tight `MaxTextSize` constraints on body text.
> - Rendered body text meets the minimums for each device class, measured, not assumed.
> - One `UIScale` controller combines device base and player preference, clamped to fit.
> - No content text uses `TextScaled`; constraints on body text are generous.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~5.2k tok. Read more: ## 2. Three scales that multiply · ## 6. An automated text audit · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

Accessibility explains how `GuiService.PreferredTextSize` changes text and which text setups ignore it. [[Responsive UI for Phone Tablet Console and PC]] covers device classes and the shipped phone rules. This note sits between them: how big text actually needs to be on each device in physical terms, how the engine's text scaling, your device `UIScale` and a player "UI size" slider stack (and where they fight), layouts that grow instead of clipping, type choices that help low-vision and dyslexic players, world-space text, and an automated audit that finds clipped labels before players do.

Sources: **Roblox docs (as of October 2026)** for engine behaviour (`GuiService`, `TextLabel`, `TextService`, `UIScale`), **measured in the reference project** where noted (anonymised), and **rule of thumb** for sizes and thresholds.

---

## 1. Readability is physical, not pixels

A 14 px label is comfortable on a laptop at arm's length, tiny on a 6 inch phone held at 30 cm, and unreadable on a TV across a room. What matters is the angle the text covers in the player's eye, which depends on the physical screen size, its pixel density, the viewing distance, and the scale factor between your authored pixels and real pixels.

Roblox gives you two useful signals here (Roblox docs, as of October 2026):

- `GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize` returns `Small`, `Medium` or `Large`, described as the physical rendering size of the viewport. It is the closest thing the engine gives you to "is this a phone?".
- `UserInputService.PreferredInput` returns the primary input the player is likely using (`Touch`, `Gamepad`, `KeyboardAndMouse`). A gamepad on a large display usually means a TV at couch distance.

Neither tells you the viewing distance. That is why a player-facing UI size setting matters even after you have a good device-based scale: you cannot measure the sofa.

### Working minimums

These are the sizes that the reference project converged on and that match common platform guidance (measured in the reference project for phones; rule of thumb elsewhere). They are **rendered** sizes after every scale has been applied, which is what you must measure.

| Context | Body text minimum | Small labels (captions, counters) | Titles |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phone (Small) | 14 px | 12 px (hard floor) | 20 px or more |
| Tablet (Medium) | 15 px | 12 px | 22 px or more |
| Desktop at arm's length | 14 px | 11 px | 20 px or more |
| TV / console (Large plus gamepad) | 24 px | 18 px | 32 px or more |

Docs set `MinTextSize` floors at 9 in their own guidance, which is a technical floor rather than a reading target. For players who raise their Roblox text size, these minimums grow automatically if your layout lets them.

---

## 2. Three scales that multiply

Most games end up with three independent sources of scale. Knowing how they combine prevents both "my text is enormous" and "my slider does nothing" bugs.

| Scale | Who sets it | What it affects | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Engine preferred text size | Player, in Roblox settings | Text only, for fixed `TextSize` labels | Ignored by `TextScaled`; respects `UITextSizeConstraint` bounds (Roblox docs, as of October 2026) |
| Device `UIScale` | You, from viewport and device | Everything under the `UIScale` | Usually one `UIScale` per `ScreenGui` |
| Player UI size | Player, in your settings | Everything, multiplied into the device `UIScale` | Clamp it |

The interactions to know:

1. **`UIScale` multiplies text, including enlarged text.** A label authored at 14 px, enlarged by the player's `Largest` preference, under a `UIScale` of 1.2, renders larger than either alone. That is usually what you want, but it means a big player UI size plus `Largest` can push long text out of fixed containers. Test the corner case, not just each setting alone.
2. **`TextScaled` defeats both text preferences.** The engine scales `TextScaled` text to fit its box, up to a maximum font size of 100 (Roblox docs, as of October 2026), regardless of the preferred text size. A `UIScale` still changes the box, so it still changes the text, but the player's text size setting does nothing. Use `TextScaled` only for decorative display text, never for content.
3. **`UITextSizeConstraint` clamps the preference.** The engine keeps the constraint's `MinTextSize` and `MaxTextSize` regardless of the preferred text size (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). A tight `MaxTextSize` on body text silently disables the accessibility setting for that label.
4. **Offsets do not scale unless a `UIScale` is above them.** Fixed pixel paddings, strokes and corner radii authored in offsets stay the same unless they live under the `UIScale`. Put every `UIScale` at the top of the tree so all offsets scale together.

### A combined scale controller

```lua
--!strict
-- UiScaleController: one place that computes the UIScale for every ScreenGui.
-- final = deviceBase * playerPreference, clamped so a reference panel still fits on screen.

local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local UiScaleController = {}

local REF_PANEL = Vector2.new(720, 520) -- the largest panel that must always fit, in authored px
local MARGIN = 0.92 -- leave 8% of the viewport free around it
local PLAYER_MIN, PLAYER_MAX = 0.8, 1.4

local playerPref = 1
local scales: { UIScale } = {}

local function deviceBase(viewport: Vector2): number
	local size = GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize
	local onTv = UserInputService.PreferredInput == Enum.PreferredInput.Gamepad
		and size == Enum.DisplaySize.Large
	-- Rule-of-thumb bases; tune against measured rendered sizes on real devices.
	if size == Enum.DisplaySize.Small then
		return 0.85
	elseif onTv then
		return 1.5
	end
	return math.clamp(viewport.Y / 900, 0.9, 1.25)
end

local function compute(): number
	local camera = Workspace.CurrentCamera
	if not camera then
		return 1
	end
	local viewport = camera.ViewportSize
	local inset = GuiService:GetGuiInset()
	local usable = Vector2.new(viewport.X, viewport.Y - inset.Y)
	local wanted = deviceBase(viewport) * playerPref
	local fit = math.min(usable.X * MARGIN / REF_PANEL.X, usable.Y * MARGIN / REF_PANEL.Y)
	return math.min(wanted, fit)
end

local function applyAll()
	local s = compute()
	for _, scale in scales do
		scale.Scale = s
	end
end

function UiScaleController.register(gui: ScreenGui): UIScale
	local scale = gui:FindFirstChildOfClass("UIScale") or Instance.new("UIScale")
	scale.Parent = gui
	table.insert(scales, scale)
	scale.Scale = compute()
	return scale
end

function UiScaleController.setPlayerPreference(value: number)
	playerPref = math.clamp(value, PLAYER_MIN, PLAYER_MAX)
	applyAll()
end

function UiScaleController.start()
	local function hookCamera()
		local camera = Workspace.CurrentCamera
		if camera then
			camera:GetPropertyChangedSignal("ViewportSize"):Connect(applyAll)
		end
		applyAll()
	end
	Workspace:GetPropertyChangedSignal("CurrentCamera"):Connect(hookCamera)
	GuiService:GetPropertyChangedSignal("ViewportDisplaySize"):Connect(applyAll)
	UserInputService:GetPropertyChangedSignal("PreferredInput"):Connect(applyAll)
	hookCamera()
end

return UiScaleController
```

Notes on the design:

- **The fit clamp wins over the player.** If a player picks 140% on a small phone, the controller gives them the largest scale that still fits the reference panel. Without the clamp, a UI size slider is a way to lock yourself out of the close button. Show the effective value next to the slider ("140% (limited to 118% on this screen)") so the player understands.
- **`ViewportDisplaySize` can change at runtime**: docs suggest listening with `GetPropertyChangedSignal` to adapt UI, without saying what triggers a change (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). The listener costs nothing.
- **Reacting to `PreferredInput`** handles the player who plugs a controller into a laptop connected to a TV. Debounce it if your UI animates on scale changes.

---

## 3. Layouts that grow

Text that can get bigger needs containers that can get bigger. Every fixed-height text box is a future clipping bug.

### 3.1 The growing stack

The pattern that survives every text size: a vertical `UIListLayout` inside a container with `AutomaticSize = Y`, children that are labels with `AutomaticSize = Y`, `TextWrapped = true`, and width set by scale (for example `UDim2.new(1, 0, 0, 0)`). Each label's height follows its text, the container's height follows its children, and the container sits inside a `ScrollingFrame` with `AutomaticCanvasSize = Y` so long content scrolls instead of clipping. [[UI Layout Objects - Lists Grids and Pages]] covers the layout objects; the accessibility point is that **height is never authored for text**.

### 3.2 Where you cannot grow

Buttons in a fixed toolbar, HUD counters, tab headers. For these:

- Keep labels short (one or two words). Long labels belong in tooltips or a details panel.
- Use `TextTruncate = AtEnd` as a last resort and make the full text reachable (long-press or select shows it). Truncation hides information; never truncate prices, counts or names that differ only at the end.
- Allow icons to carry meaning so that truncated text is not the only signal.
- Give the label a `UITextSizeConstraint` with a generous `MaxTextSize`, so it can grow until it hits the layout limit, rather than none (it overflows) or a tight one (it ignores the preference).

### 3.3 Localisation compounds it

Translations grow text. German, French and Portuguese routinely run 20 to 35% longer than English for UI strings, and some short labels double (rule of thumb). A layout that just fits English at `Medium` will clip in German at `Large`. Test the worst language at the largest size together. Localization and Localization-Ready Writing cover the string side.

### 3.4 Line spacing and line length

`TextLabel.LineHeight` takes values from 1.0 to 3.0, default 1.0 (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). For body text of more than two lines, 1.15 to 1.3 reads noticeably easier, especially for dyslexic readers (rule of thumb). Keep body lines to about 40 to 60 characters on phones and up to about 75 on desktop by capping the width of text containers with a `UISizeConstraint`, rather than letting a paragraph span a 2560 px monitor.

---

## 4. Type choices that help

### 4.1 Font

For content text, choose a font with a large x-height, open counters (the holes in a, e, o), distinct letter shapes for I, l and 1, and medium or semibold weight. Heavy display fonts (black weights) are fine for short titles and numbers but tire the eye in paragraphs. With `Font.new(family, weight, style)` you can keep one family and change weight per role, which keeps a design system coherent (Text Fonts and Rich Text).

Rules of thumb that help dyslexic readers and everyone else:

- Avoid italics for more than a few words; use weight for emphasis instead.
- Avoid ALL CAPS for anything longer than a short label. Capitals remove word shape. The reference project kept Title Case for headers for this reason (measured in the reference project).
- Avoid justified text (`TextXAlignment` is left or centre; keep paragraphs left aligned). Centred multi-line paragraphs make it hard to find the start of the next line.
- Avoid very thin fonts at small sizes; hairlines alias badly on low-density phones.

### 4.2 Outlines and plates

Text over the 3D world needs separation from an unpredictable background. The two tools:

| Tool | Best for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| `UIStroke` on text | Short labels, numbers, titles over art | At small sizes a thick stroke fills the counters of letters; keep stroke around 8 to 12% of the rendered size and never thicker than 2 px below about 16 px text (rule of thumb) |
| Plate (a panel behind the text) | Paragraphs, subtitles, tooltips | Respect `PreferredTransparency` so players who want opaque plates get them (Accessibility) |

A subtle drop shadow (a duplicated label offset by 1 to 2 px in a dark colour) is a middle ground that keeps counters open at small sizes.

### 4.3 Numbers

Numbers are often the most important text on a Roblox screen (currency, damage, timers). Make them readable at a glance:

- Abbreviate consistently ("12.4K", "3.1M"), with the suffix in the same size as the digits. Big Numbers Precision and Formatting has the formatting code.
- Use tabular (fixed-width) digits for counters that tick, so the number does not jitter horizontally. `TextLabel.OpenTypeFeatures` accepts a comma-separated list of OpenType feature tags (Roblox docs, as of October 2026); `tnum` is the standard tabular-figures tag, but whether a given Roblox font supports it is font-dependent and not something we could confirm per font. Check `OpenTypeFeaturesError` after setting it.
- Do not animate a counter so fast that the player cannot read the final value. Under reduced motion, show the final value at once.

---

## 5. World-space text

`BillboardGui` nameplates, damage numbers, interaction prompts and `SurfaceGui` signs are text too, and they suffer most.

- **Billboards that scale with distance** (sized in studs) become unreadable when far; billboards sized in offset pixels stay readable but crowd the screen. A hybrid works: scale size with distance, but clamp the rendered height to a minimum (for example 14 px) and fade out beyond a distance using `MaxDistance`.
- **Damage numbers** should be big enough to read during motion: 20 px or more rendered on phones for normal hits, larger for crits, and short-lived. Offer a setting to turn them off for players who find them noisy, and a setting to make them larger for players who rely on them.
- **`SurfaceGui` signs** depend on `PixelsPerStud` and viewing angle. Text on a sign the player passes at speed must be short. Put essential information (a door's requirement) on screen when the player is near, not only on the surface.
- **Proximity prompts** inherit some of this. Their action text should be one verb and their object text a short noun.

---

## 6. An automated text audit

Clipping bugs are easy to miss by eye because they appear only at certain sizes, languages and devices. The engine helps: `TextLabel.TextFits` reports whether the text fits within the label's bounds, and `TextBounds` gives the rendered size. A client-side audit walks every visible text object and reports problems. Run it in Studio after switching the Roblox text size to `Largest`, and with your UI size slider at the maximum.

```lua
--!strict
-- TextAudit: run on the client (for example from a debug command) after opening each screen.
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

type TextObject = TextLabel | TextButton | TextBox

export type Issue = { path: string, kind: string, detail: string }

local MIN_RENDERED_PX = 12

local function isVisible(obj: GuiObject): boolean
	local node: Instance? = obj
	while node and node:IsA("GuiObject") do
		if not node.Visible then
			return false
		end
		node = node.Parent
	end
	local gui = obj:FindFirstAncestorWhichIsA("LayerCollector")
	return gui ~= nil and gui.Enabled
end

local function check(obj: TextObject, issues: { Issue })
	if not isVisible(obj) or obj.Text == "" then
		return
	end
	local path = obj:GetFullName()
	if obj.TextScaled then
		table.insert(issues, { path = path, kind = "TextScaled", detail = "ignores PreferredTextSize" })
	end
	if not obj.TextFits then
		table.insert(issues, { path = path, kind = "Clipped", detail = `bounds {obj.TextBounds} in box {obj.AbsoluteSize}` })
	end
	-- One line of text renders roughly TextBounds.Y tall per line; approximate the glyph size.
	local lines = math.max(1, select(2, obj.ContentText:gsub("\n", "\n")) + 1)
	local approxPx = obj.TextBounds.Y / lines
	if not obj.TextScaled and approxPx > 0 and approxPx < MIN_RENDERED_PX then
		table.insert(issues, { path = path, kind = "Small", detail = `about {math.floor(approxPx)} px rendered` })
	end
	local constraint = obj:FindFirstChildOfClass("UITextSizeConstraint")
	if constraint and constraint.MaxTextSize < 18 and lines > 1 then
		table.insert(issues, { path = path, kind = "TightMax", detail = `MaxTextSize {constraint.MaxTextSize} on body text` })
	end
end

local function audit(): { Issue }
	local issues: { Issue } = {}
	local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
	for _, inst in playerGui:GetDescendants() do
		if inst:IsA("TextLabel") or inst:IsA("TextButton") or inst:IsA("TextBox") then
			check(inst :: TextObject, issues)
		end
	end
	return issues
end

for _, issue in audit() do
	warn(`[TextAudit] {issue.kind}: {issue.path} ({issue.detail})`)
end
```

Points to know about this audit:

- `TextBounds` already includes `UIScale` and the preferred text size, because it is measured in rendered pixels (the `AbsoluteSize` space). That is why the small-text check uses it rather than `TextSize`. The per-line estimate is approximate: line height and wrapped lines make it imperfect, so treat "Small" as a prompt to look.
- `TextFits` reports false for text that overflows the box, including wrapped text that runs out of height. It is the most valuable check here.
- Open each screen before running it; closed screens are skipped by the visibility check, which is deliberate (hidden templates would flood the report).
- Run it at `Medium` and at `Largest`, at minimum and maximum player UI size, and in your longest language. That is eight runs per screen, which is why it is worth scripting into a test pass (QA Checklists Before Release).

The reference project automated a similar check on phone viewports: every panel measured for rendered text below 12 px, tap targets below 44 px and elements off-screen (measured in the reference project; see [[Responsive UI for Phone Tablet Console and PC]]). Extending it to the largest preferred text size is the step most games skip.

---

## 7. When not to do this

- **Do not make everything huge by default.** Big text everywhere crowds the screen and pushes the 3D world out of view, which hurts gameplay readability. Default to comfortable sizes and let players go bigger.
- **Do not add a UI size slider before fixing the device scale.** A slider on top of a bad base just lets players choose which way it is broken.
- **Do not wrap HUD numbers.** A health value that wraps to two lines is worse than a slightly smaller one. Fixed, short, single-line text belongs in containers sized for its largest expected width.

---

## Common mistakes

- `TextScaled` for content, so the player's text size does nothing.
- Fixed-height text boxes that clip at `Largest`.
- Tight `MaxTextSize` constraints on body text.
- A UI size slider that can push the close button off screen.
- Measuring authored `TextSize` instead of rendered size.
- Thick strokes on small text that fill the letter counters.
- Long centred or justified paragraphs, and ALL CAPS sentences.
- Testing only English at default size.

## Checklist

- [ ] Rendered body text meets the minimums for each device class, measured, not assumed.
- [ ] One `UIScale` controller combines device base and player preference, clamped to fit.
- [ ] No content text uses `TextScaled`; constraints on body text are generous.
- [ ] Text containers grow (`AutomaticSize`, wrapping, scrolling) instead of clipping.
- [ ] `LineHeight` about 1.15 to 1.3 for paragraphs; line length capped.
- [ ] Outlines or plates behind text over the world; plates honour `PreferredTransparency`.
- [ ] Damage numbers and nameplates have size and visibility settings.
- [ ] Text audit run at Medium and Largest, min and max UI size, longest language.

See also: Accessibility Start Here, Accessibility, Text Fonts and Rich Text, [[Responsive UI for Phone Tablet Console and PC]], Gamepad and Console UX, Safe Areas and Insets, Layout - Scale Offset and Constraints, World-Space UI - BillboardGui and SurfaceGui, Colour-Blind Safe Design.

# SurfaceAppearance PBR Workflow

<!-- tldr:start -->
> [!tldr] TL;DR
> - Avoid: Re-importing a mesh per scene -> Import once; copy MeshParts; clone templates
> - Avoid: Mesh exported without tangents -> Re-export with tangents
> - Avoid: Judging assets in an unlit or default room -> Look-dev room with game lighting
> - Texel budget and map list decided per asset class before painting.
> - One suffix scheme; normal maps OpenGL; meshes exported with tangents.
> - Import checked: every SurfaceAppearance has the expected maps.
>
> Cost: TL;DR ~150 tok · whole note ~5.2k tok. Read more: ## 4. Import: let the importer do the wiring · ## 7. Runtime cases · ## Common mistakes · ## Checklist
<!-- tldr:end -->

The map-by-map facts about `SurfaceAppearance` (what each map means, colour spaces, AlphaMode, baking in Blender) are already in Texturing and PBR Baking and Materials MaterialVariants and SurfaceAppearance. This note is about the **workflow around them**: how to size a texture set before you paint it, how assets travel from the texturing tool into Studio without hand-pasting ids, how to keep one source of truth so instancing works, how to build a look-development room that tells the truth, how to audit a place full of PBR meshes, and how to handle the runtime cases (generated looks, pixel art, tint-driven variants). It is written for a small team that will import hundreds of assets, not one hero prop.

## 1. The shape of the pipeline

```
Plan (texel budget, map list)  ->  Author (Blender / Substance / CC0 source)
   ->  Export (named files, correct convention)  ->  Import (3D Importer or manual)
   ->  Template (one SurfaceAppearance per look, stored once)
   ->  Place (clone templates onto MeshParts)  ->  Audit (script)  ->  Look-dev check
```

Every step has one job. The two that teams skip are **Template** and **Audit**, and they are the two that decide whether your place batches well and whether a re-upload six months later takes ten minutes or two days.

## 2. Plan: budget before you paint

### Texel budget from the docs

Roblox docs (as of October 2026, texture specifications) give a PBR budget of "256x256 for every 2x2x2 unit space", stepping up to the next size when larger:

| Object bounding size (studs) | Docs guideline |
|---|---|
| 1 x 1 x 1 | 64 x 64 to 128 x 128 |
| 2 x 2 x 2 | 256 x 256 (also the maximum for non-albedo maps on rigid accessories) |
| 4 x 4 x 4 | 512 x 512 |
| 8 x 8 x 8 | 1024 x 1024 (listed as the maximum for this budget) |

The same page says Roblox supports texture resolutions up to 4096 x 4096 and, in its UV section, "up to 1024x1024 pixel spaces for texture maps". Read these together as: **the uploader accepts 4K, the guidance for in-world PBR maps tops out at 1024.** If you believe a 2048 map is justified (a huge hero statue the camera circles), test it on a low-memory phone first; the docs do not promise how such a map is downsampled on low-end devices.

### Map list per asset class

Decide which maps an asset class gets before anyone paints. Every map you skip is a texture nobody downloads.

| Asset class | Colour | Normal | Roughness | Metalness | Emissive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stylised prop, flat paint | yes | no | no (leave the slot blank) | no | no |
| Stylised prop with bevels | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| Realistic prop, non-metal | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| Weapon or armour with metal parts | yes | yes | yes | yes | optional |
| Sign, screen, lantern | yes | optional | optional | no | yes |
| Foliage card | yes (alpha) | optional | no | no | no |

Rule of thumb: roughness and metalness can usually be half the resolution of colour with no visible loss; normal maps lose detail fastest when downscaled, so keep them at colour resolution when they carry the asset's identity.

## 3. Author and export: conventions that save hours

### File naming

Pick one suffix scheme and enforce it in tools. Roblox's own character import guide uses `_ALB`, `_MTL`, `_NOR`, `_RGH` (Roblox docs). Poly Haven's CC0 sets use `_diff`, `_nor_gl`, `_rough`, `_metal`. Either works; mixing them across a project does not.

A scheme that sorts well: `<AssetName>_<Map>_<Size>.png`, for example `CrateOak_Color_512.png`, `CrateOak_Normal_512.png`, `CrateOak_Rough_256.png`.

### Export checks

- **Normal maps: OpenGL, tangent space.** The docs are explicit that world-space and object-space normal maps are not supported, and the `SurfaceAppearance` reference adds that **meshes must include tangent data**. If a mesh arrives without tangents (some generators and older exporters drop them), the normal map shades wrongly in ways that look like a bad bake. Re-export with tangents before you re-bake anything (Normal Maps and Detail Baking).
- **One UV set.** Bake everything to the UV channel you export as the first set (rule of thumb; Roblox MeshParts render one UV set for textures, and a second channel exported from Blender is not used for SurfaceAppearance as far as the docs describe).
- **Straight alpha** for any colour map whose alpha matters (TintMask, Transparency).
- **Grayscale data maps as single-channel 8-bit**, which matches the spec's "Single Channel Grayscale (8-bit)". RGB copies work but waste upload bandwidth and invite channel mistakes.

## 4. Import: let the importer do the wiring

The 3D Importer's full-release announcement lists automatic SurfaceAppearance setup when PBR textures are present in the file, and the docs say `.fbx` and `.gltf` carry PBR textures while `.obj` does not. In practice:

| Source | What you get |
|---|---|
| `.glb` / `.gltf` with PBR materials linked | MeshParts with SurfaceAppearances created and maps uploaded |
| `.fbx` with textures linked in the material | Usually the same; check the importer's warnings |
| `.obj`, or textures not linked | MeshParts only; add SurfaceAppearances manually |

The docs do not list exactly when auto-setup fails, so make "open one imported SurfaceAppearance and check all four map slots" part of every import. See 3D Importer Settings Reference for the importer options and Exporting and Validating Models for Roblox for pre-flight checks.

### Assigning maps in bulk

Map properties (`ColorMap`, `NormalMap`, ...) carry Plugin security: game scripts cannot write them. The command bar and plugins can (rule of thumb: the command bar runs with plugin-level permissions in Studio). That makes a bulk assignment script possible when you uploaded textures separately, for example through Open Cloud (Asset Upload Automation with Open Cloud).

```lua
--!strict
-- Command bar: build SurfaceAppearance templates from a table of uploaded ids.
-- Paste the table from your upload tool's output. Ids here are placeholders.
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")

type MapSet = {
	color: string?,
	normal: string?,
	rough: string?,
	metal: string?,
	alpha: Enum.AlphaMode?,
}

local SETS: { [string]: MapSet } = {
	CrateOak = {
		color = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
		normal = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
		rough = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
	},
	LanternIron = {
		color = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
		normal = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
		rough = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
		metal = "rbxassetid://0000000000",
	},
}

local folder = ServerStorage:FindFirstChild("SurfaceLooks") or Instance.new("Folder")
folder.Name = "SurfaceLooks"
folder.Parent = ServerStorage

for name, set in SETS do
	local sa = folder:FindFirstChild(name) :: SurfaceAppearance?
	if not sa then
		local created = Instance.new("SurfaceAppearance")
		created.Name = name
		created.Parent = folder
		sa = created
	end
	assert(sa)
	if set.color then sa.ColorMapContent = Content.fromUri(set.color) end
	if set.normal then sa.NormalMapContent = Content.fromUri(set.normal) end
	if set.rough then sa.RoughnessMapContent = Content.fromUri(set.rough) end
	if set.metal then sa.MetalnessMapContent = Content.fromUri(set.metal) end
	sa.AlphaMode = set.alpha or Enum.AlphaMode.Overlay
end
print("templates:", #folder:GetChildren())
```

The script writes the `*Content` properties with `Content.fromUri`, which the reference lists as the current form; the older string properties (`ColorMap`, `NormalMap`) address the same slots and are what the audit below reads. Both carry Plugin security for writing (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). Wrap command bar edits in a `ChangeHistoryService` recording if your team relies on undo (Command Bar and Studio Scripting).

## 5. Template: one source per look

This is the step that decides batching. Roblox docs (summarised in Materials MaterialVariants and SurfaceAppearance) say identical MeshParts instance only when their SurfaceAppearances are identical. Re-importing the same crate ten times creates ten uploads with ten sets of asset ids: pixel-identical, but not identical to the engine.

Rules:

1. **Every look exists once**, as a template `SurfaceAppearance` in a `SurfaceLooks` folder (`ServerStorage` for edit-time use; `ReplicatedStorage` if clients clone them at runtime).
2. **MeshParts receive clones** of the template, never fresh imports.
3. **Re-uploads update the template**, then a script re-clones it onto every user. Because every user was a clone, you can find them by comparing map ids.
4. **Meshes share too.** Instancing needs the same mesh and the same appearance. Import a crate mesh once and copy the MeshPart, rather than importing the crate per scene.

```lua
--!strict
-- Command bar: re-apply a template to every MeshPart whose SurfaceAppearance
-- matches the template's old colour map id. Run after re-uploading a texture.
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")

local TEMPLATE_NAME = "CrateOak"
local OLD_COLOR_ID = "rbxassetid://0000000000" -- the id being replaced

local template = ServerStorage.SurfaceLooks:FindFirstChild(TEMPLATE_NAME) :: SurfaceAppearance
local count = 0
for _, d in workspace:GetDescendants() do
	if d:IsA("SurfaceAppearance") and d.ColorMap == OLD_COLOR_ID then
		local parent = d.Parent
		local tint = d.Color
		local fresh = template:Clone()
		fresh.Name = "SurfaceAppearance"
		fresh.Color = tint -- keep per-instance tint
		fresh.Parent = parent
		d:Destroy()
		count += 1
	end
end
print(("re-applied %s to %d meshes"):format(TEMPLATE_NAME, count))
```

The tint question: whether two otherwise identical SurfaceAppearances with different `Color` values still instance together is not documented. If you rely on tint variety at scale (a forest of tinted rocks), measure draw calls in the MicroProfiler with tints equal and with tints varied ([[MicroProfiler Guide]], Rendering Performance).

## 6. Look-dev: a room that tells the truth

The docs warn that SurfaceAppearance appearance "depends on the user's device and graphics quality level" and that brightness and reflectivity differ between Studio and authoring tools such as Substance Painter. You need a place to judge assets that matches the game, not the authoring tool.

Build a **look-dev room** in a separate place (or a far corner of the game, streamed out):

- **Reference objects:** a matte grey sphere (colour 128, roughness 1), a chrome sphere (metal 1, roughness 0.05), a white card (sRGB 240), a black card (sRGB 30). If the grey sphere does not look mid-grey, the lighting is lying to you, not the texture.
- **Every lighting setup the asset will live in**, as switchable presets (store them as data: Stylized Lighting Recipes shows how). Lighting is selected with `Lighting.LightingStyle` (Realistic or Soft) and `PrioritizeLightingQuality` in current Studio; the older `Technology` property is deprecated and superseded by those (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). Check both styles if your game might change.
- **Matching skies.** Metals and glossy surfaces reflect the sky. CC0 HDRIs can be converted to six cube faces for a `Sky`; using the same HDRI as the Blender world and the Studio sky makes authoring-tool and Studio reflections far closer. Example: a partly cloudy daylight HDRI such as `kloofendal_38d_partly_cloudy_puresky` for an outdoor game.
- **Environment lighting values.** `Lighting.EnvironmentSpecularScale` and `EnvironmentDiffuseScale` both default to 0 (Roblox docs). At 0 specular, metalness has no effect. Set them to the game's real values in the look-dev room.
- **Quality levels.** Check at the lowest and highest graphics quality (Studio's rendering settings), and on one real phone.

A ten-minute look-dev pass catches the three most common PBR complaints: "metal looks like plastic" (environment specular 0 or dark albedo), "everything is shiny" (roughness through sRGB), and "it looked better in Substance" (authoring-tool lighting).

## 7. Runtime cases

### Changing looks during play

Game scripts can write `Color`, `AlphaMode`, `EmissiveStrength`, `EmissiveTint` and `ResampleMode`; the map properties are Plugin security (Roblox docs, `SurfaceAppearance` reference). So:

| Want | Do |
|---|---|
| Team or rarity colour | Write `Color` on a near-white or TintMask map |
| Glow pulse | Tween `EmissiveStrength` (large values clamp to white, per the docs) |
| Completely different texture | Clone a prepared template from `ReplicatedStorage` and destroy the old one |
| Damage states | Prepared templates per state (`Clean`, `Cracked`, `Broken`) swapped at thresholds |

### Generated looks: CreateSurfaceAppearanceAsync

`AssetService:CreateSurfaceAppearanceAsync(content)` builds a new SurfaceAppearance from `EditableImage` content for the keys `ColorMap`, `MetalnessMap`, `NormalMap`, `RoughnessMap` and `EmissiveMask` (Roblox docs, as of October 2026). Facts that shape its use:

- It yields and is not thread-safe.
- It currently accepts **only EditableImage content**, not asset ids.
- Maps **cannot be swapped** after creation.
- For metalness, roughness and emissive, only the red channel is read.
- `CreateEditableImage` returns `nil` if the device's editable memory budget is exhausted, so every caller needs a fallback.

That makes it a specialised tool: player-painted items, procedural patterns, previews in a customiser. It is not a way to stream normal content.

```lua
--!strict
-- Client: make a flat-colour SurfaceAppearance from a generated image, with a fallback.
local AssetService = game:GetService("AssetService")

local function makeSolidLook(color: Color3): SurfaceAppearance?
	local ok, image = pcall(function()
		return AssetService:CreateEditableImage({ Size = Vector2.new(4, 4) })
	end)
	if not ok or image == nil then
		return nil -- budget exhausted or unsupported: caller keeps the old look
	end
	local img = image :: EditableImage
	img:DrawRectangle(Vector2.zero, img.Size, color, 0, Enum.ImageCombineType.Overwrite)
	local created, sa = pcall(function()
		return AssetService:CreateSurfaceAppearanceAsync({
			ColorMap = Content.fromObject(img),
		})
	end)
	if not created then
		warn("CreateSurfaceAppearanceAsync failed:", sa)
		return nil
	end
	return sa
end
```

Check the current `EditableImage` method signatures in the docs before shipping; this API family has changed during its beta and the exact `DrawRectangle` parameters are worth re-reading (flagged as not re-verified for this note).

### Pixel art: ResampleMode

`ResampleMode` has `Default` (bilinear filtering) and `Pixelated` (nearest-neighbour, "keeps sharp pixel edges") per the docs. Pixel-art or voxel-textured games should set `Pixelated` on their templates; otherwise a 32 x 32 texture becomes a blur. It is script-writable, so it can also be a settings toggle.

## 8. Audit: find the problems before players do

Run this in the command bar before every release. It reports duplicate looks that should be clones, metalness without environment specular, transparency mode with zero part transparency on soft-alpha assets (you have to judge which those are), and MeshParts that still carry a `TextureID` under a SurfaceAppearance.

```lua
--!strict
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")

type Info = { count: number, example: Instance }
local looks: { [string]: Info } = {}
local metalUsers = 0
local transparencyZero = 0
local leftoverTextureId = 0

for _, d in workspace:GetDescendants() do
	if d:IsA("SurfaceAppearance") then
		local key = table.concat({ d.ColorMap, d.NormalMap, d.RoughnessMap, d.MetalnessMap }, "|")
		local info = looks[key]
		if info then
			info.count += 1
		else
			looks[key] = { count = 1, example = d }
		end
		if d.MetalnessMap ~= "" then
			metalUsers += 1
		end
		local part = d.Parent
		if part and part:IsA("MeshPart") then
			if d.AlphaMode == Enum.AlphaMode.Transparency and part.Transparency == 0 then
				transparencyZero += 1
			end
			if part.TextureID ~= "" then
				leftoverTextureId += 1
			end
		end
	end
end

local unique = 0
for _, info in looks do
	unique += 1
end
print(("unique looks: %d"):format(unique))
print(("metal looks in use: %d, EnvironmentSpecularScale = %.2f"):format(metalUsers, Lighting.EnvironmentSpecularScale))
print(("Transparency-mode meshes at part Transparency 0 (hard cut-outs): %d"):format(transparencyZero))
print(("MeshParts with a TextureID hidden under a SurfaceAppearance: %d"):format(leftoverTextureId))
```

How to read it: if "unique looks" is close to the number of meshes, you are not sharing; group the near-duplicates by name and template them. A leftover `TextureID` is harmless to the look (the SurfaceAppearance overrides it, per the docs) but it is an extra image download for nothing; clear it.

## 9. SurfaceAppearance or something else?

| Need | Best tool | Note |
|---|---|---|
| UV-mapped unique prop | SurfaceAppearance | This note |
| Large tiling surfaces on parts | MaterialVariant | MaterialService and Custom Materials |
| A kit of many meshes | One SurfaceAppearance on a trim sheet | Trim Sheets Atlases and Vertex Colors, Tiling Trim Sheets and Decal Tricks |
| Flat stylised colour | `MeshPart.Color`, no texture | Zero texture memory |
| Detail on a flat Part face | Decal or Texture (now with PBR map properties) | Tiling Trim Sheets and Decal Tricks |
| Terrain | MaterialVariant override or Expanded Terrain | Terrain Materials and Painting |

Nuance: a SurfaceAppearance on a mesh that only needs flat colour is the most common waste in imported kits. Generators and marketplace kits ship a 1024 colour map that is one flat swatch per island. Bake those swatches into `MeshPart.Color` (or vertex colours) and delete the texture.

## When not to use this workflow

- **One-off prototypes.** Hand-assigning ids is fine for ten assets. The template and audit steps earn their keep past about fifty assets or a second artist (rule of thumb).
- **Avatar items.** UGC has its own validation rules, texture limits and fees; follow UGC Avatar Items and Accessories instead.
- **Purely flat stylised games.** No PBR maps at all may be the right answer (Stylised vs Realistic Material Pipelines).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Re-importing a mesh per scene | Draw calls scale with prop count | Import once; copy MeshParts; clone templates |
| Mesh exported without tangents | Normal map shading looks wrong at every angle | Re-export with tangents |
| Judging assets in an unlit or default room | "Looked fine in Studio", wrong in game | Look-dev room with game lighting |
| `EnvironmentSpecularScale` left at 0 | Metal reads as plastic | Set real value; check in look-dev |
| 1024 maps on a 1-stud prop | Memory for detail nobody sees | Follow the docs' size table |
| Runtime generated looks without a fallback | Blank meshes on low-memory phones | Handle `nil` from `CreateEditableImage` |
| Pixel art with `Default` resampling | Blurry pixels | `ResampleMode = Pixelated` |

## Checklist

- [ ] Texel budget and map list decided per asset class before painting.
- [ ] One suffix scheme; normal maps OpenGL; meshes exported with tangents.
- [ ] Import checked: every SurfaceAppearance has the expected maps.
- [ ] Templates in a `SurfaceLooks` folder; meshes receive clones only.
- [ ] Re-upload procedure tested (script re-applies a template by old id).
- [ ] Look-dev room with reference spheres, game lighting presets and matching sky.
- [ ] Audit script run: unique looks, metal versus environment specular, leftover TextureIDs.
- [ ] Runtime look changes limited to writable properties or template swaps.
